collections.label: Serialisation, the Magazine and the Market

entries.category: Format and Unit
entries.name: Story Manga
entries.description: The long-form serialised narrative that is the medium's default unit, and whose origin is more contested than the standard account admits.
entries.principle: Story manga is not simply "manga that is long". It is a narrative built to be consumed in chapters weeks apart and re-read in volumes years later, which means it must satisfy two incompatible readers at once — one who needs a hook every nineteen pages and one who needs an arc that survives compression. Nearly every formal habit the medium is known for follows from that double obligation rather than from national temperament. The standard account credits Osamu Tezuka with inventing the form after the war; the scholarly record puts modern comics in Japan across the 1920s and 1930s, before his debut, and treats his contribution as consolidation and scale rather than invention. Both positions are held by serious people and the card takes neither.
entries.example: Shin Takarajima / New Treasure Island (1947) is the work the invention claim is usually attached to; Norakuro (1931) and the prewar children's-magazine serials are the evidence the claim understates; Hi no Tori / Phoenix, serialised in pieces from 1954 across three decades and four magazines, shows the form's outer limit.
entries.application: Decide which of your two readers you are writing for in any given chapter, and be deliberate when you sacrifice one. A chapter that serves only the weekly reader reads as filler in the volume; a chapter that serves only the volume reads as nothing happening. The craft is in the chapters that do both, and there are fewer of them than a plan suggests.

entries.category: Format and Unit
entries.name: Yonkoma and the Four-Panel Unit
entries.description: Four panels, read top to bottom, and a complete structure inside them.
entries.principle: The four-panel strip is the medium's smallest self-contained narrative machine, and it is not a gag format that happens to have four panels — the count is structural. The conventional reading maps the four onto kishōtenketsu: setup, development, turn, conclusion, with the weight on the third panel, which introduces something the first two did not predict. That is a different engine from the Anglophone strip's setup-and-punchline, because the turn need not be funny; it need only be unforeseen. A yonkoma artist writing to a punchline is using three panels and wasting one.
entries.example: Sazae-san (1946) ran the form as newspaper social observation for over a quarter of a century; Azumanga Daioh (1999) demonstrated that four-panel strips could accumulate into character work across volumes without ever becoming a continuous narrative; K-On! (2007) shows the same machinery serving mood rather than incident.
entries.application: If you are writing four panels, put your energy into panel three and let panel four be small. A conclusion that merely confirms the turn is doing its job. If your fourth panel is where the idea lives, you have written a three-panel setup and a caption.

entries.category: Format and Unit
entries.name: The One-Shot (Yomikiri)
entries.description: The self-contained chapter — audition piece, pressure valve, and the form most manga careers begin in.
entries.principle: The one-shot is where the serialisation system does its recruiting, and that institutional function shapes the form. A yomikiri submitted for a newcomer prize or run as a trial in a magazine has to demonstrate, in one sitting, that its author could sustain a serial — so it is read not only as a story but as evidence about a hypothetical future story. This produces a characteristic shape: a complete arc that nonetheless gestures at a world larger than it uses. A one-shot that closes too tightly reads as accomplished and unserialisable, which in this system is not a compliment.
entries.example: Many serials begin as one-shots and are rebuilt on promotion, which is why the pilot chapter and the first serialised chapter of the same property often differ structurally; Kanojo o Mamoru 51 no Hōhō (2006) and the newcomer-prize corpus published in Shōnen Jump's back pages show the audition register in its native habitat.
entries.application: Write the complete arc, then check whether a reader could believe in fifty more chapters of this world. If not, widen one element — a rule, an institution, a second character with an unresolved want — without resolving it. That deliberate loose thread is the difference between a short story and an audition.

entries.category: Format and Unit
entries.name: The Volume-First Work
entries.description: Manga written for the collected volume rather than for a magazine run, and what changes when the survey is absent.
entries.principle: A work published direct to volume, or serialised somewhere with no cancellation mechanism, is free of every constraint the rest of this pack describes — and the freedom is a mixed inheritance. There is no obligation to land a turn every nineteen pages, no reader survey, no risk of being cut at chapter thirty. What also disappears is the discipline: the weekly deadline is a bad editor with one excellent quality, which is that it never lets a scene sit. Volume-first work is where the medium's most formally ambitious pages live and also where its most self-indulgent ones do, and the difference is usually whether the author supplied a constraint to replace the one the system removed.
entries.example: Much of the Garo and Ax lineage worked this way; Onward Towards Our Noble Deaths (1973) was built as a book-length argument rather than a run; the art-manga anthologies of the 2000s show the register at its most deliberate.
entries.application: If you are working outside a serialisation system, impose a unit anyway — a chapter length, a beat count, a self-imposed deadline. Not because the system was right, but because the absence of any external shape is the specific failure mode of this format, and it looks like ambition until it is read.

entries.category: Format and Unit
entries.name: Essay Manga and Comic Reportage
entries.description: First-person and documentary work, where the drawn body of the author is the argument.
entries.principle: Essay manga puts the author on the page as a character, and the drawing style is doing epistemological work: a simplified, cartooned self is a claim about honesty rather than a shortcut. The reader accepts a level of interior access from a drawn self-portrait that the same claim in prose would have to earn, because the abstraction reads as candour rather than as artifice. This is why the register handles illness, sexuality, poverty and grief so well and handles argument so badly — the moment the drawn author starts being right about something external, the form's central move stops working.
entries.example: Sabishisugite Rezu Fūzoku ni Ikimashita Repo / My Lesbian Experience with Loneliness (2016) is the register at its most exposed; Hyakushō Kizoku (2006) runs the same machinery as comedy about agricultural labour; Onward Towards Our Noble Deaths (1973) sits at the boundary where memoir becomes testimony and the author's own reliability becomes the subject.
entries.application: Keep the drawn self simpler than everything around it. The abstraction is what buys the interiority. And if you find your drawn self explaining rather than experiencing, you have left essay manga for illustrated argument, which is a different and much less forgiving form.

entries.category: Format and Unit
entries.name: Gakushū Manga and the Commissioned Brief
entries.description: Educational and sponsored manga, where a third party owns the purpose and the craft problem is concealment.
entries.principle: Commissioned manga — school histories, corporate explainers, public-health material, government communication — is the medium's largest invisible sector, and its craft problem is unique: the brief supplies the conclusion in advance. Everything a normal narrative uses to generate interest is unavailable, because the reader knows the work is going to arrive where it was paid to arrive. What survives is the one thing a brief cannot specify, which is the shape of the misunderstanding being corrected. The good commissioned work is built around what the reader currently believes, not around what the client wants them to believe.
entries.example: The Gakushū Manga Nihon no Rekishi series has run in competing publishers' editions for decades and is how a large share of Japanese readers first encounter narrative history; Hadashi no Gen / Barefoot Gen (1973), though not commissioned, entered school libraries and acquired an educational function its author did not design.
entries.application: Build the piece around the misconception, not the fact. Give the reader a character who believes the wrong thing for a good reason, and let the correction cost that character something. A brief cannot forbid this, and it is the only route to a commissioned piece anyone finishes.

entries.category: Demographic and Its Discontents
entries.name: Shōnen and the Magazine That Defines It
entries.description: A magazine demographic routinely mistaken for a genre, and what the mistake conceals.
entries.principle: Shōnen names the readership a magazine is sold to, not the kind of story inside it. The category holds battle serials, sports, comedy, romance, horror, cooking and mystery, which have no formal property in common — so any sentence treating it as a genre has to quietly narrow it to mean "battle manga", and the narrowing is where the errors get in. What the label does reliably predict is institutional: publication cadence, chapter length, the survey's influence, the age the editorial department imagines. Those are real constraints and they are worth more to a writer than a genre label would be.
entries.example: Weekly Shōnen Jump (1968) has run works as unlike each other as Dragon Ball, Death Note and Kimetsu no Yaiba under one demographic banner; Weekly Shōnen Sunday and Weekly Shōnen Magazine (both 1959) shaped different house registers from the same nominal readership.
entries.application: When you catch yourself writing "the shōnen genre", replace it with the magazine and see whether the sentence still says anything. If it does, you meant the institution and now you have said so. If it collapses, you were describing battle manga and should name that instead.

entries.category: Demographic and Its Discontents
entries.name: Shōjo and the Grammar It Built
entries.description: The demographic that produced the medium's most distinctive page grammar, and the reason that grammar exists.
entries.principle: Shōjo is also a magazine demographic, but unlike the others it is associated with a genuine formal repertoire — overlapping and dissolving panel borders, figures breaking the frame, interiority carried by decorative field rather than by dialogue, and a treatment of time that expands a glance across a page. The reason is historical rather than essential: a readership addressed as private and interior, served by artists who were increasingly women, developed tools for rendering states rather than events. Attributing that grammar to the readership's nature rather than to the artists who built it is the standard error, and the scholarship pushes back on it, noting prewar roots the heroic 1970s account tends to erase.
entries.example: Nakayoshi (1954) and Ribon (1955) are where the readership was constituted; the 1970s work associated with the artists sometimes grouped as the Year 24 Group is where the grammar consolidated, though both the grouping and its membership are disputed; Hana to Yume (1974) carried the mature form into a second generation.
entries.application: Steal the grammar, not the subject matter. Dissolved borders and expanded glances are tools for interiority and they work anywhere. If you are writing a battle serial and need a character's decision to land, this is the page language that will do it, and nothing in it belongs to a readership.

entries.category: Demographic and Its Discontents
entries.name: Seinen and the Adult Reader's Arrival
entries.description: The demographic created when the first mass manga readership refused to stop reading.
entries.principle: Seinen exists because a readership aged and the industry followed it, which makes it the clearest evidence in the medium that demographics are market facts rather than aesthetic categories. Its formal signature is not violence or explicitness, both of which appear across every demographic, but permission for irresolution: a seinen serial may end badly, may leave its protagonist diminished, and may decline to reward persistence. That freedom comes with an institutional cost, because the magazines are smaller and the survey pressure differently shaped, so a seinen serial that fails does so faster and less visibly.
entries.example: Big Comic (1968) was founded to hold the readership that had grown out of the children's weeklies; the gekiga artists absorbed into it brought the register with them; Weekly Young Magazine and Morning extended it into the 1980s workplace.
entries.application: Use the permission deliberately. The value of this demographic is that you may leave a wound open, and the mistake is to spend that permission on content — explicitness is available everywhere — instead of on structure. Ask what your ending is allowed to withhold, and whether you would be allowed to withhold it in a weekly aimed at fourteen-year-olds. If the answer is yes, you have not used the category.

entries.category: Demographic and Its Discontents
entries.name: Josei, Redisu, and a Category That Changed Names
entries.description: The adult women's demographic, its earlier name, and what the renaming was doing.
entries.principle: The adult women's market was constituted in the 1980s under the name redisu komikku, and the shift toward josei is a change in how the readership was addressed rather than in who it was — a renaming that distanced the category from the frank sexual content the earlier label had accumulated. A writer needs both terms because the same body of work is indexed under different names in different decades, and a card or catalogue that uses only the later term will silently lose the earlier corpus. The formal territory is adult relational life at the register a shōjo magazine cannot reach: work, money, ageing, marriages that do not resolve.
entries.example: Feel Young and Kiss carry the modern register; the 1980s ladies' titles are where the market was built and are the harder half of the record to find in English-language sources.
entries.application: When you research this material, search both names and treat a gap in one as a search artefact rather than a gap in the record. And if you are writing in the register, remember the thing it can do that its neighbours cannot: let a relationship persist unresolved for years without treating that as a failure of plot.

entries.category: Demographic and Its Discontents
entries.name: Kodomomuke and the Reader Who Ages Out
entries.description: Manga for children, and the only demographic built around losing its audience on purpose.
entries.principle: Children's manga is written for a readership that will leave, and leave quickly, which inverts every serial instinct the rest of the medium runs on. There is no reward for continuity a reader cannot have accumulated, no payoff for a callback to a chapter three years old, and enormous value in an episodic structure any child can enter at any point. The industrial consequence is that the most successful children's properties are the ones designed to be entered sideways and left without loss — which is a much harder structural problem than it sounds, and is why so few of them exist relative to the market's size.
entries.example: CoroCoro Comic (1977) organised the market and the media mix around it; Doraemon (1969) is the standing demonstration that near-total episodic independence can sustain a property for decades.
entries.application: If you are writing for this readership, make every chapter a valid first chapter. That is the whole craft. Continuity is a courtesy to the child who stayed, never a requirement placed on the one who just arrived, and the moment you invert that priority you have started writing for adults who remember.

entries.category: Genre, Mainstream
entries.name: Battle Manga and the Escalating Ladder
entries.description: The escalation engine, its arithmetic problem, and the solutions the form has found.
entries.principle: A battle serial that succeeds is required to continue, and continuation means the next opponent must exceed the last, which is an arithmetic that eventually breaks the story it is serving. Every long-running work in the mode is visibly managing this, and the durable solutions are structural rather than numerical: change the axis of difficulty so the next fight is harder in a different currency; make the cost of winning rise instead of the power required; or convert the ladder into a tournament, which is a way of scheduling escalation so it looks planned. The failure mode is power creep, and it is a production artefact of success rather than an authorial mistake.
entries.example: Dragon Ball (1984) built the ladder and then demonstrated its terminal problem within its own run; Hunter × Hunter (1998) escapes it by making the rules of power a puzzle rather than a quantity; Jujutsu Kaisen (2018) escalates in constraint and cost rather than in magnitude.
entries.application: Decide early what rises. If it is a number, you have bought perhaps eighty chapters. If it is cost, or scope of consequence, or the amount of the world at risk of being understood differently, you have bought as many as you can write. Change the currency before you are forced to, because the forced change is visible on the page and readers name it.

entries.category: Genre, Mainstream
entries.name: Sports and the Spokon Inheritance
entries.description: The sports serial, and the older tradition of hardship-through-training it either inherits or refuses.
entries.principle: Sports manga has a built-in structural gift the rest of the medium envies: a match supplies a natural chapter unit, an unambiguous stake, and a clock. The genre's real variable is what it inherits from the spokon tradition, where excellence is produced by suffering under a punitive mentor and the body is something to be broken and rebuilt. Contemporary sports manga is largely a conversation with that inheritance — some works reproduce it, more of them replace privation with technique, cooperation or joy, and the choice is the most legible authorial statement the genre offers.
entries.example: Kyojin no Hoshi / Star of the Giants (1966) is the spokon template in its undiluted form; Ashita no Joe (1968) runs the tradition to its bleakest conclusion; Slam Dunk (1990) keeps the intensity and drops the punishment; Haikyū!! (2012) rebuilds the engine on cooperation and shows the tradition is fully optional.
entries.application: Take a position on suffering deliberately, because the genre will supply one by default if you do not. And use the clock: the reason these serials sustain tension across months of weekly chapters is that a match has an end the reader can see coming, and a fight in most other modes does not.

entries.category: Genre, Mainstream
entries.name: Mecha and the Piloted Body
entries.description: The piloted machine, and the difference between a robot as a character and a robot as a vehicle.
entries.principle: The mode's central formal choice is whether the machine is a body or a tool, and everything downstream follows. A machine that is a character permits the pilot to be a child and the story to be about companionship; a machine that is equipment forces the pilot to be a soldier and the story to become about institutions, supply and command. The second choice is what let the mode carry adult political material, and it also imported an obligation most works underestimate: once the machine is equipment, the reader will ask who built it, who pays for it, and who is fighting the war, and a story that has no answers will visibly decline to be asked.
entries.example: Tetsujin 28-gō (1956) is the machine as remote-controlled tool with a child at the switch; Mazinger Z (1972) puts the pilot inside and makes the body the point; Mobile Suit Gundam (1979) converts the machine into materiel and inherits the whole logistical question; Knights of Sidonia (2009) shows the equipment reading still generating structure decades on.
entries.application: Answer the supply question before chapter ten, even if you never put the answer on the page. A mecha story's credibility rests almost entirely on the reader's sense that someone off-panel is maintaining these things, and that sense is created by small specific details about repair, cost and scarcity rather than by exposition.

entries.category: Genre, Mainstream
entries.name: Magical Girl and the Transformation
entries.description: The transformation sequence as the mode's structural centre rather than its decoration.
entries.principle: The transformation is where the mode's meaning is stored. A girl acquires a second self that is older, more capable and more visible, and the specific terms of that acquisition — whether it is granted, inherited, bargained for, or imposed — is the mode's whole argument about power and adolescence. The sequence's repetition across episodes is not filler; it is ritual, and its formal cost is that a work wanting to say something new must alter the ritual rather than skip it. The mode's later, darker turn works precisely because it keeps the sequence and changes what it costs.
entries.example: Mahōtsukai Sally / Sally the Witch (1966) establishes the granted-power form; Himitsu no Akko-chan (1962) precedes it with a device rather than an inheritance and complicates every claim about which came first; Bishōjo Senshi Sailor Moon (1991) fuses the mode with the team structure and remakes the market; Mahō Shōjo Madoka Magica (2011) leaves the ritual intact and makes the bargain visible.
entries.application: If you are writing in this mode, decide what the second self costs and pay it on the page. And do not cut the transformation to save pages — repetition is the mode's grammar, and a reader who has watched the sequence nine times is exactly the reader for whom the tenth, altered, will land hardest.

entries.category: Genre, Mainstream
entries.name: Isekai and the Reincarnation Frame
entries.description: The transported-protagonist frame, its much older lineage, and the function the frame actually performs.
entries.principle: The frame is a device for managing exposition. A protagonist from the reader's world arrives in an unfamiliar one and is entitled to ask what everything is, which converts worldbuilding into dialogue and removes the narrative cost of explanation. That is the entire mechanical value, and it is why the frame recurs across decades rather than being a recent invention. Its characteristic failure is that a protagonist entitled to ask questions is also entitled to be told answers, and a serial that leans on the entitlement stops dramatising and starts briefing. The contemporary game-system variant intensifies both the benefit and the failure, because a quantified world is even easier to explain and even harder to make matter.
entries.example: Fushigi Yūgi (1992) runs the frame as shōjo romance decades before the current wave; the light-novel-to-manga pipeline of the 2010s made it a market category; Mushoku Tensei (2014) is the case usually cited as taking the frame's consequences seriously.
entries.application: Ration the questions. A newcomer protagonist should be denied an answer at least as often as they receive one, and the denials are where your world becomes a place rather than a manual. If a chapter's information could have been delivered by a signboard, you have used the frame as a convenience rather than a structure.

entries.category: Genre, Mainstream
entries.name: Horror Manga
entries.description: Horror on a monochrome page, where the medium's technical limits become its principal weapon.
entries.principle: Manga horror works on constraints that would be handicaps elsewhere. There is no soundtrack, no timing the author controls, and no colour — so dread has to be built out of composition, page-turn placement, and the reader's own pace. What the medium has instead is a uniquely fine control over detail density: a page can be almost empty and then, on the turn, unbearably full, and the eye's arrival at that page is an event the author schedules precisely. The tradition also has a distinct relationship to the body, treating physical transformation as horror's primary vocabulary rather than as its climax.
entries.example: Hyōryū Kyōshitsu / The Drifting Classroom (1972) sustains dread across a long serial rather than a short shock; Uzumaki (1998) builds an entire work on escalating pattern and detail density; Tomie (1987) runs the body-transformation vocabulary as episodic variation.
entries.application: Put your worst image on a right-hand page in the original reading direction, so the turn delivers it and the reader cannot preview it. This is the single most reliable horror technique the medium has, it is unavailable in prose and in film, and it is the reason a horror manga read in a scanned single-page view is measurably less frightening than the same work in a volume.

entries.category: Genre, Mainstream
entries.name: Historical Manga and Jidaigeki
entries.description: Period manga, its jidaigeki inheritance, and the research burden a drawn medium cannot avoid.
entries.principle: A drawn historical work makes claims a prose one can decline to make. Prose may write "a street in Edo" and stop; a page must decide the width of the street, the roofing, the signage, what the passers-by are carrying and how they wear their hair, and every one of those decisions is an assertion the reader can check. This is why the mode is research-heavy out of proportion to its prose equivalent, and why its most respected practitioners are associated with archival work as much as with drawing. The jidaigeki inheritance supplies genre structure — the wandering swordsman, the vendetta, the closed feudal institution — and a writer's main decision is how much of that structure to accept along with the period.
entries.example: Kozure Ōkami / Lone Wolf and Cub (1970) runs the jidaigeki structure at its purest; Vagabond (1998) takes a legendary figure and treats the legend itself as the subject; Golden Kamuy (2014) demonstrates the research burden discharged as pleasure rather than as duty, and carries the additional obligation of depicting a living people rather than a vanished one.
entries.application: Budget research time as drawing time, because that is what it is. And decide in advance which of your period's details you are prepared to be wrong about, so the ones you are not prepared to be wrong about get the hours. A work that is uniformly half-researched reads worse than one that is exact about three things and frankly schematic about the rest.

entries.category: Genre, Mainstream
entries.name: Gourmet and the Cooking Manga
entries.description: Food manga, and the problem of dramatising a sensation the page cannot transmit.
entries.principle: The mode's central difficulty is that taste is the one sense the page cannot reach at all, so every food manga is an exercise in indirect representation. The solutions are limited and well-mapped: render the reaction rather than the flavour; render the process, because labour is visible and taste is not; or render the social situation the meal exists inside, which is where most of the durable work in the mode actually lives. Works that attempt the flavour directly end up in a hyperbolic register that is entertaining and fundamentally unserious, which is a legitimate choice as long as it is one.
entries.example: Oishinbo (1983) built the mode's argumentative form, where a dish is the settlement of a dispute; Kodoku no Gurume / The Solitary Gourmet (1994) removes the dispute entirely and demonstrates that interior monologue over a single meal is sufficient; Shinya Shokudō / Midnight Diner (2006) puts the weight on the social situation and treats the food as an occasion for other people's stories.
entries.application: Choose your indirect route and commit. The most common failure is mixing all three — reaction, process and situation — in one scene, which dilutes each. And note that the process route is the one that rewards a drawn medium most, because a sequence of hands doing something skilled is exactly what these pages are best at.

entries.category: Genre, Mainstream
entries.name: Gambling, Mahjong and Competitive Skill
entries.description: The skill-contest serial, where the reader's ignorance of the rules is a design parameter.
entries.principle: A serial built on a specialist competition faces one hard question: how much of the game must the reader understand? The mode's answer, reached repeatedly and independently, is that the reader needs to understand the stakes exactly and the rules approximately — enough to know that this move is audacious, not enough to have played the hand themselves. The tension is therefore carried by the players' faces, by the money, and by the narration of risk, rather than by the board. This is also why the mode tolerates enormously extended single hands: once the reader is tracking the stake rather than the rules, elapsed time is a resource rather than a cost.
entries.example: Akagi (1991) sustains single mahjong hands across many chapters on almost pure nerve; Kaiji (1996) generalises the machinery to invented games and makes the stake existential; Hikaru no Go (1998) shows the same engine running on a game the reader is not expected to follow at all, where mastery is legible entirely through other players' reactions.
entries.application: Write the stake, not the rules. If a reader can tell that a move is reckless without being able to say why it is reckless, the scene is working. And take the extended-hand licence seriously — this is one of very few modes where slowing down is the mode's own preferred gear rather than a lapse.

entries.category: Genre, Mainstream
entries.name: Slice-of-Life and the Nichijō-kei Register
entries.description: The register that removes the plot engine and asks the chapter unit to carry everything.
entries.principle: Nichijō-kei withdraws the thing every other mode relies on — an escalating want — and replaces it with recurrence. What makes it work rather than stall is that the chapter unit is already a complete pleasure in this medium, so a serial that offers a well-shaped nineteen pages with no cumulative stake is offering something real rather than withholding something expected. The mode's actual difficulty is not boredom but drift: with no want to organise them, characters stop being people with positions and become a set of reliable behaviours. The good work defends against this by letting the situation, not the characters, change by small degrees.
entries.example: Yotsuba&! (2003) runs on a child's encounter with ordinary things and lets the surrounding adults accumulate a history the child cannot see; Hidamari Sketch (2004) uses the four-panel unit to keep the register honest about its own scale; Aria (2001) shows the mode absorbing an entire invented setting without acquiring a plot.
entries.application: Give the situation a slow clock even when the characters have no goal — a term ending, a season, a lease, a skill improving. It supplies the change the mode refuses to get from want, and it is what separates a serial that is calm from one that has stopped.

entries.category: Genre, Mainstream
entries.name: Iyashikei and the Healing Register
entries.description: Work made to soothe, and the discipline that keeps it from being empty.
entries.principle: Iyashikei names an intended effect rather than a subject, which makes it the one entry on this axis that is defined by what it does to a reader. The register's rule is that comfort must be earned against something — a loss already suffered, a world already ended, a solitude that is real — because comfort offered against nothing has no object and reads as vacancy. This is why so much of the strongest work in the register is quietly post-catastrophic: the calm is legible as calm only because the reader can see what it is calm about.
entries.example: Yokohama Kaidashi Kikō (1994) sets its gentleness after an unexplained and irreversible decline and never raises its voice about it; Mushishi (1999) pairs the register with episodic supernatural harm so that each resolution has something to resolve; Aria (2001) supplies the loss obliquely, through a terraformed world remembering an original it cannot return to.
entries.application: Put the wound off-panel and early. The reader does not need it dramatised and should not be given a scene about it; they need to know it is there, so that every quiet page afterwards is doing work rather than filling space.

entries.category: Desire, Relation and the Reader's Place
entries.name: BL, Yaoi and the Terms That Keep Changing
entries.description: Male-male romance made largely by and for women, across four names in fifty years, and why the names matter.
entries.principle: This is a market and movement category rather than a genre, and its terminology has changed roughly every fifteen years — shōnen-ai for the 1970s magazine work, yaoi for the 1980s doujinshi culture that grew beside it, boys' love for the 1990s commercial consolidation, and BL as the current umbrella. The terms are not synonyms and they are not a progression: each names a different production arrangement, and a researcher who searches only the current one loses the two earliest corpora entirely. Formally, the category's persistent structure is a relationship negotiated outside any social script the characters can appeal to, which is why so much of its craft attention goes to power, consent and disclosure rather than to obstacle.
entries.example: Kaze to Ki no Uta (1976) and Tōma no Shinzō (1974) are the 1970s magazine work the later terms did not yet exist to describe; June (1978) institutionalised a readership; the doujinshi circuit built the 1980s parallel economy that the commercial magazines of the 1990s then absorbed.
entries.application: Search all four terms and date what you find. And note the structural gift: with no external script for the relationship, every rule the couple lives by has to be made on the page, which is an enormous amount of free characterisation most writers in the category leave unspent.

entries.category: Desire, Relation and the Reader's Place
entries.name: Yuri and Its Two Lineages
entries.description: Female-female romance with two separate ancestries that are still visible in the work.
entries.principle: Yuri descends from two lines that were never the same thing. One is the prewar and midcentury Class S register of intense schoolgirl attachment, framed as a phase and structurally required to end — a form in which the relationship's dissolution is the genre's condition. The other is the explicitly romantic line consolidated from the 1990s, in which the relationship is a relationship and may continue. Contemporary work inherits from both, sometimes in the same volume, and the tension between them is the most common source of a reading that the ending betrayed the story: a work built on the second lineage can still reach for the first one's exit.
entries.example: Yoshiya Nobuko's early-twentieth-century schoolgirl fiction is the prose antecedent the Class S register comes from; Shōjo Kakumei Utena (1996) puts the transitional moment on the page by making the school's own rules the antagonist; Yagate Kimi ni Naru / Bloom Into You (2015) is built entirely on the second lineage and treats the first one's assumptions as something a character has to unlearn.
entries.application: Know which lineage you are writing in before the ending arrives, because the two have incompatible obligations. If your relationship is going to end, the Class S inheritance requires the ending be structural rather than circumstantial; if it is going to continue, nothing in the older register is available to you and borrowing its imagery will promise an exit you do not intend.

entries.category: Desire, Relation and the Reader's Place
entries.name: Josei Romance and the Adult Woman's Register
entries.description: Romance where the obstacle is a life already in progress.
entries.principle: The adult women's romance register runs on a structural difference the demographic label conceals: its characters have jobs, money, histories and prior relationships, so the obstacle to a romance is never merely the romance. A shōjo romance can be organised around whether two people will admit something; this one has to be organised around what admitting it would cost a life already built. That shifts the craft weight from the confession to the aftermath, and it is why the register handles divorce, ambivalence and unglamorous compromise so much better than its neighbours, and handles the grand gesture so much worse.
entries.example: Nana (2000) runs two women's ambitions against their attachments and refuses to rank them; Hachimitsu to Clover / Honey and Clover (2000) sits at the boundary where student life becomes working life and makes the unrequited case the serious one; Tokyo Tarareba Musume (2014) makes the cost of waiting the subject rather than the joke.
entries.application: Give both people something they will lose. The register's engine is not attraction but exposure — a career, a child, a lease, a reputation — and a romance in it where neither party risks anything material reads as a shōjo romance with older characters drawn into it.

entries.category: Desire, Relation and the Reader's Place
entries.name: Shōjo Romance and the Confession Structure
entries.description: The kokuhaku as a structural device rather than a cultural detail.
entries.principle: The confession is a formal gift and most work in the register underuses it. Because a declaration is a discrete, nameable, socially recognised act, it gives a romance something prose romance usually lacks: a single event that changes a relationship's status in a way both parties and the reader can date. That makes it schedulable. A serial can place it at chapter eight and spend forty chapters on consequence, or withhold it for two years and make the withholding the subject. Treating it as the ending is the default and the least interesting available choice.
entries.example: Kimi ni Todoke (2005) puts the declaration early enough that the serial is about what two people do with it; Hana yori Dango / Boys Over Flowers (1992) subordinates it to class antagonism and makes the social frame the real obstacle; Ao Haru Ride (2011) uses a second confession to re-date a relationship the reader thought was settled.
entries.application: Decide where the confession sits, and if your instinct is the final chapter, move it and see what happens. A declared relationship under pressure is dramatically richer than an undeclared one, and the medium's chapter unit is built to sustain exactly the kind of small recurring negotiation that follows.

entries.category: Desire, Relation and the Reader's Place
entries.name: Harem and the Relational Grid
entries.description: One protagonist, several candidates, and a structure that is really about scheduling.
entries.principle: The configuration is best understood as a production solution rather than a fantasy. A cast of candidates gives a serial a renewable supply of self-contained chapters — each pairing generates its own episode — while deferring the one decision that would end the serial. That is why the mode is so common in weekly publication and so rare outside it. Its structural weakness is the same as its strength: a protagonist who must not choose is a protagonist who must not change, so the mode tends to produce a static centre surrounded by characters doing all the developing.
entries.example: Urusei Yatsura (1978) runs the grid as farce and keeps its protagonist consistently, actively unworthy, which solves the static-centre problem by making it the joke; Love Hina (1998) is the template most later work follows; Gotōbun no Hanayome / The Quintessential Quintuplets (2017) commits to a resolution from the first chapter and rebuilds the mode around a question the reader can actually hold.
entries.application: If you use the grid, give the protagonist a want that is not romantic, so they can develop along an axis the deferral does not freeze. And decide early whether you are ever going to resolve it, because a serial that intends to and one that does not are structurally different from chapter one.

entries.category: Desire, Relation and the Reader's Place
entries.name: Ecchi and the Permitted Register
entries.description: Suggestive content as a magazine-standards problem, analysed as the formal constraint it is.
entries.principle: What a work may show is set by its magazine, not by its author, and the resulting register is a genuine formal constraint worth understanding rather than a matter of taste. A title running in a general-readership weekly operates under limits that shape composition, framing and the placement of incident, and much of what reads as coyness is an artist working around a standard. The craft consequence is specific: suggestion requires the reader to complete an image, which recruits them into the work in a way explicitness does not, and a writer who has the constraint imposed on them can use it rather than merely obey it. The register carries a real hazard the pack states plainly — content in this territory involving characters presented as minors is a live legal and ethical dispute that differs sharply between Japan and other jurisdictions, and this pack states that the dispute exists without adjudicating it.
entries.example: To LOVEru (2006) is the register running at the boundary of a general-readership weekly's standard and is the case usually cited in discussions of where that boundary sits.
entries.application: Treat the standard as a formal parameter, the way a poet treats a line length. Ask what the limit forces you to imply, and whether the implication is doing more work than the depiction would. And know the standard of the market you are writing for before you draft, because discovering it at revision costs pages.

entries.category: Movement, Lineage and Magazine-as-Label
entries.name: Gekiga
entries.description: The 1950s break toward an adult readership, and a term whose meaning is contested.
entries.principle: Gekiga is a movement, not a genre, and the standard account — that it named a harder-edged, more cinematic drawing style — is disputed by scholarship arguing the term was about **readership** rather than style: a claim that these comics were for adults, made at a moment when the medium was assumed to be for children. The distinction matters practically, because a writer chasing the style is chasing an effect that varies enormously between the artists grouped under the label, while a writer attending to the readership claim gets the movement's actual inheritance — permission to be unresolved, to be political, and to end badly. Its origin in the rental market rather than the magazine system also makes it the pack's clearest early evidence that the medium's formal breaks arrive from outside the survey.
entries.example: Tatsumi Yoshihiro is the artist most associated with the term's adoption and with its later historicisation; Gekiga Hyōryū / A Drifting Life (2008) is his own account of the period and is a memoir with the interests of a memoir, which is a reason to read it and a reason not to treat it as the record.
entries.application: If you are reaching for gekiga, be specific about which claim you are making. Harder line work is available to anyone. What the movement actually offers is the assumption that your reader is an adult who does not require a resolution, and that is a decision about structure, not about ink.

entries.category: Movement, Lineage and Magazine-as-Label
entries.name: The Garo Lineage and Art Manga
entries.description: The magazine that paid badly, sold little, and produced a disproportionate share of the medium's formally ambitious work.
entries.principle: Garo, founded 1964, is the medium's standing counter-example: a magazine that ran no reader survey worth the name, paid little or nothing, and consequently published work no commercial weekly could have carried. What it demonstrates is not that the serialisation system is bad but that the system optimises for one thing — a readership that keeps buying — and that some work is simply orthogonal to that. The lineage's characteristic register is the interior, the dreamlike and the deliberately ugly, and its influence runs far beyond its circulation because commercial artists read it.
entries.example: Nejishiki (1968) is the single work most often cited as the lineage's centre of gravity and is dream-logic rather than narrative; Tsuge Yoshiharu's wider Garo work established the register; COM (1967), founded by Osamu Tezuka in partial response, shows the same impulse routed through a commercial publisher and lasting a fraction as long.
entries.application: Read this lineage for permission rather than for technique. It is where the medium's evidence lives that a page need not be legible on first pass, that an ending need not resolve, and that a reader can be trusted with confusion — none of which a survey-driven weekly will ever tell you.

entries.category: Movement, Lineage and Magazine-as-Label
entries.name: The Kashihon Rental Tradition
entries.description: The postwar rental-library market, and the second economy that produced the medium's first adult work.
entries.principle: For roughly fifteen postwar years a large share of manga reached readers through rental shops rather than through purchase, and the economics of renting produced different books. A rental volume needed to be attractive on a shelf and satisfying in one sitting, was not competing for a survey position, and reached an audience that included working adults rather than only children — which is precisely why the movements that broke the medium's children's-market assumption incubated there. The tradition's disappearance under the rising weekly magazines is the clearest case in the pack of a distribution change remaking a form.
entries.example: The Osaka akahon publishers supplied the market's cheap end; the rental-market horror and gekiga volumes of the 1950s are where several later magazine careers began, and the artists carried the register with them when the shops closed.
entries.application: When you read a claim that some development began in the magazines, check the rental decade first. A great deal of what the magazine system is credited with inventing it actually recruited, and the difference matters for any argument about what the survey does and does not produce.

entries.category: Movement, Lineage and Magazine-as-Label
entries.name: Ero-guro and the Transgressive Line
entries.description: The erotic-grotesque inheritance, named plainly and analysed as craft.
entries.principle: Ero-guro descends from a 1920s and 1930s cultural movement rather than from manga, and its manga expression is deliberately transgressive work in which the disturbing image is the argument rather than an accessory to one. The pack names the content plainly because a reader will seek this material out or avoid it on exactly that basis: it is graphic, it is frequently about violated bodies, and it is not squeamish. What makes the durable work in the line durable is that the transgression is formally controlled — a composition that is beautiful and a subject that is not, held together deliberately, which is a much harder thing to build than either half alone.
entries.example: Maruo Suehiro's 1980s work is the line's most-cited modern instance and is explicitly continuous with the prewar movement's imagery; the material appeared largely outside the mainstream magazine system, which is a fact about what the survey permits rather than about the work's quality.
entries.application: If you work in this register, the discipline is control of the frame. An image that disturbs and is also composed with care reads as an argument; the same image rendered carelessly reads as an appetite, and readers reliably tell the difference even when they cannot articulate it.

entries.category: Movement, Lineage and Magazine-as-Label
entries.name: The Doujinshi Circuit as a Production System
entries.description: The self-published economy running beside the industry, and its function as a talent pipeline.
entries.principle: The doujinshi circuit is not an amateur fringe; it is a parallel production system with its own distribution, economics and audience, and it does three things the magazine system cannot. It permits work with no commercial constituency. It permits derivative work in a legal position best described as tolerated rather than licensed, which is a distinction worth stating precisely. And it functions as the medium's most effective talent pipeline, because a circle that can produce to a convention deadline twice a year has already demonstrated the exact capability a serialisation requires. Several major commercial careers begin here rather than in a newcomer prize.
entries.example: Comiket, running since 1975, is the circuit's institutional centre and the scale at which it operates is the argument; CLAMP began as a doujinshi circle before its commercial serialisation, which is the standard illustration of the pipeline working.
entries.application: If you want to learn the chapter unit, produce to a convention deadline. It is the only widely available training in the specific skill this medium runs on — a complete, satisfying, finite quantity of pages delivered on a date you did not choose.

entries.category: Movement, Lineage and Magazine-as-Label
entries.name: The Shōjo Revolution of the 1970s
entries.description: The decade the page grammar changed, and a grouping whose name and membership are both disputed.
entries.principle: Across the 1970s a cohort of artists — increasingly women, working in magazines for girls — rebuilt the medium's page: dissolved panel borders, figures crossing frames, interiority carried by decorative field, and subject matter reaching into sexuality, mortality and politics that the market had not previously admitted. The influence is not in dispute. What is disputed is nearly everything about how the cohort is described: the label commonly used for it is a retrospective critics' coinage whose originator is not established, at least one artist associated with it has objected to the term, membership is drawn at three different widths depending on the source, and the heroic decade-zero framing understates prewar roots that scholarship has since documented. The pack names the influence and marks the grouping as contested.
entries.example: Poe no Ichizoku (1972) and Tōma no Shinzō (1974) are the works most often placed at the centre of the claim; Kaze to Ki no Uta (1976) is the case usually cited for subject matter the market had not admitted; Berusaiyu no Bara / The Rose of Versailles (1972) is enormously influential and is included or excluded from the grouping depending on the source, which is itself the clearest evidence the grouping is not a settled object. A documented and public falling-out between two of the central figures, addressed in a 2021 memoir by one of them, means the cohort should not be described as a collaboration.
entries.application: Use the works and avoid the label, or use the label and say in the same sentence that it is contested. The grammar is what you actually want, it is fully transferable, and none of it requires you to take a position on who was in the group.

entries.category: Hand-Off Cards
entries.name: The Horror Serial and Its Monthly Dread
entries.description: Where manga horror hands over to the Horror pack, and the one thing it keeps.
entries.principle: Horror's mechanics — dread, the uncanny, the monster's rules, what a haunting is for — belong to the Horror pack, which carries fifty-two Japan-flagged entries and cards two of this tradition's central figures. What this pack keeps is the part that is a serialisation problem rather than a fear problem: dread sustained across a monthly gap, where the reader has four weeks to become accustomed to the last page's image and the next chapter must reopen a wound that has had time to close. That is a scheduling constraint no prose or film horror faces and no horror-craft card in the library currently addresses.
entries.example: Hyōryū Kyōshitsu / The Drifting Classroom (1972) is the standing demonstration that dread can be maintained across a long run rather than delivered in a burst; the Horror pack's own cards on the uncanny and on body horror are the fear mechanics this card defers to.
entries.application: For the mechanics of fear, use the Horror pack. Come back here for the question of what a month does to a cliffhanger, and for the page-turn scheduling that is this medium's own contribution to the effect.

entries.category: Hand-Off Cards
entries.name: Manga SF and the Mecha Line
entries.description: Where speculative manga hands over to the SF pack, and the production constraint SF does not model.
entries.principle: Extrapolation, the science primers, the cognitive-estrangement apparatus and the genre's literary history belong to the SF pack, which cites Ōtomo Katsuhiro and Shirow Masamune and cards neither of them. What this pack keeps is a constraint SF has no reason to model: a large part of the mecha line was produced under a toy-marketing obligation, in which a machine's design, its variants and the schedule on which new ones appear were commercial requirements before they were narrative ones. A great deal of what looks like escalation in the mode is a product cycle, and reading it as authorial invention gets the causality backwards.
entries.example: Mobile Suit Gundam (1979) is the case where the commercial obligation and the narrative ambition are both fully documented and visibly in tension; Kidō Keisatsu Patlabor (1988) shows the same production arrangement producing a workplace procedural instead of a war story.
entries.application: For extrapolation and the genre's arguments, use the SF pack. Come back here when you need to know why a mecha serial introduces a new machine at that specific interval, because the answer is usually not in the story.

entries.category: Hand-Off Cards
entries.name: Manga Crime and the Yakuza Story
entries.description: Where crime manga hands over to the Mystery, Crime and Thriller pack, and where it does not.
entries.principle: The investigative form — the fair-play puzzle, the procedural, the detective's epistemology — belongs to the MCT pack, and this pack defers to it entirely on how a mystery is constructed. What this pack keeps is a body of seinen crime serial that is not investigative at all: work organised around an organisation rather than a crime, in which the reader knows who did what from the first page and the tension is institutional — obligation, hierarchy, the cost of leaving. **No pack in the library currently holds this**, because MCT's collections are built around detection and this material has none.
entries.example: The seinen crime magazines of the 1980s and 1990s carried the form at scale; Gokushufudō / The Way of the Househusband (2018) is the case that demonstrates the structure by inverting it, deriving its entire comedy from an institutional register applied to domestic life.
entries.application: For anything involving detection, use the MCT pack. Come back here when the story is about belonging to an organisation rather than solving something, which is a different engine and needs different parts.

entries.category: Hand-Off Cards
entries.name: The Drawn Past and Its Claims
entries.description: Where historical manga hands over to the Historical Fiction pack, and the obligation a drawn medium cannot decline.
entries.principle: The research method, the sourcing standards, period voice and the whole question of the archive and its silences belong to the Historical pack, whose specialist collection is built on exactly that. What this pack keeps is an obligation specific to a drawn medium: a page must assert what a street, a garment and a face looked like, and cannot decline the assertion the way prose can. That makes every historical manga a series of checkable claims at a density no prose historical novel produces, and it is why the mode's research burden is different in kind rather than in degree. This card also marks the point where the pack's most contested material sits — wartime-record titles that intersect the Historical pack's own territory and are under live public dispute, which §6 states and does not adjudicate.
entries.example: Kozure Ōkami / Lone Wolf and Cub (1970) makes the period's material culture continuously visible and therefore continuously checkable; Golden Kamuy (2014) carries the additional and different obligation of depicting a living people rather than a vanished period.
entries.application: For method and for the archive, use the Historical pack. Come back here for the specific problem of a medium that must draw what it does not know, and for the discipline of deciding in advance which details you are prepared to be wrong about.

entries.category: Hand-Off Cards
entries.name: Gag Manga and Comic Timing in Panels
entries.description: Where manga comedy hands over to the Comedy pack — a debt the Comedy pack recorded itself.
entries.principle: Comic structure, the theory of the joke, satire and its targets, and the performance question belong to the Comedy pack, whose specialist collection is Structure and Timing. **Comedy explicitly declined to card gag manga pending this pack**, which makes this the second machine-checkable inter-pack debt in the library and one this pack is obliged to collect rather than merely acknowledge. What this pack keeps is timing as a spatial rather than temporal problem: in a drawn medium the reader controls the pace, so a beat is created by panel size, white space and the page turn, and the author schedules a laugh by geometry.
entries.example: Sazae-san (1946) demonstrates the four-panel unit as a complete comic machine over decades; Osomatsu-kun (1962) runs gag manga at serial length and shows the form's tolerance for total discontinuity between chapters.
entries.application: For why a joke works, use the Comedy pack. Come back here for where to put it on the page, which in this medium is most of the craft — the same joke lands or dies on whether the reveal is on the recto and how much empty space precedes it.

entries.category: Hand-Off Cards
entries.name: War Manga and the Testimony Problem
entries.description: Where war manga hands over to the War and Military pack, and the case that will not divide cleanly.
entries.principle: The representation of organised violence, the obligation to the people it happened to, and the whole testimony question belong to the War pack, which built its organising claim on precisely that gap. What this pack keeps is a case that sits in both places at once and is not resolvable by drawing a boundary: testimony published as a serial in a children's magazine, drawn by a survivor, which is simultaneously a primary historical document, a commercial serialised property subject to every constraint this pack describes, and the subject of a live and continuing public dispute about its place in school libraries. That combination exists nowhere else in the library.
entries.example: Hadashi no Gen / Barefoot Gen (1973) is that case, and the pack states its serialisation context, its documentary status and the fact of the ongoing dispute over its library placement, without adjudicating any of them; Sōin Gyokusai Seyo! / Onward Towards Our Noble Deaths (1973) is the same year's other testimony and was built as a volume rather than a serial, which is the contrast that makes the serialisation point visible.
entries.application: For the ethics and the craft of representing war, use the War pack. Come back here when the work in question was also a weekly commercial product, because that fact changes what it could say, when it could say it, and to whom — and it is invisible if you read the volume without the magazine.

entries.category: Writing to the Chapter Unit
entries.name: The Nineteen-Page Problem
entries.description: The fixed chapter length as a compositional constraint rather than an inconvenience.
entries.principle: A writer working in this medium does not choose how long a chapter is. The number is given — assume roughly nineteen pages for a weekly and something wider for a monthly — and everything else bends around it. The consequence most writers underestimate is that the constraint is on *pages*, not on words or on incident, so the real budget is panels, and a scene's cost is set by how much it must be shown rather than by how much happens. A conversation with four beats and a fight with four beats cost wildly different amounts, and a chapter plan built on events rather than on panels will overrun on the page and be discovered too late.
entries.example: Weekly Shōnen Jump serials are the most-studied case of the constraint operating at scale; Bakuman (2008) is unusual in dramatising the page budget as an explicit obstacle its characters plan around, which makes it useful as an illustration even though it is fiction about the industry rather than evidence of it.
entries.application: Plan in panels, not in beats. Count the panels your chapter needs before you write it, and when you are over, cut the scene that is cheapest to imply rather than the one that is least interesting. Implication is the only compression this medium offers that does not cost information.

entries.category: Writing to the Chapter Unit
entries.name: Opening a Chapter Cold
entries.description: The first panel after a week's gap, and what it has to do before it does anything else.
entries.principle: A chapter opens for a reader who last saw this story seven days and several other stories ago, and the first panel is doing orientation work whether the author intends it or not. The failure is to spend a page re-establishing, which is expensive and reads as a stall to anyone who has just read the previous chapter in a volume. The reliable solution is to orient through action rather than through re-statement — a first panel that shows where we are and that something is already underway does both jobs at once and costs one panel instead of five. The corollary is that the strongest chapter openings usually begin slightly *after* the moment a novelist would start.
entries.example: Death Note (2003) opens most chapters mid-manoeuvre and lets the situation reassemble itself around the reader; Vinland Saga (2005) uses a wide establishing panel that also carries new information — weather, season, an army's condition — so the orientation is never inert.
entries.application: Write your chapter's first panel last. Once you know what the chapter is, you can choose an opening image that orients and advances simultaneously, which is almost impossible to do in advance because you do not yet know what needs orienting.

entries.category: Writing to the Chapter Unit
entries.name: The Chapter's Last Panel
entries.description: The most valuable single panel in the medium, and the most commonly wasted.
entries.principle: The final panel is the only one guaranteed to be looked at for longer than a second, because a week or a month begins immediately after it. That makes it the medium's highest-leverage compositional position, and the standard use — a cliffhanger reveal — is only one of several that work. A last panel can also withhold, showing a character's reaction to something the reader has not been shown; it can recontextualise, giving the chapter's earlier events a second meaning; or it can rest, which is powerful precisely because it is rare. What it must never do is resolve everything, because that gives the reader no reason to return.
entries.example: Monster (1994) frequently ends on a face rather than an event, forcing the reader to spend a week on an interpretation; 20th Century Boys (1999) ends chapters on recontextualisation so often that the technique becomes the serial's signature.
entries.application: Ask what you want the reader holding for a week. If the answer is "what happens next", you have written a cliffhanger, which is fine and is one option. If the answer is "what did that mean", you have written something that will make them re-read, which is better and costs the same.

entries.category: Writing to the Chapter Unit
entries.name: Where the Recap Goes
entries.description: Reminding without stalling, in a form that is read twice under different conditions.
entries.principle: Every serial chapter carries a reminder burden, and the two readers it serves want opposite things — the weekly reader needs the reminder and the volume reader experiences it as repetition four pages after the fact. The technique that satisfies both is to carry the reminder inside new material: a character restates the stake while doing something else, or the information arrives attached to a fact the reader does not have. A reminder that is only a reminder is a chapter's cheapest page in the magazine and its most annoying page in the volume, and the volume is what survives.
entries.example: Hunter × Hunter (1998) routinely restates rules of its power system inside a scene where those rules are being newly tested, so the recap and the escalation are the same panels; Jujutsu Kaisen (2018) uses a character's incomplete understanding to restate for the reader without the narrative pausing.
entries.application: Never write a panel whose only function is to remind. Attach every restatement to a decision, a disagreement or a new fact. If you cannot find a carrier, the information is probably not needed and the reader has been trusted too little.

entries.category: Writing to the Chapter Unit
entries.name: Writing a Chapter That Also Reads in a Volume
entries.description: The double obligation, stated as a working method rather than as a tension to admire.
entries.principle: The chapter is the unit of sale and the volume is the unit of survival, and a serial is read in both. Structurally this means every chapter has two shapes: its own arc, and its position in a nine-or-ten-chapter block that will be bound together. The practical method is to think in blocks — plan the volume's shape first, then distribute turns across its chapters so each has one, rather than writing chapters serially and hoping a volume emerges. Working the other way round produces volumes with three climaxes in the last forty pages and nothing in the first hundred, which is the commonest structural fault in serialised work.
entries.example: Vagabond (1998) is built in visible volume-shaped movements; Fullmetal Alchemist (2001) is frequently cited for the evenness with which its turns distribute across its volumes, which is a planning achievement rather than an instinctive one.
entries.application: Sketch the volume before the chapters. Decide which chapter carries the volume's turn, which one is its low point and which one closes it, then write the chapters knowing what each has to be. This is the single most useful habit available in the form and almost nobody adopts it without being told.

entries.category: Writing to the Chapter Unit
entries.name: The Mid-Chapter Turn
entries.description: The second turn, why short chapters still need one, and where it sits.
entries.principle: A chapter with a single turn at its end is a chapter whose middle is transit. Because the page count is small, writers assume there is only room for one reversal — but a mid-chapter turn need not be large, and its function is different: it converts the chapter from a corridor into a room. Placed near the centre, a small reversal makes the reader re-evaluate what the chapter is about and gives the final panel something to land against. Without it the last panel is doing the work of the whole chapter and usually cannot.
entries.example: Chainsaw Man (2018) is unusually aggressive with mid-chapter reversals and rarely lets a chapter's premise survive to its own final page; Kimi ni Todoke (2005) shows the same structure at low volume, where the mid-chapter turn is a misread expression rather than an event.
entries.application: Find your chapter's centre and put a small reversal there — a misunderstanding, a refusal, an unexpected ally. Then check whether your ending still works. If the ending now lands harder, the turn was real; if nothing changed, you added an incident rather than a turn.

entries.category: Writing to the Chapter Unit
entries.name: Splitting a Scene Across Two Weeks
entries.description: When a scene will not fit, and the two ways to cut it.
entries.principle: Scenes routinely exceed the page budget, and there are exactly two honest responses: compress, or break. Breaking is the harder skill because the break point is not arbitrary — a scene split at its natural midpoint gives the reader a week of nothing to hold, while a scene split immediately *before* its turn gives them a week of anticipation and makes the second half open hot. The error is to split where the page count runs out, which is where the printer's constraint falls rather than where the story's does. This is also the one place where the medium's constraint reliably improves work: a forced split, chosen well, manufactures suspense the scene did not originally have.
entries.example: Kaiji (1996) builds much of its tension out of scenes broken at their point of maximum uncertainty and left there; Hikaru no Go (1998) splits long games so that each week ends on a move whose value the reader cannot yet assess.
entries.application: Choose the break before you write the scene, not when you run out of pages. Identify the scene's turn, break one beat before it, and let the second chapter open on the turn itself. If you are splitting where the pages ended, you are letting the format edit you.

entries.category: The Serial Without a Guaranteed End
entries.name: Writing Toward an Ending You May Not Reach
entries.description: Planning under the standing possibility that the serial stops before the plan does.
entries.principle: A serialised writer plans an ending they may never be allowed to write. Whether the serial continues is not their decision and the mechanism belongs elsewhere in this pack; what belongs here is the working posture, which is neither to plan nothing nor to plan a shape that only pays off at the end. The durable method is to build the story as a sequence of complete movements, each of which resolves something real, so that stopping at the end of any movement leaves a work rather than a fragment. This costs a certain kind of grand architecture and buys survivability, and in this form that is usually the right trade.
entries.example: Mushishi (1999) is episodic by design and would have been complete at almost any length; Berserk (1989) demonstrates the opposite exposure, where an unfinished long arc leaves material that cannot resolve itself.
entries.application: After every movement, ask whether the work would stand if it stopped here. If the answer is no for more than two consecutive movements, you have built a structure that requires permission you do not have. Insert a resolution you can afford to spend.

entries.category: The Serial Without a Guaranteed End
entries.name: The Arc That Can Be Cut Short
entries.description: Designing an arc with a compressible middle.
entries.principle: The practical unit of survivability is the arc, and an arc's compressibility is a design property you set when you build it. An arc whose middle is a sequence of independent obstacles can lose three of them without breaking; an arc whose middle is a single escalating chain cannot lose any link. Neither is better in the abstract — the chain is more satisfying when it runs in full — but only one of them can be shortened without visible damage, and a writer should know which they have built and choose it deliberately rather than discovering the answer under pressure.
entries.example: Hunter × Hunter (1998) builds arcs whose middles are frequently modular sets of concurrent problems; Ashita no Joe (1968) runs a chain in which each fight strictly requires the previous one, which is why its shape is so hard to abbreviate.
entries.application: Label your arc's middle as chain or set before you draft it. If it is a chain and you cannot afford one, convert two consecutive links into concurrent problems. You lose a little escalation and gain the ability to end early without amputating.

entries.category: The Serial Without a Guaranteed End
entries.name: Planting a Terminus Early
entries.description: Establishing the story's destination in the first volume, and why early is cheaper than later.
entries.principle: A story that names its destination early acquires two things at once: a promise the reader will wait for, and a structure that makes any ending legible as *the* ending rather than as a stop. The terminus need not be specific — a stated goal, a countdown, a prophecy, a named opponent — but it must be established while the work is still cheap to shape, because a terminus introduced at chapter ninety reads as a decision to wrap up rather than as the story arriving where it was going. The cost is a loss of flexibility, and it is a real cost that some writers should decline.
entries.example: Attack on Titan (2009) establishes a bounded question in its opening volume that every later development is measured against; Death Note (2003) plants a terminal condition in its first chapter and derives most of its tension from it.
entries.application: Put the destination in the first volume even if you do not yet know how you will reach it. Vagueness is permitted; absence is not. And write it as something the reader can see the story moving toward or away from, because a destination that generates no measurable progress is decoration.

entries.category: The Serial Without a Guaranteed End
entries.name: The Escape Hatch and Its Cost
entries.description: Building a place the story could stop, and the price of leaving one open.
entries.principle: Experienced serial writers build deliberate stopping points — a moment where the central relationship reaches equilibrium, or the stated goal is provisionally met — from which the story may either continue or end. The technique is sound and its cost is under-discussed: a reader can feel a hatch. A stopping point built as an option often reads as a false ending, and if the serial continues past several of them the reader learns that no apparent resolution is trustworthy, which is expensive. The discipline is to build few, build them at genuine structural joints, and make each one a real resolution of something rather than a pause.
entries.example: Slam Dunk (1990) closes on a resolution that could have been a hatch and is instead the ending, which is why it reads as decisive; Dragon Ball (1984) passes visibly through more than one point at which the story had concluded, and the later material carries the cost.
entries.application: Allow yourself two hatches in a long serial and no more. Place them where something genuinely completes. And when you pass through one and continue, open a new question in the same chapter, so the reader learns that continuing costs the story something rather than nothing.

entries.category: The Serial Without a Guaranteed End
entries.name: Writing the Ending Twice
entries.description: The short ending and the long ending, drafted together and held in reserve.
entries.principle: The most practical insurance in serialised work is to draft two endings early — one that can be executed in three chapters and one that needs fifteen — and to keep both current as the story develops. This sounds like double work and is not, because the exercise forces a writer to identify which threads are load-bearing and which are elaboration, and that knowledge improves everything in between. A writer who has never written the short version usually cannot produce it under pressure, which is precisely when it is needed, and the visible result is a compressed ending that reads as panic.
entries.example: Compressed final arcs are common across the form and are usually identifiable by a sudden change in the ratio of exposition to scene; the contrast with a serial that lands its short ending cleanly is the clearest available evidence that the short version was written in advance rather than improvised.
entries.application: Write both endings by the end of your second volume, keep them in a file, and revise them whenever the story turns. The short one is not a lesser ending — it is the same ending with the elaboration removed, and if it does not work, your long ending is carried by elaboration.

entries.category: The Serial Without a Guaranteed End
entries.name: When the Serial Outlives the Plan
entries.description: Continuing past the material you prepared, without the seams showing.
entries.principle: Success extends a serial past its plan, and the extension is where most long works acquire their structural damage. The characteristic failure is horizontal growth — more characters, more factions, more territory — because it is the easiest thing to add and it makes the world less legible with every addition. The alternative is vertical: return to something already established and reveal that it was more than the reader was told. This costs nothing in complexity, rewards the long reader specifically, and is available in almost any story that has been running long enough to have a past.
entries.example: 20th Century Boys (1999) repeatedly extends by re-examining its own established past rather than by widening; One Piece (1997) does both, and the vertical material is consistently the better-regarded half.
entries.application: When you need more story, look backwards before you look outwards. Ask what the reader believes about an established event and whether it could be incompletely true. Extension by revelation keeps the cast size flat, which is the number that actually governs whether a long serial stays readable.

entries.category: The Serial Without a Guaranteed End
entries.name: The Farewell You Owe a Long Reader
entries.description: The ending's obligation to time served, distinct from its obligation to plot.
entries.principle: A reader who has followed a serial for years is owed something the plot's resolution does not supply. Their investment is in accumulated familiarity — a cast they know, a rhythm they have kept — and an ending that resolves every narrative question while giving that accumulation no acknowledgement reads as cold, even when it is structurally perfect. The mechanism is usually a decompression after the climax in which very little happens and the reader is allowed to be with the characters without stakes. This is the one place in the form where scenes without tension are correct.
entries.example: Fullmetal Alchemist (2001) spends real page count after its resolution on ordinary futures for its cast; Vinland Saga (2005) closes movements with quiet duration rather than with incident, which is why its endings feel earned at the length they are.
