entries.application: Budget pages after the climax and defend them, because they will be the first thing cut. What they buy is not plot but acknowledgement, and a long reader can tell instantly whether an ending remembered how long they stayed.

entries.category: Character Introduction Under Survey Pressure
entries.name: The First Chapter's Cast Ceiling
entries.description: How many people a first chapter can carry, and what happens when it carries more.
entries.principle: A first chapter can establish roughly three characters the reader will retain, and the number is stubborn. Beyond it, retention does not degrade gracefully — the reader does not remember four people slightly less well, they remember the same three and file the rest as background, sometimes permanently. The pressure to exceed the ceiling is real: a writer with an ensemble wants the ensemble visible early, and the opening chapter is under scrutiny of a kind the pack's serial collection describes. Exceeding it is nonetheless the more common failure, and it is expensive because a character filed as background at chapter one is hard to promote later.
entries.example: One Piece (1997) introduces its crew across many chapters and gives each an arrival of its own rather than assembling them at the start; Haikyū!! (2012) opens on a small number of relationships and lets a large team accumulate around them.
entries.application: Count the named characters in your first chapter. If it is more than three, demote the surplus to silhouettes with no names and no lines, and introduce them properly later. A character introduced twice is fine; a character the reader has decided is scenery is not.

entries.category: Character Introduction Under Survey Pressure
entries.name: Introducing a Character Who Must Land Immediately
entries.description: The single-panel introduction, and what it must contain.
entries.principle: Under a short page budget, a character often gets one panel to become a person. What works in that panel is not backstory and not description but a *want in visible conflict with a circumstance* — someone doing something slightly wrong for a reason the reader can infer. This is why introductions built on action outperform introductions built on dialogue: an action implies a want, a want implies a history, and the reader assembles the character themselves at no page cost. An introduction that states qualities produces a description the reader has to be told twice.
entries.example: Dorohedoro (2000) introduces figures mid-behaviour and lets the reader infer everything else; Sangatsu no Lion / March Comes In Like a Lion (2007) introduces its supporting cast through small acts of care performed at inconvenient moments.
entries.application: Give the character one action that costs them something small. Not a demonstration of skill — a cost. Skill tells the reader what someone can do; a cost tells them what someone wants, and only the second one makes a person.

entries.category: Character Introduction Under Survey Pressure
entries.name: The Second Cast Wave
entries.description: When the story needs more people, and how to add them without diluting the first set.
entries.principle: Every serial reaches the point of needing new characters, and the risk is dilution: page count is fixed, so every new person is taken from someone established. The technique that avoids it is to introduce new characters *through* existing ones — as a pressure on an established relationship rather than as an addition to a roster — so the new arrival's pages simultaneously develop someone the reader already cares about. A new character who has no relation to the existing cast for several chapters is being paid for entirely out of the reader's patience.
entries.example: Slam Dunk (1990) introduces rivals as problems for specific established players rather than as free-standing figures; Fruits Basket (1998) brings each new arrival in as a disturbance to a household the reader already understands.
entries.application: Never introduce a character into empty space. Attach every arrival to an existing relationship they complicate, and the introduction pays twice. If you cannot find an attachment, the character may be arriving because you are bored rather than because the story needs them.

entries.category: Character Introduction Under Survey Pressure
entries.name: Naming, Silhouette and Instant Recognition
entries.description: Legibility as a cast-management problem, in a monochrome medium read at speed.
entries.principle: With no colour and a reader moving quickly, characters must be distinguishable by shape alone, and this is a writing problem as much as a drawing one. A cast whose members share a silhouette will be confused no matter how well they are written, and the fix is upstream: differentiate at the design stage by height, hair mass, posture and costume weight, and give each a verbal signature as well. The same logic governs names — names that share a length and a rhythm blur in a small balloon, and a reader who cannot tell two characters apart is not experiencing subtlety, they are lost.
entries.example: Hunter × Hunter (1998) maintains a very large cast partly through aggressive silhouette differentiation; One Piece (1997) is the extreme case, where nearly every figure is identifiable in outline at any scale.
entries.application: Draw your principals in solid black at thumbnail size. If you cannot tell them apart, neither can a reader at speed, and no amount of characterisation will fix it. Do the same test on the names by reading them aloud in sequence.

entries.category: Character Introduction Under Survey Pressure
entries.name: The Character Who Arrives to Be Cut
entries.description: Writing a character whose function is to be removed, without the reader feeling cheated.
entries.principle: Serialised stories need characters whose departure will matter, which means the reader must be attached to someone who is designed to leave. The failure is to signal it — a character with no future is easy to write as a foregone conclusion, and readers detect the flatness even when they cannot name it. The technique is to give the character an unrelated want that is going somewhere, so the reader is invested in a trajectory rather than in a person's survival. Their loss then costs the reader a future they had begun to imagine, which is a much larger loss than a person.
entries.example: Attack on Titan (2009) is unusually disciplined about giving short-lived figures ambitions that have nothing to do with their fate; Vinland Saga (2005) attaches departures to unfinished intentions rather than to completed arcs.
entries.application: Give every character marked for removal a plan for afterwards. Say it once, in passing, at least twenty chapters before. The reader will not consciously remember it and will feel the loss at exactly the right size.

entries.category: Character Introduction Under Survey Pressure
entries.name: Retrofitting a Minor Character
entries.description: Promoting someone the story did not originally intend to use.
entries.principle: Long serials routinely discover that a background figure has become interesting — to the writer, to readers, or both — and promotion is one of the form's genuine pleasures. The constraint is that the character's existing appearances are fixed, so the promotion must be consistent with a record the writer did not write with promotion in mind. The reliable method is to treat every prior appearance as evidence and build the character's interior life *backwards* from it, finding a reading under which their earlier behaviour was always expressive of something. Done well this reads as depth that was there all along; done carelessly it reads as a different character wearing the same face.
entries.example: Long-running ensemble serials supply many instances of the technique; Jujutsu Kaisen (2018) promotes secondary figures on the basis of established behaviour rather than by revising it.
entries.application: Re-read every panel the character appears in before you promote them, and write down what each one would mean if the character had the interior life you are about to give them. If any panel resists, that is your constraint — build around it rather than pretending it is not there.

entries.category: Character Introduction Under Survey Pressure
entries.name: The Rival as a Structural Position
entries.description: The rival as a slot in the story's machinery rather than as a character type.
entries.principle: The rival is best understood as a position that must be occupied rather than as a person with fixed attributes. Its function is to externalise the protagonist's development: a rival makes progress measurable, gives a reason for a skill to be demonstrated, and supplies opposition that does not require an antagonist. Because it is a position, it can be re-occupied — one rival can be surpassed and replaced by another without the story repeating itself, provided each occupant measures a *different* axis of the protagonist's development. Occupants who measure the same axis produce the sensation of a story running in place.
entries.example: Ashita no Joe (1968) fills the position successively with opponents who each test something different; Hikaru no Go (1998) makes the position explicit by naming the relationship the protagonist is chasing and building the whole serial on it.
entries.application: Before adding a rival, name the axis they measure — speed, resolve, technique, judgement, willingness to lose. If the axis is already occupied, either retire the current rival or change the axis. Two rivals measuring the same thing is the commonest cause of a middle that feels long.

entries.category: Dialogue, Monologue and the Interior Voice
entries.name: Dialogue That Survives a Small Balloon
entries.description: Writing lines for a container that is smaller than a sentence wants to be.
entries.principle: A speech balloon is a physical object competing with the art for space, and the practical limit is far shorter than prose instinct suggests. The consequence is not that dialogue must be terse but that it must be *front-loaded* — the meaning has to arrive in the first few words, because a balloon read at speed is often not read to its end. Subordinate clauses, qualifications and periodic sentences that withhold their verb are structurally hostile to the form. What survives is direct address, fragments, and lines whose emphasis falls early.
entries.example: Death Note (2003) is unusually dense with argument and manages it by breaking reasoning into many short balloons across many panels rather than into fewer long ones; Yotsuba&! (2003) works almost entirely in fragments and demonstrates how much characterisation short lines can carry.
entries.application: Read every line aloud and cut everything before its main verb. Then check whether the line still means what you intended. If a line needs its qualification, split it across two balloons in two panels and let the art hold the pause between them — that pause is free and a comma is not.

entries.category: Dialogue, Monologue and the Interior Voice
entries.name: Interior Monologue and the Undrawn Voice
entries.description: Thought on the page, its two conventional containers, and when each earns its keep.
entries.principle: Interior monologue is available cheaply in this medium and is therefore overused. It has one irreplaceable function — showing the gap between what a character thinks and what their face is doing — and that gap is the whole of its value. When thought merely restates what the panel already shows, it costs space and tells the reader their eyes were insufficient. The discipline is to reserve interior text for contradiction: the calm face and the frantic thought, the confident line and the private doubt. Used that way it is one of the most efficient characterisation tools in any narrative medium.
entries.example: Kaiji (1996) runs almost entirely on the distance between composed exteriors and panicking interiors; Oyasumi Punpun (2007) makes the divergence between interior voice and depicted self the work's central formal device.
entries.application: For every interior line, cover the drawing and ask whether the thought is surprising. If it is what the face already says, cut it. If it contradicts the face, you have found the reason the technique exists.

entries.category: Dialogue, Monologue and the Interior Voice
entries.name: Narration Without a Speaker
entries.description: Caption text belonging to no character, and the authority it silently claims.
entries.principle: Unattributed caption text is the medium's most authoritative register: because it belongs to nobody, the reader takes it as true. That authority is a resource and a hazard. Used for information the story genuinely wants settled — a date, a place, a fact about the world — it is efficient and invisible. Used for judgement about a character, it forecloses the reader's own reading and replaces interpretation with instruction. The distinction is not tonal but functional: ask whether the caption is establishing a fact or delivering a verdict.
entries.example: Golden Kamuy (2014) uses unattributed captions for ethnographic and material detail while leaving every judgement about its characters to scene; Pluto (2003) restricts its captions almost entirely to place and time.
entries.application: Grep your captions for evaluative words. Facts may live there; verdicts may not. If a caption is telling the reader how to feel about someone, the scene underneath it is not doing its job and the caption is concealing that.

entries.category: Dialogue, Monologue and the Interior Voice
entries.name: Silence as Dialogue
entries.description: The wordless panel as a spoken turn, and the pacing arithmetic that makes it work.
entries.principle: A wordless panel inside a conversation is a turn in that conversation — a refusal, a hesitation, an acknowledgement — and it is read as duration in a way no prose equivalent achieves. Its cost is a full panel, which under a fixed page budget is expensive, and that expense is exactly what makes it legible: the reader registers that the story spent something here. The technique fails when silences are used decoratively, because a reader who encounters several wordless panels with no communicative content stops reading them as turns and starts reading them as slow art.
entries.example: Koe no Katachi / A Silent Voice (2013) makes non-verbal turns structurally central and treats communication failure as its subject; Solanin (2005) uses silence to mark the exact moments its characters decline to say the thing that matters.
entries.application: Treat a silent panel as a line of dialogue and ask what it says. If you cannot write the sentence it replaces, it is not a turn and should be merged into an adjacent panel. Spend them where a character is choosing not to speak, which is the only place they mean something.

entries.category: Dialogue, Monologue and the Interior Voice
entries.name: The Speech Register Problem
entries.description: Politeness level and pronoun choice as characterisation, and what happens to them in translation.
entries.principle: Japanese carries social relation inside its grammar — levels of politeness, several first-person pronouns, forms of address — so a line of dialogue encodes the speaker's estimate of a relationship before it says anything. Writers use this constantly: a character who shifts register mid-scene has changed their read of who they are talking to, and that shift is often the scene's actual event. The craft point survives translation even where the mechanism does not, because the underlying move — marking relational change inside how a person speaks rather than in what they say — is available in any language, though it costs more words elsewhere.
entries.example: Nana (2000) turns much of its relational development on how two people address each other over time; Sangatsu no Lion (2007) marks the protagonist's shifting distance from an adoptive household in the way he speaks to its members.
entries.application: Decide your characters' default register toward each other, write it down, and then break it deliberately. A single unexpected shift does more relationship work than a page of stated feeling. If you are writing in a language without grammatical politeness, substitute address, contraction and sentence length — the tools are weaker but the move is the same.

entries.category: Dialogue, Monologue and the Interior Voice
entries.name: Exposition in a Medium That Can Show
entries.description: Where explanation goes when the panel has already done the work.
entries.principle: The medium's default failure with exposition is redundancy: a panel shows the situation and a balloon explains it. Because both are present the reader receives the information twice and trusts neither. The productive arrangement is division — let the art carry the physical and the spatial, and reserve language for what cannot be drawn, which is causation, intention and rule. A drawn medium is exceptionally bad at conveying *why* and exceptionally good at conveying *what*, and exposition that respects the split is nearly invisible.
entries.example: Hunter × Hunter (1998) explains rules verbally at length while never narrating what a panel is already showing; Made in Abyss (2012) delivers its worldbuilding as constraint and consequence in dialogue while leaving the world's appearance entirely to the art.
entries.application: For each exposition balloon, ask whether the panel already contains the information. If it does, cut the balloon. What survives will be causes and rules, which is what the reader actually cannot see.

entries.category: Dialogue, Monologue and the Interior Voice
entries.name: Catchphrase, Verbal Tic and the Weekly Reader
entries.description: Repeated speech as a recognition device, and the point at which it becomes a substitute for character.
entries.principle: A verbal signature does real work for a reader returning weekly to a large cast: it identifies a speaker before the reader has parsed the art, and it accumulates meaning through repetition in a way a single scene cannot achieve. Its hazard is that it is easy, and a tic can quietly become the whole of a character — a figure who says their phrase and does nothing else is a costume. The test is whether the phrase ever changes: a signature that alters under pressure, or is withheld at a moment where the reader expects it, is characterisation. One that never varies is a label.
entries.example: Long-running ensemble serials make heavy use of the device; the technique's serious form is the withheld signature, where a character's failure to say the expected thing marks a change nothing else in the scene states.
entries.application: Give the tic and then plan its violation. Decide, when you invent it, the chapter in which the character will not say it. That single omission converts a recognition device into a character, and it is free.

entries.category: The Adaptation Economy and Writing Toward It
entries.name: Writing a Scene an Adaptation Will Want
entries.description: The pull toward adaptable material, and how to notice it acting on you.
entries.principle: A serial that succeeds will be adapted, and the possibility exerts a quiet pressure on composition long before anyone commissions anything. The pressure is not corrupt in itself — writing a scene with strong physical action, clear spatial geography and a legible emotional beat is good practice regardless — but it becomes a problem when it starts selecting *against* the things the page does better than motion. Interiority carried by decorative field, a joke that depends on panel adjacency, a page whose meaning is in its layout: these are the medium's own strengths and they are precisely what does not survive the move. A writer who never notices the pull ends up writing storyboards.
entries.example: Kōkaku Kidōtai / Ghost in the Shell (1989) is dense with page-native devices — marginal annotation, dialogue running under images — that adaptations have consistently had to solve rather than transfer; Pluto (2003) works the opposite way and is built largely from staging that moves cleanly.
entries.application: Once a volume, count the scenes that could be filmed unchanged. If it is most of them, you have been writing for a camera. Deliberately build one sequence that only works on paper — the medium is what you are actually being paid for, and it is the first thing the pull removes.

entries.category: The Adaptation Economy and Writing Toward It
entries.name: The Property and the Story
entries.description: The point at which a work becomes an asset, and what that does to a writer's decisions.
entries.principle: A successful serial stops being only a story and becomes a property with several dependent products, and the writer's decisions acquire consequences outside the page. This pack states the commercial structure elsewhere; what belongs here is the working consequence, which is that certain narrative moves become expensive in a way they were not before. Killing a character, ending a relationship, closing a setting — each is a normal narrative act that, once a property exists, is also a decision about things the writer does not control. The craft response is neither to comply nor to pretend the situation is unchanged; it is to make the irreversible decisions **early**, while they are still cheap.
entries.example: Long-running properties across the form illustrate the pattern; the observable signature is a serial whose cast stops shrinking after a certain volume, which is rarely a narrative choice.
entries.application: Front-load your irreversible acts. Whatever you intend to destroy, destroy it in the first third. The story is never freer than before it is worth anything, and a writer who defers the costly decisions usually discovers they have been made for them.

entries.category: The Adaptation Economy and Writing Toward It
entries.name: What Survives the Move to Motion
entries.description: The transfer problem, read backwards as a diagnostic on your own pages.
entries.principle: Some things move to animation intact — dialogue, action geography, character design, plot — and some do not: the page turn as a beat, panel adjacency as juxtaposition, the reader-controlled pace, and the specific effect of a still image held for as long as the reader chooses. Reading your own work through that filter is a useful diagnostic even if no adaptation is ever made, because a scene that transfers *completely* is a scene that used none of the medium's own tools. This is not an argument against such scenes; it is an argument for knowing how many you have written.
entries.example: Akira (1982) contains substantial material that its own film adaptation could not carry at length, which is why the two versions diverge structurally rather than in incident; Mushishi (1999) transfers unusually cleanly, and the reason is that its effects are built from stillness and duration that animation can also produce.
entries.application: Take one chapter and mark every panel whose effect depends on the reader controlling time. If the count is zero, you have written a script. Aim for a handful per chapter, not a majority — the point is that the medium is being used, not that it is being demonstrated.

entries.category: The Adaptation Economy and Writing Toward It
entries.name: Designing for a Voice You Will Not Cast
entries.description: Writing dialogue that must work silently first.
entries.principle: Manga dialogue is read, not heard, and the reader supplies a voice. This is a genuine advantage — a reader's invented voice is always perfectly cast — and it imposes a constraint most writers only discover in adaptation: lines that depend on delivery do nothing on the page. Sarcasm without a marker reads as sincerity; a pause without a panel does not exist; emphasis has to be carried by lettering or by line break rather than by stress. Writing so that the sense survives with no performance at all is the baseline skill, and it also produces dialogue that adapts well, because a line that works unvoiced works voiced.
entries.example: Death Note (2003) carries long argumentative exchanges whose logic is entirely legible without performance; Yotsuba&! (2003) builds comic timing from panel rhythm rather than from delivery, which is why it reads as funny rather than as a description of something funny.
entries.application: Read your dialogue in a flat mental monotone. Every line whose meaning changes under that test needs a visual marker — a panel break, a lettering change, a reaction shot — or a rewrite. Do not rely on a voice you will never hear.

entries.category: The Adaptation Economy and Writing Toward It
entries.name: The Adaptation That Overtakes the Source
entries.description: When the adaptation catches up, and what the source writer does about it.
entries.principle: An adaptation produced alongside an ongoing serial can consume material faster than the serial generates it, and the writer then faces a situation with no good options: supply material out of sequence, allow the adaptation to invent, or let it stop. Each has a cost the reader will eventually see. The craft response is anticipatory — build the story so that some arcs are structurally detachable and can be released early or held back without disturbing the spine, which is the same modularity `craft-9` recommends for a different reason. Two independent pressures selecting for the same structural property is a strong argument for having it.
entries.example: The pattern is common enough across the form to be a recognised production situation; its visible signature is an adaptation whose middle section has no counterpart in the source, and a source whose later material silently absorbs or contradicts it.
entries.application: Keep two arcs in reserve that could run in any order. If the pressure never arrives you have lost nothing, and if it does you have the only currency that helps, which is material that does not need to be in a particular place.

entries.category: The Adaptation Economy and Writing Toward It
entries.name: Merchandise Logic and the Character Who Must Recur
entries.description: The recurrence pressure on a cast, named as a pressure rather than as a conspiracy.
entries.principle: Once a cast has commercial existence outside the story, some characters acquire a reason to keep appearing that has nothing to do with the narrative. Writers frequently describe this as interference and it is more often gravity: nobody instructs the author, and the character simply becomes easier to include than to exclude. The recognisable symptom is a figure who appears regularly and is never *used* — present in scenes, absent from the causal chain. The craft answer is to give every recurring character an active want, so that recurrence is paid for narratively even when the reason for it is not narrative.
entries.example: The symptom is visible across long-running ensemble serials and is most legible in works where a popular secondary figure's chapter count rises while their causal contribution does not.
entries.application: For each recurring character, ask what would change in the plot if they were absent from their last three appearances. If the answer is nothing, they are being carried. Either give them a want or reduce them to the scenes where they matter, and do it before the reader notices.

entries.category: The Adaptation Economy and Writing Toward It
entries.name: Refusing the Adaptation's Pull
entries.description: Choosing the page over the transfer, and paying for it deliberately.
entries.principle: The final card in this category exists to say that the pull can be refused and that refusal is a legitimate craft position, not a purity claim. A writer may decide that their work's central effects belong to the page and accept that this makes the work harder to adapt and less commercially extensible. The cost is real and should be stated rather than romanticised: fewer readers, less money, and in a serialisation system, plausibly a shorter run. What is bought is a work that does the thing only this medium does. Both choices are available; the failure is making one and telling yourself you made the other.
entries.example: The Garo lineage is where this refusal is most visible as a body of work rather than as an individual decision, and its economics are the argument's honest half.
entries.application: Decide once, in writing, and revisit it only on evidence. A writer who has not decided will drift toward adaptability, because every individual decision in that direction is locally reasonable and the aggregate is a different book.

entries.category: Research, Setting and the Everyday Procedural
entries.name: The Procedural Contract
entries.description: What a work promises when it takes a real occupation as its subject.
entries.principle: A serial built on a real job, sport or craft makes an implicit promise: that the reader will finish it knowing something true. This is the most reliable engine in the medium for a story with no antagonist, because competence is inherently dramatic and learning has a natural shape. The contract is strict, though — the reader is trusting the work, and the trust extends to material they cannot check. A single detectable error does not merely correct itself in the reader's mind; it retroactively devalues everything they accepted on faith, which is most of the book.
entries.example: Moyashimon (2004) builds an entire serial on agricultural microbiology and treats the science as the source of incident rather than as decoration; Gin no Saji / Silver Spoon (2011) runs the contract on agricultural-school life and derives its emotional material directly from the procedural material.
entries.application: Decide what your reader will know at the end and write it as one sentence before you start. If you cannot, you have a setting rather than a procedural, and the contract does not apply — which is fine, but do not accept the credit for a promise you are not making.

entries.category: Research, Setting and the Everyday Procedural
entries.name: Drawing a Job You Have Not Done
entries.description: The specific research problem of a medium that must show the work.
entries.principle: Prose can write "she prepared the dish" and a page cannot. Every procedural manga must decide the sequence of physical actions, the tools, the posture, the timing and the mess, and each is a checkable claim. This makes observation, not reading, the primary research method — the information a procedural needs is mostly not written down anywhere, because it is the kind of knowledge practitioners hold in their hands. The corollary is that reading about a job produces a manga that looks like reading about a job, and readers who do it will say so.
entries.example: Blue Giant (2013) is built on the physical business of playing an instrument rather than on the music as an abstraction; Uchū Kyōdai / Space Brothers (2007) derives its texture from procedure and equipment rather than from spectacle.
entries.application: Watch someone do it, and record the things nobody would think to tell you — where they put their hands between actions, what they do while waiting, what they get wrong and how they recover. That residue is what makes a drawn procedural convincing, and it is not in any book.

entries.category: Research, Setting and the Everyday Procedural
entries.name: The Expert Reader and the Error That Ends Trust
entries.description: Writing for the small readership that knows, and why they set the standard for everyone.
entries.principle: Any procedural has a minority readership who do the thing professionally, and they are disproportionately important. They are the readers who recommend the work, and they are the ones who will identify an error publicly. The temptation is to write for the majority who cannot check, and it is a bad trade: the general reader cannot tell an accurate page from a plausible one, so accuracy costs nothing with them and everything with the experts. What the expert reader actually rewards is not exhaustiveness but the correct *small* detail — the thing an outsider would never include.
entries.example: Sangatsu no Lion / March Comes In Like a Lion (2007) is respected by shogi players for the professional texture around the games rather than for the games themselves; Chihayafuru (2007) does the same for competitive karuta, where the sport's small physical realities carry the credibility.
entries.application: Put one detail per chapter that only a practitioner would recognise, and do not explain it. Explaining it converts a signal of authenticity into a lecture, and the expert reader you were writing for stops feeling addressed.

entries.category: Research, Setting and the Everyday Procedural
entries.name: Where Research Becomes Scene
entries.description: Converting what you learned into something that happens.
entries.principle: The characteristic failure of a well-researched work is a scene in which a knowledgeable character explains, and the failure is structural rather than stylistic — research arrives as information, and information is not drama. The conversion is always the same move: find the point at which the knowledge is *contested* or *insufficient*. Two practitioners disagreeing, a procedure failing, an expert meeting a case their training does not cover — each turns a fact into a position someone holds, and positions can be dramatised. Research that never produces a disagreement has not been converted.
entries.example: Oishinbo (1983) organises almost every instalment around a dispute between people who both know what they are talking about; Hataraku Saibō / Cells at Work! (2015) converts physiology into incident by personifying the process, so that mechanism becomes conflict rather than exposition.
entries.application: For each fact you intend to use, write down who could disagree with it and why. If nobody plausibly can, it is background and belongs in the art rather than in the script. The facts that survive are the ones with a second opinion attached.

entries.category: Research, Setting and the Everyday Procedural
entries.name: The Ordinary Setting and Its Specificity
entries.description: Research for a world the reader already lives in.
entries.principle: A contemporary domestic setting is the hardest research problem in the form, because the reader knows it and any generic rendering reads as absence rather than as neutrality. A room drawn without decisions is not a plain room; it is no room. The work is in specificity that carries information — a particular clutter, a particular quality of light, the wrong furniture for the income — and the reward is disproportionate, because a reader who recognises a real place extends credit to everything in it. This is the most reliably underinvested area in the medium, precisely because it looks like it needs no research.
entries.example: Solanin (2005) makes a small apartment carry the whole of its characters' economic situation; Yotsuba&! (2003) renders unremarkable suburban space with a density of observation usually reserved for invented worlds.
entries.application: Photograph or sketch the actual kind of place, not a place like it. Then remove one thing and add one thing that is specific to the person living there. Generic space is the fastest way to tell a reader that the people in it are not real either.

entries.category: Research, Setting and the Everyday Procedural
entries.name: Consulting, Credit and the Supervisor
entries.description: Working with a subject expert, and what the arrangement asks of the writer.
entries.principle: Procedural manga routinely engages a subject specialist, and the arrangement is common enough to have a standard supervision credit in the published record. The craft question is not whether to use one but what to do with the disagreements: an expert will object to things the story needs, and their objections divide into two kinds. Some are corrections, and the writer should take them. Others are objections to compression or to dramatic emphasis, and the writer should not, because the expert is optimising for accuracy and the writer is optimising for a story that is also accurate. Confusing the two produces either a false page or an unreadable one.
entries.example: Supervision credits are visible across the procedural line and are the clearest evidence in the published record that the arrangement is routine rather than exceptional.
entries.application: Ask your consultant to sort every note into "this is wrong" and "this is not how I would emphasise it". Take all of the first and argue about the second. And credit them, because the credit is what makes the next expert say yes.

entries.category: Research, Setting and the Everyday Procedural
entries.name: Knowing What You May Be Wrong About
entries.description: Allocating a finite research budget by deciding in advance where you can afford error.
entries.principle: No work is uniformly researched and pretending otherwise produces the worst outcome, which is a book that is half-accurate everywhere. The productive method is triage: decide, before drafting, which claims are load-bearing — the ones the work's authority rests on — and which are texture, then spend the hours on the first list and be frankly schematic about the second. A work that is exact about three things and openly stylised about the rest reads as confident. One that is approximately right about everything reads as careless, even when the average accuracy is higher.
entries.example: Golden Kamuy (2014) is exact where its authority is at stake and stylised elsewhere, and the difference is legible on the page; the same allocation is visible in most historical and procedural work that survives expert reading.
entries.application: Write two lists before you draft — must be right, may be wrong. Show the second list to nobody and consult it constantly. The discipline is not in the research; it is in refusing to spread it evenly.

entries.category: Collaboration: Editor, Assistant and Studio
entries.name: Bringing Work to an Editor
entries.description: What to bring, at what stage, and why the stage matters more than the quality.
entries.principle: The editorial relationship in this medium is unusually close and begins unusually early, and the writer's main lever over it is *what stage of work they present*. Bringing finished pages invites line-level notes and makes structural change expensive for everyone; bringing an idea invites the editor to co-author it. Bringing the storyboard stage — see `craft-47` — invites exactly the conversation most worth having, which is about structure while structure is still cheap. The authority the editor holds in this system is real and is described in this pack's serialisation collection; what the writer controls is the object on the table.
entries.example: The editorial relationship is documented across the industry's own accounts, and the consistent feature is early and continuous involvement rather than late review.
entries.application: Default to bringing the storyboard. If you want structural help, bring it earlier; if you have made a decision you intend to defend, bring it later and be ready to say why. Choosing the stage deliberately is most of what a writer can do to shape the relationship.

entries.category: Collaboration: Editor, Assistant and Studio
entries.name: The Note You Take and the Note You Refuse
entries.description: Sorting editorial feedback, in a system where the editor's position is strong.
entries.principle: Editorial notes divide into three kinds and conflating them is the commonest source of damage. There are diagnoses — *this section is slow* — which are almost always right, because the editor is a first reader and first readers know when they are bored. There are prescriptions — *cut this character* — which are the editor's proposed fix for the diagnosis and are frequently wrong while the diagnosis is right. And there are preferences, which are neither. A writer who refuses diagnoses becomes unpublishable; one who accepts every prescription stops being the author. Take the diagnosis, argue the prescription, and be able to tell which you are hearing.
entries.example: The pattern is documented in editors' and artists' own accounts of the relationship, where a note is often remembered as a correct problem paired with a rejected solution.
entries.application: For every note, write down the problem it implies before you write down your response. If you cannot state the problem, ask. Most bad arguments with an editor are arguments about a solution neither party has connected to a stated problem.

entries.category: Collaboration: Editor, Assistant and Studio
entries.name: Writing for Hands That Are Not Yours
entries.description: Specifying a page someone else will execute.
entries.principle: In this medium the person who conceives a page is frequently not the person who renders all of it, and the writing changes accordingly. What must be specified is intent, not appearance: *this panel is claustrophobic*, not *draw the walls close*. Specifying appearance produces a page that is technically correct and dead, because the executing artist has been given a task rather than a purpose and cannot make the hundred small decisions that purpose would have guided. The corollary is that the notes worth writing are about what the reader should feel and where their eye should go, which is exactly the information a description of appearance omits.
entries.example: The division of labour is standard across the industry, and its most-documented variant is the collective arrangement described in `craft-48`.
entries.application: For every panel you delegate, write the reader's experience and the eye-path, then stop. If you find yourself specifying an object's position, ask what the position was for and write that instead.

entries.category: Collaboration: Editor, Assistant and Studio
entries.name: What an Assistant Can Be Given
entries.description: The delegation decision, from the writer's side of it.
entries.principle: The assistant system is how this medium meets its deadlines, and this pack describes the arrangement itself in its serialisation collection. What belongs here is the authorial question: what can be handed over without the work becoming someone else's? The reliable line is between the *marked* and the *unmarked* — anything that carries the author's judgement about emphasis stays, and anything that is execution of a decision already made can go. In practice that usually means faces, key figures and the storyboard stay; backgrounds, tone, effects and much of the finishing can go. The line is not fixed and every artist draws it differently, but a line drawn by default rather than by decision tends to migrate.
entries.example: The division is visible in the published record of studios and in the credits of long-running serials, where the same names recur across a work's assistant roster for years.
entries.application: Write your line down and re-read it every six months. The thing to watch for is not delegation but drift: each individual handover is defensible and the aggregate can quietly become a different artist's book with your name on it.

entries.category: Collaboration: Editor, Assistant and Studio
entries.name: The Nemu as the Real Manuscript
entries.description: The storyboard stage, and why it is the document that matters.
entries.principle: The rough layout — panel breakdown, balloon placement, page rhythm, figures as gesture — is where nearly every decision that determines whether a chapter works is actually made. It is also the stage at which change is cheap, the stage an editor engages with, and the stage most closely equivalent to a prose manuscript. Writers who think of it as a preliminary sketch and of the finished art as the real work have the relationship backwards: the finished art executes decisions the layout already made, and a chapter that fails at layout cannot be rescued by rendering.
entries.example: The stage is standard practice across the industry and appears in accounts of the process as the object of editorial discussion rather than as an internal step.
entries.application: Spend your revision time here and your least time on finishes. If a chapter is not working, redo the layout rather than redrawing panels — you will fix it in an afternoon at this stage and not at all at the next one.

entries.category: Collaboration: Editor, Assistant and Studio
entries.name: Collective Authorship and the Divided Task
entries.description: Groups working as one author, and the division that is not the Anglophone one.
entries.principle: Collective manga authorship exists and does not map onto the Anglophone comics division of writer, penciller, inker, colourist and letterer — a model that cannot apply here in any case, since the pages are monochrome and there is no colourist role at all. The documented arrangements divide differently: a writer-and-storyboarder, a chief character designer, background artists, with some roles rotating between works. What makes such an arrangement work is that the division follows *decisions* rather than production stages, so each member owns a class of judgement rather than a step in a pipeline.
entries.example: CLAMP is the most-documented case, with a division across writing and storyboarding, character design and backgrounds, and rotation among some of those roles between projects; Fujiko Fujio worked for decades as two artists under a single name before the partnership formally separated into two credited identities.
entries.application: If you are dividing work between people, divide by judgement rather than by stage. Ask who decides what a scene means, who decides what people look like, who decides what the world looks like — and let each own their class completely rather than passing pages down a line.

entries.category: Collaboration: Editor, Assistant and Studio
entries.name: Working Under a Name That Is Not One Person
entries.description: The shared pen name, and what it does to the record and to the work.
entries.principle: A single name covering several people is common in this medium and has two consequences a writer should enter deliberately. It presents a unified authorial voice, which is a genuine artistic effect and not merely a convenience — readers relate to an author, and a group is harder to relate to. And it makes the record unreliable in ways that outlast the arrangement: attribution of individual contributions becomes difficult or impossible, and a later separation leaves a body of work that cannot be cleanly divided. Neither is an argument against it; both are things to decide in advance rather than discover.
entries.example: Fujiko Fujio's eventual separation into two credited identities left a large shared corpus whose individual attribution remains a matter of record-keeping rather than of certainty.
entries.application: If you work under a shared name, keep a private attribution record from the first page. You will not need it while the arrangement holds and you will need it badly if it ends, and reconstructing it afterwards from memory is how disputes start.

entries.category: Writing Across the Demographic Line
entries.name: Reading the Magazine Before You Write for It
entries.description: The house register, and how to find it without being told.
entries.principle: Every magazine has a register its editorial department could not fully articulate but enforces reliably — a tolerance for cruelty, a default pace, an assumption about how much the reader will re-read, a relationship to sentiment. It is learnable only by reading a run of issues rather than a run of collected volumes, because the volume strips the context that tells you what the register is. A writer who submits without doing this is not being rejected for quality; they are being rejected for register, and the note they receive will not say so because the editor experiences it as obvious.
entries.example: The differences between long-established weeklies aimed at nominally the same readership are the clearest available demonstration that the demographic label does not determine the register; each developed a distinct house tone from a similar nominal audience.
entries.application: Read six consecutive issues, not six volumes. Write down, for each, how the chapters end, how much is explained, and how cruel the work is permitted to be. That document is worth more than any amount of general advice about the demographic.

entries.category: Writing Across the Demographic Line
entries.name: Writing for a Readership You Are Not
entries.description: The oldest working situation in the medium, and the two ways it goes wrong.
entries.principle: Most writers in this medium write for a readership they do not belong to — by age, most obviously, but often by gender and by generation as well — and the medium's history includes a great deal of successful work made this way. It fails in two opposite directions. Condescension writes down, assuming the reader wants less; it is the more discussed failure and the less common one. Projection writes for the author's memory of being that reader, which is a different person in a different decade, and is the more common failure by a wide margin because it does not feel like an error from the inside.
entries.example: The 1970s shōjo work carded at `subgenre-34` was made for a readership its makers were only partly inside, and its durability is the evidence that the situation is workable; the same decade's less durable material is largely lost to projection rather than to condescension.
entries.application: Find two current readers of the age you are writing for and ask them what they are actually reading, not what they think of yours. Projection is invisible from inside and dissolves on contact with a real reader's actual habits.

entries.category: Writing Across the Demographic Line
entries.name: The Crossover Reader
entries.description: Readers outside the target demographic, who are numerous and are not the target.
entries.principle: Every successful title acquires readers outside its nominal demographic — adults reading a children's weekly, women reading a boys' magazine, and every combination — and their existence is a permanent fact rather than a surprise. The mistake is to start writing for them. A work that begins hedging between two readerships usually loses the first without securing the second, because the crossover audience came for the thing the work already was. The productive posture is to write for the target and decline to *exclude* the crossover reader — which mostly means not signalling contempt for anyone outside the demographic, a cheap discipline with a large return.
entries.example: Long-running weeklies aimed at younger readers routinely sustain substantial adult readerships without addressing them, and the addressing is the variable that distinguishes the cases that hold from the cases that dissolve.
entries.application: Write for the target. Then read for moments where the work implies that other readers are not welcome — a joke at their expense, an assumption of ignorance — and remove those. That is the whole of the technique and it costs nothing.

entries.category: Writing Across the Demographic Line
entries.name: Moving a Series Across Magazines
entries.description: What changes when a serial relocates, and what must not.
entries.principle: Serials do move between magazines, and the move is a change of register rather than merely of venue: a different page count, a different cadence, a different tolerance, and frequently a different readership age. The work has to adapt and the danger is adapting the wrong layer. Surface adaptation — adjusting how much is shown, how fast chapters move, what the register permits — is usually correct. Adapting the story's fundamental commitments to suit a new readership is usually fatal, because the readers who followed the move did so for those commitments and the new readers have not yet agreed to anything.
entries.example: Relocations are common enough across the form to be a recognised event in a serial's history, and the observable signature of one handled badly is a break in the work's tone that is not accompanied by any narrative reason for it.
entries.application: List what is surface and what is commitment before the first chapter in the new venue. Change the first list freely. Change nothing on the second for at least a volume, so the readers who followed you can see that they were right to.

entries.category: Writing Across the Demographic Line
entries.name: Age, Register and What Changes
entries.description: What actually differs between work for younger and older readerships, once the assumptions are removed.
entries.principle: The differences that survive scrutiny are narrower than the labels imply. Explicitness varies, but not reliably in the expected direction — work for younger readers frequently carries more violence and more death than its adult counterpart. What differs consistently is *how much a reader is asked to hold*: the number of simultaneous threads, the interval over which a setup may be left unresolved, and the amount of interpretation required to see what a scene is about. Work for younger readers resolves faster, carries fewer threads at once, and is more willing to state its meaning. None of that is a limit on seriousness.
entries.example: The children's and younger-readership market carries a substantial body of work dealing directly with death, war and loss, which is the standing refutation of the assumption that the difference is one of subject matter.
entries.application: Adjust load, not subject. If you are writing for younger readers, cut the number of live threads and shorten the setup-to-payoff interval, then leave your subject exactly where it was. Almost everything else you have been told about the difference is about marketing.

entries.category: Writing Across the Demographic Line
entries.name: Writing Across the Gender Line of a Magazine
entries.description: A routine working situation, stated as craft rather than as a question of entitlement.
entries.principle: Writers work across the gender line of their magazine's nominal readership constantly and in both directions, and the medium's history would be much smaller without it. Treated as craft, the problem is specific and tractable: the risk is not subject matter but *default assumption* — what a writer takes for granted about ordinary experience, which is invisible to them precisely because it is a default. That is a research problem with a research answer, and the answer is not consultation about big topics but attention to small ones, because the defaults live in the small ones.
entries.example: The 1970s shōjo cohort and the long history of women writing for boys' magazines both demonstrate the situation as normal working practice rather than as an exception requiring justification.
entries.application: Have a reader from the readership mark every place they thought "that is not how that goes" — not the big scenes, the incidental ones. The corrections will almost all be small, and small is where a default lives.

entries.category: Writing Across the Demographic Line
entries.name: The House Style and the Room Inside It
entries.description: Working inside a strong editorial register without disappearing into it.
entries.principle: A magazine with a strong house register applies real pressure toward the middle of that register, and a writer can spend a career there producing competent, indistinguishable work. The room to be distinctive exists but is not where beginners look for it: it is rarely in premise, which the register constrains hardest, and it is usually in texture — how a specific character speaks, what the work finds funny, which small moments it chooses to give a full page. Those choices are almost never the subject of an editorial note, which makes them the space that is actually available.
entries.example: Long-running weeklies contain work that is unmistakably individual while conforming entirely to the house register, which is the demonstration that the room exists; the alternative reading, that distinctiveness requires escaping the register, is not supported by the record.
entries.application: Accept the register on premise and structure, and spend your distinctiveness on texture. Pick three things — a rhythm of speech, a recurring kind of image, a category of moment you always give room — and be rigorous about them. That is what readers will recognise, and none of it will ever be noted.

entries.category: Checklists
entries.name: The Serial Premise Audit
entries.description: Run this before you write a first chapter, and again if a serial stalls in its second volume. It tests whether the premise can actually sustain serialisation, which is a different question from whether it is good.
items: Can this premise generate a chapter that ends on a turn, this week and next week and the week after? Name three.
Is there a renewable source of incident that is not the protagonist's willpower?
What is the reader waiting for? Say it in one clause. If it takes two, the promise is unclear.
Is there a destination, even a vague one, that a reader could see the story moving toward or away from?
Could this stop at chapter thirty and still be a work? If not, what would have to resolve by then?
Is the premise's engine escalation, accumulation or recurrence? Each fails differently and you should know which failure you are exposed to.
Would this be better as a one-shot? Answering yes is a result, not a defeat.

entries.category: Checklists
entries.name: The Chapter Audit
entries.description: Run this on every chapter before it goes to layout, and on any chapter that reads flat. It takes about ten minutes and catches most of what goes wrong at this scale.
items: Does the first panel orient and advance at the same time, or does it only orient?
Is there a turn at or near the middle? If not, the chapter's middle is transit.
What is the reader holding for a week after the last panel — a question, a meaning, or nothing?
Count the panels. Are you over budget, and if so which scene is cheapest to imply rather than show?
Is there a panel whose only function is to remind? Attach it to a decision or cut it.
Read every balloon and cut everything before its main verb. Does each line still mean what you intended?
Is there a silent panel? Write the sentence it replaces. If you cannot, merge it.
Does anything in this chapter only work on paper? If nothing does, you have written a script.

entries.category: Checklists
entries.name: The Volume Shape Audit
entries.description: Run this when you have drafted a block of chapters and before any of them are final, and again before the volume is bound. The volume is the unit that survives; the chapter is the unit that sells.
items: Which chapter carries this volume's turn? Name it. If none does, the volume has no shape.
Which chapter is its low point, and which one closes it?
Where are the climaxes? Three in the last forty pages and nothing in the first hundred is the commonest fault in the form.
Read the whole block at one sitting. Where does a recap land four pages after the fact?
Does the volume end somewhere a reader would wait for the next one, without ending on an arbitrary cut?
If the serial stopped at the end of this volume, what would it be? A work, or a fragment?

entries.category: Checklists
entries.name: The Cast Audit
entries.description: Run this at the end of every volume, and immediately before introducing anyone new. Cast size is the number that most reliably governs whether a long serial stays readable.
items: Count the named characters in chapter one. More than three and the surplus is probably filed as scenery.
Draw the principals as solid silhouettes at thumbnail size. Can you tell them apart?
Read the principal names aloud in sequence. Do any two blur?
For each recurring character, what changes in the plot if they are absent from their last three appearances? If nothing, they are being carried.
Does every rival measure a different axis of the protagonist's development? Two on one axis is why a middle feels long.
Is any new character arriving into empty space rather than into an existing relationship?
Does anyone marked for removal have a stated plan for afterwards?

entries.category: Checklists
entries.name: The Ending Insurance Audit
entries.description: Run this at the end of your second volume and revise it at every major turn. It exists because the short ending cannot be improvised under pressure, which is the only time it is ever needed.
items: Have you written the three-chapter ending? Not planned — written.
Have you written the fifteen-chapter ending?
If the short version does not work, which threads is the long version carrying that are elaboration rather than structure?
Is the current arc's middle a chain or a set? A chain cannot lose a link.
How many deliberate stopping points have you built? More than two and the reader learns that no apparent resolution is trustworthy.
Are there two arcs in reserve that could run in any order?
Have you budgeted pages after the climax for decompression? They will be the first thing cut and they are what a long reader is owed.

entries.category: Checklists
entries.name: The Page and Panel Audit
entries.description: Run this at the layout stage, which is the stage at which change is cheap and the stage at which nearly every decision that matters is actually made. Do not run it on finished art.
items: Is the chapter's strongest image on a page the reader cannot preview before turning?
Where does the eye enter each page, and where does it leave? Trace it.
Is any panel doing two jobs badly that two panels would do well, or the reverse?
Where is the reader's pace being controlled, and where has it been left to chance?
Is the white space distributed, or has it collected where the drawing was easiest?
Does any spread earn its scale, or is it large because the moment felt important?
If you redrew this chapter's layout from scratch in an hour, would it be better? If yes, do that rather than fixing panels.

entries.category: Checklists
entries.name: The Dialogue Audit
entries.description: Run this on a full chapter's script before layout. Read everything aloud in a flat monotone — the reader will supply a voice you cannot hear, and any line that needs performance is a line that does not work.
items: Does each line's meaning arrive in its first few words?
Does the sense survive the monotone test? If not, the line needs a visual marker or a rewrite.
For every interior monologue line: cover the drawing. Is the thought surprising, or does it restate the face?
For every caption: is it establishing a fact or delivering a verdict? Verdicts do not belong there.
Have you set each pair's default register toward each other, and broken it deliberately at least once?
Is any exposition balloon saying what its panel already shows?
Does every recurring verbal tic have a planned violation?

entries.category: Checklists
entries.name: The Demographic Audit
entries.description: Run this on any draft, and on any note you write about your own work. It exists because the error it catches is the single most common one in Anglophone writing about this medium and it is easy to commit accidentally.
items: Search your draft and your notes for the words shōnen, shōjo, seinen, josei and kodomomuke. For each, are you naming a readership or a kind of story?
If you have written any of them followed by "genre", rewrite the sentence around the magazine and see whether it still says anything.
Where you meant "battle manga", have you written "shōnen"? They are not the same claim.
Are you attributing a formal property to a demographic rather than to the artists who built it?
If you are describing an adult women's title, have you searched both josei and the earlier redisu term? A gap in one is usually a search artefact.
Does any statement about a demographic survive being tested against three titles from the same magazine that have nothing in common?

entries.category: Checklists
entries.name: The Magazine Fit Audit
entries.description: Run this before submitting anywhere, and before a serial moves venue. Rejection at this stage is usually about register rather than about quality, and the note you receive will not say so.
items: Have you read six consecutive issues of the target magazine — issues, not collected volumes?
Write down, from those issues: how chapters end, how much is explained, how cruel the work is permitted to be.
What is this magazine's default chapter length, and does your work fit it without compression?
Where does your work sit against that register — inside it, at its edge, or outside?
If you are outside, is that a decision or an accident?
On a move between magazines: which of your work's properties are surface and which are commitment? Change the first freely, hold the second for at least a volume.

entries.category: Checklists
entries.name: The Research Triage Audit
entries.description: Run this before drafting anything that makes claims about a real place, period, occupation or people. The discipline is not in the research; it is in refusing to spread it evenly.
items: Write two lists: must be right, and may be wrong. Be honest about the second.
What is the work's authority resting on? Everything on that list goes on the first list.
For each fact you intend to use, who could plausibly disagree with it, and why? Facts with no second opinion are background and belong in the art.
Have you observed the thing, or only read about it? A drawn procedural made from reading looks like it.
What are you deciding by default because you did not know? Those are the assertions to check first.
Have you recorded which claims you could not establish? An unrecorded gap becomes an assertion in the next draft.

entries.category: Checklists
entries.name: The Expert-Reader Audit
entries.description: Run this on any work built around a real occupation, sport or craft, before the first chapter is final. A minority of your readers do this professionally, and they set the standard for everyone because a single detectable error retroactively devalues everything the reader took on faith.
items: Can you state in one sentence what the reader will know at the end that they did not know at the start?
Is there one detail per chapter that only a practitioner would recognise — and is it left unexplained?
Where does the procedure fail, get contested, or meet a case it does not cover? Those are your scenes.
Have you shown the physical residue — what hands do between actions, what happens while waiting, how an error is recovered?
Has a practitioner read it? Have you sorted their notes into "this is wrong" and "this is not how I would emphasise it"?
Is the specialist credited?

entries.category: Checklists
entries.name: The What-It-Looked-Like Audit
entries.description: Run this on any historical or period work at the layout stage. A page must assert what a street, a garment and a face looked like and cannot decline the assertion the way prose can, so every panel is a checkable claim at a density prose never reaches.
items: List every material claim this chapter's art makes: clothing, architecture, tools, signage, transport, hair, food.
Which of those did you decide from evidence, and which from another drawn work? The second is inherited error waiting to compound.
Are you dating by the work's original appearance, or by a translation, licensing or export year?
Does any category string, award name or institutional label you use exist in the year you have placed it?
Where the record is thin, does the card or the page state its own evidentiary level rather than asserting confidently?
Is there a detail you have included because it reads as "period" rather than because it is documented?

entries.category: Checklists
entries.name: The Living Tradition and Cultural Borrowing Audit
entries.description: Run this whenever a work draws on a religion, folklore, or a people who are alive now. This checklist asks questions and does not answer them, because the alternative is a reference work adjudicating disputes that belong to the people in them.
items: Is this tradition living? If yes, is the work treating it as a resource, or as something practised by people who have a view about it?
What is the appropriation history here, and have you stated it rather than assumed it is settled?
Have objections been raised from within the culture? By whom, and on what basis? Record both, take no side.
Are you depicting a people who can read this? What have they said about previous depictions?
Does the work reproduce the standard genre treatment of this material, and can you say what is wrong with that treatment?
Have you consulted someone from within the tradition, and have you credited them?
Would a reader finish this better informed about why the standard treatment fails, or better equipped to repeat it?

entries.category: Checklists
entries.name: The Sensitive Content Audit
entries.description: Run this on any work carrying material a reader would seek out or avoid it for. The rule is that content is named plainly and analysed as craft — neither censored nor relished — and that live disputes are marked as disputed rather than settled on the page.
items: Name the content plainly, in one clause, without euphemism. If you cannot write the clause, you have not decided what the work is doing.
Is the content the reason a reader would come to this work, or avoid it? Both answers change how it must be handled.

Where content involves characters presented as minors: what is the legal position in the jurisdiction of publication, and in the jurisdictions of likely distribution? These differ sharply and the difference is a live dispute — establish the facts and do not adjudicate the dispute.
What is the magazine's standard, and are you working inside it deliberately or discovering it at revision?

Where a creator's record includes a criminal matter, a documented controversy or a disputed claim: state it at the level the record supports, distinguish charge from disposition, and mark disputes as disputed.

Where a subject has spoken about a sensitive matter more than twice, does your account carry every position, or has it been compressed into a claim-and-retraction shape that the record does not support?
Read the last sentence of anything you have written about this on its own. That is where adjudication hides.

entries.category: Checklists
entries.name: The Naming, Romanisation and Source Audit
entries.description: Run this before any roster is fixed and again before anything ships. It decides who is one person and what is one work, and a naive pass manufactures phantom people while an over-eager one merges two unrelated things.
items: Is every title given in its original script and a romanisation, with the English release title where one exists?
Is your romanisation policy written down — Hepburn variant, macrons, name order — rather than decided per entry?
Have you normalised for the five variant generators: macron, `ou`, `oh`, `oo`/`uu`, and name order with or without a comma?
Has anyone appeared under two forms? Ōtsuka Eiji and Eiji Otsuka are one man.
Has anything collapsed that should not have? Two different works can share a romanisation and be unrelated — the original script is the only thing that separates them.
Are you dating by original-language first appearance rather than by translation?
Have you used original-language sources, or only what has been translated? A gap in the English record is not a gap in the record.
Where a creator changed the spelling of their own name, are you using their final spelling throughout and stating the change once?

entries.category: Checklists
entries.name: The Collaboration and Credit Audit
entries.description: Run this at the start of any working arrangement and every six months afterwards. What it catches is not a decision but a drift, and drift is invisible from inside.
items: Is your delegation line written down — what stays with you, what can be handed over?
Re-read it. Has it moved? Each individual handover was defensible; the aggregate may not be.
Are you specifying intent or appearance to the people executing your pages? Appearance produces correct, dead work.
At what stage do you bring work to an editor, and is that a decision or a habit?
For each editorial note: can you state the problem it implies? Take the diagnosis, argue the prescription.
If you work under a shared name, are you keeping a private attribution record from the first page?
Is everyone who contributed credited somewhere, including the specialist consultant and the assistants?

entries.category: The Serial's Own Machinery
entries.name: The Cliffhanger Turn
entries.description: The reversal placed on a chapter's final page, and the difference between one that earns a week and one that merely delays.

examples.work: 進撃の巨人 / Shingeki no Kyojin
examples.text: Reversals are placed on final pages with unusual regularity, and most of them change what the reader believes rather than merely interrupting an action — the week is spent re-reading rather than waiting.

examples.work: DEATH NOTE / Death Note
examples.text: Chapter endings frequently reveal that a plan the reader has been following was a different plan, which converts the interval into interpretation rather than suspense.

examples.work: 東京喰種 / Tokyo Ghoul
examples.text: The device is used at high frequency, and the repetition trains the reader to expect a reversal, which is the mechanism by which a cliffhanger stops working.

examples.work: 銀魂 / Gintama
examples.text: Not a failure of the work, which is deliberately anarchic, but a demonstration of the trope's limit: a serial that undercuts its own reversals for comic effect cannot then use one sincerely, and the card exists to show that the device is spendable.

entries.category: The Serial's Own Machinery
entries.name: The Flashback at the Decisive Moment
entries.description: Backstory inserted at the point of maximum tension, and the two opposite things it can do.

examples.work: るろうに剣心 / Rurouni Kenshin
examples.text: The past arrives at points where the protagonist must decide whether to break a rule he has set himself, so each interruption supplies the price of the decision rather than its background.

examples.work: 鬼滅の刃 / Kimetsu no Yaiba
examples.text: Antagonists receive their history at the moment of defeat, which converts a fight's conclusion into a reassessment and is the clearest modern use of the device as an argument rather than as sentiment.

examples.work: はじめの一歩 / Hajime no Ippo
examples.text: Interruptions arrive reliably at the same point in a bout, and the regularity trains the reader to expect them — a flashback the reader can see coming has lost the interruption that is its whole mechanism.

entries.category: The Serial's Own Machinery
entries.name: The Time Skip
entries.description: A jump forward in story time, used to reset a cast's capability without dramatising the process.

examples.work: ONE PIECE
examples.text: The skip is placed after a defeat rather than after a victory, so the elapsed time reads as consequence and the returning cast's new capability is legible as something the reader watched them decide to acquire.

examples.work: ヴィンランド・サガ / Vinland Saga
examples.text: Elapsed time changes the protagonist's relationship to violence rather than his ability to commit it, which is the version of the device that does character work instead of power-scaling.

examples.work: 幽☆遊☆白書 / Yu Yu Hakusho
examples.text: The skip is used late and compresses material the serial had been building toward, which is the shape a skip takes when it is solving a production problem rather than a narrative one.

entries.category: The Serial's Own Machinery
entries.name: The Return of a Retired Character
entries.description: Bringing back a figure the story had finished with, and what it costs the finish.

examples.work: 無限の住人 / Mugen no Jūnin
examples.text: Returning is built into the premise as a condition rather than granted as an exception, so the serial never has to argue that a departure was reversible — the structural solution to the trope's whole problem.

examples.work: キン肉マン / Kinnikuman
examples.text: Defeated and retired figures return across decades until the roster behaves as a permanent ensemble, which is the point at which a departure stops carrying information.

examples.work: 聖闘士星矢 / Saint Seiya
examples.text: Returns recur often enough that the reader stops treating a fatal outcome as information, which is the same failure arriving by a different route.

entries.category: The Serial's Own Machinery
entries.name: The Arc Villain Who Becomes an Ally
entries.description: Converting an antagonist into a cast member, the form's most reliable way to grow a cast without introducing anyone.

examples.work: HUNTER×HUNTER
examples.text: The conversion is never free: a former antagonist retains the values that made them dangerous, remains genuinely unsafe to the people around them, and the serial declines to launder the earlier behaviour. This is the trope executed with its full cost paid, which is rare enough in the form to be worth studying directly.

examples.work: BLEACH / Bleach
examples.text: Conversions are staged as shifting institutional allegiance rather than as moral change, which sidesteps the redemption accounting entirely and is an honest solution to it.

examples.work: ドロヘドロ / Dorohedoro
examples.text: Allegiances shift readily because the world has no stable moral frame to convert between, which makes the device cheap — nothing is being crossed.

entries.category: The Serial's Own Machinery
entries.name: The Power-Up Withheld and Released
entries.description: Capability the reader knows exists and has not yet seen, held as a scheduled asset.

examples.work: 呪術廻戦 / Jujutsu Kaisen
examples.text: Withheld capability is bound to a stated rule, so the release is legible as the rule finally being satisfied rather than as an author deciding the moment had come.

examples.work: 北斗の拳 / Hokuto no Ken
examples.text: Techniques are named long before they are used, which converts anticipation into a catalogue the reader can track and makes each release feel scheduled rather than arbitrary.

examples.work: 僕のヒーローアカデミア / Boku no Hero Academia
examples.text: The device is central and heavily used, and the release points increasingly coincide with narrative need rather than with the established constraint, which is how a withheld power becomes a convenience.

entries.category: The Serial's Own Machinery
entries.name: The Chapter That Is All One Fight
entries.description: A single combat occupying a whole chapter, and what has to be true for the pages to hold.

examples.work: ベルセルク / Berserk
examples.text: Extended combat carries information about the world's physical rules and about what the protagonist is willing to become, so the pages are doing two jobs and the length is earned.

examples.work: バガボンド / Vagabond
examples.text: Fights are long and mostly still, with duration spent on decision rather than on exchange, which is the version of the device that a drawn medium does better than a moving one.

examples.work: ドラゴンボール / Dragon Ball
examples.text: Extended combat is where the form's escalation problem becomes most visible, because a fight that runs for many chapters must keep raising a quantity, and the quantity is the thing that eventually breaks.
