entries.category: The Serial's Own Machinery
entries.name: The Reset to the Status Quo
entries.description: Returning the situation to its starting state, which is a structural requirement in some formats and a failure in others.

examples.work: こちら葛飾区亀有公園前派出所 / Kochira Katsushika-ku Kameari Kōen-mae Hashutsujo
examples.text: The reset is the format's premise rather than its evasion — an episodic comic serial in which return to equilibrium is what the reader is buying, and the card exists so the trope is not read as automatically a fault.

examples.work: ドラえもん / Doraemon
examples.text: Every instalment returns to the same household in the same condition, which is what makes any chapter a valid first chapter for a readership that is constantly turning over.

examples.work: 美少女戦士セーラームーン / Bishōjo Senshi Sailor Moon
examples.text: Used here as a teaching example of the trope's cost rather than a judgement on the work: where a serial resolves a threat and restores the prior arrangement across successive arcs, the accumulated experience of the cast becomes hard to keep visible, and the work has to do extra labour to show that anything has changed.

entries.category: The Tournament and the Escalating Ladder
entries.name: The Tournament Bracket
entries.description: The competition structure, which is a scheduling device before it is a story.

examples.work: 幽☆遊☆白書 / Yu Yu Hakusho
examples.text: The bracket is used to schedule escalation so that it looks planned, which is its actual function: a reader shown a bracket knows how much story remains and how hard each remaining step will be.

examples.work: ハイキュー!! / Haikyū!!
examples.text: The structure is real competition rather than a frame, and the bracket's published shape lets the serial spend chapters on preparation without the reader losing the thread.

examples.work: 鬼滅の刃 / Kimetsu no Yaiba
examples.text: A ranked hierarchy substitutes for a bracket and supplies the same legibility, which demonstrates that the device is about visible ordering rather than about competition specifically.

entries.category: The Tournament and the Escalating Ladder
entries.name: The Preliminary Round as Cast Audit
entries.description: The early stage that exists to show the reader who everyone is.

examples.work: テニスの王子様 / Tennis no Ōjisama
examples.text: Internal ranking matches introduce a large team by making every member play, so cast establishment and plot occupy the same pages and no one arrives as a name on a list.

examples.work: 食戟のソーマ / Shokugeki no Sōma
examples.text: Qualifying rounds establish a large field efficiently, but the eliminations carry little information about the survivors, which is the point at which an audit becomes a roster.

examples.work: 弱虫ペダル / Yowamushi Pedal
examples.text: The device is used at length and the field is large enough that the audit function strains, which is the point at which an introduction sequence becomes a roster.

entries.category: The Tournament and the Escalating Ladder
entries.name: The Opponent Who Explains His Own Technique
entries.description: Exposition delivered by the person it disadvantages, and the conditions under which it is not absurd.

examples.work: アカギ / Akagi
examples.text: Explanation is addressed to an opponent in order to unsettle them, so the speech is an attack rather than an aside and the reader receives the information as a side effect of the tactic.

examples.work: テニスの王子様 / Tennis no Ōjisama
examples.text: Named techniques are announced as they are performed, which is legible and rhythmically satisfying and supplies no in-world reason for the announcement.

examples.work: ドラゴンボール / Dragon Ball
examples.text: A teaching example of the unmotivated form: where a technique is described mid-combat with no in-world reason for the speech, the reader receives the information and loses the fight's pressure, and the card exists to name the failure rather than to grade the work.

entries.category: The Tournament and the Escalating Ladder
entries.name: The Loss That Is Allowed to Stand
entries.description: A defeat that is not reversed, in a form whose economics push hard against it.

examples.work: SLAM DUNK
examples.text: The competitive outcome is permitted to be final, and the serial's ending rests on it, which is the clearest demonstration in the form that a sports serial does not require its team to win.

examples.work: ちはやふる / Chihayafuru
examples.text: Losses accumulate and shape what the protagonist is able to attempt next, so defeat functions as plot rather than as an obstacle to be erased.

examples.work: キャプテン翼 / Captain Tsubasa
examples.text: Outcomes trend heavily one way, which is a legitimate register for its readership and is also why the trope's absence is conspicuous.

entries.category: The Tournament and the Escalating Ladder
entries.name: The Tier List Made Visible
entries.description: An explicit ranking of characters' power, and the trap it sets for a serial that must continue.

examples.work: BLEACH / Bleach
examples.text: An institutional rank system is stated early and then repeatedly complicated by circumstance, so the ordering is information the reader can use rather than a promise about outcomes.

examples.work: ONE PIECE
examples.text: Published numerical values invite arithmetic the story cannot honour, and the serial spends real effort managing expectations the ranking created.

examples.work: 東京喰種 / Tokyo Ghoul
examples.text: An institutional ranking is established early and becomes a ceiling the narrative has to keep raising, which is the tier list's characteristic long-run cost.

entries.category: The Tournament and the Escalating Ladder
entries.name: The Referee and the Rules That Bind Power
entries.description: An enforced rule set as the source of tension, rather than the capability of the participants.

examples.work: 賭博黙示録カイジ / Tobaku Mokushiroku Kaiji
examples.text: Invented games with strictly enforced rules generate all the tension, and the participants' abilities are almost irrelevant, which is the purest available demonstration that constraint rather than power is what makes a contest readable.

examples.work: アカギ / Akagi
examples.text: A real game's fixed rules bound every possibility, and the serial sustains enormous tension inside a rule set the reader is not expected to fully understand.

examples.work: 遊☆戯☆王 / Yu-Gi-Oh!
examples.text: Rules are stated and then extended during play, and each extension costs the reader some of their confidence that the constraint is real.

entries.category: The Tournament and the Escalating Ladder
entries.name: The Spectator Who Explains the Fight
entries.description: The onlooker as commentary track, and how to use one without conceding that the art failed.

examples.work: はじめの一歩 / Hajime no Ippo
examples.text: Commentary comes from cornermen and rivals who have stakes in the outcome, so an explanation characterises the speaker while it informs the reader and the technique costs nothing.

examples.work: 3月のライオン / Sangatsu no Lion
examples.text: Observers supply professional assessment the reader could not derive from the board, which is the honest use of the device in a game most readers cannot follow.

examples.work: 食戟のソーマ / Shokugeki no Sōma
examples.text: Onlookers frequently narrate what the panel has already shown, which is the failure mode: a spectator explaining a visible event tells the reader their eyes were insufficient.

entries.category: The Tournament and the Escalating Ladder
entries.name: The Ladder That Runs Out
entries.description: The point at which escalation exhausts itself, and the moves available when it does.

examples.work: HUNTER×HUNTER
examples.text: Escalation is redirected from magnitude into rules and information, so later conflicts are harder without being larger — the most durable solution the form has found.

examples.work: ワンパンマン / One-Punch Man
examples.text: The ladder is exhausted in the premise rather than reached at the end, and the serial is built on what remains when escalation is unavailable from the first chapter.

examples.work: 聖闘士星矢 / Saint Seiya
examples.text: A teaching example of the ladder reaching its top: once a hierarchy of tiers has been ascended, the serial must either invent a tier above the top or change the axis, and the visible strain at that moment is what this card is for.

entries.category: Training, Mastery and the Cost of Getting Stronger
entries.name: The Training Sequence and Its Refusal
entries.description: Dramatised improvement, and what is lost when a serial skips it.

examples.work: あしたのジョー / Ashita no Joe
examples.text: Training is where the protagonist's relationship to his own body is established, and the sequences carry the argument the fights only conclude.

examples.work: 銀の匙 / Gin no Saji
examples.text: Improvement is agricultural labour rather than combat preparation, which demonstrates that the sequence is about a person acquiring competence and has nothing intrinsically to do with fighting.

examples.work: ピンポン / Ping Pong
examples.text: Improvement happens largely off the page and is reported rather than dramatised, which suits the work's interest in temperament over method and removes the sequence's evidentiary function.

entries.category: Training, Mastery and the Cost of Getting Stronger
entries.name: The Mentor Who Withholds
entries.description: The teacher who will not simply explain, and the difference between a reason and an affectation.

examples.work: ヒカルの碁 / Hikaru no Go
examples.text: Withholding is justified by the discipline itself — a game whose insight cannot be transmitted verbally — so the mentor's reticence is a fact about go rather than a personality.

examples.work: バガボンド / Vagabond
examples.text: The teacher withholds because instruction would prevent the specific realisation the student needs, and the serial makes the pedagogy explicit rather than mysterious.

examples.work: NARUTO -ナルト- / Naruto
examples.text: Withholding is frequently a scheduling device, deferring information until the plot requires it, and the reader can usually tell the difference.

entries.category: Training, Mastery and the Cost of Getting Stronger
entries.name: The Technique With a Named Cost
entries.description: Power that charges a stated price, which is the form's main defence against escalation.

examples.work: 鋼の錬金術師 / Fullmetal Alchemist
examples.text: The stated exchange principle governs the whole world and is enforced against the protagonists from the first chapter, which is why later escalation stays legible.

examples.work: 呪術廻戦 / Jujutsu Kaisen
examples.text: Costs are contractual and specific, and characters negotiate them explicitly, so power increases without the sense of quantity that breaks a ladder.

examples.work: ジョジョの奇妙な冒険 / JoJo no Kimyō na Bōken
examples.text: Abilities are narrow and rule-bound rather than powerful, and fights are won by exploiting a stated limitation, which converts combat into puzzle-solving.

entries.category: Training, Mastery and the Cost of Getting Stronger
entries.name: The Body That Pays
entries.description: Physical damage that accumulates and is not undone, in a form under constant pressure to undo it.

examples.work: あしたのジョー / Ashita no Joe
examples.text: Damage accumulates irreversibly across the serial and determines its ending, which is the form's standing demonstration that a body can be a plot.

examples.work: ベルセルク / Berserk
examples.text: Injury is permanent and visible, and the protagonist's capability is repeatedly redefined by what he has lost rather than by what he has gained.

examples.work: 北斗の拳 / Hokuto no Ken
examples.text: Damage is dramatic and largely non-cumulative, which is a register choice rather than an error and is why the serial's escalation runs on opponent scale instead.

entries.category: Training, Mastery and the Cost of Getting Stronger
entries.name: The Plateau
entries.description: The period of no improvement, which almost every serial skips and which is where the reader's belief is actually built.

examples.work: 3月のライオン / Sangatsu no Lion
examples.text: Extended stagnation is dramatised as a psychological condition rather than as an obstacle, and the serial is willing to spend volumes in it.

examples.work: BLUE GIANT / Blue Giant
examples.text: Practice occupies real page count with no visible improvement, which is what makes the eventual competence credible.

examples.work: 弱虫ペダル / Yowamushi Pedal
examples.text: Improvement is near-continuous, which is a legitimate register for the readership and also removes the plateau's evidentiary function.

entries.category: Training, Mastery and the Cost of Getting Stronger
entries.name: The Forbidden Technique
entries.description: The prohibited capability, and the difference between a rule and a countdown.

examples.work: 鋼の錬金術師 / Fullmetal Alchemist
examples.text: The prohibition is grounded in a stated moral and physical cost that the narrative enforces on its own protagonists in the first chapter, so the rule is real before it is tested.

examples.work: NARUTO -ナルト- / Naruto
examples.text: Forbidden techniques carry explicit lethal costs and characters use them anyway, which is the trope working: a prohibition that is never violated is decoration.

examples.work: るろうに剣心 / Rurouni Kenshin
examples.text: The prohibition is self-imposed rather than external, which makes every violation a decision about identity instead of a rule being broken, and the serial enforces the cost.

entries.category: Training, Mastery and the Cost of Getting Stronger
entries.name: The Skill Learned From an Enemy
entries.description: Capability acquired from an opponent, which converts a past defeat into an asset.

examples.work: ジョジョの奇妙な冒険 / JoJo no Kimyō na Bōken
examples.text: Understanding an opponent's rule is itself the victory condition, so the acquisition is the fight rather than its aftermath.

examples.work: 賭博黙示録カイジ / Tobaku Mokushiroku Kaiji
examples.text: The protagonist learns his antagonists' methods and the learning is explicitly corrosive, which is the version of the trope that costs something.

examples.work: ドロヘドロ / Dorohedoro
examples.text: Capability circulates between antagonists and protagonists without either side treating the transfer as significant, which is the trope drained of its charge.

entries.category: Training, Mastery and the Cost of Getting Stronger
entries.name: Talent Against Work
entries.description: The genre's oldest argument, and the positions a serial can actually hold on it.

examples.work: ヒカルの碁 / Hikaru no Go
examples.text: The serial declines to resolve the argument, presenting prodigies and grinders and refusing to rank the routes, which is the honest position and the rarer one.

examples.work: ハイキュー!! / Haikyū!!
examples.text: Talent is treated as real and unevenly distributed, and the work argument is made about what a person does with an unequal starting position rather than about whether the inequality exists.

examples.work: キャプテン翼 / Captain Tsubasa
examples.text: The argument resolves toward effort with little friction, which suits the readership and removes the tension the trope exists to hold.

examples.work: 巨人の星 / Kyojin no Hoshi
examples.text: A teaching example rather than a verdict: the spokon template resolves the argument by making privation itself the method, and the position is stated so absolutely that the serial cannot dramatise a counter-case — useful precisely because the trope's failure mode is visible in its founding text.

entries.category: The Confession and the Romance Structure
entries.name: The Confession as a Dated Event
entries.description: The declaration as a discrete, socially recognised act that changes a relationship's status on a date both parties and the reader can name.

examples.work: 君に届け / Kimi ni Todoke
examples.text: The declaration is placed early enough that the serial is about what two people do afterwards, which is the structural argument for treating it as an event rather than as an ending.

examples.work: ホリミヤ / Horimiya
examples.text: The relationship is established well before the serial's midpoint and the remaining chapters are about maintenance rather than pursuit, which is a much harder and less common thing to sustain.

examples.work: 花より男子 / Hana yori Dango
examples.text: Declarations recur and are repeatedly destabilised by external pressure, which keeps the romance in motion and prevents any single one of them from functioning as a dateable change of status.

entries.category: The Confession and the Romance Structure
entries.name: The Deferred Confession
entries.description: Withholding the declaration, and the difference between deferral that means something and deferral that is scheduling.

examples.work: ハチミツとクローバー / Hachimitsu to Clover
examples.text: Deferral is caused by each character's accurate assessment that speaking would cost something they are not willing to lose, so the silence is characterisation rather than delay.

examples.work: 四月は君の嘘 / Shigatsu wa Kimi no Uso
examples.text: The withholding is bound to a condition outside the relationship, which makes the deferral structural and gives the eventual disclosure a shape the reader can anticipate without predicting.

examples.work: 君に届け / Kimi ni Todoke
examples.text: Later deferrals rest on misunderstandings that a single conversation would dissolve, which is the point at which withholding becomes a scheduling device rather than a position.

entries.category: The Confession and the Romance Structure
entries.name: The Misread Signal
entries.description: Misunderstanding as an engine, and the narrow conditions under which it is not merely frustrating.

examples.work: ホリミヤ / Horimiya
examples.text: Misreadings arise from each character's established self-assessment rather than from missing information, so they cannot be solved by a conversation and are not withheld from the reader.

examples.work: ラブ★コン / Lovely Complex
examples.text: The misreading is rooted in a social embarrassment both characters feel and neither will name, which gives the device a cause the reader can respect.

examples.work: 桜蘭高校ホスト部 / Ōran Kōkō Host Club
examples.text: A teaching example rather than a verdict on the work, which is deliberately farcical: where a misunderstanding persists only because nobody asks the obvious question, the reader stops experiencing tension and starts experiencing impatience, and the device has become a stall.

entries.category: The Confession and the Romance Structure
entries.name: The Third Party Who Is Not a Villain
entries.description: The rival suitor written as a person with a legitimate claim, rather than as an obstacle.

examples.work: ハチミツとクローバー / Hachimitsu to Clover
examples.text: Every party to the several unrequited attachments is given a full interior case, and the serial declines to rank them, which is why its losses land as losses rather than as clearings.

examples.work: NANA
examples.text: Competing attachments are treated as genuine and incompatible goods, and the resolution costs somebody something real in every case.

examples.work: 俺物語!! / Ore Monogatari!!
examples.text: The third party's claim is acknowledged and then set aside quickly, which is a kindness to the reader and removes most of the pressure the device exists to supply.

entries.category: The Confession and the Romance Structure
entries.name: The Relationship That Continues Past the Yes
entries.description: Romance after acceptance, which is where the form's chapter unit is most useful and least used.

examples.work: 俺物語!! / Ore Monogatari!!
examples.text: The serial commits almost entirely to the post-acceptance period and finds its incident in small recurring negotiations, which is exactly what a weekly chapter unit is built to carry.

examples.work: 東京タラレバ娘 / Tokyo Tarareba Musume
examples.text: Attachment is written against careers, money and time already spent, so continuation is a series of costs rather than a state of rest.

examples.work: NANA
examples.text: Continuation is repeatedly interrupted by external catastrophe, which is a legitimate register and also means the ordinary maintenance of a relationship is rarely the subject.

entries.category: The Confession and the Romance Structure
entries.name: The Childhood Promise
entries.description: An obligation contracted before either party could understand it, and what makes it work rather than creak.

examples.work: 五等分の花嫁 / Gotōbun no Hanayome
examples.text: The promise is used as a puzzle rather than as a sentiment — the reader is invited to work out who made it, which converts a soft device into a structure with a solution.

examples.work: ラブ★コン / Lovely Complex
examples.text: Shared history supplies familiarity rather than obligation, which is the softer form and carries correspondingly less pressure.

examples.work: 花より男子 / Hana yori Dango
examples.text: Prior connection is revealed late and functions as confirmation of an attachment the story had already built, so it explains rather than obliges.

entries.category: The Confession and the Romance Structure
entries.name: The Confession Refused
entries.description: The declaration that is declined, and why a form built on eventual acceptance needs it.

examples.work: 四月は君の嘘 / Shigatsu wa Kimi no Uso
examples.text: Refusal is given a reason that is neither cruelty nor misunderstanding, which is the hardest version to write and the only one that leaves both parties intact.

examples.work: 大奥 / Ōoku
examples.text: Refusals are structural — imposed by rank, duty and an inverted social order — so the personal and the political are the same refusal, and neither party is at fault.

examples.work: 桜蘭高校ホスト部 / Ōran Kōkō Host Club
examples.text: Refusals are largely deflections within a comic register, which keeps the ensemble stable and prevents any of them from costing anything.

entries.category: The Confession and the Romance Structure
entries.name: The Public and the Private Register
entries.description: What a relationship is allowed to be in front of others, and the tension between the two versions.

examples.work: ベルサイユのばら / Berusaiyu no Bara
examples.text: Every attachment is conducted under observation by a court that has an interest in it, so the private register is not merely hidden but actively dangerous, and concealment is plot rather than texture.

examples.work: 東京タラレバ娘 / Tokyo Tarareba Musume
examples.text: The gap between what the characters say to each other and what they say about each other to friends is the serial's principal source of characterisation.

examples.work: 大奥 / Ōoku
examples.text: An inverted institutional order makes the public register itself the subject, and what may be shown is set by rank rather than by feeling.

entries.category: School, Club and the Institutional Frame
entries.name: The Club as a Plot Engine
entries.description: The extracurricular society as a renewable source of incident, and why it beats a friendship group.

examples.work: SLAM DUNK
examples.text: The club supplies a schedule, a hierarchy, an external opponent and a reason for unlike people to be in a room, which is four structural problems solved by one institution.

examples.work: 銀の匙 / Gin no Saji
examples.text: Club and curriculum together generate obligations the protagonist did not choose, so incident arrives without anyone needing to want anything.

examples.work: けいおん! / K-On!
examples.text: The club is a container rather than an engine, deliberately — the work is interested in the room rather than in what the room produces, which is a legitimate choice that gives up the device's main benefit.

entries.category: School, Club and the Institutional Frame
entries.name: The School Year as a Clock
entries.description: The academic calendar as a countdown the author did not have to invent.

examples.work: あずまんが大王 / Azumanga Daiō
examples.text: Three years pass in order and the calendar supplies all the change a work with no plot requires, which is the clearest demonstration that the device is doing structural work.

examples.work: 暗殺教室 / Ansatsu Kyōshitsu
examples.text: A deadline is fixed to the end of the school year in the first chapter, which converts the calendar from background into the serial's governing constraint.

examples.work: アオハライド / Ao Haru Ride
examples.text: The calendar advances and is felt mainly at its endpoints, so the clock marks time rather than applying pressure across it.

entries.category: School, Club and the Institutional Frame
entries.name: The Transfer Student
entries.description: The outsider inserted into a closed institution, which is the cheapest legitimate way to restart a static setting.

examples.work: 暗殺教室 / Ansatsu Kyōshitsu
examples.text: Arrivals are used to re-pressure an established group rather than to introduce a viewpoint, so each one changes the institution instead of merely observing it.

examples.work: 聲の形 / Koe no Katachi
examples.text: An arrival exposes what the existing group is willing to do, and the serial is about that rather than about the newcomer, which is the device used as a diagnostic.

examples.work: らんま1/2 / Ranma ½
examples.text: Arrivals are frequent and largely additive, expanding the cast without altering the arrangement they enter, which is the device as a supply line.

entries.category: School, Club and the Institutional Frame
entries.name: The Teacher Who Is Not the Antagonist
entries.description: The adult with authority written as an ally, and the structural problem that creates.

examples.work: GTO グレート・ティーチャー・オニヅカ / GTO: Great Teacher Onizuka
examples.text: The teacher is the protagonist and his authority is constantly illegitimate in the institution's eyes, which supplies the opposition the ally role would otherwise remove.

examples.work: ブルーピリオド / Blue Period
examples.text: Instructors are competent, supportive and unable to solve the protagonist's problem for him, which is the version that keeps the adult useful without removing the difficulty.

examples.work: さよなら絶望先生 / Sayonara Zetsubō Sensei
examples.text: The teacher is the protagonist and his authority is a running joke rather than a relationship, which suits the register and means the institutional question is never really put.

entries.category: School, Club and the Institutional Frame
entries.name: The Graduation Problem
entries.description: The ending a school setting schedules whether the serial wants one or not.

examples.work: あずまんが大王 / Azumanga Daiō
examples.text: The calendar's endpoint is accepted as the work's endpoint, and the serial's whole shape is legible in retrospect as having been built toward it.

examples.work: けいおん! / K-On!
examples.text: The device is confronted directly and the work's emotional weight is concentrated almost entirely in the approach to it, which is what the setting was always going to make available.

examples.work: 聲の形 / Koe no Katachi
examples.text: The institutional boundary is crossed and the story continues past it, which is a deliberate refusal of the device and costs the work the ready-made ending it declines.

entries.category: School, Club and the Institutional Frame
entries.name: The Institution That Will Not Help
entries.description: The school as an indifferent or hostile system, in a setting usually written as benign.

examples.work: 漂流教室 / Hyōryū Kyōshitsu
examples.text: The institution is removed from adult authority entirely and the children reconstruct it, which is the most direct available test of whether the structure was ever protective.

examples.work: 惡の華 / Aku no Hana
examples.text: The institution functions perfectly and is precisely what the protagonists are suffocating inside, which is the harder and more uncomfortable version of the device.

examples.work: GTO グレート・ティーチャー・オニヅカ / GTO: Great Teacher Onizuka
examples.text: Institutional failure is real and is repeatedly solved by one exceptional individual, which lets the system off in the same motion that indicts it.

entries.category: School, Club and the Institutional Frame
entries.name: The Rooftop, the Classroom and the Corridor
entries.description: A small fixed set of locations, and the meaning they accumulate through repetition.

examples.work: 惡の華 / Aku no Hana
examples.text: The same handful of spaces recur until each carries a specific charge, and the serial can then invoke a state simply by choosing a location.

examples.work: 漂流教室 / Hyōryū Kyōshitsu
examples.text: Familiar school geography is made strange without being redrawn, which only works because the reader has learned the spaces first.

examples.work: ブルーピリオド / Blue Period
examples.text: Locations are used functionally and change often, which suits a story about moving between institutions and forgoes the accumulation the device offers.

entries.category: School, Club and the Institutional Frame
entries.name: The Examination as Structure
entries.description: The test as a plot device with a date, a threshold and a public result.

examples.work: ドラゴン桜 / Dragon Zakura
examples.text: The examination supplies a fixed date, an objective threshold and a result that cannot be argued with, and the serial is built entirely on those three properties.

examples.work: ブルーロック / Blue Lock
examples.text: A selection process with published elimination rules performs the same function outside an academic setting, which demonstrates that the device is about the threshold rather than about school.

examples.work: 五等分の花嫁 / Gotōbun no Hanayome
examples.text: Academic pressure is the premise's occasion rather than its structure, and the examinations mark time without organising it.

entries.category: Transformation, Possession and the Second Body
entries.name: The Transformation Sequence as Ritual
entries.description: The repeated change into a second self, where the repetition is the grammar rather than the filler.

examples.work: 美少女戦士セーラームーン / Bishōjo Senshi Sailor Moon
examples.text: The sequence is fixed and recurs, and its consistency is what allows a later variation to carry meaning — the ritual has to be established before it can be altered.

examples.work: カードキャプターさくら / Cardcaptor Sakura
examples.text: The change is materially specific and different each time while its structure stays constant, which keeps the ritual legible and the individual instance fresh.

examples.work: キューティーハニー / Cutie Honey
examples.text: Changes are frequent and functional, treated as capability rather than as ceremony, which is an earlier and looser use of the device.

entries.category: Transformation, Possession and the Second Body
entries.name: The Body That Is Not Yours
entries.description: Occupation of a human body by something else, and the negotiation that follows.

examples.work: 寄生獣 / Kiseijū
examples.text: The occupant is neither villain nor ally but a genuinely different kind of mind with its own coherent interests, and the serial's whole argument is conducted through a working relationship between two intelligences sharing a body who never fully agree. The device is used to ask what a person is, rather than to supply a power or a horror, and it sustains that question for its entire run without resolving it cheaply. This is the trope at the fullest extent of what it can do.

examples.work: 亜人 / Ajin
examples.text: The second body is externalised and instrumental, which converts the premise into a tactical problem and demonstrates how far the device can be pushed toward mechanism.

examples.work: らんま1/2 / Ranma ½
examples.text: The changed body is treated as a comic inconvenience with no interior consequence, which is the register the work wants and is the device at its lightest load.

entries.category: Transformation, Possession and the Second Body
entries.name: The Beast Within, Bargained With
entries.description: Power obtained by admitting something into yourself, on terms.

examples.work: デビルマン / Devilman
examples.text: The bargain is made explicitly and its terms are honoured by the narrative to a conclusion the protagonist cannot survive, which is the device with its cost fully paid.

examples.work: チェンソーマン / Chainsaw Man
examples.text: Contracts are literal, itemised and transactional, so every increase in capability is a visible expenditure and the reader can track the balance.

examples.work: 犬夜叉 / Inuyasha
examples.text: The internal threat is real but is contained by an external device, which converts a bargain into a safety mechanism and removes most of its pressure.

entries.category: Transformation, Possession and the Second Body
entries.name: Possession and the Uninvited Passenger
entries.description: The occupant who was not admitted, and the difference between possession and infection.

examples.work: 寄生獣 / Kiseijū
examples.text: Arrival is accidental and unwanted on both sides, which removes the moral frame entirely and leaves two parties negotiating a situation neither chose.

examples.work: デビルマン / Devilman
examples.text: The distinction between a possession that is resisted and one that is absorbed is made the subject, and the work is explicit that the second is available to anyone.

examples.work: うしおととら / Ushio to Tora
examples.text: The uninvited party is external and adversarial rather than internal, which is a partnership story wearing the device's vocabulary.

entries.category: Transformation, Possession and the Second Body
entries.name: The Cost Written on the Body
entries.description: Change that is visible, permanent and cannot be argued away.

examples.work: うずまき / Uzumaki
examples.text: Bodily change is the work's entire vocabulary, and because it is progressive and irreversible the reader can measure elapsed damage on any page.

examples.work: 富江 / Tomie
examples.text: Damage to the body is systematically undone, and the undoing is itself the horror, which inverts the trope while depending on the reader's expectation of it.

examples.work: 亜人 / Ajin
examples.text: Injury is severe and reversible by premise, so the body records nothing and the cost has to be carried elsewhere.

entries.category: Transformation, Possession and the Second Body
entries.name: Gender and the Changed Body
entries.description: A form the medium has used for decades, across registers from farce to interiority. The pack states plainly that these works are read very differently now than when they were serialised, and records that the readings are contested rather than settling them.

examples.work: 放浪息子 / Hōrō Musuko
examples.text: The subject is treated as interior and ordinary rather than as premise or transformation, and the serial is built from small social negotiations across years — the version of this material that is about a person rather than about a device.

examples.work: ベルサイユのばら / Berusaiyu no Bara
examples.text: Presentation is imposed by circumstance and then inhabited, and the work is explicit that the social order rather than the body is what constrains its protagonist.

examples.work: ストップ!! ひばりくん! / Stop!! Hibari-kun!
examples.text: An early comic treatment whose register places the situation itself as the joke; it is historically significant to the form and its contemporary reception is disputed, which the card records without adjudicating.

entries.category: Transformation, Possession and the Second Body
entries.name: The Doppelgänger and the Copy
entries.description: The duplicate self, and the question of which one the story is about.

examples.work: 富江 / Tomie
examples.text: Copies are unlimited and identical, which removes the usual question of authenticity and replaces it with a question about what everyone around them wants.

examples.work: カードキャプターさくら / Cardcaptor Sakura
examples.text: Doubling is used to externalise a character's own unacknowledged position, so the copy is an argument rather than a threat.

examples.work: うしおととら / Ushio to Tora
examples.text: Duplication appears as an episodic threat and is resolved within its episode, which is the device used as an incident rather than as a question.

entries.category: Transformation, Possession and the Second Body
entries.name: The Return to Human Form
entries.description: Changing back, and whether the story lets the return be complete.

examples.work: チェンソーマン / Chainsaw Man
examples.text: Return is routine and the accumulated experience is not, so the body resets and the person does not, which is the honest arrangement.

examples.work: 犬夜叉 / Inuyasha
examples.text: Reversion is repeatedly available and the serial is explicit that each episode leaves a residue, which keeps a reversible device from becoming weightless.

examples.work: キューティーハニー / Cutie Honey
examples.text: A teaching example of the device's default failure rather than a judgement on the work: where reversion is complete, instant and free, the transformation cannot carry consequence, and every later work in the mode is in some sense answering this.

entries.category: The Ensemble and Its Rotations
entries.name: The Rotating Viewpoint
entries.description: Moving the camera between cast members, and what has to be true for the reader to accept losing the protagonist.

examples.work: 20世紀少年 / 20-seiki Shōnen
examples.text: Viewpoint moves across a large cast and across decades, and each shift is justified by the new holder knowing something the previous one did not, so rotation is an information structure rather than a courtesy.

examples.work: MONSTER
examples.text: Long sequences follow figures the protagonist has never met, and the serial trusts the reader to hold two investigations at once because both are converging on the same question.

examples.work: 昭和元禄落語心中 / Shōwa Genroku Rakugo Shinjū
examples.text: The serial hands its centre to a different generation partway through and treats the handover as its subject, which is the version where rotation is the argument rather than a technique.

entries.category: The Ensemble and Its Rotations
entries.name: The Ensemble Introduced One at a Time
entries.description: Sequential recruitment, and why it beats assembling a cast in chapter one.

examples.work: 東京卍リベンジャーズ / Tokyo Revengers
examples.text: Members arrive across a long run and each arrival re-pressures the existing group, so the cast grows without the reader ever being handed a roster.

examples.work: 家庭教師ヒットマンREBORN! / Katekyō Hitman Reborn!
examples.text: Arrivals are frequent and largely additive, and the serial's shift in register partway through means several early members are effectively re-introduced.

examples.work: ワンパンマン / One-Punch Man
examples.text: A very large supporting cast is introduced in blocks rather than singly, which suits a satire of ranked hierarchies and gives up the device's main benefit.

entries.category: The Ensemble and Its Rotations
entries.name: The Member Who Leaves
entries.description: A departure that is not a death, and the specific weight it carries in a form built on accumulation.

examples.work: 昭和元禄落語心中 / Shōwa Genroku Rakugo Shinjū
examples.text: Departures are professional and generational rather than dramatic, and the serial is willing to let a relationship simply end without either party being at fault.

examples.work: 進撃の巨人 / Shingeki no Kyojin
examples.text: Members leave by changing allegiance rather than by exiting, which is the harder version — the cast shrinks while everyone remains on the page.

examples.work: 銀魂 / Gintama
examples.text: The core trio is structurally permanent and departures are almost always reversed, which is what the format requires and what removes the device's weight.

entries.category: The Ensemble and Its Rotations
entries.name: The Ensemble That Outgrows Its Protagonist
entries.description: The supporting cast becoming more interesting than the centre, which is a success and a problem at once.

examples.work: 僕のヒーローアカデミア / Boku no Hero Academia
examples.text: The surrounding class accumulates enough individual want that the serial repeatedly leaves its protagonist, and the tension between his arc and theirs is visible in the page allocation.

examples.work: 家庭教師ヒットマンREBORN! / Katekyō Hitman Reborn!
examples.text: The protagonist's development is repeatedly outpaced by the cast around him, and the serial resolves this by escalating him rather than by rebalancing the pages.

examples.work: 東京卍リベンジャーズ / Tokyo Revengers
examples.text: Secondary figures are given histories more compelling than the centre's, which is a real strength and leaves the protagonist doing structural work rather than dramatic work.

entries.category: The Ensemble and Its Rotations
entries.name: The Reunion Chapter
entries.description: Bringing a dispersed cast back together, and the reason it lands harder in this form than in most.

examples.work: 20世紀少年 / 20-seiki Shōnen
examples.text: Reunion is the premise rather than an episode, and the serial gets enormous value from a reader who has watched a group disperse across real published years.

examples.work: ヴィンランド・サガ / Vinland Saga
examples.text: Returns happen after the returning party has become a different person, so the reunion is a comparison rather than a restoration.

examples.work: ちはやふる / Chihayafuru
examples.text: The device recurs at competitive intervals, which keeps the cast in contact and means no reunion has to carry accumulated absence.

entries.category: The Ensemble and Its Rotations
entries.name: The Cast Too Large to Serve
entries.description: The point at which an ensemble stops being an ensemble, named as a failure mode with a countable symptom.

examples.work: キン肉マン / Kinnikuman
examples.text: The roster accumulates across decades until most members appear without acting, which is the symptom: presence in panels, absence from the causal chain.

examples.work: 遊☆戯☆王 / Yu-Gi-Oh!
examples.text: Supporting members are retained after their function ends and are given scenes rather than decisions.

examples.work: こちら葛飾区亀有公園前派出所 / Kochira Katsushika-ku Kameari Kōen-mae Hashutsujo
examples.text: A teaching example rather than a verdict on a work that ran for four decades by design: an episodic serial can carry an unbounded cast precisely because no member needs to accumulate, and reading that as ensemble failure mistakes a format for a fault. The card is here to mark where the diagnosis does not apply.

entries.category: The Ensemble and Its Rotations
entries.name: The Group With a Job
entries.description: An ensemble bound by employment rather than by affection, which is the most durable binding available.

examples.work: 重版出来! / Jūhan Shuttai!
examples.text: The cast is a manga editorial department, and the work supplies both the reason they are in a room and the reason their disagreements matter, which is two structural problems solved by one setting.

examples.work: 働きマン / Hataraki Man
examples.text: Colleagues are bound by a magazine's production cycle and have incompatible investments in it, so conflict arises from the job rather than from personality.

examples.work: MONSTER
examples.text: Professional relationships are real and mostly instrumental, and the serial's binding is a shared pursuit rather than an institution.

entries.category: The Ensemble and Its Rotations
entries.name: The Ensemble Without a Leader
entries.description: A group with no centre, and what has to replace the protagonist's want.

examples.work: ヲタクに恋は難しい / Wotaku ni Koi wa Muzukashii
examples.text: Two couples of roughly equal weight share the serial with no hierarchy between them, and the structure holds because each pair's problem is legible without reference to the other.

examples.work: さよなら絶望先生 / Sayonara Zetsubō Sensei
examples.text: A nominal centre exists and functions as an occasion rather than as a protagonist, which suits the register and means the ensemble is a list rather than a system.

examples.work: ドラえもん / Doraemon
examples.text: The cast is fixed and hierarchy-free by design, and coherence comes from an unchanging situation rather than from anyone's want.

entries.category: Food, Work and the Procedural Everyday
entries.name: The Meal as a Scene's Structure
entries.description: Eating as a container for a scene, in a medium that cannot transmit taste.

examples.work: 深夜食堂 / Shinya Shokudō
examples.text: The meal is an occasion for someone else's story and the food is almost never the subject, which is the most reliable solution to the sense the page cannot reach.

examples.work: きのう何食べた? / Kinō Nani Tabeta?
examples.text: Preparation and eating structure a domestic relationship across years, and the recurring shape of the meal is what makes small changes in the relationship visible.

examples.work: 甘々と稲妻 / Amaama to Inazuma
examples.text: The meal is the site of a bereaved household learning to function, so every cooking sequence is doing emotional work under cover of procedure.

entries.category: Food, Work and the Procedural Everyday
entries.name: The Dish as an Argument
entries.description: Food as the settlement of a dispute, which is the mode's most productive structure.

examples.work: 美味しんぼ / Oishinbo
examples.text: Almost every instalment is organised as a disagreement between people who both know what they are talking about, and the dish is the argument's conclusion rather than its subject. This solves the mode's central problem completely — taste cannot be transmitted, but a position can be, and a reader who cannot taste the food can still tell who was right. The structure is reusable indefinitely, which is why the serial sustained it for decades, and it is the single most transferable thing in the gourmet line.

examples.work: 舞妓さんちのまかないさん / Maiko-san Chi no Makanai-san
examples.text: The dish answers a practical question about a household's needs rather than settling a dispute, which is the quieter form and demonstrates the structure works without antagonism.

examples.work: 深夜食堂 / Shinya Shokudō
examples.text: Requests are granted rather than contested, so the food resolves a person's situation instead of an argument about food.

entries.category: Food, Work and the Procedural Everyday
entries.name: Work as the Source of Incident
entries.description: The job as a renewable supply of plot, in a form that needs one badly.

examples.work: 重版出来! / Jūhan Shuttai!
examples.text: Each instalment's problem arises from the production cycle itself — a deadline, a print run, a bookshop's shelf — so incident is generated by the setting rather than imported into it.

examples.work: ブラックジャックによろしく / Black Jack ni Yoroshiku
examples.text: Cases arrive because the institution produces them, and the serial's argument is about the institution rather than about the cases.

examples.work: 働きマン / Hataraki Man
examples.text: Incident arises from the job and is frequently resolved by the protagonist's capacity for overwork, which narrows the range of problems the setting can pose.

entries.category: Food, Work and the Procedural Everyday
entries.name: The Client of the Week
entries.description: The episodic petitioner, and how a self-contained instalment can still accumulate.

examples.work: ブラック・ジャック / Black Jack
examples.text: Each petitioner is self-contained and every instalment adds a datum about the protagonist's principles, so an episodic structure accumulates a character without any continuing plot.

examples.work: ブラックジャックによろしく / Black Jack ni Yoroshiku
examples.text: Cases are episodic and cumulative in a different direction — each one adds to an indictment rather than to a portrait.

examples.work: 美味しんぼ / Oishinbo
examples.text: Petitioners are largely occasions for the dispute structure and rarely persist, which is efficient and means the accumulation happens in the argument rather than in the cast.

entries.category: Food, Work and the Procedural Everyday
entries.name: Competence as Characterisation
entries.description: Skill as the primary means of showing who someone is, which is a drawn medium's natural advantage.

examples.work: 宇宙兄弟 / Uchū Kyōdai
examples.text: Characters are distinguished by how they approach a technical problem rather than by temperament, and the serial's large cast stays legible because each has a recognisable method.

examples.work: もやしもん / Moyashimon
examples.text: Expertise is distributed unevenly across the cast and each person's blind spot is as characterising as their skill.

examples.work: BLUE GIANT / Blue Giant
examples.text: Competence is concentrated in one figure and measured largely by others' reactions, which is effective and does less work across the ensemble.

entries.category: Food, Work and the Procedural Everyday
entries.name: The Everyday Rendered at Density
entries.description: Ordinary life drawn with the attention usually reserved for invented worlds.

examples.work: 舞妓さんちのまかないさん / Maiko-san Chi no Makanai-san
examples.text: A closed working household is rendered with procedural exactness, and the density is what makes an unfamiliar institution legible without exposition.

examples.work: 甘々と稲妻 / Amaama to Inazuma
examples.text: Domestic space is specific enough to carry the household's circumstances, so the reader learns the family's situation from the kitchen rather than from a scene about it.

examples.work: 孤独のグルメ / Kodoku no Gurume
examples.text: Ordinary restaurants are rendered with a specificity that makes each one a place rather than a setting, which is the whole of the work's method.

entries.category: Food, Work and the Procedural Everyday
entries.name: The Job That Will Not Reward You
entries.description: Vocation without proportionate return, and the honest version of a mode that usually promises payoff.

examples.work: 岳 みんなの山 / Gaku: Minna no Yama
examples.text: The work is mountain rescue and it frequently fails, and the serial declines to convert the failures into lessons, which is as unsentimental as the mode gets.

examples.work: 宇宙兄弟 / Uchū Kyōdai
examples.text: Selection processes are long, arbitrary in places, and lost by people who deserved to win, and the serial treats that as a fact about institutions rather than as an injustice to be corrected.

examples.work: もやしもん / Moyashimon
examples.text: Academic labour is rendered honestly and the register is comic, so the absence of reward reads as texture rather than as cost.

entries.category: Food, Work and the Procedural Everyday
entries.name: Eating Alone
entries.description: The solitary meal, which the medium handles better than any other form and for a specific reason.

examples.work: 孤独のグルメ / Kodoku no Gurume
examples.text: Interior monologue over a solitary meal is sufficient for a whole instalment, because the reader supplies the pace and a drawn interior voice can be as expansive as the eating is slow.

examples.work: きのう何食べた? / Kinō Nani Tabeta?
examples.text: Solitary preparation and shared eating are contrasted deliberately, so eating alone means something specific rather than functioning as a mood.

examples.work: ワカコ酒 / Wakako Zake
examples.text: The solitary meal is the premise and the register is contentment rather than solitude, which is pleasant and leaves the device carrying less than it can.

entries.category: Death, Memory and the Long Farewell
entries.name: The Death That Is Not Reversed
entries.description: A permanent departure in a form under constant commercial pressure to undo one.

examples.work: PLUTO / Pluto
examples.text: Deaths are established as irreversible in the opening chapters and the serial's entire investigation depends on that, so reversibility is foreclosed structurally rather than promised morally.

examples.work: 火の鳥 / Hi no Tori
examples.text: The cycle is explicitly about the desire to undo death and consistently refuses to grant it on any terms the seeker would accept, which is the device argued rather than merely applied.

examples.work: ブラック・ジャック / Black Jack
examples.text: Outcomes are episodic and the protagonist loses often, but the episodic frame means no single loss accumulates, so permanence is asserted per instalment rather than across the work.

entries.category: Death, Memory and the Long Farewell
entries.name: The Long Farewell
entries.description: A departure the reader can see coming for volumes, and why the anticipation is the technique.

examples.work: ソラニン / Solanin
examples.text: The loss is placed early and the remainder of the work is its aftermath, which inverts the usual arrangement and makes the farewell a condition rather than an event.

examples.work: 夕凪の街 桜の国 / Yūnagi no Machi, Sakura no Kuni
examples.text: Consequences arrive across decades and generations, so the farewell is extended past any single character's death into what is inherited.

examples.work: 蟲師 / Mushishi
examples.text: Episodic losses are frequently known in advance by everyone involved, and the instalment's work is what people do with the interval rather than whether the outcome changes.

entries.category: Death, Memory and the Long Farewell
entries.name: Memory as an Unreliable Record
entries.description: Recollection treated as evidence that can be wrong, in a medium that shows the reader the memory directly.

examples.work: PLUTO / Pluto
examples.text: Recollections are shown as panels and then contradicted, which exploits the medium's specific hazard: a drawn memory carries the same authority as a drawn present.

examples.work: おやすみプンプン / Oyasumi Punpun
examples.text: The rendering of the protagonist itself encodes an unreliable self-account, so the unreliability is in the drawing rather than in the narration.

examples.work: 火の鳥 / Hi no Tori
examples.text: Recollection across the cycle is largely reliable and its unreliability is cosmic rather than personal, which is a different device wearing the same name.

entries.category: Death, Memory and the Long Farewell
entries.name: The Survivor's Account
entries.description: Testimony as narrative structure, analysed strictly as craft.

examples.work: 夕凪の街 桜の国 / Yūnagi no Machi, Sakura no Kuni
examples.text: The account is structured as two linked stories a generation apart, and the second one's protagonist does not know what the reader knows. That gap does the work an explicit account could not: the reader supplies the connection, and the material's weight arrives through inference rather than through statement. The craft lesson is transferable to any testimony — the structure withholds rather than insists, and it is more effective for it.

examples.work: はだしのゲン / Hadashi no Gen
examples.text: The account is delivered inside a children's-magazine serial structure with weekly chapter turns, and the tension between that commercial form and its documentary content is the thing no other example in the library can show.

examples.work: 岳 みんなの山 / Gaku: Minna no Yama
examples.text: Survival is repeatedly presented as arbitrary rather than earned, and the serial declines to make the survivor's account a lesson.

entries.category: Death, Memory and the Long Farewell
entries.name: Grief Without a Body
entries.description: Loss with no death in it — the departure, the estrangement, the person who is still alive.

examples.work: 弟の夫 / Otōto no Otto
examples.text: The absent party is dead before the work begins and the grief being negotiated is for a relationship that was already lost while he lived, which separates the two losses cleanly.

examples.work: ヨコハマ買い出し紀行 / Yokohama Kaidashi Kikō
examples.text: The subject is a world in gentle irreversible decline, and nothing dies on the page — the loss is entirely of a future, which is the purest available form of the device.

examples.work: ソラニン / Solanin
examples.text: Grief for an abandoned possibility runs alongside a literal bereavement, and the literal one dominates, so the device is present rather than isolated.

entries.category: Death, Memory and the Long Farewell
entries.name: The World That Outlives Everyone
entries.description: Deep time as a frame, and what it does to the stakes of an individual chapter.

examples.work: ヨコハマ買い出し紀行 / Yokohama Kaidashi Kikō
examples.text: Human timescales are placed inside a much longer one and the serial's calm is the direct product of that framing rather than of its subject matter.

examples.work: AKIRA
examples.text: The city is destroyed and rebuilt and the narrative treats both as episodes in something larger, which is what keeps its scale from collapsing into spectacle.

examples.work: ARIA / Aria
examples.text: A terraformed world remembers an original it cannot return to, and the deep-time frame supplies atmosphere rather than pressure.

entries.category: Death, Memory and the Long Farewell
entries.name: The Death Written Long in Advance
entries.description: An ending the author fixed early, and the reader's slow arrival at it.

examples.work: 無限の住人 / Mugen no Jūnin
examples.text: The terms on which the protagonist could die are stated in the first volume and the serial spends its entire length approaching them, so the ending is a contract rather than a choice.

examples.work: うずまき / Uzumaki
examples.text: The pattern's conclusion is legible from early on and the work's tension comes entirely from watching an inevitability arrive on schedule.

examples.work: 蟲師 / Mushishi
examples.text: Outcomes are fixed within each instalment rather than across the work, so the device operates at episode scale and cannot accumulate.

entries.category: Death, Memory and the Long Farewell
entries.name: The Memorial Chapter
entries.description: The instalment that exists to mark a loss rather than to advance anything.

examples.work: 弟の夫 / Otōto no Otto
examples.text: Marking is distributed across the work as small domestic acts rather than concentrated into one chapter, which is the version that avoids sentimentality by refusing the set piece.

examples.work: はだしのゲン / Hadashi no Gen
examples.text: Marking is repeated and cumulative because the losses are, and the serial's refusal to make any one of them the memorial is itself the position.

examples.work: ARIA / Aria
examples.text: Chapters of pure marking occur and are unattached to loss, which makes them atmosphere rather than memorial and shows the device needs a referent.

entries.category: The Medium Reading Itself
entries.name: The Manga About Making Manga
entries.description: The industry as subject, and what it can and cannot tell a reader about itself.

examples.work: バクマン。 / Bakuman.
examples.text: The serialisation system is dramatised in detail — the survey, the editorial meeting, the cancellation risk — and the work is a useful illustration of the machinery while being fiction about it rather than evidence of it.

examples.work: まんが道 / Manga Michi
examples.text: An account of entering the industry written by people who did, and the earliest sustained treatment of the subject in the medium itself.

examples.work: アオイホノオ / Aoi Honō
examples.text: The subject is the gap between wanting to make manga and being able to, treated as comedy, which is the register the earnest version cannot reach.

entries.category: The Medium Reading Itself
entries.name: The Autobiographical Turn
entries.description: The author as subject, and the specific credibility a drawn self carries.

examples.work: かくかくしかじか / Kakukaku Shikajika
examples.text: The drawn self is rendered less flatteringly than anyone else in the work, and that asymmetry is what buys the account its credibility.

examples.work: まんが道 / Manga Michi
examples.text: The autobiography is lightly fictionalised and says so, which is a solution to the form's central problem — total accuracy is unavailable and pretending otherwise is worse than admitting it.

examples.work: アオイホノオ / Aoi Honō
examples.text: The self-account is comic and heavily shaped, so the reader receives a persona rather than a person, which is entertaining and does less of what the form can do.

entries.category: The Medium Reading Itself
entries.name: The Fourth Wall Addressed
entries.description: Speaking to the reader, and why it is cheaper in this medium than in most.

examples.work: 吼えろペン / Hoero Pen
examples.text: Address is bound to the work's subject — the making of the page the reader is holding — so breaking the frame is continuous with the argument rather than an interruption of it.

examples.work: ギャグマンガ日和 / Gyagu Manga Biyori
examples.text: The frame is broken constantly and at speed, and the short instalment length means no strip has to survive the break.

examples.work: ボボボーボ・ボーボボ / Bobobo-bo Bo-bobo
examples.text: Address is one device among many in a work committed to total discontinuity, so it carries no particular charge — everything else is equally unmoored.

entries.category: The Medium Reading Itself
entries.name: Parody of the Form's Own Conventions
entries.description: The genre satirising its own machinery, and the knowledge it assumes.

examples.work: ボボボーボ・ボーボボ / Bobobo-bo Bo-bobo
examples.text: The battle serial's escalation, technique-naming and tournament structure are all reproduced exactly and then evacuated of stakes, which requires the reader to know the originals intimately.

examples.work: ギャグマンガ日和 / Gyagu Manga Biyori
examples.text: Historical, literary and genre conventions are parodied at strip length, and the compression is what keeps each target from being laboured.

examples.work: 行け!稲中卓球部 / Ike! Ina-chū Takkyū-bu
examples.text: The sports serial's conventions are inverted rather than parodied — the club is bad and unserious — which is funny and leaves the machinery itself untouched.

entries.category: The Medium Reading Itself
entries.name: The Author on the Page
entries.description: The creator appearing inside the work, distinct from autobiography.

examples.work: かくかくしかじか / Kakukaku Shikajika
examples.text: The author is present as both narrator and subject and the two are visibly different people separated by years, which the drawn medium can show simultaneously in a way prose cannot.

examples.work: 吼えろペン / Hoero Pen
examples.text: An authorial figure is fictionalised into a character with his own arc, which lets the work say things about the profession that a first-person account could not say about itself.

examples.work: パタリロ! / Patalliro!
examples.text: Authorial intrusion is frequent, brief and comic, functioning as punctuation rather than as a position.

entries.category: The Medium Reading Itself
entries.name: The Genre-Savvy Character
entries.description: A character who has read the same works the reader has, and what that buys.

examples.work: ヲタクに恋は難しい / Wotaku ni Koi wa Muzukashii
examples.text: Every principal is a reader of the medium, so genre literacy is characterisation rather than a device, and the work's romance runs on how each of them misapplies it.

examples.work: DEATH NOTE / Death Note
examples.text: Both principals reason explicitly about what the other will expect, which is genre-savviness converted into a tactical system rather than into commentary.

examples.work: 荒川アンダー ザ ブリッジ / Arakawa Under the Bridge
examples.text: Characters comment on the absurdity of their own situation, which is closer to a running acknowledgement than to genre literacy.

entries.category: The Medium Reading Itself
entries.name: The Reader Implicated
entries.description: Making the reader's own appetite part of the subject.

examples.work: バクマン。 / Bakuman.
examples.text: The survey the characters live under is the reader's own preference expressed as data, so a reader of the magazine it ran in is materially implicated in the mechanism the work dramatises.

examples.work: 行け!稲中卓球部 / Ike! Ina-chū Takkyū-bu
examples.text: The work's cruelty is calibrated so that the reader's enjoyment of it is uncomfortable, which is implication achieved by tone rather than by statement.

examples.work: 荒川アンダー ザ ブリッジ / Arakawa Under the Bridge
examples.text: The reader is addressed as a knowing accomplice, which is companionable rather than implicating.

entries.category: The Medium Reading Itself
entries.name: The Form Explaining Itself
entries.description: Work that teaches the reader how to read it, and the closing argument of this collection.

examples.work: ピンポン / Ping Pong
examples.text: The layouts depart far enough from convention that early chapters effectively train the reader in the work's own grammar, and by the late matches that grammar carries meaning nothing else could.

examples.work: ドラゴン桜 / Dragon Zakura
examples.text: The work's content is instruction, and it uses the medium's own explanatory tools — diagram, panel sequence, direct address — on subject matter that has nothing to do with manga, which shows those tools are general.

examples.work: パタリロ! / Patalliro!
examples.text: Conventions are named and mocked constantly, which teaches the reader the vocabulary incidentally rather than by design.

entries.category: The Magazine as Filter and Advertisement
entries.name: The Magazine Is Not the Product
entries.description: The commercial arrangement the whole medium rests on, stated plainly, because almost every craft consequence follows from it.
entries.principle: The magazine is not what the industry sells. It is a cheap, disposable, high-circulation object whose function is to identify which serials people will later buy as volumes — a filter and an advertisement, paid for by the volumes it generates. In 2024 the Japanese manga market was reported at roughly ¥704 billion, of which digital accounted for about ¥512 billion, print volumes about ¥147 billion, and **magazines about ¥45 billion** — around six per cent. The magazine has never been the revenue object and is now barely a rounding error against digital, and yet it still sets the chapter length, the deadline and the survey, because it is where the filtering happens.
entries.example: The postwar weeklies established the arrangement and the digital platforms inherited it wholesale rather than replacing it, which is the clearest evidence that the filter, not the paper, was the point.
entries.application: When a serialisation constraint seems arbitrary, ask what it does for the filter rather than what it does for the story. Nearly every one of them is optimising for a decision the publisher makes months later about which volumes to print. `subgenre-1` is the narrative form this arrangement produced.
entries._label: Serialisation, the Magazine and the Market

entries.category: The Magazine as Filter and Advertisement
entries.name: What a Magazine Sells at a Loss
entries.description: Loss-leader economics, and the specific freedoms and cruelties they produce.
entries.principle: A magazine priced to be affordable weekly and printed on paper that will not survive a year is not trying to recover its costs from the reader. That has two consequences a writer feels directly. It makes the magazine willing to carry work that is not yet profitable, because the cost of one more serial is small against the chance of finding the next volume-seller — which is why newcomers get in at all. And it makes the magazine ruthless about work that will never convert, because a serial occupying pages is occupying the filter's bandwidth rather than merely failing to earn.
entries.example: The disposable weekly format is visible in the paper stock itself, and it is the reason a volume edition is treated as the durable object and a magazine instalment as a trailer for it.
entries.application: Understand that you are being judged on conversion, not on quality in the abstract. A serial readers enjoy and do not buy is in more danger than a serial fewer readers love intensely, and the two look identical in a survey. `subgenre-3` is the audition slot this economics pays for.
entries._label: Serialisation, the Magazine and the Market

entries.category: The Magazine as Filter and Advertisement
entries.name: The Anthology as a Recommendation Engine
entries.description: Why the works are bundled, and what bundling does to a new serial.
entries.principle: An anthology magazine puts fifteen to twenty serials in front of every reader who came for one of them, which is a distribution mechanism no standalone publication has. A new serial does not need to find an audience; it needs to convert an audience already holding the book for another reason. That inverts the usual problem of publishing — discovery is free and retention is everything — and it is the single largest structural difference between this system and a market where each work is bought separately.
entries.example: A reader buying a weekly for one established serial will pass their eyes over every other serial in it, which is the mechanism by which an unknown newcomer reaches hundreds of thousands of people in week one.
entries.application: Write your opening chapters for a reader who did not choose you and is mildly annoyed to be interrupted. That is the actual reading situation, and it explains why openings in this medium are so much more aggressive than in markets where the reader has already paid for your book specifically.
entries._label: Serialisation, the Magazine and the Market

entries.category: The Magazine as Filter and Advertisement
entries.name: Position in the Issue
entries.description: Where a chapter sits in the running order, and what the position communicates.
entries.principle: Running order is not neutral. The front of the book carries the magazine's confidence, the back carries what it is willing to lose, and readers learn to read the order as a ranking even where the publisher does not intend one. The order is also functional rather than only symbolic: a serial placed early is read by more of the magazine's readers than one placed late, because not every reader finishes the book. That makes position both a consequence of standing and a cause of it, which is a feedback loop a writer should understand rather than resent.
entries.example: The convention of opening an issue with a colour instalment marks the lead position visibly, so the ranking is legible to a reader who has never thought about running order.
entries.application: Track your position over time rather than in any single week. A drift toward the back is information arriving before anyone tells you, and it is usually the earliest signal a writer gets.
entries._label: Serialisation, the Magazine and the Market

entries.category: The Magazine as Filter and Advertisement
entries.name: The Magazine's Own Readership Contract
entries.description: What a magazine has promised its readers, and why it constrains you more than genre does.
entries.principle: Each magazine has an implicit contract with its readership about tone, cruelty, explicitness and resolution, built over decades and enforced far more consistently than any genre convention. A work is rejected or reshaped for breaching that contract much more often than for being badly made, and the contract is largely undocumented — it is learned by reading the magazine rather than by being told. This is what `craft-50` sends a writer to six consecutive issues for; the reason it works is that the contract is visible in aggregate and invisible in any single instalment.
entries.example: Weeklies nominally aimed at the same readership developed markedly different house registers from the same demographic label, which is the clearest demonstration that the contract belongs to the magazine rather than to the audience bracket.
entries.application: Identify the contract before you pitch, and decide whether you are working inside it or asking the magazine to change it. Both are possible; only one of them is what a first-time contributor is being offered.
entries._label: Serialisation, the Magazine and the Market

entries.category: The Magazine as Filter and Advertisement
entries.name: The Colour Pages
entries.description: A scarce production resource, allocated as a signal.
entries.principle: Colour in a monochrome magazine is expensive and rationed, which makes its allocation a message. It marks a launch, an anniversary, an adaptation announcement or a serial the magazine is backing, and it is read as such by readers who could not articulate the convention. For the writer the practical consequence is that colour pages arrive on a schedule the editorial department sets rather than at a moment the story chose, so the story is periodically asked to supply an image worth the expense at a date it did not pick.
entries.example: Colour openings are standard on lead instalments and on launches, and their absence over a long run is as legible as their presence.
entries.application: Keep a running list of images your story could open in colour, so that when the allocation arrives you are choosing rather than improvising. This is one of the few production constraints where advance preparation converts an imposition into an opportunity.
entries._label: Serialisation, the Magazine and the Market

entries.category: The Magazine as Filter and Advertisement
entries.name: The Cover and the Lead Story
entries.description: The one slot that reaches non-readers, and what it costs to hold.
entries.principle: The cover is the magazine's only communication with people who have not bought it, and it is allocated to whatever the publisher believes will convert a browser. Holding it repeatedly is the strongest available signal of a serial's commercial standing, and it comes with an obligation: the instalment behind a cover is expected to be enterable by someone who has never read the serial. That is a genuine craft demand and it recurs unpredictably, which is why long-running serials develop a habit of periodically restating their premise without appearing to.
entries.example: A cover appearance customarily coincides with a colour opening and a lead position, so the three signals arrive together and are read as one.
entries.application: Have a way to restate your premise inside an ordinary scene, and keep it warm. You will need it whenever the cover comes round, and a chapter that stops to explain itself reads as a chapter that stopped.
entries._label: Serialisation, the Magazine and the Market

entries.category: The Magazine as Filter and Advertisement
entries.name: The Magazine as a Training Institution
entries.description: The pipeline — newcomer prizes, one-shots, assistant work — as a function of the magazine rather than of the industry.
entries.principle: Magazines run their own recruitment: newcomer awards judged in-house, one-shot slots for trial publication, and an informal apprenticeship through assistant work on established serials. This means entry is magazine-specific rather than industry-wide — a reputation built at one publisher does not automatically transfer — and it means the institution that will later cancel you is the same one that trained you. The system produces unusually rapid development and unusually narrow formation, because a newcomer learns one magazine's contract very well and the others not at all.
entries.example: The newcomer prizes that run in the back pages of the weeklies are the visible half of the pipeline; the assistant system described at `craft-46` is the invisible half, and more careers pass through it.
entries.application: Pick your magazine before you pick your story, if you can bear to. Everything about the training you receive will be specific to it, and a writer who submits everywhere is trained by nobody.
entries._label: Serialisation, the Magazine and the Market

entries.category: The Magazine as Filter and Advertisement
entries.name: What Happens When a Magazine Closes
entries.description: Cancellation from above, and the difference between a serial ending and its venue ending.
entries.principle: Magazines close, and when one does its serials face an outcome the survey never contemplated: work that was performing adequately is stopped for reasons that have nothing to do with it. Some serials transfer to a sibling magazine, which is the relocation `craft-53` describes from the writer's side; some are compressed into a hurried conclusion; some simply stop. The relevant point for a writer is that this risk is real, is uncorrelated with quality, and is a second and independent argument for the insurance `craft-12` recommends.
entries.example: Transfers between sibling magazines under one publisher are the common outcome and are visible in a serial's publication record as a change of venue mid-run.
entries.application: Know which sibling magazine your work would move to. If the answer is none, your exposure is higher than your survey position suggests.
entries._label: Serialisation, the Magazine and the Market

entries.category: The Magazine as Filter and Advertisement
entries.name: Digital Distribution and What It Replaced
entries.description: The platform era, and the honest answer about what changed.
entries.principle: Digital is now the majority of the market by a wide margin, and the temptation is to say the magazine system has been replaced. It has not been, and the distinction matters. What digital replaced is the **paper** — the filtering function was rebuilt on the platforms rather than abandoned, with view counts, rankings and comment volume standing in for the survey, and the same weekly cadence, the same chapter unit and the same cancellation logic reproduced almost exactly. Some platforms genuinely differ, notably where a work can be published without an editor at all, and those are worth studying precisely because they are the exception.
entries.example: The app-based shōnen platforms reproduce the ranked weekly structure of the print magazine closely enough that a writer trained on one can work on the other without relearning the cadence.
entries.application: Do not assume a digital venue relaxes the constraints in this collection. Ask specifically which of them it has kept, because most venues have kept nearly all of them and have added measurement the print survey never had. `subgenre-33` describes the one parallel system that never had a survey at all.
entries._label: Serialisation, the Magazine and the Market

entries.category: The Chapter Unit and Its Arithmetic
entries.name: Where Nineteen Pages Comes From
entries.description: The weekly chapter length, its actual status as a convention, and an honest statement of what is not documented.
entries.principle: The working figure for a weekly instalment is around nineteen pages, and for a monthly something in the thirty-to-forty-five range. **These are observed conventions rather than a published editorial standard**: research for this pack could not trace either number to a publisher's own stated rule, and a reference work that presents them as policy is asserting more than the record supports. What can be said is why a number in that region is stable — it is roughly what fits the magazine's page budget divided among its serials, and it is roughly what one artist and a small assistant team can produce weekly at acceptable quality. The number is a production equilibrium, not a design.
entries.example: *ONE PIECE* has run at a broadly consistent weekly length for decades, which is what makes the convention visible as a convention rather than as a rule.
entries.application: Write to the length your venue actually uses, measured from its own recent issues, and treat every published figure — including this one — as an observation to check rather than a specification. `craft-1` is the writing side of this; the number itself belongs here.
entries._label: Serialisation, the Magazine and the Market

entries.category: The Chapter Unit and Its Arithmetic
entries.name: The Page Budget as an Editorial Instrument
entries.description: Pages as the currency the editorial department actually allocates.
entries.principle: A magazine has a fixed page count per issue and must divide it among its serials, which makes pages the unit of editorial power. Granting extra pages is the cheapest way to back a serial; withholding them is the quietest way to signal doubt.
