Because the total is fixed, every extra page one serial receives is taken from another — the allocation is genuinely zero-sum within an issue, which is why it is negotiated rather than requested. The writer experiences this as a length that varies for reasons never explained.
entries.example: *ONE PIECE* has received enlarged anniversary and milestone instalments across its run while its ordinary allocation stayed level, which demonstrates that the budget is discretionary rather than fixed per serial.
entries.application: Notice your page allocation over time, and treat an unexplained increase as backing and an unexplained decrease as information. `craft-7` teaches how to split a scene when the pages run out; this is why they ran out.
entries._label: Serialisation, the Magazine and the Market

entries.category: The Chapter Unit and Its Arithmetic
entries.name: Weekly, Monthly, Quarterly
entries.description: Cadence as the variable that changes everything downstream.
entries.principle: Cadence sets the page count, the assistant headcount, the revision time and the reader's memory. A weekly gives roughly nineteen pages and seven days, which forces a small team, minimal revision, and a story that reminds constantly. A monthly gives two to three times the pages and four times the interval, which permits denser art, real revision, and a reader who has genuinely forgotten — so a monthly must restate more, not less, despite having more space. Quarterly and irregular schedules trade almost all reader retention for production freedom, and are viable mainly for work whose audience will wait.
entries.example: *火の鳥 / Hi no Tori* ran across three decades at cadences from monthly to sporadic and in four different magazines, and the variation in density between its serialised stretches is the trade that cadence buys, visible inside one work.
entries.application: Choose cadence deliberately if you have the choice, and if you do not, adjust your reminder budget to it. The commonest cadence error is a monthly written as though the reader read it last week — which is `craft-4` applied at the wrong interval.
entries._label: Serialisation, the Magazine and the Market

entries.category: The Chapter Unit and Its Arithmetic
entries.name: The Chapter-to-Volume Arithmetic
entries.description: How instalments aggregate into the object that actually sells.
entries.principle: A tankōbon volume holds roughly nine to eleven weekly chapters, which means a weekly serial produces a volume about every two and a half to three months. That number governs more of a serial's shape than any narrative principle: it sets how often the story must reach a point worth binding, how long a reader waits between purchasable units, and how much material an arc can occupy before it spans volumes and loses the reader who buys only volumes. A writer who plans in arcs without checking the arithmetic will routinely produce arcs that end four chapters into a volume, which is the least saleable shape available.
entries.example: *鋼の錬金術師 / Hagane no Renkinjutsushi* is frequently cited for the evenness of its arc distribution across volumes, which is a planning achievement rather than an instinct.
entries.application: Divide your planned arc length by ten and see where the volume boundaries fall. Then move your turns so they land near them. `craft-5` gives the writing method; this is the arithmetic it depends on.
entries._label: Serialisation, the Magazine and the Market

entries.category: The Chapter Unit and Its Arithmetic
entries.name: The Colour Opening and Its Cost
entries.description: What a colour instalment takes out of the week's production budget.
entries.principle: Colour pages are produced inside the same week as the rest of the instalment, by the same people, and the additional labour is substantial. The consequence a reader never sees is that a colour opening usually means the monochrome pages behind it received less time — so an instalment that looks like a showcase is frequently one where the interior art is weaker than the serial's norm. Understanding this converts a common reader complaint into a production fact, and it is a reason to plan the colour instalment as a lighter chapter rather than a heavier one.
entries.example: *鋼の錬金術師 / Hagane no Renkinjutsushi* held lead and colour positions repeatedly during its run, so its most-seen instalments were also its most production-stressed — routinely the same chapter.
entries.application: When colour is scheduled, write a chapter with fewer panels and simpler staging. The reader is looking at the cover image; the interior does not need to be your densest work that month. `craft-1` is how to spend a reduced panel budget deliberately.
entries._label: Serialisation, the Magazine and the Market

entries.category: The Chapter Unit and Its Arithmetic
entries.name: The Split Chapter and the Double Issue
entries.description: Irregularities in the publication calendar, and their narrative cost.
entries.principle: The magazine calendar is not uniform. Combined issues covering two weeks, seasonal breaks and holiday schedules all insert gaps that the story did not plan, and they arrive with little notice. The effect is that an interval the author designed as one week becomes three, which is enough to break a cliffhanger's tension and to erase a minor character from the reader's memory. Experienced serial writers keep a copy of the publication calendar and place their weakest intervals against the longest gaps.
entries.example: *こちら葛飾区亀有公園前派出所 / Kochira Katsushika-ku Kameari Kōen-mae Hashutsujo* published against the weekly calendar for four decades, including every combined issue in it, which is why its instalment record is the clearest available picture of where the gaps fall.
entries.application: Get the calendar and mark the gaps before you plan the arc. Put a resolution before a long gap and a question before a short one — the reverse is the commonest avoidable error in serial pacing, and `craft-3` is what the panel before each gap has to do.
entries._label: Serialisation, the Magazine and the Market

entries.category: The Chapter Unit and Its Arithmetic
entries.name: The Break Week
entries.description: The skipped instalment, what it costs, and why it is increasingly normal.
entries.principle: A serial that misses a week loses momentum, position and some readers, and the magazine loses a scheduled slot — so breaks were historically resisted hard. That has shifted, partly because the human cost of the weekly cadence became a public subject and partly because digital distribution makes an irregular schedule less damaging than it was on paper. The craft consequence is that a break is now a resource a writer can spend rather than only a failure, and spending one deliberately before a major arc is a legitimate production decision.
entries.example: *HUNTER×HUNTER* is the extreme instance of the shift, having moved from unscheduled interruption to publicly announced hiatus, which converted an exception into a stated part of its cadence.
entries.application: If you can schedule a break, schedule it **before** the chapter you need to be best, not after the one that exhausted you. The second is what happens by default and it wastes the recovery.
entries._label: Serialisation, the Magazine and the Market

entries.category: The Chapter Unit and Its Arithmetic
entries.name: Page Count as a Signal of Standing
entries.description: Reading the allocation as data about how the magazine sees you.
entries.principle: Because pages are discretionary and zero-sum, a serial's page count over time is a continuous readout of editorial confidence — more legible than position, because it is a number rather than an order. A rising allocation means the magazine is investing; a falling one usually precedes a conversation. The signal is noisy in any single week, since allocations flex around anniversaries and other serials' needs, and is reliable over a quarter.
entries.example: *こちら葛飾区亀有公園前派出所 / Kochira Katsushika-ku Kameari Kōen-mae Hashutsujo* sustained a stable allocation across four decades, which is itself the clearest possible expression of standing.
entries.application: Keep a spreadsheet of your own page counts by issue. It costs nothing, and it will tell you what your editor is not yet saying. `craft-44` is how to read the conversation when it comes.
entries._label: Serialisation, the Magazine and the Market

entries.category: The Chapter Unit and Its Arithmetic
entries.name: The Volume's Bonus Pages
entries.description: The material that exists only in the collected edition, and what it is for.
entries.principle: A volume is padded to a standard page count, which leaves a gap between the serialised chapters and the bound object. That gap is filled with author commentary, four-panel extras, character notes, unused designs and occasionally a short original story. This material is commercially functional — it gives the volume-buyer something the magazine reader did not get, which is the conversion argument the whole system runs on — and it is also where a serial's relationship with its committed readers is built.
entries.example: *あずまんが大王 / Azumanga Daiō* and the four-panel line generally use volume extras heavily, because the format's brevity leaves room and its readers are collectors.
entries.application: Plan the extras rather than improvising them at deadline. They are the only pages you write for people who have definitely already bought the book, which makes them the only place you can assume total familiarity — the inverse of the situation `craft-52` describes.
entries._label: Serialisation, the Magazine and the Market

entries.category: The Chapter Unit and Its Arithmetic
entries.name: Revision Between Serial and Volume
entries.description: The second draft the medium gives you, and how much of it to take.
entries.principle: Chapters are routinely revised for volume publication — art redrawn, dialogue adjusted, pages added, occasionally sequences restructured. This is the medium's built-in second draft and it is the reason the volume is the authoritative text rather than the magazine. The discipline is knowing what to change: fixing art produced under deadline is almost always right, and rewriting a plot point the magazine readers already experienced is almost always wrong, because it creates two incompatible versions of a story that people discuss with each other.
entries.example: *火の鳥 / Hi no Tori* exists in materially different serialised and collected states across its long publication, which is the extreme case of the same practice.
entries.application: Revise art freely, dialogue carefully, and events almost never. And record what you changed — a serial that has been revised silently is a serial nobody can cite accurately, including you. `craft-5` is the double obligation this revision exists to settle: the volume is the reader the serial could not fully serve.
entries._label: Serialisation, the Magazine and the Market

entries.category: The Reader Survey and What It Actually Controls
entries.name: What the Survey Actually Asks
entries.description: The reader questionnaire, described at the level the record supports and no further.
entries.principle: The reader survey is a questionnaire bound into or attached to the magazine, on which readers rank the instalments they most enjoyed. That much is well established and is the mechanism behind everything else in this category. Beyond it the public record thins quickly: **the sample size, the return rate and whether the responding population is stable are not documented in any source this pack could verify**, and figures in circulation are not traceable to a publisher. A writer should therefore treat the survey as a real instrument of unknown precision, which is a different thing from either a myth or a measurement.
entries.example: *重版出来! / Jūhan Shuttai!* dramatises editorial decision-making from inside a publisher and is useful for the texture of the process, while remaining fiction about it rather than evidence of it.
entries.application: Take the survey seriously as a signal and refuse to model it precisely. Any plan that depends on a specific numerical threshold is built on a figure nobody has published. `checklist-10` is the triage this applies to.
entries._label: Serialisation, the Magazine and the Market

entries.category: The Reader Survey and What It Actually Controls
entries.name: What the Survey Controls, and What It Does Not
entries.description: The boundary of the instrument's authority.
entries.principle: The survey demonstrably influences running order, page allocation, and the decision to continue or end a serial. It does not decide those things by itself. Editorial judgement, volume sales, adaptation prospects, a magazine's need for range across its lineup, and an author's standing all enter, and several of them can override a survey position in either direction. The common error is to treat the survey as an algorithm with an output; it is an input to a human decision, and the humans have their own incentives — including a strong incentive not to cancel a serial they publicly launched.
entries.example: *ヒカルの碁 / Hikaru no Go* built its readership on a game most readers could not follow, which is the shape of serial whose value to a lineup is not what a per-instalment ranking measures — and the existence of that pattern is the clearest available proof that the survey is not the whole decision.
entries.application: Ask what else your serial is good for. Volume conversion, adaptation potential, range within the lineup — each is a reason to keep you that the survey does not measure, and each is worth knowing before the conversation, and `craft-43` is how to arrive at it.
entries._label: Serialisation, the Magazine and the Market

entries.category: The Reader Survey and What It Actually Controls
entries.name: The Cancellation Threshold That Comes From Fiction
entries.description: The most widely repeated fact about this system, and its actual source.
entries.principle: A specific numerical cancellation threshold circulates widely in Anglophone discussion of the weekly system, stated with confidence and attributed to no one. **Its traceable source is *バクマン。 / Bakuman.*, a manga about the industry — that is, a work of fiction.** No publisher has published such a figure, and research for this pack found no editorial statement supporting it. This matters beyond the single number: it is a demonstration of how a fictional treatment of an industry becomes that industry's received record, and a reference work that repeats it is laundering a novel into a fact. The related claim that a serial placing last for three consecutive weeks is automatically cut is likewise **unconfirmed**.
entries.example: *劇画漂流 / Gekiga Hyōryū* is the parallel case in the other direction — an industry memoir, valuable and shaped, which is a primary account by an interested party rather than a record.
entries.application: When you encounter a precise number about this system, find who published it. If the answer is a manga, you have found a story about the industry rather than a fact about it — and the distinction is exactly what this collection exists to hold.
entries._label: Serialisation, the Magazine and the Market

entries.category: The Reader Survey and What It Actually Controls
entries.name: The Ten-Week Window and Its Cost
entries.description: The early-judgement period, and the acknowledged problem with it.
entries.principle: New serials are evaluated over an early window of roughly ten instalments, and the pressure that creates is the single largest force shaping openings in this system. A serial must establish premise, cast and appeal inside that window or it will not survive to develop them. The cost is acknowledged from inside the industry: a former editor of the largest weekly has publicly described the window as cutting too early and losing serials that would have found their readers. That is an unusual admission and it is worth carrying, because it means the constraint is understood as a constraint rather than defended as a filter.
entries.example: *進撃の巨人 / Attack on Titan* is frequently cited as a serial whose appeal was not obvious at launch, which is the shape of work the window is most likely to lose.
entries.application: Front-load ruthlessly and know what it costs you. `craft-15` and `craft-16` are the writing techniques; this is why the pressure exists, and it is also why a slow-building premise is a genuine commercial risk rather than a stylistic preference.
entries._label: Serialisation, the Magazine and the Market

entries.category: The Reader Survey and What It Actually Controls
entries.name: Not Every Magazine Runs the Same Logic
entries.description: The correction most needed in Anglophone accounts of this system.
entries.principle: The survey-driven, cancellation-heavy model is strongly associated with one publisher's flagship weekly, and Anglophone writing routinely describes it as how manga works. It is not. Monthly magazines, seinen titles, shōjo and josei magazines, and the alternative and art-manga venues run on materially different logics — longer evaluation periods, more editorial discretion, less ranking pressure, and in some cases no reader ranking at all. A writer who has internalised the weekly model and is working for a monthly is optimising for a machine that is not there.
entries.example: *ねじ式 / Neji-shiki* appeared in a magazine that operated with no survey mechanism worth the name, which is the extreme end of the same point and is why `subgenre-30` treats that lineage as the system's counter-example.
entries.application: Ask your venue directly how it evaluates a serial, and do not assume. This is the single most common false generalisation in English-language writing about the medium, and acting on it will make you write the wrong opening.
entries._label: Serialisation, the Magazine and the Market

entries.category: The Reader Survey and What It Actually Controls
entries.name: The Survey and the New Serial
entries.description: Why a launch's early positions read differently from a veteran's.
entries.principle: A new serial's survey position is measured against reader curiosity rather than reader commitment, which makes early numbers unreliable in both directions. A strong first position may reflect novelty; a weak one may reflect a readership that has not yet decided. Editorial departments know this and read a launch's **trajectory** rather than its level — a serial holding position over several weeks is generally read more favourably than one that opened higher and slid. The practical consequence is that the third to sixth instalments carry more diagnostic weight than the first.
entries.example: *NARUTO -ナルト- / Naruto* and other long-running launches are frequently discussed in terms of early trajectory rather than opening position, which reflects how the signal is actually read.
entries.application: Plan your third through sixth chapters as carefully as your first. That is where the measurement that matters is taken, and it is the stretch most writers treat as consolidation.
entries._label: Serialisation, the Magazine and the Market

entries.category: The Reader Survey and What It Actually Controls
entries.name: Survey Position and Editorial Attention
entries.description: The feedback loop between measured performance and the support that produces it.
entries.principle: Position determines how much editorial attention a serial receives, and editorial attention improves a serial — so the measurement partly causes what it measures. A well-placed serial gets a more experienced editor's time, better page allocation, colour openings and cover slots; a struggling one gets less of all of it at exactly the moment it needs more. This is not a conspiracy, it is ordinary resource allocation, and naming it is useful because it explains why recovery from a bad run is harder than the raw numbers suggest.
entries.example: *ドラゴンボール / Dragon Ball* held cover, colour and lead position together across its peak years, which is what the bundling looks like from the inside — the three visible forms of support arrive together and are withdrawn together.
entries.application: If you are sliding, ask for something specific and small rather than for confidence. A concrete request — an extra four pages for one chapter — is easier to grant than reassurance and does more.
entries._label: Serialisation, the Magazine and the Market

entries.category: The Reader Survey and What It Actually Controls
entries.name: What a Survey Cannot Measure
entries.description: The systematic blind spots of a preference ranking.
entries.principle: A ranking of enjoyment per instalment measures a specific thing and is blind to several others. It cannot see a reader who finds a chapter uncomfortable and important. It cannot see accumulated attachment, only this week's satisfaction, which structurally penalises setup, aftermath and any chapter that spends its length on consequence. And it cannot distinguish a reader who will buy the volume from one who will not. These blind spots are not incidental: they are why the system is better at producing consistently satisfying instalments than consistently satisfying books.
entries.example: *あしたのジョー / Ashita no Joe* is built on chapters whose weight is cumulative rather than immediate, which is precisely the shape a per-instalment ranking undervalues.
entries.application: Know which of your chapters the instrument cannot see, and place them where you can afford the cost. A quiet aftermath chapter placed the week after a peak is protected by the peak; the same chapter placed during a slide is not.
entries._label: Serialisation, the Magazine and the Market

entries.category: The Reader Survey and What It Actually Controls
entries.name: The Reader as an Instrument
entries.description: What it means that the audience is wired directly into production, stated without romance or complaint.
entries.principle: This system converts reader preference into production decisions faster and more directly than any other major narrative medium — the gap between a reader's opinion and a change in the work can be a matter of weeks. That is genuinely remarkable and it is neither straightforwardly good nor bad. It produces work extraordinarily well fitted to its audience, and it systematically eliminates work whose audience had not formed yet. Both effects are real, both are consequences of the same mechanism, and a writer working in the system is choosing both.
entries.example: *ドラゴンボール / Dragon Ball* is the most-cited case of a serial visibly reshaped by reader response over its run, and the reshaping is legible in the work.
entries.application: Decide in advance which parts of your story are negotiable and which are not, and write the second list down. Under weekly feedback pressure everything feels negotiable, and a writer who has not decided beforehand will find the decision has been made for them.
entries._label: Serialisation, the Magazine and the Market

entries.category: The Reader Survey and What It Actually Controls
entries.name: Life After a Bad Survey Run
entries.description: What actually happens next, and the options that exist.
entries.principle: A sustained weak run leads to a conversation, and the conversation has more outcomes than cancellation. A serial may be given a defined number of instalments to conclude, which is the origin of the compressed ending; it may be asked to change direction, which is why mid-run genre shifts are common; it may be moved to a magazine with a different readership; or it may be ended at a natural point with the author's next project already agreed. Knowing the menu matters, because a writer who believes the only outcomes are survival and cancellation will negotiate badly.
entries.example: *聖闘士星矢 / Seinto Seiya* and other long serials show visible mid-run redirections, which are the second outcome on that list rather than a loss of authorial nerve.
entries.application: Have your compressed ending written before you need it, per `craft-12`, and know which sibling magazine could take the work. Both are cheap in advance and unavailable under pressure.
entries._label: Serialisation, the Magazine and the Market

entries.category: Cancellation, the Rushed Ending and the Long Runway
entries.name: The Cancellation Conversation
entries.description: What actually happens when a serial is ended, described as a process rather than as an event.
entries.principle: Cancellation is a conversation, not a notification. An editor raises the position, the volume figures and the lineup's needs, and the outcome is negotiated — usually a number of instalments in which to finish. What is being decided is rarely whether but how many, and the number is the single most consequential thing a writer will negotiate in the serial's life. Writers who arrive at that conversation with a specific plan for three chapters and a specific plan for fifteen get a better number than writers who arrive with an argument about quality, because the editor's problem is scheduling and only one of those addresses it.
entries.example: *重版出来! / Jūhan Shuttai!* stages editorial decision-making from inside a publisher, and the texture of the conversation — commercial, unmalicious, and not about merit — is its most useful contribution to a writer's expectations.
entries.application: Arrive with `craft-12`'s two endings written and ask for the longer one. The request is concrete, it is schedulable, and it is the only form of the argument the person opposite you can act on.
entries._label: Serialisation, the Magazine and the Market

entries.category: Cancellation, the Rushed Ending and the Long Runway
entries.name: The Compressed Ending
entries.description: The rushed conclusion as a production artefact with a legible signature.
entries.principle: A compressed ending is not a failure of craft but the visible residue of an instruction, and it has a recognisable shape: the ratio of exposition to scene rises sharply, subplots are resolved by report rather than by event, and the final chapters cover more story time than any earlier stretch. Readers usually diagnose this as an author losing interest. It is almost always an author being given four chapters for fifteen chapters of material, and learning to read the signature is useful because it tells a reader what happened rather than leaving them to blame the wrong thing.
entries.example: *聖闘士星矢 / Seinto Seiya* shows visible mid-run redirection and compression, which is the shape the instruction leaves rather than a lapse in the work.
entries.application: If you are compressing, cut whole threads rather than shortening all of them. A reader forgives an abandoned subplot and does not forgive a summarised climax — and `craft-12`'s short ending exists precisely so the choice is made in advance rather than at the deadline.
entries._label: Serialisation, the Magazine and the Market

entries.category: Cancellation, the Rushed Ending and the Long Runway
entries.name: The Long Runway
entries.description: The opposite grant — permission to continue — and what it costs the story that receives it.
entries.principle: A successful serial is asked to continue, and the request is as consequential as a cancellation and much less examined. Extension arrives without a plan attached, and the author must generate material beyond the shape they designed, under a cadence that does not pause while they think. The characteristic damage is horizontal growth — more factions, more territory, more cast — because it is the easiest material to add. `craft-13` is the writing answer; the institutional point is that the grant is **not optional in practice**, since declining an extension on a performing serial is refusing the publisher its most valuable asset.
entries.example: *ONE PIECE* is the extreme case of the runway granted and used, and the visible discipline of its cast management is what a long extension demands rather than what it usually produces.
entries.application: Prepare for success as concretely as for failure. Decide now which unopened question you would open if given fifty more chapters, and make sure it is a vertical one — something already established turning out to be more than the reader was told.
entries._label: Serialisation, the Magazine and the Market

entries.category: Cancellation, the Rushed Ending and the Long Runway
entries.name: Ending on Your Own Terms
entries.description: The voluntary conclusion, its rarity, and what makes it possible.
entries.principle: A serial that ends when its author decides is unusual, and the conditions are specific: standing high enough that the publisher will not fight it, a next project the publisher wants, and — most often overlooked — an ending established early enough that stopping reads as arrival rather than as departure. The third is the one a writer controls. A serial with a planted terminus can end at that terminus and be understood; a serial without one cannot end voluntarily at all, because any stopping point looks like a decision to stop.
entries.example: *鋼の錬金術師 / Hagane no Renkinjutsushi* is frequently cited as a long serial that concluded at its planned length rather than at a commercial one, which is the outcome this card describes.
entries.application: `craft-10` says plant the terminus early for narrative reasons. This is the second reason, and for a working writer it may be the larger one: the terminus is what makes a voluntary ending legible to everyone else.
entries._label: Serialisation, the Magazine and the Market

entries.category: Cancellation, the Rushed Ending and the Long Runway
entries.name: The Serial That Is Allowed to Drift
entries.description: Continuation without support — neither cancelled nor backed — and why it is the worst outcome.
entries.principle: Between backing and cancellation sits a third state that nobody announces: a serial performing adequately, occupying a mid-table position, receiving no colour openings and no conversation, continuing indefinitely. It is the outcome writers least anticipate and it is corrosive, because there is no decision to respond to and no deadline to write toward. The story loses shape not from pressure but from its absence, and the drift is usually visible in the work long before anyone names it.
entries.example: *こちら葛飾区亀有公園前派出所 / Kochira Katsushika-ku Kameari Kōen-mae Hashutsujo* is the counter-case that proves the point: an episodic serial is **designed** for indefinite continuation and does not drift, because it never had a shape to lose.
entries.application: If nobody is talking to you, impose your own deadline and tell your editor about it. A self-declared arc endpoint converts drift into a schedule, and it is the one intervention available to a writer nobody is currently deciding about.
entries._label: Serialisation, the Magazine and the Market

entries.category: Cancellation, the Rushed Ending and the Long Runway
entries.name: The Second Serial
entries.description: What happens after a serial ends, and why the first one's ending shapes the next one's launch.
entries.principle: A magazine's relationship with a writer usually outlasts any single serial, and how a serial ended is the main input into what the writer is offered next. A voluntary conclusion at strength buys a good slot; a cancellation buys a shorter leash and often a one-shot before another serial. The consequence writers underestimate is that a badly handled compression damages the next launch as well as the current work, because the editorial memory is of the process rather than of the pages.
entries.example: *劇画漂流 / Gekiga Hyōryū* records a career as a sequence of such relationships rather than as a sequence of works, which is the more accurate shape and is why it is useful here.
entries.application: End well even when ending badly. Deliver on the number you agreed, do not overrun, and make the compression a clean decision rather than a collapse — you are being assessed on the next commission, not on this one.
entries._label: Serialisation, the Magazine and the Market

entries.category: Cancellation, the Rushed Ending and the Long Runway
entries.name: What a Cancelled Serial Leaves Behind
entries.description: The material afterlife of an ended serial, and why it matters more than it used to.
entries.principle: A cancelled serial does not disappear. Its volumes stay in print for a period, its chapters remain on digital platforms indefinitely, and the work keeps accumulating readers at a low rate for years. That changes the calculation: a serial ended at volume four is not a closed loss but a small permanent asset, and it is why publishers are more willing to start serials than the cancellation rate suggests. For the writer it means the compressed ending is read by people who will encounter it years later with no knowledge of the circumstances.
entries.example: *ゲゲゲの鬼太郎 / Gegege no Kitarō* moved across magazines and formats over decades, which is the extreme demonstration that a work's life is not bounded by any single serialisation.
entries.application: Write the compressed ending for a reader who does not know it was compressed. They are the majority of the people who will ever read it, and they have no context to forgive it with.
entries._label: Serialisation, the Magazine and the Market

entries.category: Cancellation, the Rushed Ending and the Long Runway
entries.name: The Revival
entries.description: A serial restarted after ending, and the two very different things that can mean.
entries.principle: Revivals divide cleanly. A continuation resumes an unfinished story, usually because demand became visible after the fact through volume sales or an adaptation, and its problem is that the readership has aged and the author has changed. A reboot restarts the premise for a new readership and is a different work wearing a title. Conflating them is the common error: readers arriving at a reboot expecting a continuation experience it as a betrayal of a promise nobody actually made.
entries.example: *キューティーハニー / Cutie Honey* has been restarted repeatedly across decades in forms that are reboots rather than continuations, which is what makes the distinction visible as a distinction.
entries.application: State which one you are doing, in the work, early. A single line of framing costs nothing and prevents the entire class of complaint the ambiguity generates.
entries._label: Serialisation, the Magazine and the Market

entries.category: Cancellation, the Rushed Ending and the Long Runway
entries.name: Ending Before You Are Asked To
entries.description: Pre-emptive conclusion, and the case for it.
entries.principle: A writer who can see the drift coming may conclude while still performing, and the argument for it is that every resource a good ending needs — page allocation, reader attention, editorial goodwill — is at its maximum before the decline rather than after it. The argument against is obvious and financial. What tips the balance is whether the story has more to say: a serial extended past its material converts a work people finish into a work people abandon, and abandonment is much harder to reverse than a modest early ending.
entries.example: *ヒカルの碁 / Hikaru no Go* concluded at a length its premise supported rather than at the length its popularity could have sustained, which is the decision this card is about.
entries.application: Ask, each volume, whether you still know what the next three arcs are for. When the answer stops being yes, you are already in the window where ending is a choice rather than an outcome.
entries._label: Serialisation, the Magazine and the Market

entries.category: Cancellation, the Rushed Ending and the Long Runway
entries.name: The Conclusion Nobody Reads
entries.description: Reader attrition across a long run, and what it means for where you put your best work.
entries.principle: A long serial loses readers continuously, and the readership of a final chapter is a fraction of the readership of chapter one. That is an uncomfortable fact with a clear consequence: the ending is written for the most committed and least numerous part of your audience, and it should be written for exactly that reader rather than for a general one. It also means the middle matters more than writers assume, because the middle is where the attrition happens and where most of the total reading actually occurs.
entries.example: *カムイ伝 / Kamui-den* was published in separated parts across decades, so no single readership followed the whole of it — the extreme case of an audience that cannot be assumed continuous.
entries.application: Put your most demanding material in the middle third, where the largest number of committed readers are. Save the ending for resolution and for the reader who stayed — that reader will accept difficulty, but there are fewer of them than your chapter-one numbers suggest.
entries._label: Serialisation, the Magazine and the Market

entries.category: The Tankōbon: Revision, Economics and the Real Object
entries.name: The Tankōbon Is the Book
entries.description: The collected volume as the medium's actual object, and the consequences of taking that seriously.
entries.principle: The volume is what is bought, kept, translated, shelved, lent and re-read; the magazine instalment is a disposable trailer for it. Every long-run consequence follows from that. It is why revision between serial and volume is standard rather than exceptional, why volume boundaries govern arc planning, why the volume's page count determines the bonus material, and why a work's reputation is formed by readers who never saw a single chapter in its original context. A writer who thinks of the chapter as the work and the volume as a container has the relationship exactly backwards.
entries.example: *AKIRA* is read almost entirely as volumes rather than as its original serialisation, which is the normal condition for any work that outlives its magazine run.
entries.application: Read your own work in volume form before you decide anything is finished. `craft-5` is the writing discipline; this is why it is worth the effort — the volume is the version that will be judged.
entries._label: Serialisation, the Magazine and the Market

entries.category: The Tankōbon: Revision, Economics and the Real Object
entries.name: What Gets Fixed Between Serial and Shelf
entries.description: The standard revision pass, and its actual scope.
entries.principle: Volume revision routinely covers redrawn art, corrected dialogue, added or removed pages, and occasionally restructured sequences. The scope is wider than most readers realise and narrower than most writers wish: the constraint is that the magazine version has already been read and discussed, so changes that alter **what happened** create two incompatible versions of a story people talk to each other about. Art and phrasing are safe; events are not. The distinction is not aesthetic but social.
entries.example: *火の鳥 / Hi no Tori* exists in materially different serialised and collected states across its long publication, which is the extreme instance of the same routine practice.
entries.application: Keep a revision log from volume one. You will not remember what you changed, and a work whose changes are undocumented is one nobody — including you — can cite accurately. `checklist-15` is the naming half of the same discipline.
entries._label: Serialisation, the Magazine and the Market

entries.category: The Tankōbon: Revision, Economics and the Real Object
entries.name: The Volume Cover and the Spine
entries.description: The volume's own design problem, distinct from the magazine's.
entries.principle: A volume cover works on a shelf rather than on a newsstand, which is a different job: it must be identifiable at spine width, must sit in a series that will eventually run to many volumes, and must remain coherent as the work changes over years. The spine especially is a design constraint most first-time creators never consider and every reader uses — a series whose spines do not read as a set is a series a browsing reader cannot find. This is a commercial matter that is also a real design discipline.
entries.example: *ゴルゴ13 / Golgo 13* has sustained a coherent volume identity across an extraordinary number of volumes, which is the problem at its most extreme.
entries.application: Design the spine system before volume one, not at volume five when the pattern is already broken. And decide what changes and what stays across the series — the reader needs both, and getting the ratio wrong in either direction costs recognisability.
entries._label: Serialisation, the Magazine and the Market

entries.category: The Tankōbon: Revision, Economics and the Real Object
entries.name: Volume Sales as the Real Verdict
entries.description: The number that actually decides, and how it differs from the survey.
entries.principle: The survey measures which instalment readers enjoyed most this week; volume sales measure who valued the work enough to buy it permanently. These are different populations and they frequently disagree, which is why a serial can survive weak survey positions on strong sales and why a serial can place well and still end. Volume sales are also slower — the first volume appears months into a run — so the two instruments operate on different clocks, and a writer in the early window is being judged by the faster and less meaningful one.
entries.example: *ちはやふる / Chihayafuru* built a readership on competitive karuta, a subject with no obvious mass appeal, which is the profile of a work whose volume conversion matters more than its weekly ranking.
entries.application: Know when your first volume lands, because that is when the second and better instrument starts reporting. `serial-22` covers what else enters the decision; this is the one that outweighs the survey when they disagree.
entries._label: Serialisation, the Magazine and the Market

entries.category: The Tankōbon: Revision, Economics and the Real Object
entries.name: The Backlist and the Long Tail
entries.description: Income and readership after the run ends, and why it changes what a serial is worth.
entries.principle: A completed work with volumes in print earns at a low rate indefinitely, and the aggregate over years can exceed what the serialisation paid. That is the economic reason publishers tolerate a high cancellation rate and the practical reason a writer should care about the volume edition even when the serial is ending badly. It also creates a specific asymmetry: the version that earns is the version that was revised, so effort spent on volume revision is spent on the earning object rather than on the disposable one.
entries.example: *サザエさん / Sazae-san* has remained continuously available in collected form for decades after its original run, which is the long tail at its longest.
entries.application: Do the volume revision properly even on a cancelled serial, especially on a cancelled serial. It is the only version that will still exist in five years, and it is the one a future editor will read.
entries._label: Serialisation, the Magazine and the Market

entries.category: The Tankōbon: Revision, Economics and the Real Object
entries.name: The Complete Edition and the Reissue
entries.description: Later editions — larger formats, restorations, anniversary sets — and the authorial questions they raise.
entries.principle: Successful works are reissued in larger or restored formats, and each reissue reopens the revision question at a distance of years or decades. The author is older, the work is fixed in readers' memory, and the temptation to improve is strong. The discipline is that a reissue is an **edition** rather than a rewrite: restoring colour pages, correcting reproduction and reinstating cut material are edition work; altering the story is producing a second work that will be compared unfavourably with the reader's memory of the first.
entries.example: *風の谷のナウシカ / Kaze no Tani no Nausicaä* has appeared in multiple collected formats over many years, which is the standard shape of a reissue history for a work of that standing.
entries.application: Treat a reissue as restoration. If you genuinely want to change the story, do it as a stated new version rather than as a replacement — readers accept an alternative and resent a substitution.
entries._label: Serialisation, the Magazine and the Market

entries.category: The Tankōbon: Revision, Economics and the Real Object
entries.name: Digital Volumes and the Chapter Purchase
entries.description: What digital distribution did to the volume as a unit.
entries.principle: Digital sells both volumes and individual chapters, and the chapter purchase partially dissolves the unit this whole category is built on. Where readers buy chapters, the volume's shaping function weakens — arcs no longer need to land near volume boundaries, and the bonus material has nowhere to live. Where readers buy digital volumes, almost nothing changes except the shelf. Both patterns coexist by platform and by market, which means a writer needs to know which one their venue runs on rather than assuming the print logic survived intact.
entries.example: *ワンパンマン / One-Punch Man* began outside the magazine system entirely before entering it, which is the clearest available case of a work whose unit of publication was not initially the volume at all.
entries.application: Ask your publisher how your work is actually being bought. If it is chapters, the volume-boundary planning in `craft-5` matters less and the chapter-level hook matters more; if it is volumes, nothing has changed and the print discipline holds.
entries._label: Serialisation, the Magazine and the Market

entries.category: The Tankōbon: Revision, Economics and the Real Object
entries.name: The Out-of-Print Work
entries.description: Disappearance from the record, and what it does to a medium's own history.
entries.principle: Most manga goes out of print, and a great deal of it is never digitised. The consequence for a writer is small and for the medium's history it is severe: whole registers survive only as scarce physical volumes, which means the received account of the medium is shaped by what happened to stay available rather than by what mattered. The rental-market and alternative lines are the worst affected, and any claim about what was typical in a given period should be read against the question of what survived to be counted.
entries.example: *血だるま剣法 / Chidaruma Kenpō* was withdrawn from circulation in 1962 following protest from the Buraku Liberation League — a case where a work's unavailability has a documented cause, which is unusual, and where the pack states the fact of the withdrawal without adjudicating the dispute behind it.
entries.application: When you read a generalisation about a period of this medium, ask what proportion of that period is still readable. `checklist-10`'s triage applies to historical claims as much as to procedural ones.
entries._label: Serialisation, the Magazine and the Market

entries.category: The Tankōbon: Revision, Economics and the Real Object
entries.name: Translation and the Second Market
entries.description: The export edition, named here and deliberately not developed.
entries.principle: A licensed edition is a second commercial object with its own format decisions — trim size, reading direction, how sound effects are handled, whether volumes are combined — and those decisions materially change the reading experience. This pack states that and stops. The boundary rule at §2 puts translation, the licensing apparatus and the global reception history outside the pack: they belong to a work whose subject is how manga travels, and this pack's subject is how manga is made under the Japanese serialisation system. The absence is named rather than left silent.
entries.example: *Manga! Manga! The World of Japanese Comics* is the English-language work that opened this subject and is carded here as scholarship rather than as an account this pack extends.
entries.application: If your interest is the export edition, this is not the reference for it. What you can take from here is that every decision the licensed edition makes is being made against a Japanese original whose own constraints are described throughout this collection.
entries._label: Serialisation, the Magazine and the Market

entries.category: The Tankōbon: Revision, Economics and the Real Object
entries.name: What a Volume Cannot Recover
entries.description: What is permanently lost when a serial becomes a book, and the closing argument of this category.
entries.principle: The volume is the durable object and it is not a complete record. Lost in the transfer: the week between chapters, which was a structural component of every cliffhanger; the running order and what it said about the work's standing; the other serials that surrounded it and shaped how it read; the reader survey the work was written against; and the colour openings, which are almost always reproduced in monochrome. A reader who knows a work only as volumes has read the story and has not experienced the form it was made in — and most of this collection describes things that reader cannot see.
entries.example: *あしたのジョー / Ashita no Joe* is read now as a sequence of volumes, and its original weekly reception, in which the interval between instalments was part of the experience, is not recoverable from them.
entries.application: When you study a work, find out where and how it ran. The cadence, the magazine and the position are part of the text, and `checklist-15`'s sourcing discipline is what makes them findable — reading the volumes alone will teach you the story and hide the system.
entries._label: Serialisation, the Magazine and the Market

entries.category: The Editor's Authority and the Uncredited Hand
entries.name: The Editor Has No Byline
entries.description: The single structural fact a writer from an Anglophone comics background gets wrong first.
entries.principle: The manga editor — the tantōsha, the person "in charge" — holds none of the five authorship claims a US comics writer would recognise as belonging to an editor, and holds authority over the work that exceeds any of them. The editor is not credited on the chapter, is not credited on the volume, does not own the property, and takes no royalty. The editor also decides whether the storyboard proceeds, negotiates the length of the ending, and is the reason a series changes direction in its second year. **Authority and credit are decoupled here in a way they are not in the American system**, and every disagreement a foreign writer has with the arrangement flows from expecting the two to travel together.
entries.example: *バクマン。 / Bakuman.* is the most detailed portrait of the relationship in print, and its usefulness is not its accuracy about outcomes but its accuracy about the shape of the exchange — an editor whose name never appears on the work driving decisions the author experiences as binding.
entries.application: `craft-43` tells you how to bring work to that person. This card tells you who they are before you walk in: not a gatekeeper you can go around, and not a collaborator with a claim on the result.
entries._label: Serialisation, the Magazine and the Market

entries.category: The Editor's Authority and the Uncredited Hand
entries.name: The Nemu Is Where the Authority Lands
entries.description: The stage of production at which editorial power is actually exercised, and why it is not the finished pages.
entries.principle: The nemu — the rough storyboard fixing panel order, page turns and dialogue — is what an editor reads and approves, and it is the object over which the argument happens. By the time finished pages exist the schedule has consumed the room for disagreement, so a note delivered at nemu stage is cheap and the same note delivered at inking stage is a catastrophe. The consequence for authority is direct: **the editor's leverage is greatest at the point where the work is least finished**, which is also the point at which a writer feels least defended, because a rough board looks provisional even when the structure in it is the whole plan.
entries.example: *バクマン。 / Bakuman.* stages nemu approval as the recurring site of tension rather than as an administrative step, which is the correct emphasis and a rare one in fiction about the industry.
entries.application: `craft-47` argues the nemu is the real manuscript. Read that card as craft and this one as institution: the reason to treat the board as the manuscript is that the institution already does.
entries._label: Serialisation, the Magazine and the Market

entries.category: The Editor's Authority and the Uncredited Hand
entries.name: The Editor Who Changed the Series
entries.description: The documented case that shows how far editorial direction can reach into the work.
entries.principle: Editorial intervention in a running serial is not confined to pacing notes. It reaches premise, protagonist and genre, and the historical record includes cases where the series a reader knows is the second or third answer to an editor's objection to the first. This is not a scandal inside the system and is not concealed — editors have described it in interviews and writers have described it in memoirs — but it is invisible from the finished object, because **nothing on the page records which decisions were the author's**. A writer studying a famous series is therefore studying a collaboration whose second party left no signature.
entries.example: *ドラゴンボール / Dragon Ball* is the standard case: Kazuhiko Torishima's editorial pressure on Toriyama Akira is well documented by both men, and the series' turn toward the tournament structure is usually attributed to it. The attribution is theirs, in interviews, rather than an inference from the pages.
entries.application: When you read a series' shape as authorial intent, mark the claim as uncertain. `checklist-16`'s credit audit exists for exactly this: to stop you asserting authorship of a decision the record does not support.
entries._label: Serialisation, the Magazine and the Market

entries.category: The Editor's Authority and the Uncredited Hand
entries.name: The Editor Rotates and the Serial Does Not
entries.description: The staffing fact that makes the relationship unlike a book editor's, and what it costs a long series.
entries.principle: Editors are salaried publishing employees on career tracks, moved between magazines and promoted out of hands-on work, and a serial running eight years will usually outlive two or three of them. Each handover resets the accumulated understanding of what the series is trying to do, and a new editor arrives with a mandate to improve numbers rather than to protect a plan. The practical effect is that **the institution's memory of your series is shorter than your series**, and the argument you won in year two has to be won again in year five against someone who was not there.
entries.example: *重版出来! / Jūhan Shuttai!* is set inside the editorial department rather than the studio, and its most useful contribution to a writer's expectations is showing editors as employees with their own supervisors, quotas and transfers.
entries.application: Write down the reasoning behind your structural decisions, not just the decisions. `craft-44` is about which note to refuse; refusing a note is much harder when the person giving it does not know why the alternative was rejected three years ago.
entries._label: Serialisation, the Magazine and the Market

entries.category: The Editor's Authority and the Uncredited Hand
entries.name: The Assistant System Is an Employment Arrangement
entries.description: What the assistant system is, as distinct from what it looks like on the credits page.
entries.principle: Weekly page rates are impossible for one person to meet at professional finish, so a serialised artist runs a small workshop: assistants doing backgrounds, tone, effects and inking, often living or working on site during deadline weeks. The arrangement is a genuine apprenticeship — a large share of professional mangaka came up through it — and it is also a job with hours, and it sits outside the credit system almost entirely. **The workshop is normal, expected and structural, not a shortcut or a scandal**, and treating it as an embarrassment misreads the medium's basic economics.
entries.example: *鉄腕アトム / Tetsuwan Atomu* was produced under the earliest version of this arrangement, and the Tokiwa-sō circle around Tezuka Osamu functioned as the medium's first training pipeline — several of the postwar industry's central figures passed through it as assistants or neighbours.
entries.application: `craft-45` and `craft-46` cover what you can hand to hands that are not yours. Budget for it at the planning stage: if your page design assumes only what you personally can draw weekly, you have designed a series you cannot serialise.
entries._label: Serialisation, the Magazine and the Market

entries.category: The Editor's Authority and the Uncredited Hand
entries.name: Who Pays the Assistants
entries.description: The money question, with the contested part marked as contested.
entries.principle: The standard account is that assistants are the serialised artist's expense, paid out of the page rate before the artist keeps anything, which makes a mid-list weekly serial a business that can run at a loss while looking like a success. That account is well attested in first-person industry writing. It is not uniform: practice varies by publisher and era, some assistant costs have been subsidised, and the informality of the arrangements is itself part of what makes them hard to state precisely — several researchers of the industry's labour arrangements note that the terms are frequently unwritten. **What a writer should take is the structure rather than a number**: the artist is the employer, the page rate is the pool, and volume royalties are where the income actually is.
entries.example: *サルでも描けるまんが教室 / Saru demo Kakeru Manga Kyōshitsu* is a satire of manga production by two industry insiders, and its treatment of what a serial actually earns and spends is sharper than its jokes.
entries.application: This is why `serial-44`'s point — that volume sales are the real verdict — is an economic claim and not an aesthetic one. If you are planning a career rather than a story, plan around the tankōbon.
entries._label: Serialisation, the Magazine and the Market

entries.category: The Editor's Authority and the Uncredited Hand
entries.name: Two People, One Name
entries.description: The pen name that conceals a partnership, and what happens when the partnership ends.
entries.principle: A single author name on a manga is not evidence of a single author. Duos and collectives have worked under one name throughout the medium's history, sometimes dividing story from art, sometimes dividing by series, sometimes genuinely co-writing. The reader cannot tell from the credit, the publisher has no reason to clarify, and the arrangement usually only becomes visible when it dissolves — at which point the back catalogue has to be reattributed retroactively. For a writer, the lesson is about the credit's information content: **the name on a manga tells you who is contracted, not who wrote it**.
entries.example: *ドラえもん / Doraemon* was published under the shared name Fujiko Fujio, used by Fujimoto Hiroshi and Abiko Motoo; when the partnership was dissolved in the late 1980s the two separated their names and the series' authorship was restated publicly, which is why the credit you see today differs from the credit on the early volumes.
entries.application: `craft-49` is about working under a name that is not one person. Before you attribute a technique to an author in your own notes, check whether the name is a person or a contract.
entries._label: Serialisation, the Magazine and the Market

entries.category: The Editor's Authority and the Uncredited Hand
entries.name: The Studio Under a Single Signature
entries.description: Industrial production of a serial, and the rare case where it is stated openly.
entries.principle: At the top of the market a long-running serial can be a company: a named principal setting story and direction, a permanent staff producing the pages, and a production line that continues through the principal's illness or death. This is a difference of degree from the assistant workshop rather than of kind, but past a certain size the difference of degree is the whole story, because the work is no longer something one person could produce and no longer stops when one person does. Most studios of this size present as a single author anyway; **the honest ones publish the staff, and the publication is the exception rather than the norm**.
entries.example: *ゴルゴ13 / Golgo 13* has been produced by Saitō Takao's studio on an explicit division-of-labour model that Saitō described publicly and defended as the correct way to make a long serial, and the series has continued past his death in 2021.
entries.application: `craft-48` covers collective authorship and the divided task. If you intend to work this way, decide the credit policy before the first volume, not after the studio is twelve people.
entries._label: Serialisation, the Magazine and the Market

entries.category: The Editor's Authority and the Uncredited Hand
entries.name: What the Editor Cannot Take
entries.description: The limits of the arrangement, which are real and are not where a foreign writer expects them.
entries.principle: The Japanese arrangement is not work-for-hire. Authorship rests with the manga artist, publishers acquire rights by contract rather than by default, and the practical evidence is that creators move series between publishers, revive them decades later and control adaptation participation in ways an American work-for-hire creator historically could not. The editor's authority is therefore enormous inside the serial and thin outside it: **strong over what the next chapter is, weak over who owns the series**. Set against Superhero's continuity collection, this is the sharpest institutional contrast the two packs offer.
entries.example: *劇画漂流 / Gekiga Hyōryū* records the postwar period from the author's side, and its account of moving between publishers, markets and formats is a portrait of a system in which the creator, not the imprint, is the continuous thing.
entries.application: `subgenre-29` cards the movement this example belongs to, and its history is largely a history of creators moving between markets rather than of imprints acquiring them. When you compare the two industries, compare the ownership rule first — most of the other differences are downstream of it.
entries._label: Serialisation, the Magazine and the Market

entries.category: The Editor's Authority and the Uncredited Hand
entries.name: The Credit Page and What It Omits
entries.description: How to read a manga's credits, and what a writer should record when they cannot.
entries.principle: A volume's credits typically name the author and the publisher. They may name a supervisor or researcher; they usually do not name the editor, the assistants, the letterer or the design staff, and where a collective is involved the internal division is normally invisible. This is a documentation problem before it is a fairness problem: scholarship and criticism about the medium is written from an incomplete record, and confident claims about who did what are frequently claims about who was contracted. **Absence of a credit is not evidence of absence of a contributor.**
entries.example: *聖伝-RG VEDA- / Seiden -RG VEDA-* was produced by CLAMP, a group whose membership and internal division of labour have changed across its career; the group's name on the cover is accurate and tells a reader nothing about which member did what on a given page.
entries.application: `checklist-16` audits collaboration and credit. Use it before writing about another creator's work: state what the record supports and mark the rest as unknown rather than inferring it.
entries._label: Serialisation, the Magazine and the Market

entries.category: Doujinshi, the Platform and the Systems Beside the System
entries.name: Comiket Is Infrastructure
entries.description: The self-published circuit described as a production system rather than as fan activity.
entries.principle: The doujinshi circuit is a functioning parallel industry — regular large-scale markets, tens of thousands of participating circles per event, specialist printers geared to short runs and event deadlines, and retail shops carrying self-published work. It has its own calendar, its own economics and its own distribution, and it is not a hobbyist fringe attached to the commercial industry but a second system running beside it with people and material crossing constantly in both directions. Comiket, running twice yearly since 1975, is its centre of gravity. **A writer who classifies it as fandom will not understand where the professional supply comes from.**
entries.example: *げんしけん / Genshiken* is a commercially serialised manga about a university club that produces doujinshi, and its most useful passages are procedural: the print run, the deadline, the table, the money.
entries.application: `subgenre-33` cards the circuit as a movement and lineage. This card is the operational half — read them together before writing a character who is "in doujinshi", because the specifics are the characterisation.
entries._label: Serialisation, the Magazine and the Market

entries.category: Doujinshi, the Platform and the Systems Beside the System
entries.name: The Circle, Not the Author
entries.description: The unit of production in the amateur system, and why it is not the individual.
entries.principle: The circle — a named group, sometimes one person under a group name, sometimes a durable collective — is the entity that registers for a market, holds the table, publishes the book and accumulates a reputation. It is the amateur system's version of the studio, and it has the same effect on credit: the name that carries the work is the group's. The circle also imposes the production discipline that makes the circuit a training ground, because a table booked for a fixed date is a deadline with a physical consequence, and **a deadline that cannot be renegotiated teaches scheduling faster than any amount of advice**.
entries.example: *げんしけん / Genshiken* follows a circle across production cycles rather than a single creator, which is the accurate frame, and its second half is largely about what the group owes the market date.
entries.application: If you are building a working practice rather than one book, the transferable part of this system is the fixed external date. `serial-13`'s weekly, monthly and quarterly rhythms are the commercial version of the same discipline; the circuit supplies a version of it to people with no contract.
entries._label: Serialisation, the Magazine and the Market

entries.category: Doujinshi, the Platform and the Systems Beside the System
entries.name: The Tolerated Infringement
entries.description: The legal position of derivative doujinshi, with both sides of the argument carried and neither settled.
entries.principle: A large share of doujinshi is derivative of commercially published work, and in strict copyright terms much of it is infringing. It is nevertheless widely tolerated, and the toleration is a stable equilibrium rather than an oversight. The industry-benefit argument holds that the circuit is unpaid market research, a talent pipeline and a promotional engine for the source works, and that rights holders decline to act because acting would cost them more than it recovers. The rights argument holds that toleration is a discretionary permission that can be withdrawn at any moment, that enforcement has occurred when it suited a rights holder, and that a permission structure resting on inaction protects no one reliably. Both are argued by people close to the industry; **this pack states the positions and does not settle them**, and a writer should notice that the arrangement is customary rather than legal.
entries.example: *Adult Manga: Culture and Power in Contemporary Japanese Society* examines the amateur movement's relationship to the commercial publishers directly, including the periods when that relationship was hostile rather than symbiotic.
entries.application: Write the ambiguity rather than resolving it. A character in this world is operating on custom rather than on permission, and `subgenre-33` carries the circuit's own account of how that custom came to hold.
entries._label: Serialisation, the Magazine and the Market

entries.category: Doujinshi, the Platform and the Systems Beside the System
entries.name: The Circuit as Talent Pipeline
entries.description: How amateur publication became a recruiting ground, and the part of that history usually left out.
entries.principle: Editors attend the markets, scout, and recruit; a substantial number of professional creators arrived through self-publication rather than through magazine competitions, and some brought their circle with them. The pipeline is real and is one of the medium's genuine advantages over industries with a single gate. The part usually omitted is what much of the late-1970s and 1980s amateur boom actually consisted of: **the erotic amateur market drove the circuit's growth, and the same growth produced the material that fuelled the 1990–91 harmful-manga campaign and the regulation that followed**. A history of the pipeline that mentions only the careers is not a history of the pipeline.
entries.example: *シベール / Cybele*, a 1979 amateur publication, is conventionally cited as the origin point of that erotic amateur boom, and it is cited as often in accounts of the subsequent regulatory backlash as in accounts of the careers that followed.
entries.application: If your story sends a character up this pipeline, decide what they were publishing. `checklist-14`'s sensitive content audit applies to the depiction and `subgenre-32` carries the transgressive line's own history.
entries._label: Serialisation, the Magazine and the Market

entries.category: Doujinshi, the Platform and the Systems Beside the System
entries.name: The Serial That Started on a Website
entries.description: The web-origin path into commercial publication, and what it changes about the first reader.
entries.principle: A work can now be published to an open platform, accumulate an audience without any institutional filter, and be acquired by a publisher on the strength of that audience. This inverts the classical sequence: the magazine's function was to identify what people would buy, and a web work arrives with that question already answered. What it does not do is make the institution unnecessary — the acquired work is usually redrawn, restructured or re-serialised, and the editorial relationship starts at that point. **Discovery has moved; production has not.**
entries.example: *Axis powers ヘタリア / Axis Powers Hetalia* began as a web publication and moved into commercial print and adaptation on the strength of its online readership, without a magazine having selected it first.
entries.application: `checklist-9`'s magazine fit audit still applies after acquisition, not before it. The audience you arrive with is leverage in the first conversation and is not a substitute for the conversation.
entries._label: Serialisation, the Magazine and the Market

entries.category: Doujinshi, the Platform and the Systems Beside the System
entries.name: The App, the Scroll and the Webtoon
entries.description: The digital reading formats now competing with the magazine, named specifically rather than gestured at.
entries.principle: Two distinct things are often collapsed into "digital manga". The first is the publisher app — free or cheap chapter access on a phone, with the page as the unit and the same editorial apparatus behind it, which is the magazine's function ported to a new carrier. The second is the webtoon: a Korean-origin format built for vertical scroll, usually in colour, with no page turn, no spread and no fixed panel grid, whose formal instrument is the controlled length of scroll between panels rather than the turn. **The second is a different grammar, not a delivery change**, and a writer moving between them is changing craft rather than platform. This pack's page-and-panel collection is written for the page; almost none of its turn material transfers.
entries.example: *ワンパンマン / One-Punch Man* moved from a web original to a redrawn commercial serialisation, and the redraw — rather than the original — is what carries the page-based grammar the print market expects.
entries.application: Decide which grammar you are writing before you plan a chapter. `craft-3` on the chapter's last panel assumes a page turn exists; on a scroll it does not.
entries._label: Serialisation, the Magazine and the Market

entries.category: Doujinshi, the Platform and the Systems Beside the System
entries.name: The Rental Shop System
entries.description: The postwar kashihon market, and why a dead distribution system still matters to a writer.
entries.principle: Before the weekly magazines consolidated the market, a large part of manga reached readers through rental shops: cheap volumes produced for lending rather than sale, on a distribution circuit with different economics and — crucially — a different readership. The rental audience skewed older and poorer than the magazine audience, which permitted darker, slower and more violent material than a children's weekly would carry, and the formal experiments that permission allowed did not disappear when the market did. **A separate distribution channel is a separate permission structure**, which is the general lesson and the reason this card is not merely historical.
entries.example: *黒い吹雪 / Kuroi Fubuki* is a mid-1950s rental-market work by Tatsumi Yoshihiro, produced in the conditions that shortly after produced the gekiga label itself.
entries.application: `subgenre-31` cards the rental tradition. When you find a formal move you cannot place, check whether it entered the mainstream from a channel with different constraints — most of them did.
entries._label: Serialisation, the Magazine and the Market

entries.category: Doujinshi, the Platform and the Systems Beside the System
entries.name: The Magazine That Paid in Freedom
entries.description: The alternative magazine's actual bargain, stated without romance.
entries.principle: The alternative and art magazines that shaped the medium's serious reputation ran on very small circulations and paid their contributors very little or nothing at all. The bargain was explicit: no editorial direction, no survey, no commercial obligation, and no money. It produced work that could not have appeared anywhere else, and it produced it by transferring the cost onto the creators, most of whom held other work. **Freedom in this system was purchased by the artist**, and accounts that treat the alternative magazine purely as a haven omit who paid for it.
entries.example: *赤色エレジー / Sekishoku Elegy* was serialised in Garo at the start of the 1970s and is among the strongest arguments for what the arrangement made possible; the arrangement's terms were nevertheless what they were.
entries.application: `subgenre-30` cards the Garo lineage. If you are choosing between an outlet with notes and an outlet without them, price the second one honestly before choosing it.
entries._label: Serialisation, the Magazine and the Market

entries.category: Doujinshi, the Platform and the Systems Beside the System
entries.name: The Experimental Magazine as a School
entries.description: The short-lived magazine whose real output was a generation of technique.
entries.principle: Some magazines mattered far beyond their circulation or lifespan because they functioned as a laboratory: a place where established creators could publish work with no commercial obligation, where the resulting formal experiments were read closely by younger creators, and where the argument about what the medium could do was conducted in public. Their business records look like failures and their influence does not. **Judge a magazine by what its readers went on to make**, not by how long it ran or what it sold.
entries.example: *ジュン / Jun* by Ishinomori Shōtarō, published in COM in the late 1960s, is the standard example of the experimental register such a magazine permitted — near-wordless, structurally loose, and closer to visual poetry than to story manga.
entries.application: The Page, Panel and the Turn collection's wordless-sequence material draws on this line directly. If you want to see what the medium's grammar can do without a commercial brief attached, this is the seam to read.
entries._label: Serialisation, the Magazine and the Market

entries.category: Doujinshi, the Platform and the Systems Beside the System
entries.name: What the Side Systems Send Back
entries.description: The closing argument of the collection: the parallel systems are not a sideshow, they are the supply.
entries.principle: Every system described in this category returns material to the mainstream. The rental market supplied gekiga and its adult register; the alternative magazines supplied the formal vocabulary that literary manga now takes for granted; the doujinshi circuit supplies creators, audiences and tested premises; the web platforms supply finished works with proven readerships. The traffic is continuous and it runs mostly inward. The practical consequence for a writer is that **the mainstream's next convention is currently being worked out somewhere with no editor and no survey**, and the magazine's function has always been to notice it late and buy it.
entries.example: *忍者武芸帳 影丸伝 / Ninja Bugeichō Kagemaru-den* was a rental-market work by Shirato Sanpei, and its author's subsequent central place in Garo is the clearest single line from a side system into the magazine that redefined what the medium was allowed to be.
entries.application: This closes the collection. `serial-1` argued the magazine is a filter; this card names what it filters. When you look for what manga will be doing in five years, look at the systems that do not have to sell advertising.
entries._label: Serialisation, the Magazine and the Market

entries.category: Reading Order and the Direction of Time
entries.name: Right to Left Is a Clock
entries.description: The foundational claim of the collection: on a manga page, position is time.
entries.principle: Panels are read right to left and top to bottom, and that path is not a convention laid over the story — it is the story's clock. A panel's position on the sheet states when it happens, how long after the last thing it happens, and what it is adjacent to. This is the medium's equivalent of what `literary:style-1` calls syntax performing an interpretive claim, and the difference is the whole reason this collection exists: in prose the argument is carried by grammar the reader decodes in a single linear stream, and here it is carried by **a two-dimensional arrangement the reader's eye traverses in an order the page itself dictates**. Change the arrangement and you change the sequence of time, having changed no content at all.
entries.example: *AKIRA* is the standard demonstration in English, because early US editions were mirrored to read left to right — and mirroring preserves every panel's content while reversing the clock, which is why the flipped editions read differently to anyone who has seen both.
