entries.application: Before you write a page, decide the order of its moments, then place them. `craft-47` argues the layout is the real manuscript; this card says what the layout is made of.

entries.category: Reading Order and the Direction of Time
entries.name: Where the Eye Enters
entries.description: The entry point of a page, and the diagonal that carries the eye off it.
entries.principle: A reader's eye lands at the top right and leaves at the bottom left, and everything between is a path the artist either controls or surrenders. The controlling instruments are figure direction, the tilt of panel borders, the placement of the largest black mass and the position of the first balloon. When a page reads slowly for no reason a writer can name, the usual cause is that two elements are competing to be the entry point. `craft-2` owns the question of what the first panel must *do* after a week's gap — orientation and advance in one image. This card is about something else and adjacent to it: **not what the first panel says, but how the reader finds it, and where the page then sends them**. `superhero:craft-10` states the neighbouring claim from the other drawn tradition — that the finished page is the artist's account of the scene rather than the writer's — and the entry point is the clearest case of it: a writer can specify what the first image shows and cannot specify where the eye lands.
entries.example: *ポーの一族 / Pō no Ichizoku* uses the shōjo page's diagonal freely, letting figures and decorative fields cross the reading path rather than sit inside boxes, and the eye's route through such a page is set almost entirely by figure direction.
entries.application: Print the page at thumbnail size, where content is illegible and only masses remain. If the entry point is not obvious at that scale it is not obvious at reading speed either.

entries.category: Reading Order and the Direction of Time
entries.name: The Panel That Holds Two Moments
entries.description: A single frame containing more than one instant, which prose cannot do at all.
entries.principle: A panel is not a photograph of one moment. It can hold a figure drawn twice mid-movement, a motion trail that shows the path as well as the position, an action and its consequence in the same frame, or a background whose time differs from its foreground's. The reader accepts all of these without instruction. This is the sharpest available delta against the library's prose collections: `literary:style-2` describes a long sentence accumulating clauses to enact duration, and it is still linear — the clauses arrive one at a time. **A panel holding two moments delivers them simultaneously and lets the reader order them**, which no sentence can do.
entries.example: *火の鳥 / Hi no Tori* uses the device across its run, including panels where a figure's several positions are drawn into one frame so the movement is read as a shape rather than as a sequence.
entries.application: When a beat costs you a panel you cannot afford, ask whether it can be folded into the previous frame as a second moment rather than cut. `craft-27` divides the labour — let the art carry the physical and the spatial and reserve language for cause and rule — and a second moment inside a frame is that division used for time as well as space. This is the medium's cheapest compression and the one prose writers reach for last.

entries.category: Reading Order and the Direction of Time
entries.name: The Broken Frame
entries.description: What happens to time when a figure leaves its panel.
entries.principle: A figure that crosses a border, a panel that bleeds off the sheet, a frame dissolved into a field of tone — each detaches its content from the clock the grid is keeping. The effect is not decoration. A bordered panel says *this took a measurable interval*; an unbordered one says *this is outside the count* — a state rather than an event, memory rather than action, or an emotion with no duration attached. The grammar is well established and reads reliably, which means it can be used precisely rather than atmospherically.
entries.example: *風と木の詩 / Kaze to Ki no Uta* uses dissolved and overlapping frames as a standard register rather than as an exception, and the pages where the frames return to a strict grid land as a change of tense.
entries.application: Compare this with `comedy:timing-28`, where escalation requires an axis chosen in advance. The same discipline applies: if every page has broken frames, none of them is doing anything. Establish the grid first so the departure means something — which is `page-14`.

entries.category: Reading Order and the Direction of Time
entries.name: When the Path Is Deliberately Unclear
entries.description: The rare, precise use of an ambiguous reading order, and the difference between that and a mistake.
entries.principle: Almost every page should have one obvious path. A small number of pages are better with two, or with none — a layout where the reader hesitates, backtracks, or reads a cluster as a simultaneous field rather than as a sequence. The effect is disorientation produced by the act of reading rather than described in the content, and it belongs to dream, panic, dissociation and revelation. It is also indistinguishable from incompetence unless the surrounding pages are conspicuously well ordered, so **the technique requires an established baseline more than any other in this collection**. This is the visual analogue of `literary:style-14`: the reader is made to work against the surface, and the working is the meaning.
entries.example: *ジュン / Jun* by Ishinomori Shōtarō, published in COM in the late 1960s, is the standard reference for the experimental register — largely wordless, structurally loose, and closer to visual poetry than to story manga.
entries.application: Use it once in a chapter at most, and place a strictly ordered page on either side. `serial-69` explains why so much of this vocabulary was worked out in magazines with no commercial obligation.

entries.category: The Page Turn as a Beat
entries.name: The Turn Is the Only Cut the Reader Performs
entries.description: The medium's single most powerful structural device, and the reason it is not available in prose.
entries.principle: Turning the page is a physical act the reader carries out, in their own time, without knowing what is on the other side. That makes the turn the one edit in the medium the audience executes themselves — and self-executed reveals land harder than delivered ones. `comedy:timing-1` describes the setup-and-punchline unit, an expectation installed and then replaced in a single stroke; the page turn is that unit given a body, with the reader's own hand performing the replacement. Everything else in this section is a consequence. Note the boundary with `craft-3`, which owns the chapter's last panel as the highest-leverage compositional position: that card is about what a week of waiting does to an image. **This one is about what three seconds and a hand movement do to it**, and the two positions are different — most turns are not chapter ends.
entries.example: *MONSTER* is built on the device at close to its maximum density, with reveals repeatedly placed immediately after a turn rather than at the end of the visible spread.
entries.application: Mark every turn position in your layout before you place a single panel. If your reveals are not sitting on them, you are writing a script that happens to be drawn.

entries.category: The Page Turn as a Beat
entries.name: The Spread Is the Unit, Not the Page
entries.description: What a reader actually sees at one time, which is two pages and not one.
entries.principle: An open book presents a left page and a right page simultaneously, so anything on the left half of a spread has already been seen when the reader arrives at it. The consequence is exact and constantly overlooked: **the only concealed position in the entire volume is the far side of a turn**, which in right-to-left reading is the page following the left-hand page of the current spread. A reveal placed at the bottom of a recto that the reader has been looking at for thirty seconds is not a reveal. Prose has no equivalent problem — `literary:style-1` can suspend a subject to the end of a sentence and nothing shows the reader the ending early.
entries.example: *鉄コン筋クリート / Tekkonkinkreet* composes across both halves of the spread often enough that the spread, rather than the page, is clearly the design unit — a large space treated as one field rather than two.
entries.application: `checklist-6`'s first question — is the chapter's strongest image on a page the reader cannot preview before turning — is this card made operational, and it is the one item in that audit a script cannot answer. Lay out in spreads and never in single pages. If your layout tool shows one page at a time, you are working blind on the medium's basic unit.

entries.category: The Page Turn as a Beat
entries.name: Withholding Across the Turn
entries.description: The mechanics of getting a question and its answer onto opposite sides of a turn.
entries.principle: The technique has three parts and all three are positional. Put the question in the last-read panel of the left-hand page, where the reader's eye exits. Make the question legible enough that a reader will not skip to answer it — an ambiguous one produces a shrug rather than a turn. And give the answer the dominant position on the next page, because a reveal that arrives in a small panel among five others has been diluted by everything beside it. `comedy:timing-12` is the closest prose-craft neighbour: one setup resolved twice, the second not invalidating the first. The turn's version is stronger because **the interval between the two resolutions is controlled by the reader's hand rather than by the writer's line breaks**.
entries.example: *進撃の巨人 / Attack on Titan* places its structural reveals on turn positions with unusual regularity, and the serialised chapters are noticeably built around them.
entries.application: `trope-1` cards the cliffhanger turn as a narrative device; this is its physical substrate, and the reason a cliffhanger placed one page early is not a weaker cliffhanger but an absent one. Count the turns in your chapter and list what each one hides. An unused turn is not neutral — it is the reader being told, physically, that nothing has changed.

entries.category: The Page Turn as a Beat
entries.name: The Turn That Lands on Nothing
entries.description: The most common failure in the section, and why it is usually arithmetic rather than judgement.
entries.principle: Turns fall at fixed positions determined by pagination, so a reveal written for a turn that ends up on the visible half of a spread is not weakened but spent. The cause is almost always counting: a page added or removed upstream moves every turn after it by one. `craft-1` owns the fixed chapter length as a panel budget and the decision of what to cut; this card is downstream of that decision and is about a different quantity — **not how many panels you can afford, but which sheet each one lands on after the count changes**. `comedy:timing-1` is the fence: a setup and its punchline are a unit only if the second half arrives when the audience expects the replacement, and here the arrival point is set by pagination rather than by the writer. Editors do not usually catch it, because they read the boards as a sequence of pages rather than as an object with a spine.
entries.example: *ヒカルの碁 / Hikaru no Go* is a useful positive case: its reveals sit on turns consistently enough that the layout was clearly planned around pagination rather than adjusted afterwards.
entries.application: Renumber the pages after every structural edit and re-check each reveal's parity. `checklist-6`'s page and panel audit is the place to keep the habit.

entries.category: The Page Turn as a Beat
entries.name: The Turns Move Between Serial and Volume
entries.description: A page-level consequence of the medium's two publication formats.
entries.principle: A chapter's turn positions depend on where it starts in the object it is printed in. Colour openers, advertising, front matter and a volume's chapter-break pages all shift pagination, so a chapter carefully built around turns in a magazine can have every one of those turns land differently in the collected volume — and the volume, as `serial-41` argues, is the text posterity reads. Some artists repaginate at volume stage for exactly this reason; most do not, and the effect is a body of work whose turn structure is intact in the disposable object and degraded in the durable one. This is where the analogy with `literary:style-1` finally breaks: a sentence's form travels with it into every edition, and a page's form does not survive being bound differently.
entries.example: *ワンパンマン / One-Punch Man* is an instructive case of the general problem: the commercially redrawn version is paginated for print, and the page-based grammar it carries is not the grammar of the web original it derives from.
entries.application: If you can repaginate for the volume, do it and record what changed. If you cannot, favour reveals that survive as ordinary panels — the ones that die when the turn moves are the ones that relied entirely on concealment.

entries.category: Panel, Gutter and the Shape of a Pause
entries.name: The Gutter Is the Interval
entries.description: The foundational claim of the section: the empty space between panels is where time passes.
entries.principle: Nothing is drawn in the gutter and everything happens there. Two adjacent panels state two moments; the reader supplies the transition, and the width of the gap is the medium's crudest and most reliable duration cue — narrow gutters read fast, wide ones read slow, and a gutter widened to a band of empty page reads as a held breath. This is where the comparison with prose is most instructive and most limited. `literary:style-2` describes accumulation enacting duration inside a sentence; the sentence must spend words to spend time. **A page spends silence, and silence on a sheet costs area rather than words**, which is why a wordless pause in this medium is expensive in a way its prose equivalent is not.
entries.example: *蟲師 / Mushishi* uses generous inter-panel space as a standing register, and the effect is a reading pace measurably slower than a battle serial's with no change in the amount of incident.
entries.application: `checklist-6` asks where the reader's pace is being controlled and where it has been left to chance; gutter width is the answer most layouts leave to chance. Set your widths deliberately once per chapter and treat any change as a statement. Uniform gutters are a valid choice; unconsidered ones are not a choice at all.

entries.category: Panel, Gutter and the Shape of a Pause
entries.name: Panel Size Is Duration
entries.description: The most reliable single lever on reading speed, and its limits.
entries.principle: A reader spends time roughly in proportion to a panel's area, so size is the primary control on pace — a page of eight small panels is read in a fraction of the time a page of two takes, whatever their contents. The lever has a ceiling: past a certain size the panel stops reading as *longer* and starts reading as *louder*, which is `page-13`'s subject and a different effect. `superhero:craft-9` states the neighbouring claim from the other tradition — that scale is composition rather than caption — and this card adds the temporal half: **in a serialised drawn medium, a big panel does not only assert importance, it consumes reading time, and the two effects can be used against each other**.
entries.example: *バガボンド / Vagabond* alternates dense small-panel sequences with pages given almost entirely to one image, and the contrast rather than either register is what sets the book's rhythm.
entries.application: Time yourself reading your own page. If the panel you consider most important is not the one you looked at longest, its size is wrong.

entries.category: Panel, Gutter and the Shape of a Pause
entries.name: The Tall Panel and the Held Beat
entries.description: Aspect ratio as an instrument, distinct from size.
entries.principle: A panel's shape does work its area does not. A tall narrow panel isolates a figure and reads as a beat rather than as a scene; a wide shallow one reads as a pan and carries motion across the page; a square reads as neutral and disappears. Because reading order runs right to left, a column of tall panels also delivers its beats at a fixed rhythm with no room for the eye to wander, which makes it the closest thing the medium has to a metronome. This is a distinction the prose collections cannot make at all — `literary:style-1`'s claim that form performs meaning is the right frame, and **the form performing it here is a rectangle's proportions**.
entries.example: `subgenre-8` records where this repertoire came from — the shōjo magazines are where expanding a glance across a page became standard. *ベルサイユのばら / Berusaiyu no Bara* uses the tall figure panel as a standing device, and its emotional beats are frequently carried by shape and isolation rather than by expression or dialogue.
entries.application: When a sequence reads flat, change the aspect ratios before you change the content. Three squares in a row is usually the problem.

entries.category: Panel, Gutter and the Shape of a Pause
entries.name: The Grid and the Departure From It
entries.description: Why a regular layout is what makes an irregular one legible.
entries.principle: A consistent grid — the same divisions page after page — is not a lack of ambition. It is a baseline, and every departure from it means something only in proportion to how firmly the baseline is established. Work that varies its layout on every page has no departures available, because nothing is normal. This is exactly the requirement `comedy:timing-28` states for escalation: the axis must be chosen in advance, and a sequence that escalates on everything at once escalates on nothing. **The grid is that axis, drawn.**
entries.example: `subgenre-2` argues the yonkoma's four-panel count is structural rather than incidental, which is the strongest available case for a grid as an instrument. *サザエさん / Sazae-san* runs on that unvarying four-panel vertical grid, and the constraint is precisely what lets a single departure — a panel divided, a figure crossing a border — register at all.
entries.application: Establish your grid in the first chapter and count your departures per chapter. If the number is above about three, the grid is not a baseline and your emphases are competing with each other rather than with silence.

entries.category: Panel, Gutter and the Shape of a Pause
entries.name: Where the Silence Sits
entries.description: The wordless panel as a positional decision rather than a content one.
entries.principle: `craft-25` owns the wordless panel as a conversational turn — treat a silent panel as a line of dialogue, and if you cannot write the sentence it replaces, cut it. That is what to put in it. This card is the other half: **where it goes**. A wordless panel at the end of a row reads as a pause inside a beat; at the foot of a page it reads as a stop; on the far side of a turn it reads as an answer withheld; and several in a column read as duration rather than as silence. The same panel, with the same content, does four different things depending on position, and none of that is visible from a script. `horror:craft-11` makes the neighbouring point in another genre — that intensity comes from specificity rather than magnitude — and the positional version is that a silence's power comes from where it falls, not from how many panels it occupies.
entries.example: *SLAM DUNK* is the standard case: its late sequences run long stretches with no dialogue at all, and the silence is structural — the reading pace and the position of the wordless panels carry the tension rather than any statement of it.
entries.application: Take your silent panels and move each one panel later, then read the page again. If nothing changes, the silence was decorative and `craft-25`'s test will already have told you so.

entries.category: The Spread, the Splash and Scale
entries.name: What a Splash Costs
entries.description: The foundational claim of the section: scale in this medium is bought, and the currency is the rest of the chapter.
entries.principle: A full-page image is not a large panel, it is a page, and it is subtracted from a fixed count. `superhero:craft-9` states the compositional half of this from the other drawn tradition — scale is asserted by composition rather than by a caption calling something enormous — and this card adds the economic half the serialised medium forces: **the splash is the only compositional device in the medium with a fixed, knowable price**, and the price is roughly a twentieth of a weekly chapter. That is why splashes in weekly serials cluster at first appearances, deaths and turns, and why a book that spends them evenly has usually not decided what its chapter is about. `craft-1` owns the panel budget and the decision of what to cut; this is the same arithmetic seen from the other end, where the question is not what to remove but what a single image is worth.
entries.example: *北斗の拳 / Hokuto no Ken* spends full-page images on a small, repeated set of story positions, and the regularity is legible as a policy rather than as an impulse.
entries.application: Count your splashes per chapter and name what each one buys. If you cannot say what a splash is for in a sentence, it is a drawing you liked.

entries.category: The Spread, the Splash and Scale
entries.name: The Spread Cannot Be Revealed
entries.description: The structural cost of the medium's largest image, which almost nobody prices in.
entries.principle: A double-page spread occupies both halves of what the reader sees at once, so **the reader always sees it arriving**. There is no version of a spread that lands as a surprise, because the act of turning to it exposes it whole. `page-7` establishes that the only concealed position in the volume is the far side of a turn; this is the corollary nobody likes — the biggest image in the medium is structurally the least surprising one. `comedy:timing-1`'s setup-and-punchline unit requires the replacement to arrive in a single stroke, and a spread cannot do that: it is all arrival and no installation. What a spread does instead is **hold**, which is a different and slower effect.
entries.example: *うずまき / Uzumaki* uses spreads for spatial and bodily distortion rather than for shocks, and the choice reads as an understanding of the format — the horror is in the sustained looking, not in the reveal.
entries.application: If your spread is a surprise, move it: put the surprise immediately after a turn, in a single panel, and give the spread the beat after it. Spreads are for what the reader must dwell on.

entries.category: The Spread, the Splash and Scale
entries.name: Scale Is Measured Against a Body
entries.description: How a reader judges size on a drawn page, and why an unmeasured colossus reads as small.
entries.principle: A drawn object has no size except in relation to something the reader already knows, and in practice that something is a human figure. A giant drawn alone in a frame is a shape; the same giant drawn with a person at its ankle is a giant. The corollary is that scale collapses when the comparison is removed, which is why sustained sequences of enormous things become boring — the reader loses the reference and stops converting. `horror:craft-11` makes the neighbouring argument in prose terms, that bigger is not the same as worse and fear is proportional to specificity rather than magnitude; the drawn version is more mechanical than that, because **the specificity is literally a figure in the frame doing the measuring**.
entries.example: *鉄人28号 / Tetsujin 28-gō* stages its machine against streets, buildings and a boy, and the scale reads because the comparison is present in almost every panel that needs it.
entries.application: For every large thing, name the object in the frame that measures it. If there is none, the reader is looking at an abstraction — and `page-12`'s point applies: you have bought duration and not size.

entries.category: The Spread, the Splash and Scale
entries.name: What an Establishing Panel Is Actually For
entries.description: The wide shot as a working instrument rather than a habit imported from film.
entries.principle: The wide panel is usually explained by analogy to cinema, and the analogy misleads. A film's establishing shot is unavoidable — the camera must be somewhere — while a manga page can begin inside a face and never state the room at all, so a wide panel is always a *choice to spend area on space*. It earns that area when the geography will be load-bearing later, when the distance between two figures is the content, or when the reader needs a pause. `craft-2` owns the question of what a chapter's first panel must do after a week's gap — orient and advance at once. This card is the general case rather than the chapter-opening one: **orientation is a cost, and most pages should pay it partially or not at all**. `literary:style-2`'s accretive sentence spends clauses to build a place; the page spends area, and area is the scarcer of the two.
entries.example: *風の谷のナウシカ / Kaze no Tani no Nausicaä* spends heavily on wide panels and earns it, because the ecology it establishes is the thing the plot later turns on rather than scenery.
entries.application: For each wide panel, name the later page that depends on it. If none does, redraw it as a detail — a doorway, a pair of feet, a sign — which orients for a fraction of the area.

entries.category: The Spread, the Splash and Scale
entries.name: Small Is Also Scale
entries.description: The neglected half of the section: what a tiny panel or a tiny figure does.
entries.principle: Scale runs in both directions and the downward direction is under-used. A figure rendered small inside a large frame reads as isolated, watched, or insignificant, and the effect is produced by the ratio rather than by anything in the drawing. A small panel among large ones reads as an aside, a flinch, or a fact stated quickly. Because `superhero:craft-9` frames scale as the assertion of power, the tradition it comes from tends to run the lever one way only; the reverse is available and is often the more precise instrument, since **a reader who has to look closely at a small panel has been made to lean in, and leaning in is attention you did not have to ask for**.
entries.example: *岳 みんなの山 / Gaku: Minna no Yama* repeatedly places small human figures inside large mountain frames, and the ratio carries the book's argument about the mountains more efficiently than any statement of it could.
entries.application: Take your most emotionally loaded page and try the smallest version of its key panel. If the reduction makes the moment worse, the moment was relying on volume — which `page-12` says is duration and `page-16` says is money.

entries.category: Tone, Texture and the Monochrome Palette
entries.name: Monochrome Is a Palette
entries.description: The foundational claim of the section: the absence of colour is a system with its own vocabulary, not a limitation.
entries.principle: A manga page has a full palette — black, white, and a graded range of screentone and hatching between them — and every one of those values is a decision that colour would otherwise make. Because there is no colourist in the production chain at all, those decisions belong to the artist and the assistants and are made at the same stage as everything else, which is why value in this medium is usually more consistent than colour is in a traditionally coloured comic. `literary:style-1` argues that form performs the interpretive claim rather than reporting content; **value is that argument made in a register the prose collections have no card for at all** — a page's darkness is its mood, stated before a word is read and independently of what is depicted.
entries.example: *ブラック・ジャック / Black Jack* controls value tightly across long runs, and its pages can be read for mood at thumbnail size with the content illegible — which is the practical test for whether value is doing work.
entries.application: `craft-46` covers what can be handed to an assistant; value is the case where handing it over without a stated policy produces a book whose mood changes with the schedule. Photocopy a chapter at 25% and look only at light and dark. If every page looks the same, you have a texture rather than a palette.

entries.category: Tone, Texture and the Monochrome Palette
entries.name: Screentone Is a Register
entries.description: What tone actually signals, beyond filling grey.
entries.principle: Screentone marks a change of state as reliably as a tense change does in prose: a tone-flooded panel is interior, a remembered, a suspended or an emotionally saturated one, and a page that drops to bare white line has usually changed register deliberately. The convention is strongest in the shōjo repertoire, where tone was developed into a full vocabulary of flowers, screens, gradients and starbursts, and it carries into every other demographic in diluted form. `literary:style-2` describes accumulation enacting a mind under pressure; tone accumulates in the same way and in a different dimension, because **it can saturate a panel that also carries action, which a sentence cannot do without stopping to describe**.
entries.example: *ガラスの仮面 / Garasu no Kamen* uses tone as a standing emotional register rather than as shading, and its interior states are legible at a glance from tone alone.
entries.application: `subgenre-8` records where this vocabulary came from. Mark every tone change in a chapter and ask what state it announces; if two changes announce the same state, one of them is decoration.

entries.category: Tone, Texture and the Monochrome Palette
entries.name: Spotting the Blacks
entries.description: The distribution of solid black across a page, and why it is a composition decision rather than a rendering one.
entries.principle: Solid black is the heaviest element available and the eye finds it first, so where the blacks fall determines where the reader looks and in what order — before any panel border or figure direction has an effect. Distributed evenly, blacks stabilise a page; concentrated, they create a centre of gravity that can override the reading path established in `page-2`. This is the most direct available demonstration of `superhero:craft-9`'s claim that scale and emphasis are composition rather than caption, and the drawn medium's version is blunter: **a black mass in the wrong corner will beat any amount of intention about where the reader should start**.
entries.example: *デビルマン / Devilman* is built on aggressive black masses, and its pages are legible as composition at a distance where nothing representational can be made out.
entries.application: Squint at the page until only masses remain, then check whether the heaviest one is where the beat is. `checklist-6`'s question about white space collecting where the drawing was easiest is the same test from the other side.

entries.category: Tone, Texture and the Monochrome Palette
entries.name: White Is Not Empty
entries.description: Unmarked paper as an active element with its own meanings.
entries.principle: White does three distinct jobs and they are frequently confused. It is the ground everything sits on; it is the interval, as `page-11` argues for the gutter; and it is content — an unrendered background that places a figure nowhere in particular, a standard device for isolation, shock and interior speech. The third is what gets misread as unfinished. A page whose backgrounds drop away at the emotional peak is not saving labour, it is removing the world so that nothing competes, and readers of the form take the cue without instruction. `comedy:timing-28`'s requirement — the axis chosen in advance — applies exactly: if backgrounds are absent throughout, their absence at the peak says nothing.
entries.example: *海街diary / Umimachi Diary* keeps its pages open and its backgrounds present, so the moments when the world drops away register as a change rather than as the book's normal condition.
entries.application: Count the pages in your chapter with no drawn background. If it is most of them, you are not using the device; you are working at a level of finish that has taken the device away from you.

entries.category: Tone, Texture and the Monochrome Palette
entries.name: The Line Has a Voice
entries.description: Line quality as a register, and the one thing in this collection a writer genuinely cannot specify.
entries.principle: A brushed line, a ruled line, a scratchy pen line and a clean uniform contour are four different tones of voice, and the choice sets a reader's expectations about the work's seriousness, era and emotional temperature before a single event occurs. `superhero:craft-10` is the fence and it is the honest one: in a drawn medium the finished page is the artist's account of the scene rather than the writer's, and **line quality is the part of that account a script cannot reach at all**. A writer can ask for a mood; they cannot ask for a line. What a writer can do is know what the line they are working with is capable of, and stop writing scenes that fight it.
entries.example: *ねじ式 / Neji-shiki* is inseparable from its line — the same events rendered cleanly would not produce the dream register the work is read for.
entries.application: If you are writing for an artist, describe the register and never the technique. `craft-45` covers what can be handed to hands that are not yours; the line is the clearest case of something that cannot.

entries.category: Lettering, Sound and the Drawn Word
entries.name: Lettering Is Drawing
entries.description: The foundational claim of the section: text on a manga page is a graphic element competing for the same space as everything else.
entries.principle: A balloon is an object in the composition. It has mass, position and shape; it covers art; it sits in the reading path and can redirect it; and its tail is a pointer the eye follows. `craft-22` owns the writing consequence of this — a balloon is smaller than a sentence wants to be, so the meaning must arrive in the first few words — and `craft-32` owns the performance consequence, that lines must work with no voice at all. This card owns the third thing, which is neither: **the balloon as a shape on a page**, placed before it is filled, and frequently the element that determines whether a panel is legible. `superhero:craft-10`'s point holds here too — placement is the artist's, not the writer's — but unlike the line in `page-25`, balloon order is something a script can and should specify.
entries.example: *ドラえもん / Doraemon* is a study in this, because a children's page has no tolerance for ambiguity: balloons are placed so the reading order inside each panel is unmistakable, and the placement is doing as much work as the wording.
entries.application: Draft your dialogue into a thumbnail with boxes for balloons before you write the final lines. If the boxes do not fit, the problem is the scene's structure and not its wording.

entries.category: Lettering, Sound and the Drawn Word
entries.name: The Balloon's Shape Is Tone
entries.description: The standard vocabulary of balloon forms, and what each of them commits you to.
entries.principle: The forms are conventional and read reliably: a smooth oval is neutral speech; a jagged burst is volume or shock; a cloud is thought or reverie; a broken or dotted outline is a whisper, a weakened voice, or speech the speaker cannot fully commit to; a tailless balloon is a voice with no located body; and text with no balloon at all is usually narration or interior monologue. Because the vocabulary is stable, **it does the work `literary:style-14` calls unreliable narration by other means** — a line whose content is confident inside an outline that is trembling tells the reader to disbelieve the speaker, with no narrator required to intervene. `craft-22`'s front-loading rule still governs what goes inside; this card is about the container's own statement.
entries.example: *天才バカボン / Tensai Bakabon* treats balloon form as a comic instrument in its own right, with shape and lettering carrying delivery that the words on their own would not.
entries.application: Read a page's balloons with the text masked out and ask what emotional shape the page has. If every balloon is the same oval, you have a transcript.

entries.category: Lettering, Sound and the Drawn Word
entries.name: Sound Is Drawn, Not Typed
entries.description: Onomatopoeia as an art element, and the reason it is the medium's hardest thing to translate.
entries.principle: Japanese sound effects are drawn into the image — sized, angled, distorted and integrated with the composition — and they cover two categories English mostly lacks a habit for: giongo, sounds that things make, and gitaigo, which render states and textures that make no sound at all, including silence itself. Because the characters are part of the drawing rather than a layer on top of it, replacing them damages the panel, which is why translated editions choose between overlaying, redrawing and leaving them with a small gloss, and why none of the three is satisfactory. `superhero:craft-9`'s claim that composition rather than caption carries force is literal here: **the sound effect is a compositional mass first and a word second**.
entries.example: *あしたのジョー / Ashita no Joe* integrates its effects into the drawing so completely that they read as impact and motion rather than as text laid over the art.
entries.application: If you are writing for translation, note which effects are load-bearing graphically. `serial-49` names the licensed edition as a second object with its own format decisions — sound-effect handling explicitly among them — and this is the note that should travel with the work so the same choice is not remade differently in volume three.

entries.category: Lettering, Sound and the Drawn Word
entries.name: The Author in the Margin
entries.description: Handwritten asides outside the panel, and the second voice they install.
entries.principle: Small handwritten text in the margins, between panels or squeezed beside a figure is a standing device of the form: an authorial aside, a joke, a correction, a note about the deadline. It is distinct from narration because it is visibly *outside* the fiction — different handwriting, no balloon, no place in the panel's space — and it creates a second, informal voice sitting beside the story. This is the closest thing the medium has to what `literary:style-14` describes, with the gap made physical: the reader holds the story and the person making it in view at once, and the distance between the two is the effect.
entries.example: *百姓貴族 / Hyakushō Kizoku* runs on this register, with marginal asides carrying much of the humour and effectively functioning as a second track beside the drawn account.
entries.application: `trope-77` cards the author on the page as a narrative device; this is its typographic form. Decide early whether your work has this voice, because introducing it late reads as a loss of nerve.

entries.category: Lettering, Sound and the Drawn Word
entries.name: The Order Inside the Panel
entries.description: The collection's closing card: reading order does not stop at the panel border.
entries.principle: Within a single panel the reader takes the balloons right to left and top to bottom, the same rule `page-1` states for panels on a page, and the same rule governs the relation between a balloon and the image beneath it — a balloon placed above a face is read before the expression, and placed below it, after. Almost every confusing panel in the medium is a panel whose internal order is ambiguous, and it is the most common defect a script can prevent, because unlike the line in `page-25` or the value in `page-21`, **balloon order is a writer's decision that survives into the finished page**. `comedy:timing-1` requires the setup to complete before the replacement arrives; inside a panel, that ordering is a spatial fact rather than a temporal one, and getting it backwards inverts the joke without altering a word.
entries.example: *ドラゴンボール / Dragon Ball* is exceptionally disciplined here — panel interiors are arranged so that the order of balloons, expression and action is unambiguous at speed, which is a large part of why it reads as fast as it does.
entries.application: Number the balloons in every panel of a page and read them in that order with the art covered. If the exchange makes sense and the panel does not, the order is fighting the picture — and `checklist-6` is where to catch it, at the layout stage, before anything is finished.

entries.category: Antecedents and the Manufactured Lineage (to 1862)
entries.name: The Scrolls Are Not the Ancestor
entries.description: The twelfth-century picture scrolls, what they actually are, and what they are not evidence of.
entries.principle: The Chōjū-jinbutsu-giga scrolls are the object every popular history opens with, and almost everything the popular history says about them is unsupported. The attribution to Toba Sōjō is traditional rather than established; the four scrolls are by more than one hand and were not all made at the same time; and nothing in them is serialised, printed, commercially distributed or read by a mass audience. What they demonstrate is that caricature, sequence and animal satire existed in Japan very early, which is true of most cultures with a drawing tradition. **What they do not demonstrate is descent.** The scrolls are an antecedent in the loose sense that any early sequential image is one, and the specific claim that manga comes from them is a modern argument rather than a historical finding.
entries.example: *Comics and the Origins of Manga: A Revisionist History* is the sustained argument against the descent claim, and its value here is that it treats the received lineage as a thing with a history of its own rather than as a background fact.
entries.application: When you use the scrolls in a work or a pitch, use them as an image and not as a pedigree. `checklist-15`'s discipline about sources applies to historical claims exactly as it does to names.

entries.category: Antecedents and the Manufactured Lineage (to 1862)
entries.name: What Edo Actually Supplies
entries.description: The genuine inheritance from the early-modern period, stated at the size the record supports.
entries.principle: The Edo period supplies something real and it is not a drawing style. It supplies a commercial print culture: woodblock production at scale, a literate urban readership, rental libraries, and a set of popular formats — kibyōshi picture books, Ōtsu-e, ukiyo-e series — in which word and image share a surface and are sold cheaply to strangers. **The inheritance is infrastructural rather than formal.** A kibyōshi page does not look like a manga page and does not work like one, but the existence of a mass market for cheap illustrated narrative, produced to a schedule and distributed commercially, is the condition everything later depends on.
entries.example: *マンガの読み方 / Manga no Yomikata* is the standard reference for treating manga's formal system as a system, which is what makes it useful here: it is precise about which features are old and which are not.
entries.application: If you are writing historical fiction about this period, the reading and lending economy is more usable material than the pictures — and `subgenre-31`'s rental tradition shows the same economy reappearing three centuries later.

entries.category: Antecedents and the Manufactured Lineage (to 1862)
entries.name: Hokusai Did Not Coin the Word
entries.description: A correction to the single most repeated fact about the medium's name.
entries.principle: The received account has Hokusai inventing the word *manga* for his sketchbooks of 1814. He did not. The word is in use before those volumes — Santō Kyōden used it in 1798, and Aikawa Minwa's *Manga hyakujo* appeared in the same year as Hokusai's first volume — and in none of these cases does it mean a comic. It means something closer to *sketches at random*, applied to collections of studies with no narrative and no sequence. Hokusai popularised a term he inherited, for a category that is not this one, and the modern sense arrives much later. **The error matters because it is load-bearing**: the coinage story is the hinge on which the whole descent narrative in `history-1` turns.
entries.example: *現代マンガの全体像 / Gendai Manga no Zentaizō* is useful here for its insistence that the medium's categories are historical products rather than natural kinds, which is the frame that makes the etymology legible.
entries.application: Do not use the coinage story as colour. If you need Hokusai in a work, use what he actually did, which is more interesting than the myth attached to him.

entries.category: Antecedents and the Manufactured Lineage (to 1862)
entries.name: Why the Lineage Was Built
entries.description: The construction itself as a historical object, with both positions carried.
entries.principle: A continuous native lineage from the scrolls to the present is useful to several parties, and it was assembled by them. It serves a postwar cultural argument that the medium is Japanese rather than an American import; it serves a later official interest in cultural export; and it serves the medium's own claim to seriousness. **That an argument is useful does not make it false**, and the discontinuity reading has itself been pushed too far by critics keen to see only the American inheritance. The defensible position is narrow: the formal system of modern manga assembles in the twentieth century out of imported cartoon conventions, domestic print culture and cinema; whether that assembly counts as continuity or rupture is a question about the word *continuity*. This pack states the dispute and takes no side.
entries.example: *Comics and the Origins of Manga: A Revisionist History* argues the constructed case; the continuity case has its own serious scholarship, and a card that cited only one of them would be reporting a settled question that is not settled.
entries.application: In a work, pick your position and let a character hold it — this is a live argument among people who study the medium, and a scene where two of them disagree is accurate. `checklist-13` is the audit for handling a contested cultural claim without resolving it on the reader's behalf.

entries.category: The Imported Cartoon and the Newspaper (1862–1923)
entries.name: The Cartoon Arrives on a Ship
entries.description: The foreign satirical press in the treaty ports, and the conventions it brought with it.
entries.principle: The modern cartoon enters Japan through the foreign community, in English, for a foreign readership, and the conventions come as a package: the single-panel political cartoon, the caricatured public figure, the caption beneath the image, and the periodical schedule that produces one every issue. Japanese artists read these papers, worked for them, and adapted the form for a domestic audience within a generation. **The system change that opens this period is not stylistic; it is the arrival of a printing and distribution apparatus** capable of putting the same image in front of thousands of people on a fixed date.
entries.example: *ジャパン・パンチ / The Japan Punch*, produced by Charles Wirgman in Yokohama from 1862, is the anchor object, and the word *ponchi* entering Japanese as a term for a cartoon is the clearest possible evidence of the direction of transmission.
entries.application: Note the direction and the date whenever you write about this period. `history-4`'s dispute is largely a dispute about how much weight this ship should carry.

entries.category: The Imported Cartoon and the Newspaper (1862–1923)
entries.name: The Daily Slot Made the Character
entries.description: The institution that turned cartoons into serial characters.
entries.principle: A mass-circulation daily needs something that brings a reader back tomorrow, and the recurring comic character is a cheap and effective answer. This is the mechanism that converts the single-panel cartoon into a strip with continuing characters, a fixed slot and a schedule, and it happens in Japan for the same commercial reason it happens elsewhere. Everything the pack argues about serialisation begins here in miniature: **a fixed slot, a repeating audience and a commercial reason to be liked** are already the whole apparatus, three decades before a manga magazine exists.
entries.example: *東京パック / Tokyo Puck*, founded by Kitazawa Rakuten in 1905, is the period's central publication — colour, mass circulation, and a professional operation rather than an artist's sideline.
entries.application: `serial-1` argues the magazine is a filter and an advertisement rather than the product. The newspaper strip is the earlier version of the same arrangement, and reading them together shows how old the logic is.

entries.category: The Imported Cartoon and the Newspaper (1862–1923)
entries.name: Shō-chan and the Modern Page
entries.description: The point at which the domestic strip has all the parts of the thing that follows.
entries.principle: By the early 1920s the pieces are assembled: a child protagonist, a continuing narrative rather than a gag, speech carried inside balloons rather than in captions below the frame, and publication both in a periodical and afterwards as a collected book. Each element exists elsewhere first; the assembly is what matters, and the assembly is where the children's magazine system starts. **The collected volume appears at the same moment as the serial** — the two-object economy this pack's Serialisation collection is built on is present from the beginning rather than being a later commercial refinement.
entries.example: *正チヤンの冒険 / Shō-chan no Bōken*, from 1923, is the standard reference point for the assembly, and its rapid move from newspaper to book is as significant as anything on the page.
entries.application: Read this beside `serial-41`. The tankōbon's primacy is nearly a century old, which is worth knowing before you treat it as a modern development.

entries.category: The Imported Cartoon and the Newspaper (1862–1923)
entries.name: The Profession Appears
entries.description: When drawing comics becomes a job, with a studio, a salary and a title.
entries.principle: A profession requires more than practitioners: it requires a reliable buyer, a rate, a name for the work and somewhere to learn it. Those arrive together in this period. Rakuten is the usual candidate for the first professional cartoonist in the modern sense — salaried by a newspaper, running a studio, training successors — and the significance is structural rather than biographical. **Once the work has an employer, it has a house style, a schedule and an apprenticeship**, and all three are still the medium's basic conditions a century later.
entries.example: *田吾作と杢兵衛の東京見物 / Tagosaku to Mokubē no Tokyo Kenbutsu*, from 1902, is the strip usually named as the first in the Western sense in a Japanese newspaper, and the professional apparatus around it is the period's real innovation.
entries.application: `craft-56` covers the house style and the room inside it. The room was small in 1902 and is not much larger now; what changed is who sets the walls.

entries.category: Strips, Children's Magazines and the War (1923–1945)
entries.name: The Children's Magazine Is the Real Ancestor
entries.description: The institution the entire later system descends from, and it is not a scroll.
entries.principle: The interwar children's monthlies establish every structural feature the postwar industry runs on: serialised strips competing inside one magazine for a young readership, a publisher choosing the lineup, collected volumes as the profitable object, and characters that generate merchandise. This is the actual ancestry — a business model rather than a drawing tradition — and it is why the periodisation in this collection cuts where it does. **The system is inherited; the graphic language is rebuilt after the war.**
entries.example: *タンクタンクロー / Tanku Tankurō*, from the mid-1930s, shows how complete the commercial apparatus already was: a strongly designed character built for recognition and reuse, running in a children's monthly.
entries.application: When you need the origin of a convention, look for the magazine that paid for it. `serial-3`'s account of the anthology as a recommendation engine — a new serial carried by the established ones beside it — describes a machine that has been running since the 1920s.

entries.category: Strips, Children's Magazines and the War (1923–1945)
entries.name: Norakuro's Two Careers
entries.description: The period's most popular character, and what happened to it, stated plainly.
entries.principle: The defining children's strip of the 1930s follows a stray dog through military life, and it is genuinely funny, genuinely popular and genuinely a recruiting poster. As the war expanded, work of this kind was absorbed into the state's purposes — directly, through content, and structurally, through a profession organised into an official association in 1940 and a paper supply the state controlled. **Stated, analysed, not excused**: the strip's craft is real, its wartime function is real, and a history that mentions only one of them is not a history. The useful lesson for a writer is mechanical rather than moral — a popular character with an institutional setting is the most easily repurposed object a medium has.
entries.example: *のらくろ / Norakuro* by Tagawa Suihō is the case, and the interest is precisely that the comic and the propaganda are the same body of work rather than separable phases of it.
entries.application: `checklist-14`'s sensitive content audit applies whenever you use this material. Do not write it as a fall from innocence; the commercial and the official uses ran together from early on.

entries.category: Strips, Children's Magazines and the War (1923–1945)
entries.name: The Colonial Frame
entries.description: The racial content of the period's popular children's work, carried rather than skipped.
entries.principle: A significant strand of interwar children's manga is set in the empire's periphery and depicts colonised peoples through caricature that was standard at the time and is indefensible now. The scholarship reads this as more than incidental offensiveness: the visual conventions are doing translation work, positioning the Japanese reader as modern against a drawn primitive, and that positioning is the content rather than a blemish on it. **A pack that omitted this would be describing a different medium's history.** It is stated at the level the record supports and analysed as craft — what the caricature is for, structurally — without either defending or performing outrage.
entries.example: *冒険ダン吉 / Bōken Dankichi* is the standard case, and Thomas Lamarre's reading of racial translation in the wartime corpus is the scholarship to consult rather than a summary of it.
entries.application: If you draw on this period, you are drawing on this too. `checklist-13`'s questions about depicting people who can read your work are the right instrument, and `history-4`'s rule holds: state the dispute where there is one, and do not resolve it for the reader.

entries.category: Strips, Children's Magazines and the War (1923–1945)
entries.name: What the War Left Behind
entries.description: The material conditions at the end of the period, and the two things that survived them.
entries.principle: By 1945 the industry as an industry is gone: paper is rationed to nothing, magazines have merged or closed, and the professional body is an arm of the state. Two things survive and both matter. The first is the *format* — serialised strips in a children's magazine, collected into volumes — which is reconstructed within two years because everyone remembers how it worked. The second is a habit of collective professional organisation that outlasts the purpose it was created for. **What does not survive is continuity of content**, and the postwar rebuild is genuinely a rebuild, which is the strongest evidence available for the rupture side of `history-4`.
entries.example: *Manga! Manga! The World of Japanese Comics* remains the standard English account of the postwar reconstruction, and its framing of the immediate postwar as a fresh commercial start is well supported by what the publishers actually did.
entries.application: If your story crosses 1945, the industry your characters worked in does not exist on the other side. That is a plot, not a background detail.

entries.category: Two Postwar Economies (1945–1964)
entries.name: Two Cheap Economies and a Red Book
entries.description: The Osaka akahon market, the work that broke out of it, and the credit that gets dropped.
entries.principle: The immediate postwar market is not the Tokyo magazine market. It is cheap, fast, poorly printed volumes — *akahon*, red books — produced and sold largely in Osaka, outside the surviving publishing establishment, for children with very little money. The work that comes out of it changes the medium's direction, and the standard account attributes that change to a cinematic page grammar arriving all at once. **That claim is contested and this card carries both sides**: prewar precedents for cinematic staging exist and are named in the scholarship, the deflationary reading has itself been over-corrected, and the honest statement is that a formal repertoire already in circulation was consolidated and made dominant. A second correction belongs here too: the breakout work is co-credited, and the collaborator's name is routinely dropped.
entries.example: *新宝島 / Shin Takarajima*, 1947, is the work; the credit it carries includes Sakai Shichima, whose contribution is disputed and whose name disappears from most popular accounts, which is a documentation problem before it is a fairness one.
entries.application: Read this beside `page-1`. The page grammar that card describes has a history, and the history is an argument rather than an invention story.

entries.category: Two Postwar Economies (1945–1964)
entries.name: The Rental Shops and Why They Ended
entries.description: The second postwar economy, its readership, and a correction to the received account of its collapse.
entries.principle: Alongside the akahon trade runs the kashihon rental circuit: volumes produced for lending rather than sale, distributed through neighbourhood shops, read by an audience older and poorer than the magazine audience. The different readership permits different material — slower, darker, more violent — and the formal experiments that permission allows outlive the market. **The received account says television killed it. The record says otherwise**: cheap weekly magazines arrive in 1959 and undercut it, and rising household incomes make renting a book less attractive than owning a cheap one. Television is the environment, not the mechanism.
entries.example: *忍者武芸帳 影丸伝 / Ninja Bugeichō Kagemaru-den* is the period's most consequential rental-market work, and its author's later centrality to the alternative magazines is the clearest line from this economy into the mainstream.
entries.application: `subgenre-31` cards the tradition and `serial-67` cards the system. When you explain a market's death, name the competitor and the price, not the new technology.

entries.category: Two Postwar Economies (1945–1964)
entries.name: Gekiga Names Itself
entries.description: A word invented on purpose, by whom, and what inventing it was for.
entries.principle: In 1957 a young artist working in the rental market coins a term to distinguish what he is doing from *manga*, a word that by then means work for children. The coinage is a claim to seriousness and an act of positioning, made by a group that shortly formalises itself, and it works: the word survives, the category it names becomes the adult end of the medium, and the argument it was making is now so settled that the word has gone soft. **The lesson is that a category can be created deliberately by people who need one** — which is worth remembering whenever a taxonomy looks natural.
entries.example: *劇画漂流 / Gekiga Hyōryū* is the participant's own long account of the period, and it is the primary source for the coinage, the group and the intent behind both.
entries.application: `subgenre-29` cards gekiga as a movement. Note that pass H's planted control was a false attribution of exactly this coinage; it is a fact people misremember with confidence, and the correct form is Tatsumi Yoshihiro, 1957.

entries.category: Two Postwar Economies (1945–1964)
entries.name: 1959: The Weekly Arrives
entries.description: The system change that this entire pack is organised around, and its date.
entries.principle: In March 1959 two weekly manga magazines for boys launch within days of each other, and the medium's clock changes. A monthly's production rhythm allows a work to be composed; a weekly's does not, and everything this pack's Serialisation collection describes — the chapter unit, the survey, the cancellation conversation, the assistant workshop — is a consequence of a schedule that cannot be met by one person working alone at a considered pace. **The weekly is the pack's organising claim in its historical form.** It is also the moment the rental market's clock runs out, as `history-14` describes.
entries.example: *巨人の星 / Kyojin no Hoshi* is a product of the system rather than of the launch, and its serialised shape — escalation, arcs, a cast introduced under pressure — is what the weekly rhythm produces once it has settled.
entries.application: Everything in `serial-11` through `serial-20` dates from here. If you want to know why a manga chapter is the length it is, this is the year to point at.

entries.category: Break, Expansion and the Adult Reader (1964–1989)
entries.name: Two Answers to the Same Problem
entries.description: The alternative magazines, what they were reacting to, and how differently they reacted.
entries.principle: By the mid-1960s the weekly system is dominant and its constraints are obvious to the people inside it, and two responses appear within three years. One is a magazine that pays almost nothing and imposes almost nothing, becoming the home of politically serious long-form work and of the medium's avant-garde. The other is a magazine founded by the industry's central figure as a laboratory and a training ground, publishing formal experiment alongside criticism. **Both are answers to the weekly's constraints and they are opposite answers** — one refuses the commercial apparatus, the other tries to build a better one inside it — and both fail commercially while succeeding at what they were for.
entries.example: *カムイ伝 / Kamui-den* is the clearest case of what the first arrangement made possible: a long, politically argumentative historical work that no weekly of the period would have carried.
entries.application: `subgenre-30` and `serial-68` cover the lineage and the bargain. If you are choosing an outlet, this is the period that priced the choice.

entries.category: Break, Expansion and the Adult Reader (1964–1989)
entries.name: The Reader Who Did Not Stop
entries.description: The demographic expansion that turned a children's medium into a general one.
entries.principle: The postwar generation that grew up on weekly manga did not put it down, and the industry followed them upward: adult men's magazines from the late 1960s, young men's titles through the 1970s, and women's equivalents behind them. This is the period in which the medium stops being a children's format with adult exceptions and becomes a general publishing category with a full demographic grid. The consequence for craft is the arrival of subject matter — work, sex, politics, money, illness — that a children's weekly cannot carry, and the arrival of readers who will follow a serial for twenty years. **Demographic expansion, not formal innovation, is what makes the medium's later scale possible.**
entries.example: *ゴルゴ13 / Golgo 13*, serialised from 1968 in the first of the adult men's magazines, is the period's emblematic launch and has outlasted almost everything around it.
entries.application: `subgenre-9` and `subgenre-10` card the demographics. Note what the grid actually is — a market segmentation, as `checklist-8` insists, and not a set of genres.

entries.category: Break, Expansion and the Adult Reader (1964–1989)
entries.name: Who Rebuilt Shōjo, and Who Counts
entries.description: The most consequential formal transformation in the medium's history, and a membership question that is not settled.
entries.principle: Through the 1970s a cohort of women creators takes over shōjo magazines from a largely male preceding generation and rebuilds the form: psychological interiority, dissolved and overlapping panel layouts, ambitious historical and science-fictional subject matter, and explicit treatment of sexuality and gender. The formal repertoire they build is the medium's most distinctive, and it spreads into every other demographic. **Who exactly belongs to the named group is contested and this card says so**: the label is applied with different widths by different critics, several creators central to the transformation are excluded by the narrow definition, and some of those named have disputed the framing. The transformation is not in doubt; the roster is.
entries.example: *トーマの心臓 / Tōma no Shinzō* is among the works always cited for the shift, and its formal apparatus — interior monologue carried by layout rather than by narration — is the repertoire in mature form.
entries.application: `subgenre-34` cards the movement and `page-22` cards the tone vocabulary it produced. When you name members, name your source's definition too, because the lists genuinely differ.

entries.category: Break, Expansion and the Adult Reader (1964–1989)
entries.name: The Circuit Forms Beside the Industry
entries.description: The self-published market's arrival as a permanent second system.
entries.principle: A large amateur market organises itself from the mid-1970s: a regular convention, circles as production units, specialist short-run printers, and shops carrying self-published work. It grows through the late 1970s and 1980s alongside the commercial industry, supplies it with creators and audiences, and develops its own conventions and economics. **This is the last of the medium's structural components to arrive**, and after it the system described by the rest of this pack is complete: magazine, volume, adaptation, and a parallel amateur circuit feeding all three.
entries.example: *シベール / Cybele*, a 1979 amateur publication, is conventionally cited as the origin point of the erotic amateur boom that drove much of the circuit's growth — and, as `serial-64` records, of the material that fuelled the regulation campaign a decade later.
entries.application: `serial-61` and `subgenre-33` card the circuit as system and as movement. For a work set in this period, the amateur scene is the more interesting location, because nothing about it was settled yet.

entries.category: Peak Circulation, Contraction, Platform (1989–)
entries.name: Panic, Ordinance and Jurisdiction
entries.description: The regulation history, stated as a divergence between jurisdictions rather than as a verdict.
entries.principle: A 1989 criminal case produced a moral panic about manga and its readers, and a campaign against so-called harmful manga followed in 1990–91, with publishers adopting self-regulation under pressure. A Tokyo ordinance in 2010 renewed the argument in a new form. The legal position on drawn material differs sharply by country — Japan's 2014 child-pornography law explicitly excludes drawn work, while the United Kingdom, Canada and Australia criminalise it — and a third position exists in local ordinances that restrict distribution rather than possession. **The pack states the divergence as a fact about jurisdictions.** It does not use the divergence as a defence of any work and does not use it as an indictment of the medium, and it takes no position on which jurisdiction is right.
entries.example: *Adult Manga: Culture and Power in Contemporary Japanese Society* is the standard scholarly treatment of the campaign period and of the publishers' response to it, including the parts of that response that were commercial rather than principled.
entries.application: `checklist-14` is the audit. If you write about this history, note which of the three positions your characters are living under, because the answer changes what is at stake for them.

entries.category: Peak Circulation, Contraction, Platform (1989–)
entries.name: The Peak Belonged to the Magazine
entries.description: The circulation curve, with its dates checked.
entries.principle: The best-selling weekly's average print circulation reached **6.53 million copies**, a record for any manga anthology, with the New Year double issue at the turn of 1994–95 — the received form of this fact says 1995 and the issue went on sale in late 1994, which is why both dates circulate. From there the curve falls continuously for three decades. In the April–June quarter of 2026 the same magazine's average print circulation was **985,000 copies, below one million for the first time in its history**. That is a decline of roughly 85% from the peak, in the medium's flagship object. **What it measures is the magazine**, which is the point of the next card.
entries.example: *ドラゴンボール / Dragon Ball* was the engine of the peak years, and the magazine's circulation history is inseparable from the run of a small number of serials of that scale.
entries.application: `serial-1` explains why this number was never the industry's revenue. A falling circulation is a falling advertisement, and the advertisement was never what was being sold.

entries.category: Peak Circulation, Contraction, Platform (1989–)
entries.name: The Market Went the Other Way
entries.description: The inverted fact: the medium's money grew while its most visible object shrank.
entries.principle: The decline narrative is true of magazines and false of the medium. The Japanese manga market reached an all-time high of **¥704.3 billion in 2024**; **2025's ¥692.5 billion is the first contraction in seven years**, and the split that year was **¥527.3 billion digital against ¥165.2 billion print — roughly 76% to 24%**. The medium did not shrink between the magazine's peak and now; it changed carrier, and the carrier it changed to is not counted by circulation figures at all. **A metric that measures one object will report the death of a medium that has merely stopped using it**, which is a general caution and not a manga-specific one.
entries.example: *進撃の巨人 / Attack on Titan* is a useful marker of the transition period: a serial whose commercial scale was built on volumes, adaptation and international sales rather than on the circulation of the magazine it appeared in.
entries.application: When you cite a figure about the medium's health, **say what it measures** — magazine circulation, publisher shipment value, retail sales, print only or print and digital. Four of those five numbers are commonly reported as "manga sales" and no two of them are the same quantity. `checklist-10`'s instruction to record the claims you could not establish is the nearest audit; the type discipline itself is stated here because it has no other home in the pack.

entries.category: Peak Circulation, Contraction, Platform (1989–)
entries.name: What the Platform Changed
entries.description: The collection's closing card: the current system, described as a system rather than as a trend.
entries.principle: Four things have changed and none of them is the magazine disappearing. Distribution moved to apps and to purchase-by-chapter, which decouples reading from a weekly lineup. Discovery moved partly to open platforms, so a work can arrive with an audience rather than be given one. Translation moved to near-simultaneous release, so the international market is now a first market rather than a later one. And a formally distinct competitor exists — the vertical-scroll webtoon — whose grammar is not this medium's. **What has not changed is the editorial apparatus, the assistant workshop, the volume as the durable object, or the fact that somebody decides what runs.** The filter has a new carrier; it is still a filter.
entries.example: *ワンパンマン / One-Punch Man* traverses the whole of it — an open-platform origin, a commercial redraw for the page, and an international readership that arrived with the work rather than after it.
entries.application: `serial-65` and `serial-66` card the paths and the formats. If you are planning a career rather than a story, the question this history leaves you with is which carrier you are writing for, because the page grammar in `page-1` through `page-30` is not portable to all of them.

entries.category: Reading the Page: Order, Eye-Path and Cognition
entries.name: Reading a Page Is a Learned Skill
entries.description: The finding that undermines the most common assumption about the medium.
entries.principle: Sequential images are widely assumed to be self-explanatory — a transparent, near-universal code needing no instruction, which is why they are used as test material for everything from intelligence to theory of mind. The converging evidence says otherwise. Cross-cultural, developmental and clinical work indicates that understanding a visual narrative depends on **exposure to and practice with a particular graphic system**, and that readers unfamiliar with the system read it slowly, wrongly, or not as a sequence at all. For a writer the consequence is direct: the conventions in this pack's Page collection are a language your reader has learned, and a reader who has not learned it is not a slow reader but a non-speaker. (robustness: robust)
entries.example: The review synthesising this evidence is Cohn's *Visual narrative comprehension: Universal or not?* (2020), which assembles cross-cultural, developmental and clinical findings against the transparency assumption.
entries.application: When you write for readers outside the form, do not simplify the story — teach the grammar. `page-1`'s clock is the first thing a new reader has to acquire, and nothing else works until they have it.

entries.category: Reading the Page: Order, Eye-Path and Cognition
entries.name: The Eye Goes Where the Page Sends It
entries.description: Evidence that fixations land on informative regions, and that those regions carry the sequence.
entries.principle: Where readers look inside a panel is not idiosyncratic. In one experimental series, panels were re-cropped to show only the regions a separate group of readers had fixated; those cropped panels were rated **easier** to understand than panels cropped to non-fixated or incongruous regions, and produced viewing times close to the unmodified original despite carrying much less information. Modifying such a panel also changed how the *following* panels were read. Two things follow for a writer: **the informative region is a real and locatable thing**, and its treatment propagates forward rather than staying local. (robustness: unreplicated)
entries.example: Foulsham & Cohn's zoom experiments (2020) are the source; three self-paced experiments from one laboratory, which is why the tier on this card is not *robust*.
entries.application: Identify the one region in each panel that carries the beat, and compose so nothing competes with it. `page-2`'s entry point is the page-level version of the same claim, and this is its evidence at panel level.

entries.category: Reading the Page: Order, Eye-Path and Cognition
entries.name: The Brain Reads Sequence Like Language
entries.description: The electrophysiological evidence, and what it does and does not license you to say.
entries.principle: Manipulating a sequence of images produces the same electrophysiological signatures as manipulating a sentence — an N400 to semantic discontinuity, a P600 to structural violation, anterior negativities to processing load — across multiple laboratories and paradigms. This is the strongest evidence in the collection, and it licenses a narrower claim than it is usually made to carry. It supports: **the mechanisms recruited to comprehend sequential images overlap substantially with those recruited for language.** It does not support the claim that comics *are* a language in any strong sense, which is a theoretical position argued separately and answered by researchers who explain the same data with general event cognition. (robustness: robust)
entries.example: Cohn's cognitive model of visual narrative comprehension (2019) synthesises the ERP evidence; Coopmans & Cohn's co-reference study (2022) is a representative single experiment within it.
entries.application: Use this when you need to justify treating layout as grammar rather than decoration, and stop there. Overclaiming from it is how a real finding becomes a slogan.

entries.category: Reading the Page: Order, Eye-Path and Cognition
entries.name: Building a Model, or Updating One
entries.description: The two distinct things a reader does at a break, and why the size of the break decides which.
entries.principle: A reader holds a working model of the situation, and what happens at a gap depends on the gap's size. At a small omission the existing model is **updated** — the reader infers the missing step and carries on, cheaply. At a large discontinuity the model is **rebuilt** from scratch, which costs measurably more time and reads as a new scene. Recent work separates the two using viewing time, segmentation and comprehensibility together, having previously been hard to distinguish. The craft consequence is that **a gap is not a dial with a single scale**: below a threshold you are asking for an inference, above it you are asking for a reconstruction, and the second is far more expensive to spend on something trivial. (robustness: unreplicated)
entries.example: Brich, Papenmeier, Huff and Merkt's construction-versus-updating study (2024) is the source; a single study with eighty participants, hence the tier.
entries.application: Audit your scene breaks by asking which of the two you are requesting. `page-11`'s gutter is the small case and `craft-7`'s split scene is the large one, and confusing them is why some transitions read as jumps.

entries.category: Identification, the Blank Face and the Reader's Place
entries.name: The Blank Face, and What Actually Supports It
entries.description: The collection's most useful idea, with its evidentiary status stated plainly.
entries.principle: The argument is familiar: a simplified, less individuated face lets a reader project themselves into a character, while a rendered, specific face holds them at the distance of observation — which is why so much manga pairs a schematic protagonist with detailed backgrounds and detailed antagonists. It is a good argument. It explains a real and widespread design pattern, working artists use it deliberately, and it makes predictions a writer can act on. **It is also a craft claim rather than a finding**: pass P searched the indexed literature for empirical work on schematic faces and reader identification and located none.
