This card carries the idea because it is useful and carries its status because the alternative is a reference work presenting a persuasive argument as settled science.
entries.example: The pattern is easy to observe in *ドラえもん / Doraemon*, where the schematic child protagonist sits against comparatively specific settings and adults — the observation is solid; the mechanism is the part that is argued rather than measured.
entries.application: Use the technique and hold the explanation loosely. `page-25`'s point stands either way: the line makes a register, and a schematic line makes a different one from a rendered line, whatever the reason turns out to be.

entries.category: Identification, the Blank Face and the Reader's Place
entries.name: The Panel That Shows Nothing
entries.description: What happens when the medium hands the reader an event with the event removed.
entries.principle: A conventionalised panel — the star-shaped burst of impact, blown up to fill a frame and stripped of all representational content — depicts a narrative culmination and shows none of it. Experimentally, such panels demand more inference than a depicted event and **remain coherent in sequence**, which is the surprising half: removing the content does not break the narrative, and the reader supplies a culmination they were never shown. The general principle is larger than the device. **A convention can carry a narrative role with no content at all**, provided the sequence around it establishes the role, and the reader's supplied version is often stronger than a drawn one. (robustness: unreplicated)
entries.example: Cohn & Wittenberg's action-star experiments (2015) are the source; two experiments, hence the tier.
entries.application: When a moment is hard to draw well, consider not drawing it. `page-15`'s positional rule applies — where the omission sits decides whether it reads as withholding or as a mistake.

entries.category: Identification, the Blank Face and the Reader's Place
entries.name: Zoom Before, Zoom After
entries.description: Why the order of a wide shot and its close-up changes what the close-up does.
entries.principle: A panel that shows a detail of a scene is processed differently depending on whether it comes before or after the panel showing the whole. Following the wide shot, it resolves a reference already established and reads as attention being directed. Preceding it, it is a reference waiting to be filled, and the reader holds it open — a measurably different processing state, with distinct electrophysiological and oscillatory signatures. **The same two panels in the opposite order are not the same sequence**, which is obvious once stated and routinely ignored in drafting. (robustness: unreplicated)
entries.example: Coopmans & Cohn's study of co-reference in visual narrative (2022) is the source; a single EEG study, hence the tier.
entries.application: For every detail panel, decide whether you want the reader oriented first or curious first. `page-19`'s argument about the cost of wide panels is the other half of this decision.

entries.category: Identification, the Blank Face and the Reader's Place
entries.name: Where the Reader Is Standing
entries.description: The implied viewing position as a relationship, not a camera setting.
entries.principle: Every panel puts the reader somewhere: behind a shoulder, at eye level with a child, above a room, inside a character's sightline. The position is read as a relationship rather than as geometry — a low angle on a figure is deference or threat, a high one is exposure or pity, and a sustained over-the-shoulder position makes the reader a companion rather than a witness. What makes this different from film's version is that a manga page shows several positions at once, so **the reader's place is not a track through the story but a pattern across the sheet**, and inconsistency in it registers as a wobble in whose story this is.
entries.example: *岳 みんなの山 / Gaku: Minna no Yama* holds a consistent relationship to its protagonist across page after page, and the moments where it pulls to a great distance are legible as a change in that relationship rather than as a change of shot.
entries.application: Mark the implied position on every panel of a page and look for the outlier. `page-18`'s scale-against-a-body applies here too: the reader measures their own position the same way.

entries.category: Attachment, Parasocial Relationship and the Circuit
entries.name: A Week Is Not a Pause
entries.description: What serialised release does to a reader that continuous reading does not.
entries.principle: Weekly release inserts real time into the reading, and real time is not empty. Between chapters a reader speculates, rereads, discusses, and — crucially — lives, so the story accumulates associations with a period of their life that a volume read in an afternoon never acquires. This is a claim about ordinary memory rather than a special property of the medium, and it explains something writers frequently misdiagnose: the same chapter is a different object weekly and collected. **A cliffhanger that sustains seven days of speculation is a bore at the turn of a page**, and a quiet chapter that reads as a lull in a volume can be a welcome exhalation in a week.
entries.example: *ONE PIECE* is the extreme case — readers who have followed it weekly for decades hold a relationship to it that no first-time volume reader can assemble, however carefully they read.
entries.application: Decide which reader you are writing for and accept the cost, or write for both and check both. `serial-42`'s account of what changes between serial and volume is where the practical work happens.

entries.category: Attachment, Parasocial Relationship and the Circuit
entries.name: Ten Years With the Same Face
entries.description: Duration as the mechanism behind manga's characteristic reader attachment.
entries.principle: Attachment to a fictional character is ordinary and not medium-specific; what long-running manga supplies is an unusual amount of **duration**, and duration does most of the work. A reader who has seen a character weekly for a decade has accumulated more encounters with that face than with most of the people in their life, and the accumulation is what produces the response — not depth of characterisation, and not identification. This has an uncomfortable corollary that the medium's commercial structure exploits without needing to state: **a character who simply persists will out-perform a better character who does not**, which is why the industry's long serials are so hard to end.
entries.example: *こちら葛飾区亀有公園前派出所 / Kochira Katsushika-ku Kameari Kōen-mae Hashutsujo* ran for forty years, and its readers' relationship to its cast is a product of that span more than of any single arc.
entries.application: If you are planning a long serial, plan what accumulates. `trope-66`'s long farewell exists because the duration has to be paid back, and `craft-14`'s farewell card is the writing side of the same debt.

entries.category: Attachment, Parasocial Relationship and the Circuit
entries.name: Attachment That Makes Things
entries.description: The doujinshi circuit read as attachment in material form.
entries.principle: The distinctive thing about this medium's fandom is not intensity but **productivity**: attachment routinely takes the form of making something — a book, a circle, a table at a market, a continuation of the story in a direction the original declined. That changes the relationship's character. A reader who has drawn a character is not consuming a work; they are in an argument with it, and the argument has a physical object attached. It also feeds back, since a portion of those readers become professionals, as `serial-64` records. **A medium whose readers make things has a different relationship with its audience than one whose readers only buy**, and it is worth being clear-eyed that this is a strength and a source of friction at once.
entries.example: *げんしけん / Genshiken* is the standing depiction of exactly this — a group whose relationship to what it loves is mediated through producing more of it.
entries.application: If your work invites continuation, expect continuation. `serial-63` states the legal position and does not resolve it, which is also the right posture for a creator deciding what to tolerate.

entries.category: Attachment, Parasocial Relationship and the Circuit
entries.name: What Ending Does to a Long Reader
entries.description: Why the endings of long serials are received so badly so often, stated structurally.
entries.principle: A long serial's ending has to satisfy a reader whose investment was built by duration, and duration is the one thing an ending cannot supply. The reader is not primarily asking whether the plot resolves; they are asking what the last decade was, and no final chapter can answer a question that size. This is why endings of very long works are received harshly by comparison with endings of short ones, and why the reception often improves years later when the work is read as a whole. It is not a failure of craft peculiar to this medium. **It is a structural mismatch between what was accumulated and what a conclusion is able to discharge**, and the practical response is to discharge some of it earlier.
entries.example: *ドラゴンボール / Dragon Ball*'s conclusion has been read very differently at different distances from its serialisation, which is the pattern rather than an isolated case.
entries.application: Pay the reader in instalments. `craft-14`'s farewell is not the last chapter's job alone — arcs that close properly along the way leave the ending less to carry.

entries.category: Repetition, Long Duration and the Serial Reader
entries.name: Repetition Is Not Redundancy
entries.description: Why the recurring element in a weekly serial does work that would be a fault in a novel.
entries.principle: The catchphrase, the recurring pose, the technique announced by name and the fixed opening are frequently read as lazy by readers trained on prose. In a weekly, they are load-bearing. A reader returning after seven days needs re-entry that costs nothing, and a recognisable element supplies it instantly — recognition is cheaper than recall, and the repeated element is a handhold rather than a filler. The difference between this and genuine redundancy is whether the element **also advances something on the occasion of its use**: the same phrase, delivered in circumstances that change what it means, is a device; delivered unchanged, it is wallpaper.
entries.example: *ONE PIECE*'s named techniques function this way — the naming is re-entry for the weekly reader and escalation for the fight at once.
entries.application: For each repeated element, name what changed this time. `craft-28`'s catchphrase card is the drafting rule; this is why the rule exists.

entries.category: Repetition, Long Duration and the Serial Reader
entries.name: The Gap Does Work You Do Not Control
entries.description: What readers do to a story between instalments, and what it costs to contradict it.
entries.principle: Between chapters, readers speculate — individually and, since the 1990s, collectively and in public. The consequence is that a serial's reader arrives at the next chapter holding expectations the author did not write and often does not know about, and those expectations have been rehearsed. A resolution that matches the popular guess feels inevitable in the good sense or predictable in the bad one; a resolution that contradicts it must be strong enough to survive comparison with something a reader has already enjoyed imagining. **The gap is not neutral time and the author is not the only one working during it.**
entries.example: *ヒカルの碁 / Hikaru no Go* is a useful case of a serial whose structure keeps giving readers exactly enough to speculate with, which is a design decision rather than an accident of subject.
entries.application: Decide what your chapter's last panel invites the reader to imagine, because they will. `page-8`'s withholding rule is about controlling which question they hold, and this card is why the choice of question matters more than the withholding.

entries.category: Repetition, Long Duration and the Serial Reader
entries.name: What a Reader Actually Retains
entries.description: The honest account of long-serial memory, and how it should change your plotting.
entries.principle: Over hundreds of chapters a reader retains far less than an author assumes and something different in kind: not plot mechanics but **relationships, a few images, and the shape of how things went**. Names of minor characters, the sequence of arcs and the details of earlier rules go first. Long serials that depend on a reader holding precise information from four years ago are relying on a capacity most readers do not have and a minority does — the minority is loud, which is how authors are misled about the average. The practical form of this is not simplification but restatement: information that matters now should be available now.
entries.example: *鋼の錬金術師 / Hagane no Renkinjutsushi* is the counter-model worth studying — a long serial that re-establishes its rules at the moment each becomes load-bearing rather than assuming recall.
entries.application: For every payoff, ask when the reader last saw the setup. If it was more than a year of serialisation ago, restage it — `craft-4`'s recap rule tells you where to put it so it does not read as a recap.

entries.category: Repetition, Long Duration and the Serial Reader
entries.name: Why They Stay
entries.description: The collection's closing card: what actually keeps a reader across years, as against what writers assume.
entries.principle: The assumption is that readers stay for the plot, and the evidence of the medium's own history is that they stay for **the reliability of the encounter** — a familiar world available on a known schedule, in which they have accumulated time. Plot is what makes an individual chapter worth reading; it is not what makes a decade worth continuing. This is why serials survive weak arcs and why strong works with irregular publication lose readers who liked them. Set against the rest of this pack, it is the reader-side statement of the organising claim: **the serialisation system shapes the work because it shapes the relationship**, and the relationship is built out of regularity before it is built out of quality.
entries.example: *サザエさん / Sazae-san* ran for decades on an unvarying formal and publication rhythm, and its readership was built by exactly the reliability the strip's form advertises.
entries.application: Protect the schedule before you protect the ambition. `serial-13`'s rhythms and `checklist-1`'s premise audit are both, read from here, questions about whether the relationship you are proposing is one you can actually sustain.

entries.category: Gekiga and the Kashihon Line
entries.name: Tatsumi Yoshihiro
entries.description: The man who named the adult end of the medium and spent fifty years arguing about what he meant.
entries.meta: Yoshihiro Tatsumi in English-market credits · 1935–2015 · Osaka, then Tokyo · rental market, then the alternative magazines.
entries.knownFor: Coining *gekiga* in 1957 as a name for what he and the Gekiga Kōbō group were already doing — short, bleak, adult stories for the rental shops — and then watching the word be absorbed by the industry it was invented to stand apart from.
entries.signature: Small, unhappy men in postwar rooms; a flat, unemphatic drawing style that refuses to dramatise; and endings that stop rather than resolve. The refusal of dramatic emphasis is itself the argument, and it is the opposite of the story-manga generation's inheritance from cinema.

works.title: 劇画漂流 / Gekiga Hyōryū
works.note: His long memoir of the period, and the primary source for the coinage, the group and the intent behind both

works.title: 黒い吹雪 / Kuroi Fubuki
works.note: Rental-market work from the year before the word existed

works.title: 幽霊タクシー / Yūrei Takushī
works.note: The short bleak form at its most characteristic

entries.category: Gekiga and the Kashihon Line
entries.name: Shirato Sanpei
entries.description: The rental market's most politically serious talent, and the reason Garo was founded.
entries.meta: Sanpei Shirato in English-market credits · 1932–2021 · the kashihon circuit, then Garo.
entries.knownFor: Long historical works that use ninja and peasant material to make a materialist argument about class, and for being the creator whose serialisation the magazine Garo was created to carry.
entries.signature: Historical action drawn with genuine research and organised around economic causation rather than heroism — a form in which the fight scene and the argument about landholding are the same scene.

works.title: カムイ伝 / Kamui-den
works.note: The work Garo was founded to serialise

works.title: 忍者武芸帳 影丸伝 / Ninja Bugeichō Kagemaru-den
works.note: Rental-market, and the clearest single line from that economy into the alternative magazines

entries.category: Gekiga and the Kashihon Line
entries.name: Saitō Takao
entries.description: The industrial production of a serial, defended openly by the man who built it.
entries.meta: Takao Saito in English-market credits · 1936–2021 · rental market, then the adult magazines.
entries.knownFor: Running his serial as a company on an explicit division of labour — story team, backgrounds, figures — and arguing publicly that this is the correct way to make a long work rather than a compromise. The series continued past his death.
entries.signature: A production system rather than a hand: consistent, legible, unsentimental staging that survives changes of personnel, which is precisely what it was designed to do.

works.title: ゴルゴ13 / Golgo 13
works.note: The studio model's proof, still running

works.title: 劇画漂流 / Gekiga Hyōryū
works.note: Not his work; he is a participant in the period it records

entries.category: Gekiga and the Kashihon Line
entries.name: Hirata Hiroshi
entries.description: The samurai line of gekiga, and a work withdrawn from circulation.
entries.meta: Hiroshi Hirata in English-market credits · 1937–2021 · rental market, then seinen magazines.
entries.knownFor: Historical samurai work drawn in a dense, calligraphic brush line, built around duty, humiliation and the body's cost — the register the rental market permitted and the children's weeklies could not carry.
entries.signature: Brushwork that treats a face as terrain, and compositions that hold a figure in the moment before violence rather than during it. **One work was withdrawn from circulation after a complaint that its depiction of an outcast community was discriminatory** — the complaint, the withdrawal and the subsequent debate about censorship and representation are all part of the record, and this pack states them without adjudicating between them.

works.title: 血だるま剣法 / Chidaruma Kenpō
works.note: Withdrawn after the complaint described above; later reissued, and contested in both directions

entries.category: Gekiga and the Kashihon Line
entries.name: Kojima Gōseki
entries.description: The draughtsman half of the medium's most exported partnership.
entries.meta: Goseki Kojima in English-market credits · 1928–2000 · rental market, then the adult magazines.
entries.knownFor: The drawing on a long samurai serial that reached English readers earlier and more completely than almost any other manga, and did much of the work of establishing what Anglophone readers thought manga looked like.
entries.signature: Ink held back to almost nothing, then spent all at once; long silent sequences of landscape and weather that carry duration rather than information, which is `page-15`'s positional argument decades before anyone screened for it.

works.title: 子連れ狼 / Kozure Ōkami

entries.category: Gekiga and the Kashihon Line
entries.name: Koike Kazuo
entries.description: The writer half of the same partnership, and a teacher whose students ran the industry.
entries.meta: Kazuo Koike in English-market credits · 1936–2019 · adult magazines, and the Gekiga Sonjuku school.
entries.knownFor: Writing serials he did not draw — an uncommon arrangement in a medium whose default is a single credited author — and running a school whose students include several of the industry's later central figures.
entries.signature: Character before plot, stated as doctrine and taught that way: a premise is worth nothing until the person inside it is specific enough to generate incident by themselves. **This pack reads him as an author who did not draw, which is the arrangement `craft-48` describes and `serial-58` prices.** He is already carded as `western:Kazuo Koike`, where the reading is his place in that genre's samurai-western exchange; here he is a case in the medium's authorship model, and the two cards are about different things.

works.title: 子連れ狼 / Kozure Ōkami

entries.category: Garo, COM and the Art-Manga Lineage
entries.name: Tsuge Yoshiharu
entries.description: The alternative magazine's central figure, and the medium's first genuinely interior work.
entries.meta: Yoshiharu Tsuge in English-market credits · 1937–2026 · rental market, then Garo.
entries.knownFor: Short works that abandon plot for dream logic, memory and depressive flatness, published in a magazine that paid almost nothing and imposed nothing — the bargain `serial-68` prices.
entries.signature: An apparently plain drawing style used for material that is not plain at all; travel, failure and inertia treated as subjects rather than as obstacles; and a refusal of resolution that reads as honesty rather than as withholding.

works.title: ねじ式 / Neji-shiki
works.note: The dream work the whole lineage is measured against

works.title: 紅い花 / Akai Hana
works.note: The quieter register, and arguably the better case for what he does

entries.category: Garo, COM and the Art-Manga Lineage
entries.name: Hayashi Seiichi
entries.description: Animation training brought into the alternative magazine, and what it did to the page.
entries.meta: Seiichi Hayashi in English-market credits · born 1945 · animation, then Garo.
entries.knownFor: Bringing a designer's and animator's eye to Garo — flat colour fields, poster composition, pop imagery — in service of work about postwar disappointment rather than about style.
entries.signature: Panels composed as graphic design rather than as illustration, with figures reduced to shape and silhouette, and a tonal register that stays cool while the material is not.

works.title: 赤色エレジー / Sekishoku Elegy
works.note: Serialised in Garo at the start of the 1970s

entries.category: Garo, COM and the Art-Manga Lineage
entries.name: Maruo Suehiro
entries.description: The ero-guro line's most technically accomplished practitioner, and the hardest card in the block.
entries.meta: Suehiro Maruo in English-market credits · born 1956 · the alternative and underground magazines.
entries.knownFor: Work in the ero-guro tradition — erotic-grotesque imagery drawn with meticulous prewar-poster technique — which is genuinely admired as drawing and genuinely disturbing as content, and which this pack neither recommends nor writes around.
entries.signature: Immaculate line and period design used for atrocity and sexual violence, with the gap between manner and matter as the deliberate effect. **The critical argument runs in both directions and both sides are serious**: that the beauty of the rendering is a critique of the appetite it serves, and that it is that appetite's most effective delivery system. `checklist-14` is the audit; this pack states the dispute and takes no side.

works.title: 少女椿 / Shōjo Tsubaki
works.note: The best-known work and the centre of the argument above

entries.category: Garo, COM and the Art-Manga Lineage
entries.name: Takano Fumiko
entries.description: The art-manga line's most formally exacting figure, and one of very few women working in it.
entries.meta: Fumiko Takano in English-market credits · born 1957 · Garo and the alternative magazines.
entries.knownFor: Short works of unusual formal precision — timing, panel rhythm and omission handled with a control that other cartoonists cite more often than general readers know her name.
entries.signature: Extreme economy: a sequence built from the two or three panels that cannot be removed, with the rest inferred. The reader does more work than in almost any other manga and does not notice, which is `psychology-4`'s updating case executed deliberately.

works.title: 絶対安全剃刀 / Zettai Anzen Kamisori
works.note: The collection that established the reputation

entries.category: Garo, COM and the Art-Manga Lineage
entries.name: Tsurita Kuniko
entries.description: The only woman who was a regular contributor to Garo in its central years.
entries.meta: Kuniko Tsurita in English-market credits · 1947–1985 · Garo.
entries.knownFor: Work published in the alternative magazine from her late teens, dealing with gender, illness and self-determination in a register the shōjo magazines of the period had no room for and the men's alternative magazines had not attempted.
entries.signature: Sparse line and abrupt structure, with protagonists whose gender is unstable or unstated — decades before that became a legible subject in the commercial market. She died at 38, and the small size of the surviving body of work is part of why the lineage in `subgenre-30` is usually described as male.

works.title: 紅い花 / Akai Hana
works.note: Not her work; listed as the Garo context her own work sat inside

entries.category: Garo, COM and the Art-Manga Lineage
entries.name: Matsumoto Taiyō
entries.description: The art-manga sensibility operating successfully inside the commercial seinen market.
entries.meta: Taiyo Matsumoto in English-market credits · born 1967 · Spirits and the seinen magazines.
entries.knownFor: Work with the formal ambition of the alternative line and the distribution of the mainstream — an arrangement that had not obviously been available in the preceding generation.
entries.signature: Elastic, hand-drawn perspective; architecture that bends around the figures; spreads treated as single spatial fields rather than as two pages, which `page-7` cards as the design unit.

works.title: 鉄コン筋クリート / Tekkonkinkreet
works.note: The spatial approach at its fullest

entries.category: Doujinshi-Origin Creators and the Circle System
entries.name: Ōkawa Nanase
entries.description: The circle that became a studio, and the writer at its centre.
entries.meta: Nanase Ohkawa in English-market credits · born 1967 · doujinshi circuit, then commercial serialisation.
entries.knownFor: Leading the group that moved from self-published work to commercial serialisation intact — the clearest single case of the pipeline `serial-64` describes — and writing across shōjo, shōnen and seinen magazines under one collective name.
entries.signature: Story construction built for a collective: densely plotted, structurally symmetrical, and designed so that scripting and drawing can be separated cleanly, which is what makes the group's output rate possible at all. The group's membership and internal division of labour have changed across its career, and `serial-60`'s point applies — the name on the cover is accurate and tells a reader nothing about who did what.

works.title: 聖伝-RG VEDA- / Seiden -RG VEDA
カードキャプターさくら / Cardcaptor Sakura
works.note: The group working in the shōjo market at its widest reach

entries.category: Doujinshi-Origin Creators and the Circle System
entries.name: Azuma Hideo
entries.description: A career that runs through the amateur market's most consequential and most contested episode.
entries.meta: Hideo Azuma in English-market credits · 1950–2019 · commercial magazines and the doujinshi circuit.
entries.knownFor: Work at the origin of the late-1970s erotic amateur boom, and, two decades later, a memoir of homelessness and alcoholism that became one of the medium's most respected pieces of autobiographical reportage.
entries.signature: A light, rounded, apparently harmless line applied to material that is not harmless, and later to his own worst years without self-pity. **The amateur work is where the record has to be complete**: it is conventionally cited as the origin point of the boom that grew the circuit, and it is cited just as often in accounts of the 1990–91 regulation campaign that followed. `history-21` states the jurisdictional divergence; this card states the sequence and adjudicates neither.

works.title: シベール / Cybele
works.note: The amateur publication at the centre of both accounts

works.title: 失踪日記
works.note: The memoir of homelessness and alcoholism

entries.category: Doujinshi-Origin Creators and the Circle System
entries.name: Kio Shimoku
entries.description: The professional who cards the amateur system from inside, in a commercial magazine.
entries.meta: Shimoku Kio in English-market credits · born 1974 · Afternoon.
entries.knownFor: A serial about a university circle producing doujinshi, published commercially, which functions as the most detailed procedural account of the circuit available in the medium itself — print runs, deadlines, tables, money.
entries.signature: Ordinary drawing in service of exact social observation; the comedy comes from accuracy rather than from exaggeration, and the production detail is correct enough to be used as reference.

works.title: げんしけん / Genshiken
works.note: The procedural account `serial-61` and `serial-62` both cite

entries.category: Doujinshi-Origin Creators and the Circle System
entries.name: Himaruya Hidekaz
entries.description: The web-origin path into print, in its clearest early form.
entries.meta: Hidekaz Himaruya in English-market credits · born 1985 · personal website, then commercial print.
entries.knownFor: A work published to an open website that accumulated a readership with no institutional filter and was subsequently acquired for print and adaptation — the inversion `serial-65` describes, in which discovery precedes selection.
entries.signature: Very short, gag-driven strips built for scroll-reading and repeat visits, with a cast of national personifications whose treatment is affectionate, stereotype-based, and has drawn objection on exactly that ground; the objection is part of the record.

works.title: Axis powers ヘタリア / Axis Powers Hetalia

entries.category: Doujinshi-Origin Creators and the Circle System
entries.name: ONE
entries.description: The web-original serial redrawn for print, and what that redraw actually changed.
entries.meta: ONE · a single-element pen name; no family-given order exists to gloss, and the exemption is declared in config with this reason.
entries.knownFor: A webcomic drawn with deliberate crudity that acquired an enormous readership on its writing alone, then a commercial redraw by a different artist that preserved the writing and replaced the page grammar.
entries.signature: Comic timing built on anticlimax — a structure that sets up escalation and then declines it — which survives the change of artist intact and is the clearest evidence that the writing and the drawing are separable here.

works.title: ワンパンマン / One-Punch Man
works.note: Web original; the commercial redraw is the version `serial-66` and `page-10` discuss

entries.category: Essay, Documentary and Reportage Manga
entries.name: Saibara Rieko
entries.description: The essay line's most commercially successful and most uncomfortable practitioner.
entries.meta: Rieko Saibara in English-market credits · born 1964 · newspapers, magazines and the essay-manga market.
entries.knownFor: Autobiographical work about family, money, gambling and alcohol, published in a mainstream newspaper strip and in essay collections, and refusing the reassurance the form usually supplies.
entries.signature: A deliberately rough, childlike line used for material — addiction, bereavement, the household economy — that would be unbearable rendered realistically. The gap between the drawing's register and the content's is the technique, and it is the same gap `author-9` uses in the opposite direction.

works.title: 毎日かあさん / Mainichi Kaasan

entries.category: Essay, Documentary and Reportage Manga
entries.name: Hanawa Kazuichi
entries.description: Reportage from inside a prison, by someone who was in it.
entries.meta: Kazuichi Hanawa in English-market credits · born 1947 · the alternative magazines, then reportage.
entries.knownFor: A documentary account of three years in a Japanese prison, drawn after his release, which is the medium's most cited piece of first-person institutional reportage.
entries.signature: Obsessive procedural detail — meals, cell layout, the schedule — rendered with a precision that turns monotony into structure. There is almost no drama and the absence is the point: the account's authority comes from its refusal to shape the experience into a story.

works.title: 刑務所の中 / Keimusho no Naka

entries.category: Essay, Documentary and Reportage Manga
entries.name: Oguri Saori
entries.description: The domestic essay strip as cross-cultural observation, and the ceiling of the form.
entries.meta: Saori Oguri in English-market credits · born 1966 · essay-manga market.
entries.knownFor: A long-running essay series about daily life in an intercultural marriage, which sold at a scale the essay form rarely reaches and made the four-panel domestic observation a commercial category in its own right.
entries.signature: Small observations rendered without editorial: the misunderstanding is stated, both parties are treated as reasonable, and the strip declines to conclude. The restraint is what keeps the material from becoming a catalogue of national traits, which is the form's standing failure mode.

works.title: ダーリンは外国人 / Daarin wa Gaikokujin
works.note: The series that made the category

entries.category: Essay, Documentary and Reportage Manga
entries.name: Tatsuta Kazuto
entries.description: Reportage from inside the Fukushima Daiichi decommissioning, and a contested account.
entries.meta: Kazuto Tatsuta in English-market credits · a pen name; the creator worked at the site and published under it · essay and reportage manga.
entries.knownFor: A first-person account of working as a contract labourer on the Fukushima Daiichi decommissioning, drawn from direct experience and serialised commercially.
entries.signature: Procedural, undramatic documentation of shift work, dosimetry and equipment, with the author's own limited vantage stated as a limit rather than smoothed over. **The reception divided and both positions are serious**: the account has been valued as rare first-hand documentation of conditions almost nobody outside the site can describe, and criticised for a matter-of-factness that readers have argued understates the hazard and the contracting structure around it. `checklist-11`'s expert-reader audit is the relevant instrument, and this pack does not settle the dispute.

works.title: いちえふ 福島第一原子力発電所労働記 / Ichi-efu: Fukushima Daiichi Genshiryoku Hatsudensho Rōdōki

entries.category: Educational and Commissioned Manga
entries.name: Asari Yoshitoo
entries.description: The science-explanation serial, done at a standard the category rarely reaches.
entries.meta: Yoshitoo Asari in English-market credits · born 1962 · children's science magazines and SF comedy.
entries.knownFor: A long-running science-education serial for children that explains mechanisms rather than reciting conclusions, and is respected by readers who came to it as adults — a rare outcome for commissioned educational work.
entries.signature: Genuine explanation staged as comedy, with the demonstration drawn rather than described; the joke and the mechanism are the same panel, which is why the material survives being read for pleasure.

works.title: まんがサイエンス / Manga Science

entries.category: Educational and Commissioned Manga
entries.name: Shimizu Akane
entries.description: The commissioned-explanation form reaching the mainstream through genre rather than through pedagogy.
entries.meta: Akane Shimizu in English-market credits · born 1991 · Shōnen Sirius.
entries.knownFor: A serial personifying the cells of the human body as workers, which teaches immunology accurately while running as an ensemble workplace comedy, and which reached an audience far outside the educational market.
entries.signature: Anthropomorphism disciplined by accuracy — each character's behaviour is constrained by what the cell actually does, so the story cannot drift from the science without breaking the cast. `trope-55`'s group-with-a-job is the structure it runs on.

works.title: はたらく細胞 / Hataraku Saibō

entries.category: Educational and Commissioned Manga
entries.name: Aihara Kōji
entries.description: The how-to manual as satire, and the most honest account of the industry's economics in the medium.
entries.meta: Koji Aihara in English-market credits · born 1963 · with Takekuma Kentarō, in the seinen magazines.
entries.knownFor: A parody instructional serial on how to make manga, co-authored with a critic, which teaches the conventions accurately in the course of mocking them and is used as an actual reference despite itself.
entries.signature: The satire works because the underlying description is correct — page rates, assistant costs, editorial pressure and genre formula are all reported accurately and then ridiculed, which is why `serial-56` cites it for economics rather than for jokes.

works.title: サルでも描けるまんが教室 / Saru demo Kakeru Manga Kyōshitsu

entries.category: The Prewar and Early Postwar Shōjo Line
entries.name: Matsumoto Katsuji
entries.description: The prewar shōjo page, and the modern girls' comic before the war interrupted it.
entries.meta: Katsuji Matsumoto in English-market credits · 1904–1986 · prewar girls' magazines.
entries.knownFor: Illustration and comics for girls' magazines from the 1930s, including a work now cited as an early instance of a modern, cinematic shōjo page — decades before the transformation usually dated to the 1970s.
entries.signature: Fashion-illustration line and a designer's page sense, applied to comic narrative; the girl protagonist as a stylish modern subject rather than as a moral lesson, which was itself the innovation.

works.title: 謎のクローバー / Nazo no Clover
works.note: Cited as an early modern shōjo page

works.title: くるくるクルミちゃん / Kurukuru Kurumi-chan

entries.category: The Prewar and Early Postwar Shōjo Line
entries.name: Kurakane Shōsuke
entries.description: The immediate postwar girls' strip, and the commercial machine around it.
entries.meta: Shosuke Kurakane in English-market credits · 1914–1973 · postwar girls' magazines and newspapers.
entries.knownFor: A hugely popular postwar girls' serial that ran across magazine, radio, film and stage — an early and complete instance of the media-mix that `craft-30` treats as a modern condition.
entries.signature: Gentle domestic comedy built on a single legible character trait, drawn in a soft rounded line, with the merchandise potential visible in the design itself.

works.title: あんみつ姫 / Anmitsu Hime

entries.category: The Prewar and Early Postwar Shōjo Line
entries.name: Watanabe Masako
entries.description: One of the first women to make a career in shōjo, and one of the longest careers in the medium.
entries.meta: Masako Watanabe in English-market credits · born 1929 · postwar girls' magazines onward.
entries.knownFor: Working professionally in shōjo from the early 1950s — when the field's creators were still largely men — and continuing for over six decades, into the josei market that did not exist when she started.
entries.signature: European settings, melodrama structured around inheritance and social class, and a willingness to let a heroine be unhappy for a long time; the register the 1970s generation inherited and then rebuilt.

works.title: ガラスの仮面 / Garasu no Kamen
works.note: Not her work; the theatrical-melodrama line she helped establish

entries.category: The Prewar and Early Postwar Shōjo Line
entries.name: Mizuno Hideko
entries.description: The bridge between the Tokiwa-sō generation and the shōjo transformation.
entries.meta: Hideko Mizuno in English-market credits · born 1939 · the boys' and girls' magazines, then shōjo.
entries.knownFor: Being the one woman in the Tokiwa-sō circle, and then producing work in the 1960s that put romance, sexuality and a girl's own desire at the centre of a shōjo serial — the material the 1970s generation is usually credited with introducing.
entries.signature: Full-figure fashion drawing and a colour sense carried over from illustration, with narrative built on the heroine's wanting rather than on her being chosen. She is the standing counter-example to any account that begins the transformation in 1970.

works.title: リボンの騎士 / Ribon no Kishi
works.note: Not her work; the Tezuka serial the period is usually dated from

entries.category: The 1970s Shōjo Revolution
entries.name: Hagio Moto
entries.description: The transformation's central figure, and the contested roster she is always the first name on.
entries.meta: Moto Hagio in English-market credits · born 1949 · Shōjo Comic, then Petit Flower and the josei magazines.
entries.knownFor: Science fiction and psychological work in shōjo magazines from the early 1970s — vampires, boarding schools, cloned children, families that do damage — with a formal apparatus built to carry interiority rather than incident.
entries.signature: Time handled as layered rather than sequential: memory, present and anticipation share a page, with panel borders dissolving where the distinction stops mattering. **The Year 24 Group she is invariably named in is a critical construction, not a membership list.** Different critics apply it with different widths, several creators central to the same transformation are excluded by the narrow definition, and some of those named have disputed the framing — including on the ground that it treats a generation of individual careers as a movement. `history-19` states the dispute; this card names it because her card is where readers meet the label first.

works.title: ポーの一族 / Pō no Ichizoku
トーマの心臓 / Tōma no Shinzō

entries.category: The 1970s Shōjo Revolution
entries.name: Takemiya Keiko
entries.description: The creator who forced the market open, and then taught it.
entries.meta: Keiko Takemiya in English-market credits · born 1950 · Shōjo Comic and Manga Shōnen, later a university presidency.
entries.knownFor: A long serial about love between boys, fought for over years against editorial refusal and finally serialised, which opened the commercial space the BL category later occupied — and a second career as an educator running a manga faculty.
entries.signature: Decorative page architecture — flowers, screens, dissolved frames — used structurally rather than ornamentally, with the decoration carrying the emotional register that the dialogue withholds. `page-22` cards the vocabulary; this is where much of it was built.

works.title: 風と木の詩 / Kaze to Ki no Uta
works.note: The serial she fought to publish

works.title: 地球へ… / Terra e…
works.note: The science fiction, and her widest readership

entries.category: The 1970s Shōjo Revolution
entries.name: Ōshima Yumiko
entries.description: The quietest member of the generation, and the one whose formal risks were largest.
entries.meta: Yumiko Oshima in English-market credits · born 1947 · Shōjo Comic and the shōjo monthlies.
entries.knownFor: Work that abandons plot for psychological state, including a long serial narrated by a cat-eared girl whose species is never resolved, and shorter work dealing directly with the sexual abuse of a child — the subject of the work rather than an incident inside it.
entries.signature: Interior monologue running free of any panel, so that the page reads as thought with pictures rather than as pictures with captions. **The child-abuse material is stated here because omitting it would misdescribe the body of work**; `checklist-14` is the audit and the work's own treatment is neither sensational nor consoling.

works.title: 綿の国星 / Wata no Kuni Hoshi

entries.category: The 1970s Shōjo Revolution
entries.name: Yamagishi Ryōko
entries.description: The historical and the uncanny in shōjo, and a name the narrow roster leaves out.
entries.meta: Ryoko Yamagishi in English-market credits · born 1947 · Ribon, then the shōjo monthlies.
entries.knownFor: A historical serial about a prince with supernatural powers and an unreciprocated love for another man, which is among the period's most ambitious works, and an early work usually cited as the first yuri manga.
entries.signature: Classical Japanese material rendered with a dancer's attention to posture and gesture — she trained in ballet — and a willingness to make the reader uncertain whether what is on the page is happening. **She is the clearest case of the roster problem `author-29` names**: central to the transformation by any account of the work, and included or excluded from the Year 24 label depending on which critic is counting.

works.title: 日出処の天子 / Hi Izuru Tokoro no Tenshi
アラベスク / Arabesuku
白い部屋のふたり / Shiroi Heya no Futari
works.note: Usually cited as the first yuri manga

entries.category: The 1970s Shōjo Revolution
entries.name: Ikeda Riyoko
entries.description: The historical epic that made shōjo a mass-market category rather than a girls' one.
entries.meta: Riyoko Ikeda in English-market credits · born 1947 · Margaret.
entries.knownFor: A serial set in the French Revolution, built around a woman raised as a man in the royal guard, which sold at a scale the category had not previously reached and became stage, film and television.
entries.signature: Political history staged as personal melodrama without either half being decorative — the revolution is researched and the romance is the reason anyone is reading, and the work refuses to treat that combination as a compromise.

works.title: ベルサイユのばら / Berusaiyu no Bara
works.note: The serial and the franchise around it

entries.category: The 1970s Shōjo Revolution
entries.name: Satonaka Machiko
entries.description: A career begun at sixteen, and the industry politics half of the generation.
entries.meta: Machiko Satonaka in English-market credits · born 1948 · shōjo weeklies and monthlies.
entries.knownFor: Debuting as a teenager after winning a newcomer prize, producing historical and contemporary work across five decades, and taking a public role in the industry's professional bodies and in the copyright arguments of the digital period.
entries.signature: Directness — a heroine who states what she wants in the first chapter and pursues it — which reads as unremarkable now and separated her sharply from the period's prevailing register of longing and deferral.

works.title: ガラスの仮面 / Garasu no Kamen
works.note: Not her work; the ambition-driven register she shares with it

entries.category: The 1970s Shōjo Revolution
entries.name: Kihara Toshie
entries.description: The generation's supernatural-historical line, and the member who is least often named.
entries.meta: Toshie Kihara in English-market credits · born 1948 · shōjo monthlies.
entries.knownFor: Historical and supernatural work in the same years and often the same magazines as the better-known names, with a body of work of comparable size and a critical profile that has never matched it.
entries.signature: Japanese historical settings treated as genuinely strange rather than as costume, with the supernatural admitted matter-of-factly; the register is closer to a ghost story told at home than to gothic.

works.title: 日出処の天子 / Hi Izuru Tokoro no Tenshi
works.note: Not her work; the historical-supernatural line she also worked in

entries.category: The 1970s Shōjo Revolution
entries.name: Miuchi Suzue
entries.description: The unfinished serial as a fifty-year institution.
entries.meta: Suzue Miuchi in English-market credits · born 1951 · Hana to Yume.
entries.knownFor: A serial about a teenage actress that began in 1976, has run intermittently ever since, and remains unfinished — one of the medium's clearest live cases of the relationship duration builds and the ending problem `psychology-12` describes.
entries.signature: Theatrical melodrama executed without irony: the performances inside the story are staged on the page as performances, with the reader placed in the audience rather than backstage.

works.title: ガラスの仮面 / Garasu no Kamen

entries.category: Shōjo Romance and the Modern Magazine
entries.name: Takeuchi Naoko
entries.description: The magical-girl serial that fused two genres and rebuilt an export market.
entries.meta: Naoko Takeuchi in English-market credits · born 1967 · Nakayoshi.
entries.knownFor: A serial that put the transforming magical girl into a team-based battle structure — a combination neither category had used — and became one of the medium's largest international properties.
entries.signature: Transformation staged as ritual rather than as mechanism, with the sequence repeated deliberately so that its variations register, which is `trope-41`'s ritual reading and `psychology-13`'s repetition argument in one device. **She is carded as `superhero:Naoko Takeuchi`, where the reading is the team-superhero structure her work exports into.** This pack reads her from the other side: a shōjo creator whose magazine, readership and formal vocabulary are the ones this collection describes, and whose battle structure is the import rather than the origin.

works.title: 美少女戦士セーラームーン / Sailor Moon

entries.category: Shōjo Romance and the Modern Magazine
entries.name: Yoshizumi Wataru
entries.description: The 1990s shōjo romance at its most exactly engineered.
entries.meta: Wataru Yoshizumi in English-market credits · born 1963 · Ribon.
entries.knownFor: A romance serial built on a deliberately complicated relational grid — two teenagers, two sets of parents remarrying across the pair — which became the decade's model for how much complication a shōjo romance could carry.
entries.signature: Emotional bookkeeping: every character's state is tracked and updated each chapter, so the reader always knows exactly who is holding what, which is what allows the plot to be as tangled as it is without becoming confusing.

works.title: ママレード・ボーイ / Marmalade Boy

entries.category: Shōjo Romance and the Modern Magazine
entries.name: Kamio Yōko
entries.description: The longest-selling shōjo serial, and the class antagonism inside it.
entries.meta: Yoko Kamio in English-market credits · born 1966 · Margaret.
entries.knownFor: A serial about a working-class scholarship student against a group of wealthy boys, which ran for a decade, sold enormously, and was adapted across Asia more widely than almost any other manga.
entries.signature: Romance built on class humiliation rather than on misunderstanding — the obstacle is money and status and stays money and status — which is why the structure travelled to markets whose romance conventions differ from Japan's.

works.title: 花より男子 / Hana yori Dango
works.note: The serial and its regional adaptations

entries.category: Shōjo Romance and the Modern Magazine
entries.name: Obana Miho
entries.description: Comedy and childhood damage in the same serial, at the same time.
entries.meta: Miho Obana in English-market credits · born 1970 · Ribon.
entries.knownFor: A serial about a child actress that reads as broad comedy and carries, without changing register, material about neglect, bullying and a mother's withdrawal.
entries.signature: Tonal simultaneity — the joke and the injury occupy the same page rather than alternating — which is unusual in any medium and depends on the drawing carrying the second register while the dialogue carries the first.

works.title: こどものおもちゃ / Kodomo no Omocha

entries.category: Shōjo Romance and the Modern Magazine
entries.name: Nakajo Hisaya
entries.description: The disguise plot as a structure for writing about gender without arguing about it.
entries.meta: Hisaya Nakajo in English-market credits · born 1973 · Hana to Yume.
entries.knownFor: A long-running serial about a girl who enrols at a boys' school in disguise, which uses a very old comic device to spend hundreds of chapters on what it is like to be read as the wrong thing.
entries.signature: Farce discipline — the disguise's rules are fixed early and never bent for convenience, so every scene's tension comes from the rules rather than from authorial mercy, which is `trope-46`'s changed-body card in its comic register.

works.title: 花ざかりの君たちへ / Hanazakari no Kimitachi e

entries.category: Shōjo Romance and the Modern Magazine
entries.name: Shiina Karuho
entries.description: The confession structure slowed down to its limit.
entries.meta: Karuho Shiina in English-market credits · born 1975 · Bessatsu Margaret.
entries.knownFor: A serial that takes a straightforward premise — a shy girl, a popular boy, a mutual liking — and extends it over years by treating every small misreading as a full event.
entries.signature: Extreme temporal magnification: a single conversation can occupy a chapter, with the interior monologue and the drawn pause doing the work that plot does elsewhere. `trope-25`'s dated-confession structure is the frame, and this is the extreme case of deferring it without cheating.

works.title: 君に届け / Kimi ni Todoke

entries.category: Josei and the Adult Woman's Register
entries.name: Yazawa Ai
entries.description: Fashion, ambition and money, written for readers who had left school.
entries.meta: Ai Yazawa in English-market credits · born 1967 · Ribon, then Cookie.
entries.knownFor: Serials about young women's careers, bands, clothes and self-invention, which moved shōjo's readership into adulthood without changing the emotional seriousness, and one long serial left unfinished on medical hiatus.
entries.signature: Clothes as characterisation, drawn with a designer's specificity so that a change of outfit is a change of state; and an unusual willingness to let ambition and friendship damage each other. **She is carded as `romance:Ai Yazawa`, where the reading is the romance genre's treatment of the couple.** Here she is a josei creator, and the delta is that this pack reads the career and the money as the subject and the romance as one of its costs.

works.title: NANA
ハッピー・マニア / Happy Mania
works.note: Not her work; the josei register she works beside

entries.category: Josei and the Adult Woman's Register
entries.name: Yoshida Akimi
entries.description: Half a century of work across three demographics, in the same steady voice.
entries.meta: Akimi Yoshida in English-market credits · born 1956 · shōjo magazines, then seinen and josei.
entries.knownFor: A long career spanning a hard-edged crime serial in a shōjo magazine and, decades later, a quiet family serial in a monthly — the same author working at the two extremes of the medium's register.
entries.signature: Restraint that reads as confidence: no emphasis, no decorative pages, dialogue that stops early, and emotional events staged in the flattest possible way so the reader has to do the arithmetic.

works.title: 海街diary / Umimachi Diary

entries.category: Josei and the Adult Woman's Register
entries.name: Anno Moyoco
entries.description: The josei serial at its least consoling.
entries.meta: Moyoco Anno in English-market credits · born 1971 · josei and seinen magazines.
entries.knownFor: Work about women's ambition, appetite and self-destruction that declines to make its protagonists likeable, and a body of work spanning josei, seinen and the historical.
entries.signature: Compulsive energy in the line itself — hatching and motion where another artist would use stillness — matched to protagonists who cannot stop. The style and the subject are the same observation twice.

works.title: ハッピー・マニア / Happy Mania

entries.category: Josei and the Adult Woman's Register
entries.name: Yoshinaga Fumi
entries.description: The creator who moved from the amateur BL circuit into the historical epic, and kept the same instrument.
entries.meta: Fumi Yoshinaga in English-market credits · born 1971 · doujinshi, then BL magazines, then josei.
entries.knownFor: A gender-reversed Edo historical epic, a long-running domestic serial about a gay couple's cooking, and a career that began in the self-published BL circuit — the pipeline `serial-64` describes, ending somewhere the pipeline is not usually credited with reaching.
entries.signature: Conversation as structure. Whole chapters are two people talking while doing something ordinary, with the historical or political argument carried entirely inside the exchange, and the panel work kept plain so nothing competes with the talk.

works.title: 大奥 / Ōoku
きのう何食べた? / Kinō Nani Tabeta?

entries.category: Josei and the Adult Woman's Register
entries.name: Higashimura Akiko
entries.description: Comic self-exposure as the josei register's most commercially successful mode.
entries.meta: Akiko Higashimura in English-market credits · born 1975 · josei magazines.
entries.knownFor: Serials about women in their thirties failing to arrange their lives as planned, written with an autobiographical looseness that made the essay register commercially central to josei.
entries.signature: Speed — rough, fast drawing with the correction lines left in — which reads as candour and lets a chapter turn from farce to something painful in a single panel without the tonal seam showing.

works.title: 東京タラレバ娘 / Tokyo Tarareba Musume

entries.category: Josei and the Adult Woman's Register
entries.name: Konari Misato
entries.description: The contemporary josei serial about leaving the arrangement rather than fixing it.
entries.meta: Misato Konari in English-market credits · working from the 2010s · josei magazines.
entries.knownFor: A serial about a woman who quits her job, her relationship and her flat after a breakdown, and rebuilds slowly — a structure with no romantic resolution as its object and no return to the starting arrangement.
entries.signature: Small material detail carrying psychological state: what is in the fridge, what the rent is, what the neighbours are like. The recovery is legible through logistics rather than through declaration.

works.title: 凪のお暇 / Nagi no Oitoma

entries.category: BL, Yaoi and Yuri
entries.name: Ozaki Minami
entries.description: The doujinshi circuit's first mass-market BL crossover.
entries.meta: Minami Ozaki in English-market credits · born 1963 · doujinshi, then commercial BL.
entries.knownFor: A commercially serialised work that came directly out of the self-published circuit and sold at a scale that demonstrated a market the publishers had not been serving.
entries.signature: Melodrama at maximum intensity — obsession, injury, declaration — with the visual register borrowed from shōjo's decorative apparatus and used at a pitch shōjo magazines would not have permitted.

works.title: 絶愛-1989- / Zetsuai -1989

entries.category: BL, Yaoi and Yuri
entries.name: Nakamura Shungiku
entries.description: BL as a stable commercial category with a house structure.
entries.meta: Shungiku Nakamura in English-market credits · born 1980 · commercial BL magazines.
entries.knownFor: Two long parallel serials set in adjacent workplaces, which established a durable model for BL as an ongoing commercial property rather than as a single-volume category.
entries.signature: Workplace comedy carrying the relationship rather than the other way round; the couples are stable and the incident comes from the job, which is what makes the serials extendable at all.

works.title: 純情ロマンチカ / Junjō Romantica
世界一初恋 / Sekai-ichi Hatsukoi

entries.category: BL, Yaoi and Yuri
entries.name: Nakamura Asumiko
entries.description: The literary end of the category, and the argument the category has with itself.
entries.meta: Asumiko Nakamura in English-market credits · born 1976 · BL and josei magazines.
entries.knownFor: Work in the BL category that is unusually restrained and formally deliberate, and that engages directly with the criticism the category has attracted — most seriously from gay male critics who have argued that a genre about relationships between men, written and read largely by women, has obligations it has not always met.
entries.signature: Elongated figures, wide margins and long silences; the erotic content is present and is not the engine, which is precisely the position in the internal argument her work takes. **The argument is live and both sides are held by serious people** — that the category is a space for women to write desire outside the constraints placed on it elsewhere, and that its conventions have at times misrepresented the lives of the men it depicts. `checklist-13` is the audit; this pack states the dispute and does not settle it.

works.title: 同級生 / Dōkyūsei

entries.category: BL, Yaoi and Yuri
entries.name: Shimura Takako
entries.description: Yuri and trans narrative written as ordinary adolescence.
entries.meta: Takako Shimura in English-market credits · born 1973 · seinen and josei magazines.
entries.knownFor: Serials about girls in love with girls and about trans childhood, published in general magazines rather than in category titles, and written without the melodramatic apparatus the subjects usually attract.
entries.signature: Very quiet pacing and a plain line, with the significant moment placed in an unemphatic panel and left there; the refusal of emphasis is the ethical position as well as the style.

works.title: 青い花 / Aoi Hana

entries.category: BL, Yaoi and Yuri
entries.name: Nakatani Nio
entries.description: The contemporary yuri serial that argues with its own genre.
entries.meta: Nio Nakatani in English-market credits · working from the 2010s · Dengeki Daioh.
entries.knownFor: A serial in which one protagonist cannot feel romantic attraction and the other loves her anyway, which takes the category's central convention and asks what happens if it is refused.
entries.signature: Dialogue that circles the point for chapters, with the layout using empty space to hold the unsaid; the structure `trope-31`'s refused confession describes, extended across an entire work rather than used as a beat.

works.title: やがて君になる / Yagate Kimi ni Naru

entries.category: BL, Yaoi and Yuri
entries.name: Takashima Hiromi
entries.description: The yuri slice-of-life serial, and the category's quietest commercial form.
entries.meta: Hiromi Takashima in English-market credits · working from the 2010s · yuri magazines.
entries.knownFor: A long-running slice-of-life serial about two schoolgirls in an established relationship, which spends its length on ordinary days rather than on getting together.
entries.signature: The relationship as the premise rather than the goal, which removes the genre's usual engine and replaces it with domestic incident — the same structural move `trope-29`'s continuing-relationship card describes, sustained for a whole serial.

works.title: あさがおと加瀬さん。 / Asagao to Kase-san.

entries.category: Antecedents: Newspaper Cartooning and the Prewar Strip
entries.name: Kitazawa Rakuten
entries.description: The first professional cartoonist in the modern sense, and the apparatus he built around the job.
entries.meta: Rakuten Kitazawa in English-market credits · 1876–1955 · newspapers and his own magazine.
entries.knownFor: Founding the colour satirical magazine that anchors the period, being salaried by a newspaper to produce cartoons on a schedule, and running a studio that trained the next generation — the profession's arrival rather than an individual talent.
entries.signature: Western cartoon conventions adapted rather than copied: the caricature and the panel come from the foreign press, the subjects and the visual shorthand are domestic. `history-8`'s argument that the job precedes the art form runs through his career.

works.title: 東京パック / Tokyo Puck
田吾作と杢兵衛の東京見物 / Tagosaku to Mokubē no Tokyo Kenbutsu
works.note: Usually named as the first newspaper strip in the Western sense

entries.category: Antecedents: Newspaper Cartooning and the Prewar Strip
entries.name: Okamoto Ippei
entries.description: The newspaper cartoon as writing, by a man who was also a writer.
entries.meta: Ippei Okamoto in English-market credits · 1886–1948 · newspapers.
entries.knownFor: Developing a form combining drawing and extended prose in newspapers, and founding the professional association that organised cartoonists as a trade — the institutional half of the same arrival.
entries.signature: The picture and the text as equal partners rather than caption and illustration, which is a different lineage from the balloon-carried strip and is one reason the medium's prehistory resists a single line of descent.

works.title: 東京パック / Tokyo Puck
works.note: Not his; the magazine culture he worked inside

entries.category: Antecedents: Newspaper Cartooning and the Prewar Strip
entries.name: Tagawa Suihō
entries.description: The 1930s' defining children's strip, and the war it served.
entries.meta: Suiho Tagawa in English-market credits · 1899–1989 · children's monthlies.
entries.knownFor: A strip about a stray dog in military life that was the decade's most popular children's serial, ran through the war's expansion, and functioned as recruitment as well as comedy.
entries.signature: Clean, geometric character design built for instant recognition and reuse — the merchandising logic `craft-34` describes, decades early. **The craft and the function are stated together**: the strip is genuinely well made, it served the war, and a card that separated those would be doing the evasion §6 exists to prevent. `history-10` carries the same account at period level.

works.title: のらくろ / Norakuro

entries.category: Antecedents: Newspaper Cartooning and the Prewar Strip
entries.name: Shimada Keizō
entries.description: The colonial adventure strip, carried rather than skipped.
entries.meta: Keizo Shimada in English-market credits · 1900–1973 · children's monthlies.
entries.knownFor: An adventure serial set on a South Seas island, enormously popular with children in the 1930s, whose depiction of the islanders is racial caricature of a kind that was conventional then and is indefensible now.
entries.signature: Bright, energetic adventure staging — and a visual system that positions the Japanese boy protagonist as modern against a drawn primitive, which the scholarship reads as the content rather than as a blemish on it. `history-11` states the argument and the reading; this card states that the popularity and the caricature are the same object.

works.title: 冒険ダン吉 / Bōken Dankichi

entries.category: Antecedents: Newspaper Cartooning and the Prewar Strip
entries.name: Shishido Sakō
entries.description: The American apprenticeship, brought back and applied to a Japanese strip.
entries.meta: Sako Shishido in English-market credits · 1888–1969 · newspapers and children's magazines.
entries.knownFor: Working in the United States as a young man, absorbing the American newspaper strip's staging directly rather than through imported copies, and returning to produce work whose panel-to-panel motion was noticeably ahead of its domestic contemporaries.
entries.signature: Movement broken into stages across panels in the American manner — a figure's action carried by the cut rather than by lines drawn inside a single frame — which is the imported half of `history-5`'s transmission argument in one career.

works.title: 冒険ダン吉 / Bōken Dankichi
works.note: Not his; the children's-magazine market he worked in

entries.category: Antecedents: Newspaper Cartooning and the Prewar Strip
entries.name: Asō Yutaka
entries.description: The newspaper family strip, and the first domestic hit built on ordinary life.
entries.meta: Yutaka Aso in English-market credits · 1898–1961 · newspapers.
entries.knownFor: A daily strip about an unemployed man and his household that ran through the interwar years and established the newspaper family comedy as a Japanese form rather than an imported one.
entries.signature: Ordinary domestic incident treated as sufficient material, with the comedy coming from circumstance rather than from gag construction — the register the postwar four-panel newspaper strip inherits wholesale, and which the postwar yonkoma strip carries to its longest run.

works.title: 東京パック / Tokyo Puck
works.note: Not his; the cartoon-magazine culture the newspaper strip grew out of

entries.category: Tezuka and the Story-Manga Generation
entries.name: Fujiko F. Fujio
entries.description: Half of a partnership that published as one name for thirty years, and the children's serial that outlived everything.
entries.meta: Fujiko F. Fujio · a pen name published in this form in both markets; the gloss exemption is declared in config with this reason · children's monthlies and Korokoro Comic.
entries.knownFor: The children's science-fiction serial that is among the most widely read works in the medium's history, published for decades under a shared name that concealed a two-person partnership until it was dissolved in the late 1980s.
entries.signature: A gag structure with a fixed engine — a problem, a gadget, a misuse, a consequence — repeated for thousands of instalments without exhausting itself, and drawn with a clarity built for readers who are learning to read. `serial-57`'s point about the shared name is this career, and `page-26`'s balloon discipline is best studied here.

works.title: ドラえもん / Doraemon

entries.category: Tezuka and the Story-Manga Generation
entries.name: Abiko Motoo
entries.description: The other half, and the darker line the shared name hid.
entries.meta: Motoo Abiko in English-market credits · 1934–2022 · children's monthlies, then seinen.
entries.knownFor: Working under the shared pen name for three decades while producing work of a completely different temperature — black comedy and adult horror — and being routinely misattributed as a result.
entries.signature: Everyday cruelty rendered in a children's-comic line, so the discomfort comes from the mismatch. **The partnership is the documented case that `serial-57` and `serial-60` both rest on**: two people, one credit, and a back catalogue that had to be re-attributed publicly after the split.

works.title: ドラえもん / Doraemon
works.note: Not his; the shared credit it was published under

entries.category: Tezuka and the Story-Manga Generation
entries.name: Tezuka Osamu
entries.description: The most consequential career in the medium, and the claim about it that is not settled.
entries.meta: Osamu Tezuka in English-market credits · 1928–1989 · akahon, then every magazine that mattered.
entries.knownFor: An output of extraordinary size across children's, adult and experimental work; the founding of an animation studio whose economics shaped the adaptation system; and the magazine COM, which functioned as a laboratory for the next generation.
entries.signature: Story-manga at length — hundreds of pages sustaining a single narrative, with a cast reused across unrelated works like a repertory company. **The received claim that he invented the medium's cinematic page grammar is contested and this card carries both sides**: prewar precedents exist and are named in the scholarship, the deflationary correction has itself been over-applied, and the defensible statement is that a repertoire already in circulation was consolidated and made dominant. `history-13` carries the same dispute.

works.title: 新宝島 / Shin Takarajima
火の鳥 / Hi no Tori
ブラック・ジャック / Black Jack
アドルフに告ぐ / Adolf ni Tsugu

entries.category: Tezuka and the Story-Manga Generation
entries.name: Ishinomori Shōtarō
entries.description: The most prolific career on record, and the transformation format it exported.
entries.meta: Shotaro Ishinomori in English-market credits · 1938–1998 · every demographic, and the commissioned market.
entries.knownFor: An output large enough to hold a certified record, spanning children's adventure, the transforming-hero format, experimental work in COM, and an economics primer in comics form.
entries.signature: Format invention rather than a house style — the cyborg team, the insect-masked hero, the wordless experimental sequence and the explanatory diagram are all his, and share almost nothing visually. **He is carded as `superhero:Shotaro Ishinomori`, where the reading is the transforming hero's export into that genre.** Here the reading is the range: a career that treats the medium as a set of formats to be built rather than a form to be mastered, which `history-17`'s laboratory magazine is part of.
