works.title: マンガ日本経済入門 / Manga Nihon Keizai Nyūmon

entries.category: Tezuka and the Story-Manga Generation
entries.name: Yokoyama Mitsuteru
entries.description: The giant robot with a pilot outside it, and the historical epic almost nobody in English has read.
entries.meta: Mitsuteru Yokoyama in English-market credits · 1934–2004 · children's and seinen magazines.
entries.knownFor: The remote-controlled giant robot that established the mecha line, an early magical-girl serial, and enormous historical adaptations that occupied the second half of his career.
entries.signature: Plain, legible staging that puts the machine's scale in relation to streets and people — `page-18`'s measurement argument in its founding case. **He is carded as `superhero:Mitsuteru Yokoyama` for the robot's place in that genre's power fantasies.** This pack reads the control relation instead: the boy is outside the machine holding a box, which is a different proposition about power from a body that transforms, and the whole mecha line descends from that difference.

works.title: 鉄人28号 / Tetsujin 28-gō
魔法使いサリー / Sally the Witch

entries.category: Tezuka and the Story-Manga Generation
entries.name: Sakai Shichima
entries.description: The co-credit that disappears from the story, and what that omission is evidence of.
entries.meta: Shichima Sakai in English-market credits · 1905–1969 · the Osaka akahon market.
entries.knownFor: Being the co-credited collaborator on the 1947 akahon volume conventionally treated as the medium's postwar turning point — and being absent from most popular accounts of it.
entries.signature: An akahon professional's economy: fast, cheap, built for a market with no margin. **The extent of his contribution is disputed** — accounts differ on how much of the story and layout were his, and the dispute has never been resolved from the surviving evidence. This pack cards him because `serial-60`'s rule cuts both ways: absence of a credit is not evidence of absence of a contributor, and neither is the presence of a famous name beside it. `history-13` states the same omission at period level.

works.title: 新宝島 / Shin Takarajima
works.note: Co-credited; the contribution is disputed and the dispute is not settled here

entries.category: Tezuka and the Story-Manga Generation
entries.name: Chiba Tetsuya
entries.description: The draughtsman who made defeat legible, across sixty years.
entries.meta: Tetsuya Chiba in English-market credits · born 1939 · children's, boys' and sports magazines.
entries.knownFor: Drawing the boxing serial that is the medium's standard reference for an ending, and a long career across shōjo, shōnen and sports that has made him the industry's most quietly respected figure.
entries.signature: Bodies that carry damage honestly — posture, weight, exhaustion — so that a fight reads as cost rather than as spectacle. The final image of his best-known work is cited more than any other single panel in the medium, and it is a still figure rather than a blow.

works.title: あしたのジョー / Ashita no Joe

entries.category: Tezuka and the Story-Manga Generation
entries.name: Terada Hiroo
entries.description: The Tokiwa-sō circle's organiser, and the career the system did not carry.
entries.meta: Hiroo Terada in English-market credits · 1931–1992 · children's monthlies.
entries.knownFor: Being the senior figure in the apartment building where much of the story-manga generation lived and trained, and producing gentle sports and school work that fell out of favour as the market's register hardened in the 1960s.
entries.signature: Wholesome children's comedy with an explicit ethic — he refused to draw the violence the shift to weeklies rewarded, and the refusal ended his commercial career. **The training pipeline `serial-55` describes had losers as well as graduates**, and this is the card that says so.

works.title: 新宝島 / Shin Takarajima
works.note: Not his; the akahon moment the circle formed around

entries.category: Shōnen Battle and the Weekly System
entries.name: Toriyama Akira
entries.description: The weekly system's most efficient page, and the editorial relationship that shaped it.
entries.meta: Akira Toriyama in English-market credits · 1955–2024 · Weekly Shōnen Jump.
entries.knownFor: A gag serial and then a battle serial that became the template most later Jump serials are measured against, and a working relationship with an editor whose pressure both men described publicly.
entries.signature: Legibility above everything — clean silhouettes, uncluttered backgrounds, action staged so the geometry is never in doubt, and a page that can be read at speed by a child on a train. **He is carded as `superhero:Akira Toriyama` for the escalating-power structure his work exports.** This pack reads the production side instead: a page designed for weekly consumption under a survey, and a series whose direction is documented as a negotiation rather than a plan. `history-3`'s Torishima account is the same relationship from the editor's side.

works.title: ドラゴンボール / Dragon Ball

entries.category: Shōnen Battle and the Weekly System
entries.name: Oda Eiichirō
entries.description: The longest-running serial of the modern weekly era, and what sustaining it requires.
entries.meta: Eiichiro Oda in English-market credits · born 1975 · Weekly Shōnen Jump.
entries.knownFor: A serial running since 1997 with a planned ending stated from early on, an enormous cast, and volume sales at a scale no contemporary matches.
entries.signature: Density — panels crowded with incidental cast, jokes and detail — combined with a long-range structure in which minor material from years earlier becomes load-bearing. `psychology-15`'s memory problem is the standing risk, and the work manages it by restaging rather than by assuming recall.

works.title: ONE PIECE

entries.category: Shōnen Battle and the Weekly System
entries.name: Kishimoto Masashi
entries.description: The battle serial's most systematic power taxonomy, and the international readership it built.
entries.meta: Masashi Kishimoto in English-market credits · born 1974 · Weekly Shōnen Jump.
entries.knownFor: A ninja serial whose techniques form an explicit, learnable system, and which was among the first Jump serials whose international readership was visibly part of its commercial life during serialisation rather than after.
entries.signature: Rules a reader can hold: named techniques with stated costs and a hierarchy that stays consistent, which is `trope-13`'s tier list made visible and `trope-19`'s named cost in their most disciplined form.

works.title: NARUTO -ナルト- / Naruto

entries.category: Shōnen Battle and the Weekly System
entries.name: Kurumada Masami
entries.description: The armoured team serial, and the merchandise structure built into the fiction.
entries.meta: Masami Kurumada in English-market credits · born 1953 · Weekly Shōnen Jump.
entries.knownFor: A serial whose protagonists wear constellation-themed armour, which was designed to be manufactured and became one of the earliest cases of a toy line and a manga being planned together.
entries.signature: Escalation by tier, with each opponent introducing a rank above the last, and a design language built for three dimensions. **He is carded as `superhero:Masami Kurumada` for the armoured team's place in that genre.** This pack reads the commercial mechanism: `craft-34`'s merchandise logic is not a consequence of the serial's success here, it is in the premise.

works.title: 聖闘士星矢 / Seinto Seiya

entries.category: Shōnen Battle and the Weekly System
entries.name: Horikoshi Kōhei
entries.description: The American superhero genre re-imported into the weekly system, and the changes that required.
entries.meta: Kohei Horikoshi in English-market credits · born 1986 · Weekly Shōnen Jump.
entries.knownFor: A serial that takes the American superhero premise wholesale — a society of powered people, a hero licence, a school for heroes — and runs it on the Japanese school-serial and tournament structure.
entries.signature: The two traditions visible at once: costume and power design out of American comics, plot architecture out of Jump. **He is carded as `superhero:Kohei Horikoshi` for the genre inheritance.** Here the reading is the reverse direction — what the weekly system does to an imported genre, which is to put it in a school, give it a tournament, and run it under a survey. `subgenre-16` and `trope-9` are the machinery it was fitted to.

works.title: 僕のヒーローアカデミア / My Hero Academia

entries.category: Shōnen Battle and the Weekly System
entries.name: Togashi Yoshihiro
entries.description: The battle serial pushed past its own conventions, at the cost of the schedule.
entries.meta: Yoshihiro Togashi in English-market credits · born 1966 · Weekly Shōnen Jump.
entries.knownFor: Two major serials, the second of which has run intermittently for decades with long hiatuses, and both of which take the tournament structure apart while using it.
entries.signature: Rule systems elaborate enough to be argued about, and a willingness to spend chapters on negotiation, strategy or exposition where the format expects a fight. **The hiatus history is part of the record and is not gossip**: it is the clearest live case of `serial-13`'s rhythms being the thing a career is actually built on, and of `psychology-16`'s argument that readers stay for reliability.

works.title: HUNTER×HUNTER

entries.category: Shōnen Battle and the Weekly System
entries.name: Arakawa Hiromu
entries.description: The battle serial planned to its ending, by a creator who also cards her own farm.
entries.meta: Hiromu Arakawa in English-market credits · born 1973 · Shōnen Gangan, and the essay market.
entries.knownFor: A shōnen serial with a stated endpoint reached on schedule — rare enough to be the standing counter-example to the format's structural pressures — and an autobiographical essay series about her family's dairy farm.
entries.signature: Rules honoured. The alchemical system's central law is fixed in the first chapter and every subsequent development obeys it, which is `psychology-15`'s restaging discipline done as design rather than as repair. **She is carded as `fantasy:Hiromu Arakawa` for the magic system's place in that genre.** This pack reads the serialisation: a weekly-format work that resisted the extension pressure `serial-31` describes, and finished.

works.title: 鋼の錬金術師 / Hagane no Renkinjutsushi
百姓貴族 / Hyakushō Kizoku

entries.category: Shōnen Battle and the Weekly System
entries.name: Isayama Hajime
entries.description: The serial that carried its ending's argument from the first chapter, and the reception that followed.
entries.meta: Hajime Isayama in English-market credits · born 1986 · Bessatsu Shōnen Magazine.
entries.knownFor: A monthly serial that became the decade's largest international manga property, and whose conclusion was received with unusual public disagreement.
entries.signature: Structural withholding — information the reader needs is held for years and then delivered as a reframing rather than as a reveal, which is `page-8`'s withholding at the scale of a whole work. **The divided reception of the ending is on the record and this card states it without ruling on it**, which is also `psychology-12`'s structural point: a decade of accumulation is not dischargeable by a final chapter.

works.title: 進撃の巨人 / Attack on Titan

entries.category: Shōnen Battle and the Weekly System
entries.name: Takahashi Rumiko
entries.description: The most commercially successful woman in the medium, working in the boys' magazines throughout.
entries.meta: Rumiko Takahashi in English-market credits · born 1957 · Weekly Shōnen Sunday.
entries.knownFor: Four decades of long-running serials in a boys' weekly, comedy and action in roughly equal measure, and volume sales among the highest recorded for any creator.
entries.signature: A relational engine rather than a plot: a fixed group of characters whose incompatible wants generate incident indefinitely, which is why the serials can run for hundreds of chapters without an escalating threat. `trope-27`'s relational grid is this method carded.

entries.category: Sports and the Spokon Line
entries.name: Kajiwara Ikki
entries.description: The writer who defined the sports serial, and the ideology inside it.
entries.meta: Ikki Kajiwara in English-market credits · 1936–1987 · boys' weeklies.
entries.knownFor: Writing — not drawing — the serials that established the spokon form: endurance, cruelty in training, self-abnegation, and a mentor who withholds.
entries.signature: Suffering as the mechanism of worth, stated as doctrine rather than implied. **The ideology is legible and dated and both are worth saying**: it produced the medium's most affecting work about failure, and its account of what a body owes an ambition belongs to a specific postwar moment. `trope-17` and `trope-20` are the machinery; this is where it was assembled.

works.title: 巨人の星 / Kyojin no Hoshi
あしたのジョー / Ashita no Joe

entries.category: Sports and the Spokon Line
entries.name: Kawasaki Noboru
entries.description: The other half of the spokon form's founding partnership.
entries.meta: Noboru Kawasaki in English-market credits · born 1941 · boys' weeklies.
entries.knownFor: Drawing the baseball serial that established the form, in a heightened register that made the training sequence a set piece rather than a transition.
entries.signature: Expressionist distortion in service of effort — the pitch drawn as a physical ordeal, with speed lines, sweat and facial strain pushed past realism. The style dates precisely, and the dating is why later sports manga reads as a reaction to it.

works.title: 巨人の星 / Kyojin no Hoshi

entries.category: Sports and the Spokon Line
entries.name: Yamamoto Sumika
entries.description: The spokon structure moved into shōjo, and what changed when it got there.
entries.meta: Sumika Yamamoto in English-market credits · born 1949 · Margaret.
entries.knownFor: A tennis serial in a girls' magazine that took the endurance-and-mentor structure and ran it with a female protagonist, at a scale that made the sports serial a shōjo category as well as a shōnen one.
entries.signature: The mentor relationship written as emotional rather than disciplinary, and rivalry treated as intimacy — which is the shōjo apparatus applied to spokon material and is the reason the transfer worked rather than reading as an imitation.

works.title: エースをねらえ! / Ace o Nerae!

entries.category: Sports and the Spokon Line
entries.name: Inoue Takehiko
entries.description: The sports serial after spokon, and a second career in brush and ink.
entries.meta: Takehiko Inoue in English-market credits · born 1967 · Weekly Shōnen Jump, then seinen magazines.
entries.knownFor: A basketball serial that replaced the endurance ideology with technique and team dynamics, a wheelchair-basketball serial, and a long historical work drawn substantially in brush.
entries.signature: Anatomical accuracy in motion, and long wordless sequences where the reading pace is set entirely by panel size and silence — `page-15`'s positional argument and `page-12`'s duration lever, executed at a level the collection cites rather than explains.

works.title: SLAM DUNK
バガボンド / Vagabond

entries.category: Sports and the Spokon Line
entries.name: Ishizuka Shinichi
entries.description: The procedural sports serial, where the opponent is not a person.
entries.meta: Shinichi Ishizuka in English-market credits · born 1971 · Big Comic Original.
entries.knownFor: A mountain-rescue serial whose subject is competence and altitude rather than competition, and which is researched to a standard that mountaineering readers accept.
entries.signature: Human figures held small inside large frames so the mountain does the measuring — `page-20`'s downward scale as the book's central argument — and a refusal to make death dramatic.

works.title: 岳 みんなの山 / Gaku: Minna no Yama

entries.category: Seinen and the Adult Magazine
entries.name: Urasawa Naoki
entries.description: The suspense serial built entirely on the withheld answer.
entries.meta: Naoki Urasawa in English-market credits · born 1960 · Big Comic Spirits and Big Comic Original.
entries.knownFor: Long suspense serials whose structure is a question posed early and deferred for years, and which have made him the most internationally visible seinen creator of his generation.
entries.signature: Faces — ordinary, specific, unglamorous — carrying almost all the tension, with the plot advanced by expression across a sequence of close panels rather than by incident. `page-8`'s withholding is his working method at the scale of a whole serial, and `psychology-14`'s point about readers filling the gap is the risk his structures run deliberately.

works.title: MONSTER
20世紀少年 / 20th Century Boys

entries.category: Seinen and the Adult Magazine
entries.name: Hirokane Kenshi
entries.description: The salaryman serial, and the medium taking the office seriously as a subject.
entries.meta: Kenshi Hirokane in English-market credits · born 1947 · Morning.
entries.knownFor: A serial following a corporate employee's career from section chief upward across decades of real-time promotion, which made the workplace a durable seinen category — the magazine demographic it ran in, not a genre.
entries.signature: Procedural accuracy about corporate structure — meetings, factions, transfers, the politics of a posting — treated as inherently dramatic, which is `trope-59`'s work-as-incident card in its founding case.

works.title: 課長島耕作 / Kachō Shima Kōsaku

entries.category: Seinen and the Adult Magazine
entries.name: Kawaguchi Kaiji
entries.description: The political thriller as a serious argument about Japan's postwar settlement.
entries.meta: Kaiji Kawaguchi in English-market credits · born 1948 · Morning and Big Comic.
entries.knownFor: Serials built on constitutional and military what-ifs — a submarine crew declaring independence, an invasion scenario — that were debated in the national press as political propositions rather than only as fiction.
entries.signature: Procedural realism about institutions under pressure: the cabinet meeting, the chain of command and the press conference are staged with the same care as the action, and the argument is carried by the procedure.

works.title: 沈黙の艦隊 / Chinmoku no Kantai

entries.category: Seinen and the Adult Magazine
entries.name: Iwaaki Hitoshi
entries.description: The body-horror premise worked through as an ethical problem.
entries.meta: Hitoshi Iwaaki in English-market credits · born 1960 · Afternoon.
entries.knownFor: A serial about a parasite that takes over a boy's right hand and the negotiated coexistence that follows, which treats its horror premise as a question about what a person owes other species.
entries.signature: A plain, almost diagrammatic drawing style that makes the transformations legible rather than lush, and an argument advanced through conversation between the boy and the thing in his hand. `trope-44`'s uninvited passenger is this work carded.

works.title: 寄生獣 / Kiseijū

entries.category: Seinen and the Adult Magazine
entries.name: Kariya Tetsu
entries.description: The food serial as journalism, and a writer who took the consequences.
entries.meta: Tetsu Kariya in English-market credits · born 1941 · Big Comic Spirits.
entries.knownFor: Writing the long-running gourmet serial that made food a major manga genre, and suspending it after a sequence on radiation exposure near Fukushima produced a national controversy.
entries.signature: Argument staged as a contest — two dishes, two positions, a verdict — which turns instruction into drama and is why the format spread. **The controversy is part of the record and both sides are serious**: that the sequence reported what people at the site told the author, and that a fiction serial reporting health effects carries an evidential burden it did not meet. `checklist-11` is the audit; this pack states the dispute and does not settle it.

works.title: 美味しんぼ / Oishinbo

entries.category: Seinen and the Adult Magazine
entries.name: Fukumoto Nobuyuki
entries.description: The gambling serial, where the mechanism is the drama.
entries.meta: Nobuyuki Fukumoto in English-market credits · born 1958 · Young Magazine and Kindai Mahjong.
entries.knownFor: Serials in which the tension comes entirely from a fully explained game with money and life attached, and from protagonists who are not good people.
entries.signature: Interior monologue at enormous length while nothing physical happens; a distinctive pointed-nose figure style; and rules explained so completely that the reader can check the protagonist's reasoning, which is what makes the tension survive the explanation.

works.title: 賭博黙示録カイジ / Tobaku Mokushiroku Kaiji

entries.category: Seinen and the Adult Magazine
entries.name: Manabe Shōhei
entries.description: The debt-collection serial, and the seinen magazine's least consoling register.
entries.meta: Shohei Manabe in English-market credits · born 1969 · Big Comic Spirits.
entries.knownFor: A serial about an illegal moneylender and the people who borrow from him, structured as a rotating set of cases in which most borrowers are destroyed.
entries.signature: Documentary specificity about money — interest rates, collection practice, the exact sums — with the misery presented as arithmetic rather than as tragedy. `trope-60`'s client-of-the-week structure, run without the mercy the format usually supplies.

works.title: 闇金ウシジマくん / Yamikin Ushijima-kun

entries.category: Seinen and the Adult Magazine
entries.name: Taniguchi Jirō
entries.description: The quiet register, and the creator European readers met first.
entries.meta: Jiro Taniguchi in English-market credits · 1947–2017 · seinen magazines, and the European market.
entries.knownFor: Slow, undramatic work about walking, memory and food, and an unusually direct relationship with the French-language market where his reputation stood highest.
entries.signature: Architectural precision and unhurried panel rhythm — a page can be a man walking past shops — with emotion carried by place rather than by event. `trope-64`'s eating alone and `trope-62`'s everyday density are both his method.

works.title: 孤独のグルメ / Kodoku no Gurume

entries.category: Horror and the Uncanny
entries.name: Mizuki Shigeru
entries.description: The folklorist of the medium, and one of its most serious war witnesses.
entries.meta: Shigeru Mizuki in English-market credits · 1922–2015 · kashihon, then children's and adult magazines.
entries.knownFor: The yōkai serial that made folklore a permanent manga genre, and a body of war work drawn from his own service in the Pacific, where he lost an arm and survived an engagement most of his unit did not.
entries.signature: Photographically dense backgrounds with cartoon figures moving through them — the world rendered seriously and the inhabitants not — which is the visual argument that the supernatural is ordinary. **The war work is testimony and is stated as such**: it contradicts the official account he was given, it names the command decisions, and it was produced over decades against a market that preferred the yōkai.

works.title: ゲゲゲの鬼太郎 / Gegege no Kitarō
墓場鬼太郎 / Hakaba Kitarō
総員玉砕せよ! / Sōin Gyokusai Seyo!

entries.category: Horror and the Uncanny
entries.name: Umezu Kazuo
entries.description: Children's horror at full intensity, by the creator who proved children would take it.
entries.meta: Kazuo Umezu in English-market credits · the creator's own preferred Latin styling is **Umezz** and most English editions use it; the pack cards the modified-Hepburn form and states the divergence once, per `checklist-15` · 1936–2024 · girls' and boys' magazines.
entries.knownFor: Horror serials published in children's magazines — a class of schoolchildren transported to a wasteland, a body-swap sequence, a snake-woman — at an intensity adult horror rarely reaches.
entries.signature: Faces distorted past anatomy at the moment of terror, and a willingness to let children die and stay dead. The distortion is the technique `page-25` describes: the line changes register and the reader is told, before reading a word, that the rules have gone.

works.title: 漂流教室 / Hyōryū Kyōshitsu

entries.category: Horror and the Uncanny
entries.name: Itō Junji
entries.description: The single-rule horror, executed with unusual formal discipline.
entries.meta: Junji Ito in English-market credits · born 1963 · horror magazines and seinen.
entries.knownFor: Short horror built on one impossible premise applied without exception, and a serial in which a town is infected by a geometric shape.
entries.signature: Immaculate fine-line rendering of ordinary rooms and faces, deformed by a single rule, on a regular panel grid that makes the deformation measurable. **He is carded as `horror:Junji Ito`, where the reading is his place in that genre's canon and his award record.** This pack reads the production frame instead: the short horror serial as a magazine format, and the grid discipline as page grammar `page-14` cards.

works.title: 富江 / Tomie
うずまき / Uzumaki

entries.category: Horror and the Uncanny
entries.name: Hino Hideshi
entries.description: The grotesque line of horror manga, and the autobiographical wound underneath it.
entries.meta: Hideshi Hino in English-market credits · born 1946 · horror magazines and the kashihon-descended market.
entries.knownFor: Horror built on deformity, mutation and family cruelty, much of it framed autobiographically, and a body of work that circulated in English translation earlier than most of the genre.
entries.signature: A deliberately crude, childlike line applied to viscera, so the horror arrives through the mismatch rather than the rendering. **He is carded as `horror:Hideshi Hino`, where the reading is the genre's grotesque tradition.** Here the reading is the market: this work exists because the kashihon-descended horror magazines had a readership the mainstream weeklies would not serve, which is `serial-67`'s permission-structure argument.

works.title: 蔵六の奇病 / Zōroku no Kibyō

entries.category: Horror and the Uncanny
entries.name: Furuya Usamaru
entries.description: The formal experimenter working in the transgressive line.
entries.meta: Usamaru Furuya in English-market credits · born 1968 · Garo, then seinen magazines.
entries.knownFor: Beginning in the alternative magazine with a strip of one-page formal experiments, then moving into commercial seinen with work about adolescence, suicide and cruelty.
entries.signature: Each page a different pastiche or formal system — the experiment is the unit — with a fine-art training visible in the composition. The transgressive content is real and the interest is structural, which is the same pairing `author-9`'s card describes and a different resolution of it.

works.title: パレポリ / Palepoli

entries.category: SF, Mecha and the Speculative Line
entries.name: Nagai Gō
entries.description: Three formats invented in five years, and the censorship fight that came with them.
entries.meta: Go Nagai in English-market credits · born 1945 · Weekly Shōnen Jump and Weekly Shōnen Magazine.
entries.knownFor: The piloted giant robot, the transforming heroine, and a demon-possession serial whose ending is among the medium's bleakest — plus a gag serial that triggered a national campaign by parents' and teachers' groups against indecency in children's manga.
entries.signature: Escalation without a brake: whatever the premise permits, the work does, which is why the same career produced both a toy franchise and an apocalypse. **He is carded as `superhero:Go Nagai` for the piloted robot's place in that genre.** This pack reads the censorship history instead — the campaign against his gag serial is an early instance of the pressure `history-21` describes, two decades before the case that made it national.

works.title: マジンガーZ / Mazinger Z
デビルマン / Devilman
キューティーハニー / Cutie Honey

entries.category: SF, Mecha and the Speculative Line
entries.name: Matsumoto Leiji
entries.description: Space opera with a melancholy the genre had not carried before.
entries.meta: Leiji Matsumoto in English-market credits · 1938–2023 · boys' magazines and the anime industry.
entries.knownFor: Long space serials built around departure, mortality and unfinished obligation, and a central role in the animation boom that carried them.
entries.signature: Elongated figures, dense machinery and long silent panels of ships against black — the visual grammar of vastness — with narratives that treat travel as loss rather than as adventure.

works.title: 銀河鉄道999 / Ginga Tetsudō 999

entries.category: SF, Mecha and the Speculative Line
entries.name: Ōtomo Katsuhiro
entries.description: The work that changed what manga looked like, and what Western readers thought it was.
entries.meta: Katsuhiro Otomo in English-market credits · born 1954 · Young Magazine.
entries.knownFor: A long science-fiction serial about psychic children and a destroyed Tokyo, whose draughtsmanship and page construction reset the seinen standard, and whose English edition was many readers' first manga.
entries.signature: Architectural precision and a fixed camera discipline borrowed from film — consistent eyelines and geography across a sequence, which the medium had largely not bothered with — plus destruction rendered as engineering rather than as spectacle.

works.title: AKIRA

entries.category: SF, Mecha and the Speculative Line
entries.name: Shirow Masamune
entries.description: The densest information design in the medium, and the argument it forces about readability.
entries.meta: Masamune Shirow in English-market credits · born 1961 · Young Magazine and specialist SF publishers.
entries.knownFor: Cyberpunk serials whose technical and political apparatus is elaborated in marginal notes running alongside the story, and which have been enormously influential outside manga.
entries.signature: Text density that competes with the art deliberately — footnotes, diagrams, technical asides — which is the exact inverse of `craft-27`'s division of labour and is worth studying as the counter-case rather than as a failure.

works.title: 攻殻機動隊 / Kōkaku Kidōtai

entries.category: SF, Mecha and the Speculative Line
entries.name: Miyazaki Hayao
entries.description: A manga made in the gaps of a film career, and more ambivalent than the films.
entries.meta: Hayao Miyazaki in English-market credits · born 1941 · Animage.
entries.knownFor: A long ecological serial drawn intermittently over twelve years alongside his animation work, which is darker, denser and more politically unresolved than the film made from its first act.
entries.signature: Pages crowded with ecological and military detail, tiny lettering, and an argument that refuses the resolution the adaptation supplies. **He is carded as `fantasy:Hayao Miyazaki` for the films' place in that genre.** This pack cards the manga, which is a different object with a different ending, and `craft-33`'s adaptation-that-overtakes-the-source is the exact case.

works.title: 風の谷のナウシカ / Kaze no Tani no Nausicaä

entries.category: SF, Mecha and the Speculative Line
entries.name: Hoshino Yukinobu
entries.description: Hard science fiction in manga, sustained across a career.
entries.meta: Yukinobu Hoshino in English-market credits · born 1954 · seinen and SF magazines.
entries.knownFor: Anthology and serial science fiction working from real physics, palaeontology and archaeology, in a tradition closer to written SF's problem stories than to the medium's usual speculative register.
entries.signature: A premise stated as a scientific situation and worked through honestly, with the human material kept deliberately spare — the form `subgenre-36`'s hand-off card points at, and one of the few places manga does written SF's job.

works.title: 2001夜物語 / Nisen'ichiya Monogatari

entries.category: Comedy, Gag and Yonkoma
entries.name: Akatsuka Fujio
entries.description: The gag manga's inventor of nonsense, and the studio behind it.
entries.meta: Fujio Akatsuka in English-market credits · 1935–2008 · boys' and girls' weeklies.
entries.knownFor: Gag serials built on absurdity rather than on situation, a stable of catchphrase characters who outlived their strips, and a production studio that made the output rate possible.
entries.signature: Nonsense with internal consistency — the rules are insane and they are rules — plus characters designed as pure recognisable shapes, which is why they survived into merchandise, television and common speech. `psychology-13`'s repetition argument is this career's mechanism.

works.title: 天才バカボン / Tensai Bakabon

entries.category: Comedy, Gag and Yonkoma
entries.name: Hasegawa Machiko
entries.description: The four-panel family strip that became a national institution, by one of the first professional women in the medium.
entries.meta: Machiko Hasegawa in English-market credits · 1920–1992 · newspapers.
entries.knownFor: A newspaper yonkoma about an ordinary family that ran for nearly three decades, and whose television adaptation has run continuously since 1969.
entries.signature: The four-panel unit used with complete discipline — setup, development, turn, conclusion, no overspill — and domestic material that dates precisely enough to function as a social record of postwar Japan. `subgenre-2` cards the form; this is the case that proves the count is structural.

works.title: サザエさん / Sazae-san

entries.category: Comedy, Gag and Yonkoma
entries.name: Akimoto Osamu
entries.description: Forty years without a missed week, and an ending chosen rather than imposed.
entries.meta: Osamu Akimoto in English-market credits · born 1952 · Weekly Shōnen Jump.
entries.knownFor: A comedy serial that ran weekly in the same magazine for four decades — the longest continuous run in that magazine's history — and ended on the creator's decision rather than on a survey result.
entries.signature: A fixed comic premise refreshed by subject rather than by escalation: the cast never changes and the topic always does, which is the only structure that survives that many instalments. `psychology-10`'s duration argument and `serial-13`'s rhythms have no better single case.

works.title: こちら葛飾区亀有公園前派出所 / Kochira Katsushika-ku Kameari Kōen-mae Hashutsujo

entries.category: Comedy, Gag and Yonkoma
entries.name: Azuma Kiyohiko
entries.description: The four-panel school comedy, and the register that came to define an era of it.
entries.meta: Kiyohiko Azuma in English-market credits · born 1968 · Dengeki Daioh.
entries.knownFor: A four-panel school serial with no plot and no antagonist, which established the low-stakes ensemble comedy as a commercial category, and a later serial about a child's first encounters with ordinary things.
entries.signature: Comic timing built on the absence of event, with the humour arising from character reaction to nothing much; and a clean, uncluttered page that gives the four-panel unit room to breathe. `subgenre-21`'s nichijō-kei register is largely this work's inheritance.

works.title: あずまんが大王 / Azumanga Daiō

entries.category: Comedy, Gag and Yonkoma
entries.name: Ishii Hisaichi
entries.description: The newspaper four-panel as political and social observation, sustained for fifty years.
entries.meta: Hisaichi Ishii in English-market credits · born 1951 · newspapers and magazines.
entries.knownFor: Daily four-panel strips combining domestic comedy with political and literary satire, produced at a volume that has few parallels, and a persistent presence in the national press.
entries.signature: A minimal, almost crude line that puts everything on the writing, and a turn in the third panel that is frequently a change of subject rather than a change of situation — the yonkoma structure used for argument rather than for jokes.

works.title: ののちゃん / Nono-chan

entries.category: Editors and the Editorial System
entries.name: Nagai Katsuichi
entries.description: The editor who founded a magazine to publish one serial, and kept it running for thirty years.
entries.meta: Katsuichi Nagai in English-market credits · 1921–1996 · rental-market publishing, then Garo.
entries.knownFor: Founding the alternative monthly in 1964 in order to serialise a single long work, and then sustaining it for three decades as the home of the medium's avant-garde on a business model that barely functioned.
entries.signature: Editorial permission as a policy: almost no direction, almost no payment, and almost no rejection of work on commercial grounds — the bargain `serial-68` prices and `history-17` reads as one of two opposite answers to the weekly system's constraints.

works.title: カムイ伝 / Kamui-den
works.note: Not his work; the serial the magazine was founded to carry

entries.category: Editors and the Editorial System
entries.name: Torishima Kazuhiko
entries.description: The documented case of an editor changing a series, described by both parties.
entries.meta: Kazuhiko Torishima in English-market credits · born 1952 · Weekly Shōnen Jump, later a publishing executive.
entries.knownFor: Editing a debut creator through many rejected drafts into a gag serial and then a battle serial, and describing the process publicly in enough detail that it is the standard evidence for how far editorial authority reaches.
entries.signature: Direction rather than correction — an editorial method that argues about premise and protagonist rather than about pacing, exercised at nemu stage where `serial-52` says the leverage actually sits. **He holds no credit on any of it**, which is `serial-51`'s claim in its clearest instance, and `history-3` carries the same case at period level.

works.title: ドラゴンボール / Dragon Ball
works.note: Not his work; the series the record attributes his pressure to

entries.category: Editors and the Editorial System
entries.name: Ōtsuka Eiji
entries.description: The editor who became the theorist of the thing he had been editing.
entries.meta: Eiji Otsuka in English-market credits · born 1958 · manga magazines as editor, then criticism and scriptwriting.
entries.knownFor: Editing in the commercial magazines, writing serials, and producing the theoretical account of consumption in which audiences buy fragments of a larger fictional world rather than individual stories — an argument the industry's media-mix later made look descriptive.
entries.signature: Structural analysis from inside the machine: he argues about the medium's economics and its narrative grammar as one subject, which is why the theory is usable rather than only interpretive. His work is among the sources `history-3` and `history-4` draw on for the constructed-lineage argument. **The survey often attributed to him in English-language citation is Kure Tomofusa's**, and this pack's own Creator card carried that misattribution until screen 33's attribution half was built (§3.37).

works.title: 物語消費論 / Monogatari Shōhiron

entries.category: Editors and the Editorial System
entries.name: Nishimura Shigeo
entries.description: The editor-in-chief who wrote the memoir, and why that is rare.
entries.meta: Shigeo Nishimura in English-market credits · born 1937 · Weekly Shōnen Jump.
entries.knownFor: Editing and then running the boys' weekly through the years of its steepest growth, and publishing a first-person account of how the magazine was actually assembled — lineup decisions, survey handling, the negotiation of cancellations.
entries.signature: The editorial department as an institution with quotas and internal politics, described from inside by someone who ran it. **Most of what a reference work can say about editorial practice comes from a small number of memoirs like this one**, which is a documentation condition worth stating: the system is described mainly by the few participants who chose to describe it. `serial-54`'s rotating editor is his account made general.

works.title: ドラゴンボール / Dragon Ball
works.note: Not his work; the magazine and period his account covers

entries.category: Editors and the Editorial System
entries.name: Suzuki Toshio
entries.description: The magazine editor who became the producer, and the media-mix seen from the commissioning side.
entries.meta: Toshio Suzuki in English-market credits · born 1948 · Animage, then film production.
entries.knownFor: Editing the animation magazine that commissioned a manga serial from a film director, and then producing the films — a career that runs along the seam `craft-29` through `craft-35` describe from the writer's side.
entries.signature: Commissioning as authorship-adjacent work: deciding what gets made, by whom, in which medium, and in what order. **This is the media-mix as a financial structure rather than as an aesthetic**, and it is carded here because the person who decides that a manga should exist is doing something the credits do not record.

works.title: 風の谷のナウシカ / Kaze no Tani no Nausicaä
works.note: Not his work; the serial his magazine commissioned

entries.category: Assistants, Studios and Collective Authorship
entries.name: Buronson
entries.description: The writer of a serial whose art everyone can picture and whose script nobody credits.
entries.meta: Buronson · a single-element pen name; no family–given order exists to gloss, and the exemption is declared in config with this reason · born 1947 · Weekly Shōnen Jump and seinen magazines.
entries.knownFor: Writing the post-apocalyptic martial-arts serial that defined 1980s shōnen violence, and continuing as a writer-for-artists across four decades.
entries.signature: Structural economy — an escalating opponent ladder with a stated moral frame, set out so an artist can stage it without further instruction. The writer-artist split he works in is the arrangement `craft-48` cards and `serial-58` prices, and it remains uncommon enough that readers routinely attribute the whole work to the artist.

works.title: 北斗の拳 / Hokuto no Ken

entries.category: Assistants, Studios and Collective Authorship
entries.name: Hara Tetsuo
entries.description: The artist half of the same partnership, and the studio that produced it.
entries.meta: Tetsuo Hara in English-market credits · born 1961 · Weekly Shōnen Jump.
entries.knownFor: Drawing that serial at weekly pace with a workshop behind him, and later running his own studio and imprint.
entries.signature: Heavy hatching, extreme musculature and a fixed set of impact conventions, executed at a consistency only a workshop makes possible. **The weekly page rate is the constraint that produces the studio**, which is `serial-55`'s employment argument seen from the artist's side rather than the assistant's.

works.title: 北斗の拳 / Hokuto no Ken

entries.category: Assistants, Studios and Collective Authorship
entries.name: Ōba Tsugumi
entries.description: A pen name whose holder has never been identified, and the attribution everyone repeats anyway.
entries.meta: Tsugumi Ohba in English-market credits · a pen name; the holder's identity has not been disclosed and living status is recorded as unknown · Weekly Shōnen Jump.
entries.knownFor: Writing two major serials for the boys' weekly, including one about making manga inside that magazine — a work whose subject is the very authorship apparatus its own credit conceals.
entries.signature: Dense procedural plotting built on rules and negotiation rather than on physical action, drawn by a separate artist throughout. **The widely repeated identification of this name with a known creator is an inference, not a disclosure**: the publisher has never confirmed it and the holder has never claimed it. This pack states the inference exists, states that it is unconfirmed, and does not assert it — which is `serial-60`'s rule applied to the one case where the missing credit is deliberate rather than institutional.

works.title: バクマン。 / Bakuman.

entries.category: Assistants, Studios and Collective Authorship
entries.name: Obata Takeshi
entries.description: The artist who works to other people's scripts, repeatedly and by choice.
entries.meta: Takeshi Obata in English-market credits · born 1969 · Weekly Shōnen Jump.
entries.knownFor: Drawing several major serials to scripts by different writers, each in a visibly different register, which is unusual in a medium whose default is a single author doing both.
entries.signature: Adaptive style — the line, the panel density and the character design change with the writer rather than staying constant — which is the clearest available evidence that in this medium the artist's account of the scene is a choice and not a signature. `superhero:craft-10`'s claim, tested by one person taking both sides of it.

works.title: バクマン。 / Bakuman.
ヒカルの碁 / Hikaru no Go

entries.category: Critics, Scholars and Translators
entries.name: Natsume Fusanosuke
entries.description: The critic who gave the medium a vocabulary for its own page.
entries.meta: Fusanosuke Natsume in English-market credits · born 1950 · criticism, broadcasting and academia.
entries.knownFor: Developing a formal vocabulary for manga expression — panel, frame, line, the treatment of the balloon — that made it possible to discuss the medium's grammar in its own terms rather than in film's or literature's.
entries.signature: Close reading of the page as a technical object, with the argument advanced by looking at how a specific panel is built. **Much of what this pack's Page collection can say in the vocabulary it uses descends from this line of criticism**, which is why `page-1` through `page-30` are possible as cards rather than as impressions.

works.title: マンガの読み方 / Manga no Yomikata
works.note: The collaborative volume he is central to

entries.category: Critics, Scholars and Translators
entries.name: Yomota Inuhiko
entries.description: The comparatist who put manga beside film and literature without flattening it.
entries.meta: Inuhiko Yomota in English-market credits · born 1953 · academia and criticism.
entries.knownFor: A theoretical account of manga's expressive principles written from within comparative literature and film studies, and a long career arguing for the medium as a serious object across all three.
entries.signature: Analysis that borrows tools from adjacent disciplines and states where they stop working, which is the discipline this pack's screen 18 was built to enforce on itself — name what the neighbouring form cannot say.

works.title: 漫画原論 / Manga Genron

entries.category: Critics, Scholars and Translators
entries.name: Shimizu Isao
entries.description: The historian of the cartoon, and the continuity argument's most serious advocate.
entries.meta: Isao Shimizu in English-market credits · 1939–2021 · history and criticism.
entries.knownFor: Decades of archival work on Japanese cartoon and caricature history, and the argument that modern manga descends continuously from Edo and Meiji picture traditions rather than being assembled from imported conventions.
entries.signature: Primary-source history — periodicals, prints, publication records — rather than interpretation, which is what makes the continuity argument he advances difficult to dismiss even where it is disputed. **`history-4` carries that dispute two-sided, and this card names the side it belongs to**, because a pack that states a controversy and then cards only its opponents has adjudicated it after all.

works.title: 東京パック / Tokyo Puck
works.note: Not his work; the period his archival work recovered

entries.category: Critics, Scholars and Translators
entries.name: Frederik L. Schodt
entries.description: The translator and critic who built the Anglophone account of the medium almost single-handed.
entries.meta: Frederik L. Schodt · an Anglophone writer whose card name is already in his own order; the gloss exemption is declared in config with this reason · born 1950 · translation and criticism.
entries.knownFor: The 1983 survey that introduced manga to English-language readers as a serious medium with a history, a later volume covering the decades after it, and translation work including a long collaboration on the medium's foundational science-fiction serial.
entries.signature: Explanation without condescension in either direction — neither treating the medium as exotic nor pretending the cultural distance is nil — which is why the survey is still cited forty years on. `history-12` uses it for the postwar reconstruction, and much of the English-language record's shape is downstream of what he chose to cover first.

works.title: Manga! Manga! The World of Japanese Comics

entries.category: Critics, Scholars and Translators
entries.name: Sharon Kinsella
entries.description: The scholar who read the industry as an industry, including the parts it prefers not to discuss.
entries.meta: Sharon Kinsella · an Anglophone scholar whose card name is already in her own order; the gloss exemption is declared in config with this reason · sociology and Japanese studies.
entries.knownFor: A study of the commercial manga industry, the amateur movement and their relationship, covering the publishers' editorial control, the 1990–91 regulation campaign, and the periods when the professional and amateur systems were hostile rather than symbiotic.
entries.signature: Sociology rather than appreciation: the object of study is the production system and the power inside it, and the argument is built from interviews and institutional evidence. `serial-63`, `serial-64` and `history-21` all rest on this work, and this card closes the collection where `author-1` opened it — with the system rather than the page.

works.title: Adult Manga: Culture and Power in Contemporary Japanese Society

entries.category: Gekiga and the Kashihon Market
entries.name: 黒い吹雪 / Kuroi Fubuki
entries.author: Tatsumi Yoshihiro
entries.awards: None. The kashihon market sat outside the prize system of its period, which is a fact about the prizes rather than about the work.
entries.description: Rental-market volume. The long rental-market volume from the year before the word gekiga existed. A crime story told at length for an audience the…
entries.text: Rental-market volume. The long rental-market volume from the year before the word gekiga existed. A crime story told at length for an audience the children's magazines were not serving, and the clearest available evidence that the formal shift later named gekiga was underway before it had a name. The interest for a writer is structural: the length, the pacing and the willingness to stay with an unpleasant protagonist are all permissions the rental economy granted and the magazine economy withheld, which is `serial-67`'s argument in its earliest form. English-language readers meet it as *Black Blizzard*, and the roster records that divergence because the two titles will otherwise generate two entries.

entries.category: Gekiga and the Kashihon Market
entries.name: 幽霊タクシー / Yūrei Takushī
entries.author: Tatsumi Yoshihiro
entries.awards: None; see `work-1` on the rental market and the prize system.
entries.description: Anthology serial. The cover that carried the word gekiga for the first time. Published in a rental-market anthology, and significant less for the…
entries.text: Anthology serial. The cover that carried the word gekiga for the first time. Published in a rental-market anthology, and significant less for the story than for the label on it: this is the point at which a term invented to distinguish adult work from children's manga appears in print. `history-15` cards the coinage and `subgenre-29` cards the movement; this card exists because a category's first use is a datable event and worth being able to point at. The 1957 date rests on the Japanese record, and the pack states it rather than the rounder 1950s attribution that circulates in English.

entries.category: Gekiga and the Kashihon Market
entries.name: 忍者武芸帳 影丸伝 / Ninja Bugeichō Kagemaru-den
entries.author: Shirato Sanpei
entries.awards: None recorded from the period; the work's reputation was made by readership and by the later Garo association rather than by a prize.
entries.description: Rental-market volume. The rental market's most consequential long work, and the line from it into the alternative magazines. Seventeen volumes of…
entries.text: Rental-market volume. The rental market's most consequential long work, and the line from it into the alternative magazines. Seventeen volumes of ninja warfare organised around class and economics rather than around heroism, produced for the rental shops and read by university students as a political argument. Two things follow. The first is that a rental-market work could carry material no children's weekly would have taken, which is `history-14`'s permission-structure point. The second is that its author's later centrality to Garo is the clearest single line from a side system into the magazine that changed what the medium was allowed to be — `serial-70`'s closing argument, with this work as its evidence. English citation usually shortens the title, and the roster holds the full form.

entries.category: Gekiga and the Kashihon Market
entries.name: 墓場鬼太郎 / Hakaba Kitarō
entries.author: Mizuki Shigeru
entries.awards: None. The rental market's economics did not include prize eligibility.
entries.description: Rental-market volume. The kashihon original that the famous version is not. The first version of a yōkai character later rebuilt for a children's…
entries.text: Rental-market volume. The kashihon original that the famous version is not. The first version of a yōkai character later rebuilt for a children's weekly under a different title, and a distinctly harsher object than its successor — the protagonist is amoral, the stories end badly, and the audience was adults renting cheaply rather than children buying. **The roster separates this from its later namesake deliberately**, and the pack's own Creator collection got that separation wrong once before screen 33 caught it. Two works, two titles, two markets, one character: exactly the phantom-duplicate shape `checklist-15` audits for.

entries.category: Gekiga and the Kashihon Market
entries.name: 血だるま剣法 / Chidaruma Kenpō
entries.author: Hirata Hiroshi
entries.awards: None; the work was out of circulation for four decades.
entries.description: Rental-market volume. A withdrawn work, the complaint that withdrew it, and a dispute the pack does not settle. A samurai revenge story withdrawn by…
entries.text: Rental-market volume. A withdrawn work, the complaint that withdrew it, and a dispute the pack does not settle. A samurai revenge story withdrawn by its publisher roughly a month after release, following protest by the Osaka branch of the Buraku Liberation League over its treatment of buraku origins, and reissued in 2004 with redactions. **Both positions are on the record and neither is adjudicated here**: that the depiction reproduced a discriminatory account of a community that could read it, and that a withdrawal secured by organised protest set a precedent about who decides what stays in print. `checklist-13` and `checklist-14` are the instruments. For a writer the case is not primarily about censorship — it is about `craft-38`'s expert reader, arriving as a community with a stake rather than as a specialist with a correction.

entries.category: Gekiga and the Kashihon Market
entries.name: 子連れ狼 / Kozure Ōkami
entries.author: Koike Kazuo · Kojima Gōseki
entries.awards: No award is asserted on this card; the pack's award pass did not establish one it could state with the body and indexing year §7 requires.
entries.description: Weekly serial. The gekiga register's most exported work, and a writer-artist partnership at full stretch. An assassin and his infant son move…
entries.text: Weekly serial. The gekiga register's most exported work, and a writer-artist partnership at full stretch. An assassin and his infant son move through Edo in a sequence of largely self-contained commissions, and the form is the argument: an episodic structure that can run indefinitely, carried by a partnership in which the writing and the drawing are separately credited — the arrangement `craft-48` cards and `serial-58` prices. Its English edition reached readers earlier and more completely than almost any other manga, which is why the Anglophone idea of what gekiga looks like is substantially this book. `page-15`'s silences are worth studying here: whole sequences run wordless and the pace is set by panel size alone.

entries.category: Gekiga and the Kashihon Market
entries.name: 劇画漂流 / Gekiga Hyōryū
entries.author: Tatsumi Yoshihiro
entries.awards: Tezuka Osamu Cultural Prize, Grand Prize, 2009 — awarded for the collected volume, and the award year differs from the 1995 serialisation year this card is dated by, per §7.
entries.description: Anthology serial. The period's primary source, written forty years later by a participant. A long autobiographical account of the rental market, the…
entries.text: Anthology serial. The period's primary source, written forty years later by a participant. A long autobiographical account of the rental market, the gekiga group and the coinage, serialised in a dealer's catalogue and collected in 2008. It is the most detailed source available for a period the industry recorded badly, and **it is a memoir**: its account of Tezuka's remarks about gekiga is reconstructed rather than contemporaneous, and research pass T marks it as a source to attribute rather than to cite as record. Writers should read it as testimony with a position, which is `checklist-10`'s distinction between what must be right and what may be wrong.

entries.category: Garo, COM and Art Manga
entries.name: カムイ伝 / Kamui-den
entries.author: Shirato Sanpei
entries.awards: None. The magazine paid little and entered nothing.
entries.description: Monthly serial. The serial a magazine was founded to carry. A long historical work about caste, land and revolt, for which the publisher Nagai…
entries.text: Monthly serial. The serial a magazine was founded to carry. A long historical work about caste, land and revolt, for which the publisher Nagai Katsuichi founded Garo in 1964 — the clearest case in the medium of an institution built around a single work rather than the reverse. Its politics are explicit and its structure is unusual: the nominal protagonist recedes for long stretches while the villages, the economics and the seasons carry the narrative. `history-17` cards the magazine as one of two opposite answers to the weekly system, and `author-107` cards the editor who chose to answer that way.

entries.category: Garo, COM and Art Manga
entries.name: 紅い花 / Akai Hana
entries.author: Tsuge Yoshiharu
entries.description: One-shot. The quiet end of the alternative magazine's achievement. A short story about a river, a girl who runs a teahouse and a boy fishing, in…
entries.text: One-shot. The quiet end of the alternative magazine's achievement. A short story about a river, a girl who runs a teahouse and a boy fishing, in which almost nothing happens and the reticence is the content. It is the strongest available argument that the alternative magazines' value was not transgression but permission — nothing here would have been refused by a weekly on grounds of content, and no weekly would have run it, because it has no hook. `psychology-4`'s updating case is the reading experience: the gaps are small and constant, and the reader assembles a great deal from very little.

entries.category: Garo, COM and Art Manga
entries.name: ねじ式 / Neji-shiki
entries.author: Tsuge Yoshiharu
entries.description: One-shot. The dream work the whole art-manga lineage is measured against. A boy with a severed artery moves through a seaside town looking for a…
entries.text: One-shot. The dream work the whole art-manga lineage is measured against. A boy with a severed artery moves through a seaside town looking for a doctor, in a sequence with dream logic and no resolution, and it is probably the most written-about short work in the medium. Its usefulness to a working writer is narrower than its reputation: it demonstrates that a reader will follow a sequence with no causal chain provided the images are specific, and that `page-5`'s deliberate ambiguity requires an otherwise disciplined page to read as intention rather than as incompetence.

entries.category: Garo, COM and Art Manga
entries.name: ジュン / Jun
entries.author: Ishinomori Shōtarō
entries.description: Monthly serial. The experimental register a laboratory magazine existed to permit. Largely wordless, structurally loose sequences closer to visual…
entries.text: Monthly serial. The experimental register a laboratory magazine existed to permit. Largely wordless, structurally loose sequences closer to visual poetry than to story manga, published in the magazine Tezuka founded as a laboratory, and the standard reference for what a commercial obligation's absence makes possible. `serial-69` cards the magazine as a school and `page-15` cards the positional grammar this work uses without naming; the creator's name is carded under the post-1986 respelling he adopted, per `checklist-15`.

entries.category: Garo, COM and Art Manga
entries.name: 赤色エレジー / Sekishoku Elegy
entries.author: Hayashi Seiichi
entries.awards: None. The magazine's contributors were largely unpaid, which `serial-68` prices.
entries.description: Monthly serial. Poverty, work and a relationship failing, in the alternative magazine's flattest register. Two young people in Tokyo, animation…
entries.text: Monthly serial. Poverty, work and a relationship failing, in the alternative magazine's flattest register. Two young people in Tokyo, animation work, no money and a relationship that does not survive the period — drawn in flat graphic fields by an artist trained in animation, with pop imagery used against the material rather than with it. The formal interest is the drawing's refusal to intensify: nothing in the line signals that a scene is the sad one. `page-25`'s argument about the line as a register is unusually visible here, because the register never changes and the reader supplies the change.

entries.category: Garo, COM and Art Manga
entries.name: 絶対安全剃刀 / Zettai Anzen Kamisori
entries.author: Takano Fumiko
entries.awards: Japan Cartoonists Association Award, Excellence Prize, 1983 — awarded to the 1982 collection; the card is dated by the 1978 first appearance, per §7.
entries.description: One-shot. The most formally exact short work in the collection, by a creator other cartoonists cite more than readers do. The commercial debut, and…
entries.text: One-shot. The most formally exact short work in the collection, by a creator other cartoonists cite more than readers do. The commercial debut, and a demonstration of omission as a working method: the sequence keeps only the panels that cannot be removed and the reader supplies the rest without noticing the work being asked of them. **The 1978 date will look wrong to readers who know the 1982 collection**, which is precisely why the roster holds it. `psychology-4`'s distinction applies exactly — these are updates, not reconstructions, and the difference is why the omissions do not read as gaps.

entries.category: Garo, COM and Art Manga
entries.name: 少女椿 / Shōjo Tsubaki
entries.author: Maruo Suehiro
entries.description: Volume-first work. The ero-guro line's best-known volume, and the actions taken against its adaptation. A girl orphaned into a travelling freak…
entries.text: Volume-first work. The ero-guro line's best-known volume, and the actions taken against its adaptation. A girl orphaned into a travelling freak show, drawn with meticulous prewar-poster technique, and the standing test case for the argument this pack refuses to settle: whether the beauty of the rendering critiques the appetite it serves or delivers it more effectively. **Both readings are held by serious critics** and `author-9` carries the same dispute from the creator's side. One factual distinction the record requires: the manga has remained in print, while the 1992 animated adaptation was seized by Japanese customs in 1999 and its screening restricted for years — the actions concern the film. `checklist-14` is the audit.

entries.category: Garo, COM and Art Manga
entries.name: 鉄コン筋クリート / Tekkonkinkreet
entries.author: Matsumoto Taiyō
entries.awards: No award is asserted on this card.
entries.description: Weekly serial. The art-manga sensibility running inside a commercial weekly, and what that bought. Two street children in an invented city, drawn…
entries.text: Weekly serial. The art-manga sensibility running inside a commercial weekly, and what that bought. Two street children in an invented city, drawn with elastic perspective and architecture that bends around the figures, published in a major commercial weekly rather than in the alternative magazines the style descends from. That placement is the card's point: by the 1990s the formal ambition of the Garo line could be carried by a Shogakukan weekly, which changed what the alternative magazines were for. `page-7`'s spread-as-unit argument has no better case in the collection — the two-page field is this work's basic compositional object. The 1993 date rests on secondary sources; the publisher record was not reached.

entries.category: Doujinshi-Origin and the Circuit
entries.name: シベール / Cybele
entries.author: Azuma Hideo and others
entries.awards: None; the amateur circuit has no prize system of this kind.
entries.description: Doujinshi. The self-published volume conventionally placed at the origin of a boom and of the campaign against it. A self-published anthology from…
entries.text: Doujinshi. The self-published volume conventionally placed at the origin of a boom and of the campaign against it. A self-published anthology from April 1979, documented as Japan's first male-oriented lolicon doujinshi and cited in two literatures at once — as the origin point of the erotic amateur boom that grew the circuit into a talent pipeline, and as the origin point of the material that fuelled the 1990–91 harmful-manga campaign. **The pack states the sequence and adjudicates nothing.** The legal position on drawn material involving minors diverges sharply by jurisdiction, as `history-21` records: Japan's 2014 statute explicitly excludes drawn work, several other jurisdictions criminalise it, and local ordinances form a third position. That divergence is stated here as a fact about jurisdictions and is used as neither defence nor indictment.

entries.category: Doujinshi-Origin and the Circuit
entries.name: 聖伝-RG VEDA- / Seiden -RG VEDA-
entries.author: CLAMP
entries.awards: No award is asserted on this card.
entries.description: Monthly serial. A doujinshi circle's commercial debut, arriving intact as a group. The commercial debut of a circle that had been self-publishing,…
entries.text: Monthly serial. A doujinshi circle's commercial debut, arriving intact as a group. The commercial debut of a circle that had been self-publishing, and the clearest case of the pipeline arriving whole rather than as an individual recruit — the byline is a collective and stays one. `serial-64` cards the pipeline and `serial-60` cards the credit problem this creates: the name on the cover is accurate and tells a reader nothing about who did what, which becomes material when a group's membership changes across its career. The pack's own Creator collection notes a live cross-pack disagreement about one member's name form; that is a Creators matter and `author-13` carries it.

entries.category: Doujinshi-Origin and the Circuit
entries.name: げんしけん / Genshiken
entries.author: Kio Shimoku
entries.awards: No award is asserted on this card.
entries.description: Monthly serial. The circuit as subject rather than as origin, published commercially. A university club produces doujinshi, and the serial follows…
entries.text: Monthly serial. The circuit as subject rather than as origin, published commercially. A university club produces doujinshi, and the serial follows the production cycle rather than the fandom: the print run, the deadline, the table at the market, the money. It is the most detailed procedural account of the amateur system available inside the medium, which is why `serial-61` and `serial-62` both cite it. Note what it is not — the work is commercial, monthly and edited, and its accuracy about an unedited system is a reported accuracy rather than a native one.

entries.category: Doujinshi-Origin and the Circuit
entries.name: Axis powers ヘタリア / Axis Powers Hetalia
entries.author: Himaruya Hidekaz
entries.awards: No award is asserted on this card.
entries.description: Volume-first work. The web-origin path into print, and the objection that followed it abroad. Short gag strips personifying nations, published to a…
entries.text: Volume-first work. The web-origin path into print, and the objection that followed it abroad. Short gag strips personifying nations, published to a personal website and acquired for print on the strength of that readership — discovery preceding selection, which is `serial-65`'s inversion. **The commonly cited 2006 web date could not be established to a reliable source and the card is dated by the confirmed 2008 volume**, with the divergence stated rather than smoothed. The 2009 anime announcement drew organised objection in South Korea to the Korea character, including a petition and discussion in the National Assembly; the objection and the work's defenders are both on the record and this pack takes no side.

entries.category: Doujinshi-Origin and the Circuit
entries.name: ワンパンマン / One-Punch Man
entries.author: ONE
entries.awards: No award is asserted on this card.
entries.description: Web serial. One title, two versions, and the redraw that carries the page grammar. A superhero parody published to a personal site with deliberately…
entries.text: Web serial. One title, two versions, and the redraw that carries the page grammar. A superhero parody published to a personal site with deliberately crude drawing, which acquired an enormous readership on its writing alone and was then redrawn commercially by a different artist. **Two versions under one title is a phantom-duplicate generator inside a single work**, and the roster holds the web original as the carded object with the 2012 redraw recorded separately. For a writer the case is the cleanest available separation of writing from drawing: the comic timing survives the change of artist unaltered, which `author-17` reads as evidence and `page-10` reads as a warning about what does not survive repagination.

entries.category: Essay, Documentary and Reportage
entries.name: 刑務所の中 / Keimusho no Naka
entries.author: Hanawa Kazuichi
entries.awards: Japan Media Arts Festival, Manga Division, Excellence Award, 2000.
entries.description: Volume-first work. Three years inside a prison, drawn by the person who served them. A documentary account of imprisonment following the author's…
entries.text: Volume-first work. Three years inside a prison, drawn by the person who served them. A documentary account of imprisonment following the author's 1994 firearms conviction, built almost entirely from procedure: meals, cell layout, the schedule, the exact texture of monotony. There is no arc and the absence is the method — the account's authority comes from refusing to shape the experience into a story. **The conviction is stated as record and not as verdict**, which is the same discipline `author-19` applies. `craft-37`'s problem of drawing a life you have not lived is inverted here, and `trope-62`'s everyday density is the technique.

entries.category: Essay, Documentary and Reportage
entries.name: 毎日かあさん / Mainichi Kaasan
entries.author: Saibara Rieko
entries.awards: Japan Media Arts Festival, Manga Division, Excellence Award, 2005; Tezuka Osamu Cultural Prize, Short Work Prize, 2005. Both award years differ from the 2002 first-appearance year this card is dated by, per §7.
entries.description: Newspaper strip. The newspaper essay strip that refused to be consoling. A daily autobiographical strip about raising children, running a household…
entries.text: Newspaper strip. The newspaper essay strip that refused to be consoling. A daily autobiographical strip about raising children, running a household and an alcoholic former husband's decline, published in a national newspaper until 2017. The register is the achievement: a rough, childlike line carrying material — addiction, bereavement, money — that realistic rendering would make unbearable. **It depicts named living family members**, which is a standing ethical condition of the form rather than an incident, and `checklist-14` applies to any writer working this way.

entries.category: Essay, Documentary and Reportage
entries.name: ダーリンは外国人 / Daarin wa Gaikokujin
entries.author: Oguri Saori
entries.awards: No award is asserted on this card.
entries.description: Volume-first work. The essay manga's largest commercial success, and the form's ceiling. Observational strips about daily life in an intercultural…
entries.text: Volume-first work. The essay manga's largest commercial success, and the form's ceiling. Observational strips about daily life in an intercultural marriage, which sold at a scale that made the domestic essay a commercial category in its own right. The technique is restraint: the misunderstanding is stated, both parties are treated as reasonable, and the strip declines to conclude — which is what keeps the material from becoming a catalogue of national traits, the form's standing failure. It depicts a named living person, and the reader should notice that the generalisations are the risk the restraint is managing.

entries.category: Essay, Documentary and Reportage
entries.name: 失踪日記 / Shissō Nikki
entries.author: Azuma Hideo
entries.awards: Japan Media Arts Festival, Manga Division, Grand Prize, 2005; Tezuka Osamu Cultural Prize, New Artist Prize, 2006.
entries.description: Volume-first work. Homelessness and alcoholism, drawn without self-pity by a creator who lived both. A first-person account of two disappearances…
entries.text: Volume-first work. Homelessness and alcoholism, drawn without self-pity by a creator who lived both. A first-person account of two disappearances and a period of alcoholism, drawn in the same light rounded line the author used for gag manga, with the mismatch doing the work. Parts had appeared earlier; the alcoholism section was drawn new for the volume. Read beside `work-16`: the same creator sits at the origin of the erotic amateur boom and at the top of the medium's autobiographical reportage, and **a reference work that carded only one of those would be describing a career that did not happen**.

entries.category: Essay, Documentary and Reportage
entries.name: 百姓貴族 / Hyakushō Kizoku
entries.author: Arakawa Hiromu
entries.awards: No award is asserted on this card.
entries.description: Anthology serial. The farm essay serial, by a creator better known for a battle serial. Short comic essays about growing up on a Hokkaidō dairy farm…
entries.text: Anthology serial. The farm essay serial, by a creator better known for a battle serial. Short comic essays about growing up on a Hokkaidō dairy farm — livestock, weather, agricultural economics — produced alongside the author's commercial serials and carrying the procedural authority of someone describing work they actually did. `craft-36`'s procedural contract is met here by biography rather than by research, which is the cheapest way to meet it and the only one not available on request. The English market knows a different, unrelated farming work by the same author; the roster separates them.

entries.category: Essay, Documentary and Reportage
entries.name: いちえふ 福島第一原子力発電所労働記 / Ichi-efu: Fukushima Daiichi Genshiryoku Hatsudensho Rōdōki
entries.author: Tatsuta Kazuto
entries.description: Weekly serial. Reportage from inside a decommissioning site, and a contested account of it. A first-person account of contract labour on the…
entries.text: Weekly serial. Reportage from inside a decommissioning site, and a contested account of it. A first-person account of contract labour on the Fukushima Daiichi decommissioning, drawn from direct experience under a pen name, documenting shift work, dosimetry, equipment and the contracting chain. **The reception divided and both positions are serious**: that it is rare first-hand documentation of conditions almost nobody outside the site can describe, and that its matter-of-factness understates the hazard and the labour structure. The work's own strapline disclaims exposé status, and the author's statements on radiation risk are themselves contested. `checklist-11` is the instrument; this pack does not settle it.

entries.category: Educational and Commissioned Manga
entries.name: マンガ日本経済入門 / Manga Nihon Keizai Nyūmon
entries.author: Ishinomori Shōtarō
entries.awards: No award is asserted on this card.
entries.description: Volume-first work. The commissioned explanation that opened instructional manga to adults. An introduction to the Japanese economy in comics form,…
entries.text: Volume-first work. The commissioned explanation that opened instructional manga to adults. An introduction to the Japanese economy in comics form, commissioned by a financial newspaper and read by adults in large numbers — the case that established instructional manga as an adult category rather than a children's one. The craft question it settles is whether explanation survives the form: it does, provided the drawing carries the mechanism rather than illustrating a lecture, which is `craft-27`'s division applied to exposition that cannot be shown.

entries.category: Educational and Commissioned Manga
entries.name: まんがサイエンス / Manga Science
entries.author: Asari Yoshitoo
entries.awards: No award is asserted on this card.
entries.description: Monthly serial. Children's science explanation held to an adult standard. A long-running science serial for children that explains mechanisms rather…
entries.text: Monthly serial. Children's science explanation held to an adult standard. A long-running science serial for children that explains mechanisms rather than reciting conclusions, and is read with respect by adults who first met it as children. **The commonly cited 1988 start is a year late**: the publisher-magazine record puts the first instalment in the October 1987 issue, and holding that distinction is what stops a roster carrying two entries for one serial. The method is comedy and demonstration in the same panel, which is why the material survives being read for pleasure.

entries.category: Educational and Commissioned Manga
entries.name: サルでも描けるまんが教室 / Saru demo Kakeru Manga Kyōshitsu
entries.author: Aihara Kōji · Takekuma Kentarō
entries.awards: No award is asserted on this card.
entries.description: Weekly serial. The instructional manual as satire, and the most honest account of the industry's economics in the medium. A parody course in how to…
entries.text: Weekly serial. The instructional manual as satire, and the most honest account of the industry's economics in the medium. A parody course in how to make manga, co-authored by a cartoonist and a critic, which teaches the conventions accurately in the course of ridiculing them and is used as a genuine reference despite itself. The satire works because the description underneath it is correct — page rates, assistant costs, editorial pressure and genre formula are all reported straight, which is why `serial-56` cites it for economics rather than for jokes.

entries.category: Educational and Commissioned Manga
entries.name: はたらく細胞 / Hataraku Saibō
entries.author: Shimizu Akane
entries.awards: Kodansha Manga Award, Shōnen Division, 2017 — the award year differs from the 2015 first-appearance year, per §7.
